title: The Barber's Tale of his Fourth Brother
summary: The barber stroked his chin and recounted the adventure of his fourth brother, Al-Kuz:
keywords: the barber's tale of his fourth brother
full_text:
The barber stroked his chin and recounted the adventure of his fourth brother, Al-Kuz:

"My fourth brother, Al-Kuz, was a butcher in Baghdad who owned a well-stocked stall in the meat bazaar. He was prosperous and respected, but he possessed a fatal flaw: whenever an opportunity arose to make an extraordinary profit without labor, his common sense vanished like steam.

One morning, an aged stranger with a white beard and piercing eyes approached the stall. He purchased a fat quarter of mutton, paid with crisp, shining gold dinars, and departed without asking for change. For five successive days, the stranger returned, buying meat and paying with the same bright gold coins. Al-Kuz, overjoyed by this wealthy patron, locked the coins in a special cedar chest beneath his counter.

On the sixth day, when the butcher went to open his chest to purchase new sheep from the Bedouin drovers, he unlocked the lid and gasped in horror. The cedar chest contained not a single gold coin, but only dried round leaves cut from the fig tree! The mysterious stranger had been an adept in optical illusions, projecting a temporary glamour over worthless foliage.

Enraged by the fraud, Al-Kuz stood in his stall, shouting curses against all magicians. At that moment, an honest customer stepped up and asked to purchase a cut of beef. Al-Kuz, blinded by fury, mistook the innocent citizen for the sorcerer’s accomplice, seized his meat cleaver, and threatened the crowd. The neighbors summoned the police, who searched the stall and discovered the cedar chest filled with strange leaves.

The superstitious magistrate declared that Al-Kuz was practicing unlawful witchcraft in the meat market! The butcher was sentenced to fifty lashes, his stall was confiscated, and he was banished beyond the city walls. He came to my house penniless and bruised, weeping over his ruined trade, learning too late that easy gold often turns to withered leaves in the hand of the greedy."
moral: Greed and dealing in dubious goods bring sudden ruin upon the merchant who abandons fair trading.

title: The Barber's Tale of his Fifth Brother
summary: The barber then laughed merrily as he remembered his fifth brother, Al-Nashshar, whose name became a proverb across the East:
keywords: the barber's tale of his fifth brother
full_text:
The barber then laughed merrily as he remembered his fifth brother, Al-Nashshar, whose name became a proverb across the East:

"My brother Al-Nashshar was a lazy fellow who inherited one hundred silver dirhams upon our father’s death. Instead of investing in steady trade, he spent the entire sum purchasing a large wicker basket filled with fragile glassware—crystal bottles, cut-glass bowls, and delicate perfume flasks. He set his basket against a sunny wall in the market square, rested his back against the bricks, folded his arms, and began to weave magnificent daydreams.

'With these hundred dirhams of glassware,' he murmured to himself, 'I shall make two hundred dirhams in profit. With those two hundred, I shall buy fine Syrian pottery and double my money to four hundred. Within two years, I shall amass ten thousand dirhams and buy a magnificent shop in the jewelers' bazaar. I shall trade in pearls, diamonds, and rubies until I am worth a hundred thousand dinars!

Then,' he whispered, closing his eyes in ecstasy, 'I shall demand the hand of the Grand Vizier’s daughter in marriage. On our wedding night, when she enters my chamber adorned in jewels and bows humbly to offer me a cup of spiced wine, I shall pretend to be proud and haughty. I shall turn my face away to test her submissiveness. And when she kneels and begs for my regard, I shall draw back my foot and kick her thus, to teach her who is master!'

Lost in his grandiose illusion, Al-Nashshar lashed out with his right foot in earnest! His heavy leather boot struck the wicker basket squarely in the center. The basket flipped into the street, crashing against the cobblestones with a deafening shatter. Crystal, colored glass, and perfume bottles were pulverized into a thousand worthless shards!

Al-Nashshar opened his eyes and saw his entire fortune lying in glittering dust at his feet. He tore his hair, beat his breast, and wept bitter tears while the entire bazaar erupted in uncontrollable laughter. He had destroyed his reality in the pursuit of an arrogant shadow."
moral: Daydreaming of haughty triumph without laying the foundation of labor shatters one's hopes into dust.

title: The Barber's Tale of his Sixth Brother
summary: The barber concluded the saga of his family with the story of his sixth brother, Shakkashik, who was celebrated for his quick mind:
keywords: the barber's tale of his sixth brother
full_text:
The barber concluded the saga of his family with the story of his sixth brother, Shakkashik, who was celebrated for his quick mind:

"My youngest brother, Shakkashik, was once reduced to absolute poverty. Starving and in rags, he knocked upon the door of a magnificent palace in Baghdad belonging to a noble prince of the famous Barmecide clan. The prince, who was renowned for his whimsical humor, invited Shakkashik into his grand dining hall.

'Welcome, friend!' cried the Barmecide prince. 'Wash your hands and partake of my hospitality!' The servants set before them empty porcelain dishes, empty crystal carafes, and silver spoons. The prince took up his spoon, pretended to dip it into an empty bowl, and smacked his lips: 'Taste this superb lentil soup seasoned with fresh coriander! Have you ever tasted anything so delicious?'

Shakkashik, though his stomach was gnawing with hunger, immediately perceived that the prince was testing his wit and manners. Instead of growing angry, Shakkashik joined the game. He dipped his own empty spoon, chewed on thin air, and exclaimed: 'By heavens, my lord, the coriander is roasted to perfection, and the broth is fit for a caliph!'

Next, the host offered an imaginary roast lamb stuffed with pistachios. Shakkashik pretended to tear off a juicy leg, chewed vigorously, and praised the delicate spice. Course after course of nonexistent delicacies were served, followed by phantom honey pastries and imaginary vintage wine from Shiraz.

When the prince offered a fourth imaginary goblet of wine, Shakkashik pretended to drink deeply, swayed in his seat, rolled his eyes, and suddenly slapped the noble prince on the cheek! The prince gasped: 'What means this insolence?' Shakkashik bowed low and pleaded: 'Forgive me, my generous host! The excellence of your vintage was so potent that it intoxicated your humble guest, and he lost his wits!'

The Barmecide prince laughed until tears streamed down his cheeks. Delighted by Shakkashik’s humor, patience, and brilliant adaptability, he ordered a real, sumptuous banquet to be served at once. He clothed my brother in robes of honor and made him the chief steward of his palace for twenty years."
moral: True wit and good humor in the face of misfortune can turn a mockery into a feast of honor.

title: Nur al-Din Ali and the Damsel Anis Al-Jalis
summary: In the city of Basra lived a wise vizier named Al-Fazl, who served King Muhammad bin Sulayman. The king had commissioned him to purchase ...
keywords: nur al-din ali and the damsel anis al-jalis
full_text:
In the city of Basra lived a wise vizier named Al-Fazl, who served King Muhammad bin Sulayman. The king had commissioned him to purchase a maiden of supreme beauty, intelligence, and musical talent. The vizier found such a maiden, named Anis al-Jalis, who had mastered calligraphy, grammar, history, and the playing of the lute.

Before presenting her to the king, the vizier brought her to his own palace to rest. There, his noble son, Nur al-Din Ali, beheld her, and the two young people fell deeply in love. Realizing that true affection cannot be commanded by royal decree, the vizier permitted them to wed, but warned his son to live with modest prudence.

When the elder vizier passed away, a jealous rival vizier, Al-Muin, reported to the king that Nur al-Din had kept the royal maiden for himself. Faced with royal displeasure, Nur al-Din and Anis al-Jalis fled Basra by night, boarding a riverboat that carried them to the golden city of Baghdad.

Penniless in the great capital, they sought shelter in an enchanted pleasure garden on the banks of the Tigris. The keeper of the garden, an aged shaykh named Ibrahim, was so charmed by the young couple's modesty and Anis al-Jalis’s sublime lute playing that he brought them fruit, sweetmeats, and illuminated the garden pavilions with hundreds of colored candles.

The Caliph Harun al-Rashid, cruising the river in his royal barge, saw the brilliant illumination and sailed to the terrace in disguise. Listening from behind the rose trellises, the Caliph was enraptured by the maiden’s singing and Nur al-Din’s poetic wit. Revealing his identity, the Caliph did not punish them; instead, he admired their unwavering fidelity, granted them a royal pardon, and dispatched a royal decree to the King of Basra appointing Nur al-Din as governor in his father’s place.
moral: Sincere devotion, eloquence, and artistic excellence win the favor of monarchs and conquer all obstacles.

title: Tale of Ghanim bin Ayyub
summary: Ghanim bin Ayyub was a handsome and virtuous young merchant of Damascus who traveled to Baghdad with a rich caravan of silk and spices. H...
full_text:
Ghanim bin Ayyub was a handsome and virtuous young merchant of Damascus who traveled to Baghdad with a rich caravan of silk and spices. Having sold his goods for a handsome sum, he spent his evenings walking peacefully along the outskirts of the city.

One night, finding himself outside the gates after curfew, he took shelter in an ancient tomb in the cemetery. Near midnight, three slaves entered bearing a heavy iron chest. They dug a deep trench, buried the chest, and departed. Suspecting foul play, Ghanim waited until they were gone, dug up the chest with his dagger, and pried open the lid.

To his astonishment, he found lying within an exquisite maiden who had been drugged with sleeping vapors. Ghanim lifted her out, warmed her with his cloak, and brought her secretly to his rented house. When she revived, she revealed that her name was Kutan-al-Qulub, the favorite court singer of Queen Zubaydah, and that jealous rivals in the harem had drugged and buried her alive out of malicious envy.

For months, the noble Ghanim gave her sanctuary in his house, treating her with the utmost reverence and modesty, never violating her trust or asking for any return save her safety. When the Caliph Harun al-Rashid discovered that his favorite singer was alive, slanderous tongues accused Ghanim of abducting her. The Caliph ordered Ghanim's house seized, his mother and sister arrested, and a price put upon his head.

Ghanim escaped in the disguise of a water-carrier, enduring months of hunger and disease. Meanwhile, Kutan-al-Qulub was brought before Harun al-Rashid. Weeping, she swore on the sacred books that Ghanim was the purest, most honorable of men, who had preserved her life and dignity with saintly virtue. The remorseful Caliph summoned Ghanim, embraced him as a brother, gave him Kutan-al-Qulub in marriage, and appointed him to the highest council of state.
moral: Chaste honor, unshakeable integrity, and loyalty under trial are rewarded with the highest honors.

full_text:
While the three slaves were carrying the chest containing Kutan-al-Qulub to the cemetery, they sat upon a tombstone to rest, and the first attendant, Bukhayt, explained how he had entered royal service:

"In my youth, I was a farm hand in Upper Egypt, but I possessed a mischievous disposition that took delight in sowing mischief between peaceful neighbors. If I saw two farmers working harmoniously, I would whisper to the first that his companion was stealing his irrigation water, and whisper to the second that his neighbor had cursed his oxen.

One day, my master, an honest cattle breeder, purchased a spirited bull. Desiring to test my cunning, I whispered to the master’s wife that her husband intended to sell her bridal jewelry, and told the master that his wife had consulted an astrologer to leave him. Both flew into a furious temper, shouting accusations across the courtyard.

In the confusion of their quarrel, the farm gate was left unlatched. The spirited bull charged out into the vegetable gardens, knocked over the beehives, and trampled the master’s prize melons. The furious bees swarmed upon the household, stinging the master, his wife, and myself until we looked like spotted leopards!

When the uproar subsided and the master discovered that my deceitful whispers had orchestrated the entire catastrophe, he seized an ox-whip and gave me a hundred lashes. He shaved my head, branded my forehead with the mark of a slanderer, and sold me to a foreign caravan driver for three silver coins. That painful day taught me that he who lights the fire of malice in another’s home will find his own beard singed by the flames."
moral: Sowing discord between others creates a fire that eventually consumes the troublemaker himself.

title: Tale of the Second Eunuch Kafur
summary: The second attendant, Kafur, laughed and recounted his own strange history to his companions:
keywords: tale of the second eunuch kafur
full_text:
The second attendant, Kafur, laughed and recounted his own strange history to his companions:

"I was purchased as a boy by a wealthy merchant in Aleppo. At the slave market, my former master told the buyer: 'This lad is strong, honest, and diligent, but he has one incurable flaw: once every year, he tells one single lie!' The merchant laughed, thinking: 'What harm can a single lie do in twelve months?' and paid the price.

For eleven months I served him with flawless loyalty, managing his storehouses, tending his horses, and guarding his ledger. My master praised my fidelity before all his friends. But when the twelfth month arrived, my annual impulse overcame my reason.

My master had ridden out to his country vineyard to host a banquet for his fellow merchants, leaving me to guard his city mansion. In the afternoon, I tore my tunic, smeared dust upon my head, and ran through the streets to the master's house, wailing: 'Alas! The master’s country pavilion has collapsed into the river! He and all his guests are drowned beneath the ruins!'

The mistress shrieked, broke her porcelain mirrors, tore her silken draperies, and collapsed in convulsions. The servants wept, and the neighbors gathered in lamentation. I then ran all the way to the vineyard, where my master was drinking sherbet with his companions, and shouted: 'Woe! The city mansion has caught fire, and your wife and children have perished in the flames!'

The merchant fell from his divan, tore his beard, and galloped madly toward the city. When he reached his gate, he met his wife running toward him in mourning clothes. When they discovered that both were alive and that neither house nor pavilion had suffered harm, they turned upon me in fury. 'Why did you invent such monstrous falsehoods?' roared the merchant.

I bowed meekly and replied: 'Did you not purchase me with the condition of one lie per year? Rejoice, master, for this was only a half-lie, and the year is now fulfilled!' My master, recognizing the peril of his bargain, expelled me from his house forever, proving that even a single lie can shatter a family’s peace."
moral: A single half-truth spoken out of malice can overthrow an entire household and cause irreparable ruin.

full_text:
In the ancient city of Baghdad, long before the Abbasid dynasty, reigned King Omar bin al-Nu'uman, a sovereign of mighty valor who held dominion over Syria, Iraq, and the Arabian peninsula. He possessed an army of a hundred thousand horsemen, a treasury overflowing with tribute, and two valiant sons: Prince Sharrkan, famed for his mastery of the lance, and Prince Zau al-Makan, renowned for his learning and wisdom.

When the Emperor of Constantinople declared war against the realm, King Omar dispatched Sharrkan at the head of twenty thousand horsemen to defend the northern frontiers. Sharrkan marched into the rugged mountains of Anatolia, where he became separated from his troops in an enchanted valley surrounded by cedar forests.

There, beside a marble hermitage, he encountered Princess Abrizah, the daughter of the King of Greece. Though adversaries by allegiance, both possessed souls of supreme nobility and chivalry. They matched their martial prowess in single combat, wrestling with such grace and skill that neither took advantage of the other. Defeated by her agile wit, Sharrkan was moved by her honor and sought to forge a lasting peace between their nations.

Meanwhile, back in Baghdad, King Omar fell into the snares of courtly intrigue and treacherous advisers who preferred endless warfare to honorable treaties. When the king died, it fell upon the two brothers, Sharrkan and Zau al-Makan, to set aside their differences, unite their armies, and discover that true strength lies not in the slaughter of adversaries, but in establishing a reign of justice, religious tolerance, and peaceful commerce across the Mediterranean world.
moral: Great empires and martial glory are hollow unless governed by wisdom, chivalry, and noble restraint.

title: Tale of Taj al-Muluk and Princess Dunya
summary: Taj al-Muluk, the Crown Prince of the Green City in Persia, was a youth of peerless charm, yet he refused to look upon any maiden, until ...

full_text:
Taj al-Muluk, the Crown Prince of the Green City in Persia, was a youth of peerless charm, yet he refused to look upon any maiden, until an old merchant showed him a painted portrait of Princess Dunya of the Isle of Camphor. Dunya had secluded herself in a remote fortress, vowing never to wed, having dreamed that a hunter had trapped a gentle dove in a net.

Determined to win her heart through subtlety and grace, Taj al-Muluk traveled to the Isle of Camphor disguised as a silk merchant, accompanied by his faithful friend Aziz. Instead of demanding her hand with an army, the prince opened a magnificent shop in the bazaar, displaying rare tapestries, pearls, and paintings.

Knowing that Princess Dunya loved beautiful gardens, Taj al-Muluk engaged the royal master painter to decorate the interior of the princess's private garden pavilion. Upon the central wall, the prince commissioned a breathtaking fresco depicting a lush forest: a hunter’s net lay open, but in this painting, a noble falcon was depicted cutting the cords with its talons, freeing the dove, while a stag protected the flock.

When Princess Dunya entered the pavilion, she gazed upon the painting with wonder. The master painter explained: 'Princess, this artist wishes you to see that not all who approach are hunters; some come as guardians to free the captive soul from fear.'

Moved to tears by the beauty of the art and the delicacy of the sentiment, Princess Dunya asked to meet the painter-merchant. When Taj al-Muluk appeared before her, his modesty, eloquence, and noble spirit confirmed the truth of his art. Her guarded heart melted like spring snow, and their joyous union united the two realms in enduring peace.
moral: Art, patience, and gentle perseverance can open the most guarded heart and heal past sorrows.

title: Tale of Aziz and Azizah
summary: While guiding Prince Taj al-Muluk on his quest, the faithful counselor Aziz wept as he recounted the tragic history of his youth and his ...
full_text:
While guiding Prince Taj al-Muluk on his quest, the faithful counselor Aziz wept as he recounted the tragic history of his youth and his cousin Azizah:

"In Damascus, my cousin Azizah and I were betrothed from our childhood. Her love for me was pure as morning dew, and her mind was gifted with the interpretation of poetry and omens. Yet in my youthful folly, I was easily distracted by every passing illusion.

One afternoon, as I walked through the perfumers’ souk, a mysterious lady dropped an embroidered handkerchief bearing the symbol of an open iris from an upper window. Captivated, I showed the handkerchief to Azizah. Instead of reproaching me with jealousy, my saintly cousin examined the cloth and interpreted the riddle: 'Cousin, she bids you meet her in two days at the hour of the second prayer.'

Time and again, Azizah used her superior wisdom to decipher the secret signs of my pursuit, guiding me away from perilous traps and preparing aromatic foods for my journeys, while her own heart broke in silence. She never spoke a word of anger, caring only for my well-being, though grief consumed her health day by day.

On the day of her passing, she placed a golden ring upon my finger and whispered her final counsel: 'When you meet with deceit, remember the words: Faithful love endures beyond the grave, while fickle passion vanishes like smoke.'

Only when she was laid to rest did the veil fall from my eyes. I realized that in pursuing fleeting shadows, I had neglected the truest, most angelic soul on earth. Stricken with remorse, I renounced worldly vanity and devoted my life to helping other travelers recognize the precious worth of sincere devotion before it is lost forever."
moral: Selfless devotion and unrequited fidelity are noble virtues, but one must never take true love for granted.

title: Tale of the Hashish Eater
summary: In a crowded quarter of Cairo lived an idle young man named Bakkar who refused to learn a trade, preferring to spend his pennies on herba...
full_text:
In a crowded quarter of Cairo lived an idle young man named Bakkar who refused to learn a trade, preferring to spend his pennies on herbal smoke that induced vivid, waking dreams. One sultry afternoon, he sat upon a stone bench before an ancient public fountain, closed his eyes, and drifted into an elaborate reverie.

In his dream, he was no longer an impoverished beggar in patched wool, but the Grand Sultan of the Orient! He rode through the gates on a magnificent Arabian steed caparisoned in velvet and pearls. Heralds blew silver trumpets, courtiers bowed to the dust, and crowds showered him with rose petals and gold coin.

Entering the royal palace, he ascended the throne of ivory and gold. He summoned his treasurer and commanded a million dinars to be distributed among the poor of Cairo. He ordered forty ships to set sail for the Spice Islands and decreed a feast of roasted peacocks for the whole city. Then, imagining his royal guards stood before him awaiting his command to march upon his enemies, he shouted aloud with royal majesty: 'Charge! Spare none who oppose my will!'

Lost in his delusion, Bakkar leaped from the stone bench, flailed his arms wildly, and dove headfirst into the public fountain! The icy water instantly shattered his dream. He spluttered, choked on fountain moss, and scrambled out into the street drenched from head to foot, his turban floating away in the gutter.

A crowd of laughing washerwomen and schoolboys gathered round, clapping their hands at the dripping 'Sultan' who had conquered nothing but a horse-trough. Shivering with cold and burning with shame, Bakkar realized that illusions provide a moment of mock majesty at the cost of enduring dignity. From that afternoon, he threw away his herbs, took an apprenticeship with a cooper, and discovered the genuine satisfaction of an honest day's labor.
moral: Chasing artificial illusions weakens the spirit; true happiness is built on clear-headed reality.

title: Tale of Hammad the Badawi
summary: In the vast red sands of the Najd lived Hammad, a Bedouin chief renowned across the desert for his skill with the lance, his generous hea...
full_text:
In the vast red sands of the Najd lived Hammad, a Bedouin chief renowned across the desert for his skill with the lance, his generous hearth, and his unyielding adherence to the laws of nomadic honor. His tent was pitched beside an isolated desert crossroads, where a lantern burned all night on a tall pole to guide lost wayfarers.

One stormy night, when a violent sandstorm raged across the dunes, a lone horseman galloped up to Hammad’s tent, leaped from his exhausted mare, and begged for sanctuary according to the ancient laws of the desert. Hammad took the stranger's reins, ushered him into the tent, wrapped him in dry camel-hair cloaks, and slaughtered his prize young camel to prepare a hot feast.

As the guest sat before the hearth fire, the light illuminated his face. Hammad recognized him immediately: he was the chief of a rival clan who, in a border skirmish months before, had slain Hammad’s only brother! Hammad’s heart seized with grief and wrath, but he did not lay a finger upon his weapon or alter the warmth of his countenance.

For three days, Hammad served the guest with princely courtesy, pouring bitter coffee and serving roasted meat, according to the inviolable law that grants three days of unconditional protection to whoever breaks bread under one's tent. On the fourth morning, when the guest prepared to depart, Hammad led out the guest’s horse, fed and rested, and handed him a bag of dates and a full waterskin.

Hammad looked the rival chief in the eye and said quietly: 'Know, O guest, that you slew my brother in battle, and my heart bled every hour you sat at my hearth. But you sought my hospitality, and under Hammad’s roof, a guest is sacred. Today you leave my territory in peace. But if we meet tomorrow in the open desert, our blades must settle the score of our clans.'

The rival chief was so moved by such peerless chivalry and moral greatness that he threw down his sword, fell upon Hammad’s neck, and pledged eternal brotherhood between their tribes, ending forty years of desert warfare with a single act of sacred hospitality.
moral: Desert chivalry, hospitality to the stranger, and honoring the guest are sacred codes that triumph over enmity.

title: The Birds and Beasts and the Carpenter
summary: In an ancient forest, the beasts of the field and the birds of the air held a council. A young lion, proud of his claws and majestic roar...
keywords: the birds and beasts and the carpenter
full_text:
In an ancient forest, the beasts of the field and the birds of the air held a council. A young lion, proud of his claws and majestic roar, asked the elder wolf what creature in the world was the most dangerous. The wolf shuddered and answered: 'Beware of the son of Adam! He possesses neither sharp fangs nor iron talons, yet by his craft and cunning, he traps the elephant in a pit, harnesses the ox to his plow, and cages the falcon in the sky.'

The young lion scoffed at this warning and set forth to conquer this mysterious creature. On the forest trail, he met a horse with an iron bit between its teeth. 'Who did this to you?' asked the lion. 'The son of Adam,' sighed the horse. Next, he met an ox with a ring in its nose and a heavy wooden yoke. 'The son of Adam has tamed me,' moaned the ox.

Continuing deeper into the woods, the lion encountered a slender man carrying an axe, an adze, and several heavy wooden planks upon his shoulder. 'Are you the son of Adam?' growled the lion. The carpenter bowed meekly: 'I am indeed a carpenter, a humble servant of Adam.'

The lion roared: 'Prepare to perish, for I am the king of the beasts!' The carpenter did not tremble. He said calmly: 'O king of the forest, slay me if you will, but first grant me leave to complete this wooden house I am building to shelter a noble beast from the coming winter tempests.'

Curious, the lion examined the sturdy wooden chest the carpenter was assembling. 'Is it large enough for a great monarch like me?' asked the lion. 'Test it yourself, sire,' invited the carpenter, holding open the sliding door.

The lion stepped inside the chest and curled his tail. Swiftly, the carpenter slid the heavy wooden lid into place, drove three iron nails through the latch, and smiled down through the air holes. The trapped lion roared in frustration, but the carpenter said: 'Learn, O beast, that brute strength is nothing before the patient craft of the mind.' Leaving the lion safely confined until he promised peace, the carpenter returned to his village.
moral: Human craft and intellect, when guided by prudence, can build shelters that tame the fiercest perils.

title: The Hermits
summary: Upon the summit of a high mountain in Syria lived two hermits who had abandoned the cities of men to devote their lives to solitary conte...
full_text:
Upon the summit of a high mountain in Syria lived two hermits who had abandoned the cities of men to devote their lives to solitary contemplation. They slept in caves, dressed in coarse goat hair, and subsisted entirely on wild berries, acorns, and mountain spring water.

After forty years of asceticism, the elder hermit began to feel a secret pride in his breast. He thought: 'Surely, no mortal on earth is as holy, pure, and beloved of the angels as I, who have never touched coin or spoken with sinners for four decades.'

That night, a voice came to him in a vision: 'If you wish to see a servant whose devotion is truly accepted, descend into the valley and visit Abu Yusuf the water-carrier in the town of Homs.'

Astonished and humbled, the hermit took his staff and walked down the rocky trails until he reached the bustling bazaar of Homs. He found Abu Yusuf, a humble, sun-darkened laborer who carried two heavy goat-skins of water through the sweltering streets, distributing cool water to thirsty travelers, weary porters, and beggars without demanding payment.

The hermit approached him at dusk and asked: 'What great austerities do you practice, O water-carrier, that the heavens praise your name?' Abu Yusuf laughed gently and replied: 'I know nothing of austerities, venerable father. I have a family to feed and neighbors who thirst. Each morning, I fill my skins at the river, give water to all who ask in the name of mercy, forgive those who speak harshly to me, and share my crust of bread with the stray dogs at my gate.'

The hermit bowed his head to the earth, weeping in profound realization. He saw that forty years of proud isolation in the mountains could not equal a single day of selfless, humble service to suffering humanity. Returning to his companion, he opened his mountain cave to lost shepherds and weary wanderers, discovering that true devotion is love in action.
moral: True spiritual perfection is found not in haughty seclusion, but in active benevolence toward humankind.

summary: On the reeds of a tranquil lake lived a graceful water-fowl and an ancient tortoise. Despite the difference in their natures—the bird gif...
full_text:
On the reeds of a tranquil lake lived a graceful water-fowl and an ancient tortoise. Despite the difference in their natures—the bird gifted with swift wings to soar among the clouds, and the tortoise bound to crawl slowly upon the muddy shore—they had forged a bond of unbreakable friendship. Each evening, the water-fowl would perch upon a floating log, sharing tales of distant rivers, while the tortoise offered the patient, earthy wisdom of a creature who had seen a hundred seasons.

One summer, an unprecedented drought struck the land. Day after day, the sun burned like molten brass, and the lake shrank until only a shallow puddle of bitter mud remained. The fish perished, and the green reeds withered into dry straw.

The water-fowl ruffled its plumage in distress and said: 'My dear companion, the water is gone. If I remain here, I shall starve. I must spread my wings and fly across the mountains to the great river of Egypt, where water flows in abundance. But my heart breaks to leave you behind to perish in the dry mud.'

The tortoise wept and replied: 'You can fly across the skies, but I can only crawl three paces an hour. Take me with you, brother, or watch me die!'

The water-fowl reflected deeply and devised a clever plan: 'Find a sturdy reed of wild bamboo. Take the middle of the reed firmly between your jaws, and bite with all your might. I shall take one end of the reed in my beak, and my cousin the crane will take the other end. Thus we will bear you through the air across the mountain peaks. But mark this warning well: whatever you see or hear, do not open your mouth to utter a single word!'

The tortoise bit the reed, and the two birds took flight, carrying their friend high into the azure sky. As they flew over a village, the peasants pointed up in astonishment, shouting: 'Look at the clever birds carrying a slow tortoise!'

Remembering the bird's strict counsel, the tortoise held his tongue with heroic willpower, keeping his jaws clenched until they safely landed upon the lush, green banks of the Nile. The water-fowl praised his friend's self-control, and they lived together in abundance, proving that true friendship and obedience to wise advice conquer the greatest perils.
moral: A true friend provides steady companionship and practical wisdom in times of greatest adversity.

title: The Wolf and the Fox
summary: In a rocky gorge lived a powerful, tyrannical wolf who forced a clever fox to be his servant. Whenever the fox caught a hare or found a w...
full_text:
In a rocky gorge lived a powerful, tyrannical wolf who forced a clever fox to be his servant. Whenever the fox caught a hare or found a wild honeycomb, the wolf would snarl, bare his fangs, and snatch the prize, leaving the fox only bones and bitter roots. The fox endured the humiliation patiently, waiting for an opportunity to liberate himself from the tyrant’s yoke.

One autumn afternoon, as the wolf rested under a pomegranate tree, his stomach rumbled with insatiable hunger. He kicked the fox and growled: 'Go into the valley and fetch me fat meat, or I shall devour you before nightfall!'

The fox bowed meekly and ran toward the village. In the orchard of an affluent farmer, he discovered a deep pit dug by the peasants to catch wild boars. The pit was covered with slender reeds and concealed with fresh green turf, with a savory roasted kid placed in the center as bait.

Returning to the wolf, the fox whispered with breathless excitement: 'Rejoice, O mighty master! In the orchard below lies a roasted kid so tender that the grease drips from its ribs, guarded by neither dog nor man! Because of my loyalty to you, I did not touch a morsel, leaving the feast for your royal jaws.'

The greedy wolf leaped to his feet, saliva dripping from his jowls. Without pausing to examine the ground, he galloped into the orchard and leaped straight toward the roasted kid. The fragile reeds snapped under his heavy weight, and the wolf crashed down into the bottom of the deep pit, trapped between sheer walls of stone.

The wolf howled in terror and pleaded: 'Help me out, faithful companion! Throw down a rope or call the other beasts to pull me up!'

The fox stood safely at the lip of the pit, looked down with a calm smile, and said: 'For three years you bullied the weak, stole their sustenance, and threatened their lives. Now learn that he who builds his kingdom on terror will find that his own greed digs the pit of his downfall.' The fox trotted merrily away into the woods, free at last, while the village watchmen arrived to secure the captured beast.
moral: Tyranny and bullying provoke subtle wit, and the arrogant oppressor is ultimately trapped by his own greed.

title: Tale of the Falcon and the Partridge
summary: Upon the crags of a rocky mountain perched a royal falcon with feathers of iron-grey and eyes like burnished amber. From his dizzying hei...
keywords: tale of the falcon and the partridge
full_text:
Upon the crags of a rocky mountain perched a royal falcon with feathers of iron-grey and eyes like burnished amber. From his dizzying height, he looked down upon a gentle gray partridge that was pecking seeds among the stones of the valley.

The falcon swept down with a rush of wind, pinned the partridge beneath his talons, and mocked him: 'Look at you, frail bird! You spend your life scratching in the dirt, terrified of every shadow, while I soar among the thunderclouds and feast from the wrist of kings!'

The partridge trembled, but spoke with quiet dignity: 'O noble hunter, do not boast of your strength. You fly high, yet a bird in the clouds is visible to all, while the creature of the earth knows how to find refuge among the stones.'

The falcon laughed scornfully: 'What refuge could hide you from my piercing gaze? Watch how I strike down any prey that dares defy me!'

To display his magnificent aerial prowess before delivering the final blow, the falcon released the partridge, leaped into the air, and began climbing in great spirals toward the clouds. He folded his wings, plunged like a lightning bolt toward the valley floor, aiming to seize the partridge in mid-flight with a spectacular dive.

However, the partridge slipped quietly beneath the overhanging ledge of a granite boulder, blending perfectly with the mottled grey stone. The swooping falcon, blinded by the sun and intoxicated by his own speed, could not check his downward momentum. He struck the solid rock face with tremendous force, breaking his wings and shattering his talons.

The humble partridge stepped out from beneath the ledge, looked at the fallen hunter with pity, and said: 'He who flies too high on the wings of pride will find the earth unyielding when he falls.' The partridge flew safely into the thicket, leaving the humbled bird of prey to reflect on the virtue of modest quietude.
moral: Boastful arrogance invites disaster, while humble discretion preserves life and safety.

title: The Mouse and the Ichneumon
summary: In the hollow of an ancient banyan tree lived a field mouse, while in the roots below burrowed an ichneumon—the fierce mongoose that hunt...
full_text:
In the hollow of an ancient banyan tree lived a field mouse, while in the roots below burrowed an ichneumon—the fierce mongoose that hunts snakes and rodents. For years, the mouse lived in perpetual dread of the mongoose, never daring to leave its hole without sniffing the wind.

One afternoon, a fowler set a broad net of fine hemp around the base of the banyan tree, baiting it with roasted sesame cakes. The mouse, lured by the fragrant scent, crept into the net, only to feel the cords snap tight around it. At that same moment, a wild cat leaped from the branches, intending to devour the trapped mouse, but the cat too became entangled in the outer mesh!

Meanwhile, up on a high bough perched an owl, watching with hungry eyes, ready to pounce upon whichever victim struggled free. The mongoose poked its nose out from the roots, seeing the cat trapped, but spotted the owl poised to strike from above.

The mouse, perceiving the intricate web of danger, called out to the cat: 'O hunter! We are both trapped in the fowler's net. If the owl strikes, we are both dead. But if you swear by your honor not to harm me, my sharp teeth can gnaw through the hempen cords, freeing us both before the fowler returns!'

The cat, seeing no other hope of survival, swore a solemn oath of peace. The mouse gnawed the thick ropes around the cat’s neck and paws with furious speed. The moment the cat leaped free, it chased the mongoose into the roots and scared the owl away into the sky.

The cat then turned to the mouse and purred: 'Come out of your hole, brave companion, and let me embrace you as my savior!'

The wise mouse remained safely inside its burrow, peeking through a narrow crack, and answered: 'Friendship born of shared peril is noble, but when the peril has passed, nature returns to its old paths. I honor our treaty, but I shall keep my burrow between your claws and my fur!' The mouse survived, demonstrating that prudence must outlive temporary alliances.
moral: Mortal adversaries must unite when a shared danger threatens, but caution must remain when the peril passes.

title: The Cat and the Crow
summary: In an orchard of fig trees lived a quiet tabby cat and a noisy, conceited crow who nested in the tallest poplar. The crow spent his days ...
full_text:
In an orchard of fig trees lived a quiet tabby cat and a noisy, conceited crow who nested in the tallest poplar. The crow spent his days strutting upon the branches, cawing loudly to the sky, boasting of his glossy black feathers, his sharp beak, and his ancient lineage.

Whenever the cat crept softly through the grass to catch grasshoppers, the crow would mock her: 'Look at you, poor four-legged creature! You have to slink through the dust on belly and paws, while I command the winds and fill the valley with my royal song!' The cat flicked her ears, kept her counsel, and said nothing.

One morning, a fowler entered the orchard carrying a hunting bow and sticky lime-twigs. The cat, sensing danger with her acute instincts, slipped silently beneath the dense thorns of a blackberry bramble, keeping her tail tucked and her body motionless, blending completely with the dark earth.

The crow, by contrast, remained upon his high perch, flapped his wings, and began cawing with deafening pride, believing that his loud voice would intimidate the intruder. 'Hear my battle-cry, human!' cawed the crow. 'None dare disturb my orchard!'

The fowler looked up, guided directly by the bird’s ceaseless noise. He fitted a slender reed arrow to his bow, drew the string to his ear, and loosed the shaft. The arrow struck the crow in the wing, sending him fluttering and tumbling from his high branch down into the blackberry bush.

The cat stepped out quietly from her thorny refuge, looked at the wounded, trembling crow, and said gently: 'Brother, the hunter did not possess magic eyes; your own tongue was the compass that guided his arrow to your heart. Had you possessed the wisdom to keep silent in times of peril, your feathers would still be dry in the tree.' The cat helped the humbled crow into a safe hollow in the roots, teaching him that quiet humility is a fortress that pride can never build.
moral: Quiet discretion and humility provide safety, while noisy vanity attracts the hunter's eye.

title: The Fox and the Crow
summary: In a quiet grove beside an olive press, a black crow perched upon a high branch, holding in his yellow beak a large wedge of savory sheep...
full_text:
In a quiet grove beside an olive press, a black crow perched upon a high branch, holding in his yellow beak a large wedge of savory sheep's cheese which he had carried off from a dairy window. As he prepared to enjoy his breakfast, a hungry red fox trotted by and caught the pungent aroma of the cheese.

Looking up into the boughs, the fox realized that he could neither climb the smooth trunk nor shake the branch. Sitting on his haunches, the fox tilted his head and spoke with honeyed sweetness: 'O noble monarch of the air! How radiant are your feathers in the morning sun! Surely the eagle himself cannot match the gloss of your ebony wings, nor the peacock the grace of your noble posture.'

The crow looked down, flattered by the praise, yet kept his beak firmly clenched around the cheese.

The fox sighed with theatrical admiration: 'If your voice is but half as sweet as your plumage is magnificent, you must surely be the undisputed king of all songbirds! How I long to hear a single melody from that royal throat, that I may bow before you as your humble servant.'

Drunk with pride and eager to prove his musical majesty, the foolish crow stretched his neck, flapped his wings, and opened his beak wide to let out a loud, grating: 'Caw! Caw!'

The moment his beak parted, the heavy cheese slipped from his grasp and tumbled straight down through the branches. The fox caught it neatly in his jaws before it touched the earth, swallowed it with relish, and smiled up at the crow: 'Thank you for the delicious cheese, my fine singer! In return, let me give you a piece of advice worth more than a basket of cheese: Never trust a flatterer, for he lives entirely at the expense of those who listen to him!'
moral: Flattery is the food of fools; he who listens to sweet falsehoods will surely lose his prize.

title: The Flea and the Mouse
summary: In the opulent bedchamber of a wealthy chamberlain lived a little house mouse who had hollowed out a snug nest behind the cedar wainscoti...
full_text:
In the opulent bedchamber of a wealthy chamberlain lived a little house mouse who had hollowed out a snug nest behind the cedar wainscoting. The mouse was prudent and modest, venturing out only in the dead of night to gather bread crumbs and melon seeds from the carpet, never chewing the fine tapestries or disturbing the master's sleep. Because of this discretion, the chamberlain never set traps or brought cats into the room.

One chilly evening, a wandering flea hopped through the window and begged for shelter: 'Brother mouse, the autumn frost is bitter outside. Grant me leave to warm myself by your nest for a single night, and I swear by the hospitality of the floorboards never to cause you grief.'

The kind mouse took pity on the shivering insect, fed him a drop of honey, and allowed him to rest. But as midnight struck, the aroma of the sleeping chamberlain’s warm bed proved too tempting for the flea’s greedy nature.

'Stay where you are!' warned the mouse. 'Our master sleeps soundly, but if you bite him, he will awaken in wrath, and both of us will perish.'

The arrogant flea scoffed at the warning: 'A tiny creature like me needs only one hearty sip. I shall be as light as a feather.' He hopped onto the bed, burrowed into the silk quilt, and bit the chamberlain so sharply on the neck that the nobleman leaped up shouting with pain!

The chamberlain summoned his servants with torches and brooms, commanding them to search every inch of the bedding, the curtains, and the wainscoting. The nimble flea leaped into a crack in the wall and escaped into the garden, but the poor, innocent mouse was discovered in his nest behind the baseboard.

The servants overturned the nest, driving the mouse into exile in the cold night. As the mouse shivered beneath a dry leaf, he lamented: 'Woe to him who welcomes an undisciplined guest! He who cannot control his own appetite brings ruin upon the roof that sheltered him.'
moral: Greed and impatience in a guest bring disaster upon both himself and his generous host.

title: The Saker and the Birds
summary: A fierce hunting saker—a falcon of great speed and deadly talons—grew weary of serving the royal falconer. One afternoon, breaking his si...
full_text:
A fierce hunting saker—a falcon of great speed and deadly talons—grew weary of serving the royal falconer. One afternoon, breaking his silver jesses during a chase, he escaped into a tranquil valley where flocks of doves, linnets, and starlings lived in peaceful harmony.

Perching upon a flowering almond bough, the falcon smoothed his sharp plumage, softened his fierce yellow glare, and called out to the fluttering songbirds: 'O gentle birds of the grove, do not flee from me! For years I was compelled by human masters to hunt my feathered brethren, but my soul has turned from violence. I come to offer you my protection! With my wings to guard you, no hawk or serpent shall ever dare approach your nests.'

The young and inexperienced doves fluttered near, marveling at the falcon's majestic stature and soothing speech. 'How wonderful!' cooed a fledgling. 'The king of hunters has become our guardian!'

However, an elderly ringdove who had nested in the valley for ten summers perched safely upon a high thornbush and warned the flock: 'Stay back, my children! Judge a hunter by his nature, not by his afternoon sermon. When did the falcon's curved beak ever learn to crack millet seeds? When did those razor talons ever learn to cradle a fledgling without drawing blood?'

To test the falcon's sincerity, the old dove rolled a ripe fig along the branch toward the raptor: 'If you have truly joined our fellowship, O noble saker, partake of the fruit of the tree with us.'

The saker looked at the sweet fig with disgust, his sharp eyes flashing with suppressed hunger. Unable to contain his predatory instinct any longer, he lunged with outstretched claws to strike the old dove! But the cautious dove had anticipated the attack and dropped into the thorny thicket where the falcon’s broad wings could not follow.

The entire flock took wing and scattered into the safety of the rocky clefts, while the frustrated falcon flew away hungry. The birds praised the ancient ringdove, learning that honeyed promises cannot change the fangs of a predator.
moral: A reputation for cruelty cannot be undone by sudden words of friendship; true trust requires proven action.

title: The Sparrow and the Eagle
summary: From the dizzying heights of a craggy mountain peak, an immense imperial eagle folded his wings, plunged like a thunderbolt into the gree...
full_text:
From the dizzying heights of a craggy mountain peak, an immense imperial eagle folded his wings, plunged like a thunderbolt into the green meadow below, and seized a fat young lamb in his talons, bearing it effortlessly back to his aerie to feed his hungry eaglets.

Sitting upon a nearby hawthorn bush, a tiny brown sparrow observed the majestic feat with eyes burning with envy and foolish ambition. 'What is there in this feat that I cannot accomplish?' chirped the sparrow conceitedly. 'He has feathers, wings, and a beak, and I possess feathers, wings, and a beak! If an eagle can carry a lamb, surely I can carry a full-grown ram!'

Puffing up his tiny breast feathers, the sparrow fluttered high into the air, fluttered his little wings with all his might, and dove down onto the back of a huge ram that was grazing among the clover.

With a triumphant chirp, the sparrow dug his tiny claws into the thick, matted wool of the ram's fleece. But alas! The ram felt nothing more than the landing of a thistle-down, and continued calmly chewing his cud. When the sparrow attempted to lift the massive beast into the sky, he could not stir a single hair. Worse still, when he tried to take flight, his sharp little claws had become hopelessly tangled in the dense, oily curls of the sheep's wool.

The sparrow beat his wings in a frenzy, screeching and fluttering, but he was held fast as if in a spider’s web.

Presently, the shepherd boy walked by carrying his crook. Seeing the frantic little bird thrashing upon the ram’s back, the boy laughed heartily, reached out his hand, and untangled the bird's feet. He clipped the sparrow's flight feathers, placed him in a wicker cage, and took him home to his little sister.

When the girl asked: 'Brother, what kind of bird is this?' the boy laughed: 'If you ask him, he will tell you he is an eagle; but if you look at his wings, you will see he is only a foolish sparrow who mistook his ambition for ability.'
moral: Do not attempt burdens beyond your strength merely out of foolish imitation of the mighty.

title: The Hedgehog and the Wood Pigeons
summary: Beside an ancient palm grove lived a family of wood pigeons who nested in the crown of a tall date palm. The tree was laden with clusters...
keywords: the hedgehog and the wood pigeons
full_text:
Beside an ancient palm grove lived a family of wood pigeons who nested in the crown of a tall date palm. The tree was laden with clusters of sweet, honeyed dates, but the birds dropped many ripe dates upon the grass as they fed. Beneath the roots dwelt a cunning hedgehog whose prickly coat hid a mind steeped in trickery.

Longing to devour all the dates himself, the hedgehog donned an ascetic’s cloak made of woven palm fiber, tied a string of prayer beads around his neck, and sat at the foot of the palm tree with eyes cast down, murmuring prayers and fasting.

The gentle pigeons looked down from their leafy bower and marveled at his apparent holiness. 'Look at our neighbor the hedgehog!' cooed the mother pigeon. 'He has abandoned the pleasures of the world and spends his days in humble devotion. Let us descend and seek his spiritual counsel.'

The elder pigeon descended to the grass, bowed respectfully, and said: 'Peace be upon you, venerable hermit. Will you share with us your pearls of wisdom?'

The hedgehog wiped an imaginary tear and sighed: 'Peace be upon you, noble birds. I have realized that true peace comes only from renouncing earthly stores. He who hoards grain and fruit in high trees lives in constant anxiety. If you wish your souls to be light as the desert breeze, bring down all your dates and pile them at my hermitage, that I may distribute them to the poor and needy creatures of the forest.'

The pious pigeons, touched by his eloquent words, spent the entire day flying up and down, carrying every single ripe date from the treetop and stacking them in a massive mound before the hedgehog's burrow.

As night fell, the hedgehog threw off his prayer beads, kicked aside his ascetic's cloak, and rolled himself over the mound of dates, impaling dozens of the fruit upon his sharp spines! Laughing heartily at the gullible birds, he dragged his prize into his subterranean cave, leaving the cold, hungry pigeons on their bare palm tree to weep over the false piety that had stripped them of their winter food.
moral: Beware of hypocrites who don the cloak of piety merely to strip the innocent of their possessions.

summary: An honest grain merchant was leading a sleek, well-fed donkey laden with two sacks of fine wheat to the central market of Cairo. Walking ...
keywords: the merchant and the two sharpers
full_text:
An honest grain merchant was leading a sleek, well-fed donkey laden with two sacks of fine wheat to the central market of Cairo. Walking behind the beast, the merchant held the halter loosely in his hand, humming a cheerful tune.

Two notorious confidence tricksters, observing the plump donkey and the merchant's relaxed demeanor, resolved to steal the animal. The first sharper whispered to his partner: 'Take the donkey by the pack-saddle and lead him down the side alley to the cattle market; I shall handle the halter and the merchant!'

While the second thief quietly slipped the halter off the donkey's ears and led the beast away, the first thief slipped the halter over his own neck and walked quietly behind the merchant in the donkey's footsteps!

After walking several streets, the thief suddenly stopped short, bracing his feet against the cobblestones. The merchant pulled on the rope, found it resisted, and turned around. To his utter amazement, he saw not his grey donkey, but a grown man wearing the halter around his neck, looking down with tearful remorse!

'By heavens!' gasped the merchant. 'Who are you, and where is my donkey?'

The trickster sighed deeply and wept: 'O generous master, know that I was born a human being, but because in my youth I spoke disrespectfully to my pious mother, she cursed me, and I was transformed into a donkey! For five years I have carried sacks of wheat and turned water-wheels to atone for my sin. Today, my mother’s heart softened, she prayed for my deliverance, and at this very hour my human form was restored to me!'

The merchant was struck with pious awe and horror. 'Forgive me, brother!' cried the merchant. 'May heaven witness that I did not know you were a human being when I loaded you with wheat!' He took the halter off the man's neck, gave him five dirhams for charity, and sent him away with blessings.

The next morning, the merchant went to the livestock market to purchase another beast. To his absolute bewilderment, he saw his exact same grey donkey standing in a dealer's pen! The merchant walked up, leaned close to the donkey's ear, and whispered sternly: 'Ah, you incorrigible rascal! You have gone and quarreled with your poor mother again, haven't you? By my honor, you may find another fool to buy you this time!'
moral: Greedy tricksters who scheme to swindle others often end up outwitting and exposing themselves.

title: The Thief and His Monkey
summary: In the bustling port of Alexandria lived a cunning pickpocket who owned a trained monkey of remarkable agility. The monkey had been taugh...
full_text:
In the bustling port of Alexandria lived a cunning pickpocket who owned a trained monkey of remarkable agility. The monkey had been taught to slip through open high windows, climb up silk curtains, and snatch gold coins, rings, and brooches from dressing tables while the owners were downstairs at dinner. Through this deceitful practice, the thief amassed a fortune in gold without performing a single day of honest labor.

Desiring to enjoy his wealth in safety, the thief boarded a merchant vessel sailing for Constantinople. In his heavy leather belt were sewn a thousand stolen gold dinars, and the monkey sat beside him upon the deck.

As the ship sailed across the sunny waters of the Mediterranean, the thief took out his gold coins to count his treasure, gloating over his cleverness. The monkey, watching his master closely, remembered how he had been trained to snatch glittering objects.

When the thief fell asleep beneath the awning, the monkey seized the heavy purse of a thousand dinars, leaped up the ropes of the mainmast, and perched upon the highest yardarm!

The thief awakened, saw his monkey with the treasure, and turned pale with terror. He whistled, waved nuts and sweetmeats, and pleaded: 'Come down, dear friend! That is our livelihood!'

The monkey chattered merrily, opened the purse, and took out two gold coins. He threw one coin down onto the wooden deck into his master’s lap, and hurled the second coin far out into the azure sea! Again he reached into the purse: one coin dropped to the ship, and the next splashed into the waves.

The passengers and sailors gathered on deck, laughing and cheering as the monkey systematically divided the fortune: one coin for the thief on earth, and one coin returned to the deep waters of the ocean!

When the last coin was thrown, the monkey tossed the empty leather purse into the sea and climbed down to his master. The thief sat among five hundred coins, weeping over his lost half. An aged captain placed a hand upon his shoulder and said: 'Do not weep, brother. The monkey was a wiser judge than the magistrate: five hundred coins were earned by your labor in feeding him, and five hundred were stolen from the innocent. The sea has reclaimed what belonged to greed.'
moral: Ill-gotten gains cannot be concealed forever; justice finds its way through the most unexpected instruments.

title: The Foolish Weaver
summary: In a quiet village near Isfahan lived an honest weaver who produced durable linen cloth for coats and sails. Though his trade did not mak...
full_text:
In a quiet village near Isfahan lived an honest weaver who produced durable linen cloth for coats and sails. Though his trade did not make him wealthy, it provided warm bread, honey, and olive oil for his family, and his neighbors respected him for his even stitching.

One spring morning, a traveling troupe of acrobats arrived in the village square. The crowd gathered with breathless excitement as a master rope-dancer climbed a high mast, balanced upon a slender rope stretched between two minarets, leaped into the air, and landed with supreme grace upon his toes. The spectators threw handfuls of silver coins, cheering the acrobat's daring skill.

The weaver watched with wide eyes, his heart consumed by sudden envy. 'What a fool I am!' he thought bitterly. 'I sit hunched over a wooden loom all day long, throwing a wooden shuttle back and forth for a few miserable copper pennies, while this man dances in the air for ten minutes and fills his purse with silver dinars! Tomorrow, I too shall become a famous rope-dancer!'

He returned home, kicked his loom into the corner, and refused to weave another thread. Climbing up to the flat roof of his house, he tied a slender clothesline between two tall chimney pots. Without practicing, without testing the rope, and without taking off his heavy wooden clogs, the foolish weaver stepped boldly onto the slender cord!

The moment his full weight pressed upon the rope, the line snapped like dry grass. The weaver tumbled head over heels from the roof, crashed through his neighbor’s wicker chicken coop, and landed flat on his back in a trough of muddy ditch-water, spraining both his wrists and bruising his ribs.

His wife and neighbors ran out with smelling salts and pulled him from the mud. As the village bonesetter bandaged his fractured wrists, the weaver groaned in agony: 'Cursed be the pride that made me despise my shuttle! The loom was built for my hands, but the sky was meant for eagles and acrobats.' He returned to his loom the moment his bones healed, never again casting envious eyes upon the feats of others.
moral: Do not abandon your proven skill to pursue flashy accomplishments for which you possess neither training nor talent.

title: The Sparrow and the Peacock
summary: In the royal gardens of the Sultan lived a magnificent peacock whose plumage shimmered with sapphire, emerald, and gold. His tail spread ...
full_text:
In the royal gardens of the Sultan lived a magnificent peacock whose plumage shimmered with sapphire, emerald, and gold. His tail spread like a celestial fan decorated with a hundred eyes, and he strutted across the marble terraces, admired by princes and ambassadors.

In a hedge of wild jasmine nearby nested a humble brown sparrow. Every morning, the sparrow would look upon the peacock with deep sorrow, lamenting his own plain feathers: 'How unfair is destiny!' chirped the sparrow. 'I am clad in dusty grey wool, unnoticed by all, while the peacock walks in robes of emerald and gold, the jewel of the court!'

One afternoon, the king of a neighboring realm arrived for a diplomatic treaty. Seeing the peacock, the foreign monarch exclaimed: 'Never have I seen a bird of such sublime splendor! I must possess him for my royal menagerie.'

The royal hunters immediately trapped the peacock with nets, clipped his magnificent wing feathers so that he could never fly, placed a golden ring around his ankle, and shut him inside a heavy iron cage suspended inside a gilded salon.

That evening, the sparrow fluttered through the open palace window and perched upon the gilded bars of the peacock's cage. The splendid bird sat with drooping head, weeping bitter tears: 'Woe is me, little sparrow! My gorgeous plumage has become my prison. I am locked in iron bars, unable to run across the grass or feel the cool morning breeze, displayed as a prisoner for the amusement of strangers.'

The humble sparrow looked at his own plain brown feathers, puffed his wings, and flew freely out through the high window into the vast azure sky. He dipped his wings in the cool fountain spray, chirped happily among the jasmine blossoms, and thanked the heavens for his humble attire, knowing that contentment and liberty are worth more than all the glittering cages of kings.
moral: Plain simplicity carries freedom and safety, while ostentatious beauty often becomes a golden cage.

title: Tale of Ali bin Bakkar and Shams al-Nahar

full_text:
In the golden reign of Harun al-Rashid, Prince Ali bin Bakkar, descendant of ancient Persian kings, resided in Baghdad. He was celebrated across the city for his supreme elegance, generosity, and mastery of poetry. One afternoon, visiting the grand jewelers’ souk of Abu al-Hasan, he beheld Shams al-Nahar, the favorite lady of the court, whose countenance shone like the morning sun.

A deep and mutual affection sprang between them, founded on shared reverence for music, poetry, and noble character. Knowing the perilous boundaries of courtly protocol, they met only in secret garden pavilions, exchanging verses of sublime beauty while the lutes played in the moonlight.

Yet the shadow of discovery hung heavy over their heads. When rumors reached the palace, court guards surrounded the pavilion. With swift presence of mind, Abu al-Hasan helped the young prince escape across the river, while Shams al-Nahar returned with composure to the palace, shielding her beloved from royal wrath.

Separated by impassable walls and weighed down by sorrow, Ali bin Bakkar fell into a burning fever in his Baghdad residence, attended by his devoted companions. Shams al-Nahar, confined to the palace, poured her heart into letters of unmatched eloquence, affirming that true love seeks not selfish triumph, but the spiritual elevation and honor of the beloved.

When the Caliph Harun al-Rashid finally discovered their secret correspondence, he was so moved by the chaste purity and poetic nobility of their devotion that his wrath melted into profound compassion. Though fate decreed their earthly parting, their memory was preserved in the songs of Baghdad as an enduring testament to love that transcends all worldly pride.
moral: True devotion endures with dignity through severe trials, finding purity of soul beyond worldly obstacles.

title: Tale of Kamar al-Zaman
summary: Prince Kamar al-Zaman, son of King Shahriman of the Khaledan Isles, was a youth of such blinding beauty that his name meant 'Moon of the ...
full_text:
Prince Kamar al-Zaman, son of King Shahriman of the Khaledan Isles, was a youth of such blinding beauty that his name meant 'Moon of the Age.' Yet he was so devoted to scholarship, archery, and jurisprudence that he refused his father’s commands to marry, desiring only to rule with wisdom. In anger, his father confined him to an ancient tower.

At that same hour, in the distant empire of China, Princess Budur, whose beauty was famed across the eastern seas, likewise refused all royal suitors, preferring to study astronomy and statecraft, and was placed in a pavilion by her father.

During the night, a benevolent jinni named Danhash and an angelic peri named Maymunah met above the clouds. Arguing over which mortal youth was the fairer in all the world, they lifted Princess Budur from China and placed her gently upon the couch beside Kamar al-Zaman in his tower.

When the prince awakened, he was dazzled by the sleeping maiden’s radiance. Believing his father had placed his bride beside him, he slipped his own royal talismanic ring onto her finger, took her ring in exchange, and kissed her brow before sleep overcame him. When the spirits carried Budur back to China, she awoke with Kamar al-Zaman’s ring upon her hand, her heart consumed by love for the prince she had seen in her vision.

Both kingdoms were plunged into confusion as prince and princess searched the world for their mysterious counterpart. Kamar al-Zaman traveled disguised as an astrologer, while Princess Budur, escaping in the robes of a prince, governed the city of the Ebony Isles with supreme justice.

Recognizing the talismanic ring during an astrological assembly, the royal lovers were joyfully reunited. Their fathers set aside their anger, celebrating a royal union that joined the empires of the West and the East in perpetual friendship.
moral: Destiny unites noble souls across vast distances through faith, steadfastness, and pure intention.

title: Ni'amah bin al-Rabi'a and Naomi
summary: In the city of Kufa lived a noble young gentleman named Ni'amah, whose family had raised an orphan maiden named Naomi from her childhood....
full_text:
In the city of Kufa lived a noble young gentleman named Ni'amah, whose family had raised an orphan maiden named Naomi from her childhood. As they grew into youth, Naomi mastered calligraphy, jurisprudence, and music, and their mutual affection blossomed into marriage.

The tyrannical governor of Basra, Al-Hajjaj, hearing of Naomi’s peerless gifts, sent his guards to abduct her by stealth, presenting her as a gift to the Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik in Damascus. Devastated by the loss of his beloved bride, Ni'amah swore never to rest until he had found her.

Taking his purse of gold, Ni'amah rode across the Syrian desert to Damascus. He sought the counsel of a venerable physician, who advised him not to storm the royal palace with steel, but to use art and patience. Ni'amah disguised himself as a master physician's apprentice, carrying rare elixirs and a golden medicine chest.

His gentle manners and medical skill gained him entrance to the palace infirmary. One afternoon, while preparing scented pastilles in the inner courtyard, he heard a sweet voice singing from behind a silk lattice—it was Naomi, singing verses of longing for her home in Kufa!

Recognizing her voice, Ni'amah inscribed a verse of reassurance upon the back of a silk fan and had it conveyed to her chamber. Through the assistance of the kind court matron who recognized their pure fidelity, the lovers were brought before the Caliph.

Instead of ordering their execution, the Caliph Abd al-Malik was deeply touched by Ni'amah’s fearless journey across the desert and Naomi’s unwavering fidelity. The Caliph bestowed royal gifts upon them, granted them a magnificent mansion in Kufa, and praised their enduring devotion as an example for all his realm.
moral: Steadfast loyalty, courteous resourcefulness, and mutual respect conquer the most formidable fortresses.

title: Ala al-Din Abu al-Shamat
summary: Ala al-Din Abu al-Shamat was the beloved son of the chief merchant of Cairo. Raised in piety, trade, and horsemanship, he embarked with h...
full_text:
Ala al-Din Abu al-Shamat was the beloved son of the chief merchant of Cairo. Raised in piety, trade, and horsemanship, he embarked with his father’s blessing on a great merchant caravan across the Sinai toward Baghdad.

On the road, the caravan was ambushed by desert brigands, and Ala al-Din was stripped of his goods. Alone in the desert, he placed his trust in providence, walked until he reached the gates of Baghdad, and found employment with an elderly jeweler who recognized his honesty and treated him as an adopted son.

When the old jeweler died, he bequeathed his shop and his fortune to Ala al-Din. The young merchant's prosperity, handsome countenance, and open-handed charity won the hearts of the citizens, but it also aroused the burning jealousy of Habazlam, the chief magistrate’s son, who plotted his destruction.

Habazlam stole the Caliph’s golden crown and state mantle from the imperial treasury and secretly buried them beneath the flagstones of Ala al-Din's warehouse. The city watch searched the premises, discovered the royal insignia, and dragged the innocent youth to the scaffold.

Just as the executioner raised his scimitar before the palace, Ahmad al-Danaf, the captain of the honorable vigilantes of Baghdad, burst through the crowd with evidence of Habazlam’s conspiracy. The Caliph Harun al-Rashid ordered the magistrate's son arrested, restored Ala al-Din’s honor with royal robes, and made him the chief inspector of all the markets of the empire.
moral: Divine protection shields the innocent from the most venomous conspiracies of treacherous rivals.

title: Hatim of the Tribe of Tayy
summary: Among the nomadic tribes of ancient Arabia, none was more celebrated than Hatim of the noble tribe of Tayy. His open hand was like the ra...
keywords: hatim of the tribe of tayy
full_text:
Among the nomadic tribes of ancient Arabia, none was more celebrated than Hatim of the noble tribe of Tayy. His open hand was like the rain of spring; he never turned away a beggar, never refused a traveler shelter, and slaughtered his prize horses whenever a stranger arrived at his campfire.

The King of Rome, hearing of Hatim’s fame, felt an itch of royal jealousy. He thought: 'Can a mere desert nomad surpass an emperor in magnificence?' The king dispatched an envoy with secret orders to test Hatim’s generosity to the uttermost: the envoy was to demand Hatim’s favorite stallion, a black Arabian steed famed for unmatched speed and beauty, which Hatim loved above all his possessions.

The royal envoy arrived at Hatim’s camp during a torrential winter storm. The desert was flooded, game was impossible to find, and the livestock were grazing three days' journey away. Hatim welcomed the shivering stranger into his tent, dried his garments before the fire, and served him a sumptuous roast of savory meat.

After the banquet, the envoy stood and delivered the Roman emperor’s request: 'O Hatim, my master demands your famous black stallion as a token of your renowned generosity.'

Hatim’s eyes filled with tears, and he struck his hands together in sorrow. 'Alas, noble guest!' cried Hatim. 'Why did you not speak your request when you first stepped across my threshold? When you arrived drenched and starving in the midnight storm, I had no meat to set before you, and the herds were far away. Rather than let my guest sleep hungry, I slaughtered my beloved black stallion with my own hands to prepare your supper!'

The Roman envoy was struck dumb with awe. He fell at Hatim’s feet and wept: 'By heavens, your fame is but a shadow of your reality! You sacrifice your greatest treasure to feed a stranger without knowing his name.' The emperor, upon receiving the report, acknowledged that Hatim’s open heart was richer than all the gold mines of Rome.
moral: Boundless generosity and selflessness disarm the fiercest envy and elevate a name above all earthly crowns.

title: Tale of Ma'an the Son of Zaidah
summary: Ma'an bin Zaidah was the governor of Iraq and the northern marches, renowned throughout the caliphate for his extraordinary forbearance, ...
keywords: tale of ma'an the son of zaidah
full_text:
Ma'an bin Zaidah was the governor of Iraq and the northern marches, renowned throughout the caliphate for his extraordinary forbearance, mildness of temper, and princely generosity. Three cynical courtiers in Basra wagered one hundred camels that they could provoke the governor into losing his temper.

A daring desert poet accepted the challenge. He dressed in ragged goat-skins, entered Ma'an’s grand hall without greeting him with royal titles, and shouted: 'Do you remember, O Ma'an, when your shoes were made of camel-hide and you tended goats in the hills?'

The courtiers gasped at the insolence, but Ma'an smiled gently and replied: 'I remember it well, brother; it was a peaceful life, and I thank heaven for the humble beginnings that taught me gratitude.'

The poet stepped closer and recited an insulting verse: 'Now that you sit on a cushioned divan, you think yourself a prince, yet your lineage is lower than the dust!'

Ma'an answered with undisturbed calm: 'A man’s true lineage is his conduct, my friend. If my deeds are worthy, my origin matters little; and if my deeds are evil, no noble ancestry can redeem me.'

The poet, enraged by his failure to ruffle the governor, shouted: 'Give me five hundred pieces of gold at once, you miserly son of a shepherd, or I shall mock you across every market from Basra to Damascus!'

Ma'an turned to his treasurer and said with boundless courtesy: 'Give this man a thousand pieces of gold: five hundred for his bold poetry, and five hundred because his clothing is thin and the winter frost approaches.'

The poet dropped his staff, fell upon his knees before the governor, and kissed his robe: 'By the Creator of all things, O Ma'an, your forbearance is a fortress that no tongue can breach! I came to provoke your anger for a wager, but your magnanimity has conquered my soul forever.' Ma'an smiled, raised the poet to his feet, and welcomed him as a friend of his court.
moral: Patience and forbearance under insult prove true nobility more than swords and royal decrees.

title: The City of Labtayt
summary: In the ancient kingdom of Andalusia stood the royal city of Labtayt, which is Toledo. In the center of the city rose an ancient, mysterio...
full_text:
In the ancient kingdom of Andalusia stood the royal city of Labtayt, which is Toledo. In the center of the city rose an ancient, mysterious palace whose gates had never been opened since the founding of the realm. Each king, upon ascending the throne, placed a new iron lock upon the massive bronze doors, until twenty-four locks gleamed upon the portals.

When the haughty King Roderic seized the crown, the venerable bishops and counselors brought him the twenty-fifth lock. But Roderic shook his head with arrogant disdain: 'Why should I add another lock like a frightened child? I am a monarch of valor! I shall break open these gates and discover what treasure my ancestors have locked away from my eyes.'

The elders fell upon their knees, pleading: 'Do not do this, sire! The ancient prophecy decrees that as long as the palace remains sealed, our kingdom shall flourish in peace, but if the locks are broken, strangers shall conquer our land.'

Deaf to their pleas, Roderic commanded his smiths to cut the twenty-four locks with iron chisels. The heavy bronze gates swung open with a groan of thunder, revealing a vast, dark hall paved with jasper and lined with statues of gold. In the center stood an ebony table bearing an ancient wooden coffer decorated with pearls.

Roderic seized the coffer, pried open the lid, and found within a scroll of parchment. When he unrolled the scroll, a painted fresco illuminated the hall: upon it were depicted Arabian horsemen armed with scimitars and lances, riding swift steeds across desert sands. Below the painting was written an ancient inscription:

'When these locks are broken and this coffer is unsealed, warriors wearing these turbans and bearing these lances shall cross the sea and conquer the kingdom of Andalusia.'

Roderic trembled, seized with sudden dread. He ordered the gates resealed, but it was too late. Within the year, the fleet of Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the straits, and Roderic’s army was scattered at the Guadalete, proving that he who scoffs at ancestral warnings invites his own destruction.
moral: Arrogance that tramples ancestral wisdom and breaks sacred locks unleashes unforeseen catastrophe.
