title: The Caliph Hisham and the Arab Youth
summary: The Umayyad Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik rode out hunting across the northern steppes of Syria with a splendid retinue of emirs, falcon...
keywords: the caliph hisham and the arab youth
full_text:
The Umayyad Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik rode out hunting across the northern steppes of Syria with a splendid retinue of emirs, falconers, and palace guards. While pursuing a desert gazelle, the Caliph became separated from his escort and rode near an isolated well where a young Bedouin boy was watering his flock of sheep.

The Caliph’s stallion was thirsty, and Hisham called out with imperious authority: 'Ho, boy! Draw water for the horse of the Commander of the Faithful!'

The Bedouin boy looked up with untroubled eyes, his head held high: 'Your stallion may drink when my sheep have finished, O traveler. The beasts of the poor have thirsted all day under the sun, and the water of the earth belongs equally to all living creatures.'

Hisham frowned, his pride wounded: 'Do you know to whom you speak with such bold speech, insolent child? I am Hisham, the ruler of all the Faithful from Morocco to Samarkand!'

The boy smiled with calm dignity and replied: 'If you are indeed the shepherd of the people, O Caliph, remember that a true shepherd watches over the weakest lamb before he feeds his own horse. Power is a trust from the heavens, not a rod to strike down the humble.'

Hisham was astonished by the youth’s fearlessness and the philosophical depth of his reply. At that moment, the royal guards galloped up, drawing their swords to punish the boy for his lack of deference.

'Hold your hands!' commanded Hisham. 'This desert child has taught your Caliph more wisdom in three breaths than all the flatterers in my court have spoken in twenty years.' The Caliph dismounted, embraced the boy, rewarded his tribe with five hundred sheep and a fertile oasis, and took the youth to his capital to be trained in the highest councils of the realm.
moral: Inborn eloquence and sharp intellect outshine royal power and command respect from emperors.

title: Ibrahim bin al-Mahdi and the Barber-Surgeon
summary: Prince Ibrahim bin al-Mahdi, uncle of the Caliph Al-Ma'mun, was a man of royal blood and celebrated musical genius. Following a bitter po...
keywords: ibrahim bin al-mahdi and the barber-surgeon
full_text:
Prince Ibrahim bin al-Mahdi, uncle of the Caliph Al-Ma'mun, was a man of royal blood and celebrated musical genius. Following a bitter political rebellion in Baghdad, Ibrahim's faction was defeated, and the Caliph put a reward of one hundred thousand gold dinars upon his uncle’s head, dead or alive.

Disguised in a tattered woollen mantle, Prince Ibrahim wandered the alleys of Baghdad, pursued by royal guards. Exhausted and desperate, he slipped into a modest mud-brick house and threw himself before the master, an impoverished barber-surgeon named Abu Ahmad.

'I am a man fleeing for my life,' gasped Ibrahim. 'If the guards find me, I perish. Protect me for the sake of ancient honor!'

Abu Ahmad asked no questions. He hid the prince in his small attic, shared his meager supper of lentils and bread, and tended his blistered feet with soothing oils.

The next morning, the town crier passed the window, proclaiming the reward of one hundred thousand dinars for Ibrahim’s capture. The barber turned to his guest with tears in his eyes: 'My lord, I recognized your noble voice last night from the days when you sang at the palace. You are worth a king's ransom, but under Abu Ahmad’s roof, a guest is worth all the gold in creation. Stay here until the storm passes.'

For three weeks, the poor barber shared his crust of bread with the royal prince. When peace was restored and the Caliph Al-Ma'mun proclaimed a universal amnesty, Ibrahim walked boldly into the imperial palace. The Caliph, moved by his uncle's poetic plea, embraced him and granted full pardon.

Ibrahim then stepped forward and said: 'Sire, I ask one favor: summon Abu Ahmad the barber.' Before the entire court, Ibrahim recounted the barber's heroic fidelity. The Caliph appointed Abu Ahmad chief physician of the royal hospital, granted him a palace on the Tigris, and decreed that true nobility is found not in crowns, but in the faithful heart of an honest man.
moral: Loyalty, hospitality to a fugitive in peril, and honorable gratitude create friendships that outlive empires.

title: The City of Many-Columned Iram
summary: In the reign of the Umayyad Caliph Mu'awiyah, an Arab traveler named Abdullah ibn Qilab was searching for a lost camel in the great south...
full_text:
In the reign of the Umayyad Caliph Mu'awiyah, an Arab traveler named Abdullah ibn Qilab was searching for a lost camel in the great southern wilderness of the Rub al-Khali—the Empty Quarter. As a violent sandstorm cleared, Abdullah beheld a sight that made him doubt his own senses: rising from the red dunes stood the towering walls of a magnificent city, built entirely of golden bricks and silver tiles.

Entering through massive gates of carved sandalwood studded with rubies, Abdullah walked through silent, empty streets lined with colossal palaces supported by thousands of translucent pillars carved from alabaster and chrysolite. In the courtyards flowed clear canals over beds of pearls and emeralds, and trees made of burnished gold bore fruits of amber and turquoise. Yet not a single human footstep broke the silence, and not a single bird sang in the branches.

Filled with awe and dread, Abdullah gathered a handful of pearls from the dry riverbed, mounted his camel, and fled back to the civilized cities of Yemen.

When news of his discovery reached the Caliph, Abdullah was brought to Damascus. The Caliph summoned the venerable sage Ka'ab al-Ahbar and asked: 'Is there truly such a city in the desert, or was this traveler delirious with thirst?'

The sage unrolled ancient chronicles and answered: 'It is the truth, O Commander of the Faithful. That is Iram of the Pillars, built by King Shaddad of the ancient tribe of Ad. In his supreme arrogance, Shaddad sought to build a paradise on earth that would rival the celestial heavens. For five hundred years, he gathered all the gold, gems, and pearls of the world to build his city. But when he approached its gates to inaugurate his glory, a celestial cry of wrath struck him and his host, and they perished in an instant. The city was swallowed by the drifting sands, hidden forever from human eyes, save for a lone traveler who would find it to remind the mighty that all earthly pride is nothing but passing dust.'
moral: Arrogant pride that builds monuments to rival the heavens vanishes like dust before the desert wind.

title: Isaac of Mosul
summary: Isaac of Mosul was the chief court musician of the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, universally acknowledged as the greatest master of the lute an...
full_text:
Isaac of Mosul was the chief court musician of the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, universally acknowledged as the greatest master of the lute and the voice in all the Islamic world. His melodies moved emperors to tears and his compositions were sung from Cordoba to Baghdad.

One sultry afternoon, desiring to escape the formalities of the court, Isaac walked through the quiet residential quarters of Baghdad. Passing a secluded garden enclosed by high walls, his ear was caught by the sound of a lute being played with such breathtaking subtlety, technical perfection, and soulful depth that Isaac stood frozen on the cobblestones.

A youthful voice sang verses of heartbreaking beauty, modulating across complex melodic modes with effortless grace. Isaac listened, his heart alternating between awe and astonishment. He realized that this unknown lutenist possessed a genius that rivaled—and perhaps surpassed—his own.

Instead of turning away in envious bitterness, Isaac knocked upon the gate. A modest young man named Ziryab, poorly dressed but with eyes burning with artistic devotion, opened the door.

Isaac smiled warmly, embraced the youth, and said: 'Young master, I am Isaac of Mosul. I have spent my life mastering the lute, yet your playing has opened a new fountain of wonder in my soul. You must not hide your light in a courtyard; the world must hear your song!'

Isaac brought Ziryab to the palace, presented him to the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, and stepped back to let the young artist perform before the court. The Caliph was enchanted, rewarding Ziryab with wealth and honor. Years later, Ziryab traveled to Andalusia, where he founded the legendary conservatory of Cordoba, revolutionizing music and poetry across Europe.

Isaac’s generosity was celebrated as a rare example of true greatness: a master who nurtured his own rival, proving that art belongs not to the ego, but to the beauty of all humankind.
moral: A true master of art recognizes and honors talent in others without the poison of petty jealousy.

title: The Sweep and the Noble Lady
summary: In Baghdad lived a humble chimney sweep named Ali, whose skin and garments were permanently blackened by soot. He earned only a few coppe...
keywords: the sweep and the noble lady
full_text:
In Baghdad lived a humble chimney sweep named Ali, whose skin and garments were permanently blackened by soot. He earned only a few copper coins each day cleaning the hearths and chimneys of the grand mansions, yet his heart was clean, and he never touched a coin that was not his own.

One morning, Ali was summoned to clean the wide marble fireplace in the private salon of a noble lady of the Abbasid court. While scraping the soot from the flue, his brush struck a loose brick inside the chimney wall. Dislodging the brick, a velvet jewelry case fell out and landed at his feet.

Ali opened the case and caught his breath: inside rested a diamond necklace of immense value, sparkling like stars against the black soot. The salon was empty; no one had seen him discover it, and the dust on the box proved it had been hidden for years.

Ali held the case in his soot-stained hands. A voice within whispered: 'Take it! With this single jewel, you and your children will be wealthy forever; you will never scrape a chimney again.'

Ali closed the lid firmly, shook his head, and replied to his conscience: 'Wealth bought by theft is blackened with a soot that water can never wash clean.'

He carried the case downstairs and handed it directly to the noble lady. The lady gasped with astonishment: the necklace was an ancestral heirloom lost twenty years earlier during a fire, and she had long mourned its loss.

'O sweep!' cried the lady. 'You could have hidden this beneath your tunic, and no soul would have known! Why did you return it?'

Ali bowed humbly: 'I am a poor man, my lady, but my father taught me that honesty is a treasure that thieves cannot steal and fire cannot burn.'

Moved to tears by his integrity, the noble lady gifted Ali a thousand gold dinars, purchased him a comfortable house, and made him the chief steward of her estates, proving that a pure heart shines brighter than the rarest diamond.
moral: Honesty in the face of poverty and temptation is the truest badge of nobility.

title: The Mock Caliph
summary: One evening, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, disguised as an ordinary merchant alongside his vizier Ja'afar and Masrur, sailed down the Tigri...
full_text:
One evening, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, disguised as an ordinary merchant alongside his vizier Ja'afar and Masrur, sailed down the Tigris in a small rowing boat to inspect the peace of his capital. As their boat drifted beneath the grand arched bridge, they saw a magnificent royal barge approaching, illuminated with hundreds of lanterns and silk banners.

Upon the gilded deck sat a young man dressed in the exact robes, black turban, and mantle of the Caliph! Beside him stood a mock vizier, a mock executioner, and fifty armed attendants who treated him with imperial deference. The young mock-caliph listened to petitions, distributed sacks of gold to the poor boatmen, and held court with regal majesty.

Harun al-Rashid was astonished. 'Who is this bold youth who dares to play the Caliph upon my own river?' he whispered to Ja'afar.

The next morning, the Caliph sent guards to arrest the mock-caliph and bring him to the palace. The youth, whose name was Mohammed Ali, was brought in chains before the real throne. He turned pale with terror, fell prostrate to the marble floor, and pleaded for his life.

'Explain yourself!' commanded Harun al-Rashid. 'Why did you mimic my sacred office?'

Mohammed Ali wept and confessed: 'O Commander of the Faithful, I am the son of a wealthy jeweler who left me an enormous fortune. Having neither wife nor children, I dreamed of feeling the joy of a monarch who delivers justice and wipes away the tears of the poor. Every evening, I hired musicians and distributed my father’s gold to the destitute, pretending to be you, whom I revere above all men! I had no treason in my heart, only a foolish desire to play at benevolence.'

Harun al-Rashid smiled at the youth’s extraordinary confession. 'Your intention was generous,' said the Caliph, 'yet authority without responsibility causes confusion in the realm. From this day forward, you shall not play the Caliph upon a boat; I appoint you my royal almoner, and you shall distribute my own imperial treasury to the needy every Friday.' Thus the youth’s dream became reality through lawful duty.
moral: Generosity and theatrical playfulness must never overstep the boundaries of civic order and respect for law.

title: Ali the Persian
summary: In the court of Harun al-Rashid, an old traveler named Ali the Persian related a comical dispute he had once brought before the Chief Jud...
full_text:
In the court of Harun al-Rashid, an old traveler named Ali the Persian related a comical dispute he had once brought before the Chief Judge of Baghdad:

"In my youth, I was walking through the leather-tanners’ bazaar carrying a small, tattered leather bag containing a few copper coins, an olive, and an iron needle. A notorious sharper seized the bag from my hand, shouting: 'Help, citizens! This thief has stolen my property!' We wrestled over the bag until the watchmen dragged us both before the Chief Judge.

The judge looked sternly at the sharper: 'What does your bag contain?'

The sharper puffed his chest and recited without drawing breath: 'My lord, this bag contains two bottles of rosewater, two crystal carafes, a pair of gilded scissors, twenty rolls of Persian silk, four silver spoons, a pair of dancing boots, an iron anvil, two brass candlesticks, three camels, a flour mill, and a caravan of fifty mules!'

The judge rubbed his temples in disbelief. He then turned to me: 'And what does your bag contain, O Persian?'

Perceiving that the sharper was attempting to overwhelm the court with impossible nonsense, I resolved to match his absurdity. I bowed low and recited:

'May heaven preserve our noble judge! Inside this small leather bag rests a marble palace with forty pillars, two thousand sheep with their shepherds, the city of Cairo with all its mosques, the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, the mountains of the Moon, an orchard of ten thousand date palms, three royal armies with their war elephants, and the grand judge himself sitting upon his bench!'

The court erupted in uncontrollable laughter. The Chief Judge laughed until his turban slipped over his eyes. When order was restored, the judge opened the little bag and pulled out the single olive, the copper coins, and the iron needle.

Turning to the blushing sharper, the judge gave him twenty lashes for his fraudulent claim, awarded me my bag with ten gold dinars for my witty defense, and sent us on our way, proving that the best cure for ridiculous bluster is a dose of equal wit."
moral: Empty bluster and ridiculous exaggeration reveal their own absurdity when subjected to calm scrutiny.

title: Harun al-Rashid and the Slave-Girl
summary: The Caliph Harun al-Rashid sat in his golden pavilion overlooking the Tigris, listening to the performance of a newly arrived court singe...
full_text:
The Caliph Harun al-Rashid sat in his golden pavilion overlooking the Tigris, listening to the performance of a newly arrived court singer named Tawaddud. She had been educated by the finest masters of Baghdad, not merely in the arts of the lute and singing, but in the deepest disciplines of the mind.

Desiring to test her renown, the Caliph summoned his chief scholars: the grand theologian, the royal physician, the imperial astronomer, and the master philosopher. 'Examine this maiden,' decreed the Caliph, 'and let us see if her wisdom matches her fame.'

The theologian questioned her on the principles of jurisprudence, the traditions of the ancients, and the subtleties of ethics; she answered every inquiry with citations and flawless logic. The physician examined her in anatomy, herbal remedies, and the diagnosis of fevers; she explained the circulation of humors and the properties of medicinal roots with precision.

The astronomer challenged her on the movements of the planets, the constellations of the zodiac, and the calculation of lunar eclipses; she charted the celestial spheres upon a brass astrolabe without a moment's hesitation. Finally, the philosopher asked her the deepest riddles of human existence, which she answered with profound humility, poetry, and grace.

The venerable scholars stood, bowed before her, and confessed to the Caliph: 'O Commander of the Faithful, her learning surpasses that of your entire council! She is a living library of wisdom.'

Harun al-Rashid, deeply impressed by her extraordinary dedication to knowledge, granted her freedom, bestowed upon her a magnificent estate in Baghdad, and rewarded her teacher with royal honors, demonstrating that true beauty resides in the cultivated mind and the noble character.
moral: Intellect, cultural refinement, and artistic wisdom elevate the spirit and inspire noble rulers.

title: Tale of the Lover Who Feigned Himself a Thief
summary: In the city of Basra lived a noble young man named Wafiq who was deeply in love with the daughter of an affluent neighbor. Their affectio...
keywords: tale of the lover who feigned himself a thief
full_text:
In the city of Basra lived a noble young man named Wafiq who was deeply in love with the daughter of an affluent neighbor. Their affection was pure and mutually shared, but her strict father had forbidden any communication between them.

One starlit evening, driven by longing, Wafiq climbed the outer garden wall merely to catch a glimpse of her walking among the rosebushes. As he peered down from the parapet, the watchmen of the city happened to patrol the alley. Seeing a young man climbing the wall of a wealthy merchant's home, the guards shouted: 'A thief! Catch the burglar!' and seized him.

Wafiq realized his dilemma: if he spoke the truth and explained his presence, he would save himself from punishment, but the innocent maiden's reputation would be tarnished forever across the gossip of the bazaars. If he remained silent or claimed to be a thief, he faced the executioner's scimitar.

Choosing chivalric honor over self-preservation, Wafiq held his tongue and confessed before the magistrate: 'I climbed the wall to steal the merchant’s gold. Punish me as the law decrees.'

The magistrate sentenced him to have his right hand severed in the public square. On the appointed morning, as the executioner raised the blade, a veiled lady rushed through the crowd, crying: 'Hold your hand, O judge! This man is no thief!'

The maiden threw herself before the magistrate and revealed the noble truth: 'He climbed the wall out of pure love for me, and confessed to a crime he never committed to shield my name from scandal! If anyone must be punished, punish me, but do not harm the noblest soul in Basra!'

The magistrate, the merchant, and all the citizens were moved to tears by such heroic chivalry and mutual fidelity. The merchant embraced the young man, granted him his daughter’s hand in marriage with a handsome dowry, and praised the courage that had chosen honor over life itself.
moral: Selfless chivalry that risks one's own life to protect another's honor is ultimately vindicated by truth.

title: Ja'afar the Barmecide and the Bean-Seller
summary: Ja'afar the Barmecide, Grand Vizier to Caliph Harun al-Rashid, was accustomed to walking through the narrow alleys of Baghdad in simple m...
keywords: ja'afar the barmecide and the bean-seller
full_text:
Ja'afar the Barmecide, Grand Vizier to Caliph Harun al-Rashid, was accustomed to walking through the narrow alleys of Baghdad in simple merchant attire to observe the life of the common people. One chilly winter evening, when the icy north wind blew from the mountains, Ja'afar found himself in a desolate lane near the eastern wall, shivering with cold and having missed his evening meal.

Smelling the savory aroma of cooking, he approached a tiny, lantern-lit stall where an old bean-seller named Abu Salih was ladling hot, steaming fava beans into clay bowls, sprinkling them with ground cumin, coarse salt, and fragrant olive oil.

Ja'afar stepped up and searched his pockets, only to discover that he had forgotten his purse at the palace. Embarrassed, the great vizier said: 'Peace be upon you, elder. I am a stranger who has lost his purse; I have not a single copper fals to offer you.'

The old bean-seller smiled warmly, wrapped his coarse woollen shawl tighter, and replied: 'Enter, brother! Food is a gift from the heavens, not a merchandise to withhold from the hungry.' He handed Ja'afar a steaming bowl heaped with hot beans and two fresh barley flatbreads, saying: 'Eat in peace, and warm your bones.'

Ja'afar ate with hearty gratitude, finding the humble meal sweeter than any feast served upon royal gold.

The next morning, royal horsemen rode into the lane, bearing an imperial decree from the Grand Vizier. Abu Salih was brought to the palace, trembling with fear. But Ja'afar descended from his dais, embraced the bean-seller before all the courtiers, and said: 'Yesterday, you fed the hungry without asking for coin; today, the Barmecide repays your bread with gold.'

Ja'afar gifted him a thousand dinars, a comfortable house, and made him the chief provider of grain for the city orphanages, proving that an open heart in a mud stall can outshine the splendor of empires.
moral: Generosity from the humble poor carries more spiritual weight than the lavish gifts of kings.

title: Abu Mohammed hight Lazybones
summary: In Baghdad lived a young man named Abu Mohammed, so notorious for his indolence that the whole neighborhood called him Lazybones. From da...
full_text:
In Baghdad lived a young man named Abu Mohammed, so notorious for his indolence that the whole neighborhood called him Lazybones. From dawn until dusk, he lay curled upon a sheepskin mattress on his mother’s porch, refusing to fetch water, sweep the yard, or earn a single copper, while his poor mother spun cotton late into the night to feed him.

One day, an aged traveler from Khorasan arrived at the house, looking for a strong youth to accompany him on a trading voyage down the Persian Gulf. Seeing Abu Mohammed's broad shoulders, the traveler gave the mother five gold dinars and promised: 'Mother, give your son into my care. I shall cure his sloth or bring him back laden with silk.'

Dragged aboard the merchant vessel, Abu Mohammed at first groaned and wept, wishing only for his mattress. But as the ship sailed through perilous uncharted seas, fierce tempests broke the masts. Thrown upon a desert island, the lazy youth was forced by hunger to gather firewood, catch fish with his bare hands, and scale sheer cliffs to find fresh spring water.

In the mountains of the island, they discovered an ancient cavern guarded by an enchanted ape who held an emerald talisman. To secure the talisman, Abu Mohammed had to dive into a whirlpool and swim against the current. Remembering his mother’s tears and his wasted years, the youth gathered his courage, plunged into the churning waters, and retrieved the talisman with heroic determination.

Returning to Baghdad with chests of pearls, Abu Mohammed kissed his mother’s hands, built her a palace with blooming gardens, and opened a free craft school for the youth of the city. He never returned to his lazy ways, proving that labor and purpose give life its true fragrance.
moral: Overcoming sloth and embracing honest duty unlocks the true treasures of character and fortune.

title: Generous Dealing of Yahya bin Khalid
summary: Yahya bin Khalid, the patriarchal head of the illustrious Barmecide family, was celebrated throughout the Islamic world for his exquisite...
keywords: generous dealing of yahya bin khalid
full_text:
Yahya bin Khalid, the patriarchal head of the illustrious Barmecide family, was celebrated throughout the Islamic world for his exquisite tact, boundless charity, and princely magnanimity.

One morning, an impoverished gentleman of noble lineage named Mansur entered Yahya’s reception hall. Mansur had inherited vast estates, but famine and crop failures had reduced him to absolute destitution; he was heavily indebted to creditors and had pawned his family’s ancestral silver to buy bread.

Too proud to beg publicly in the marketplace, Mansur stood quietly among the petitioners, his head bowed with sorrow.

Yahya bin Khalid noticed his downcast eyes and noble bearing. Instead of offering him a humiliating handout of copper before the crowd, Yahya summoned Mansur to his private library. He embraced him warmly, sat him upon his own divan, and asked: 'Brother, how may the house of Barmak serve a noble soul like you?'

Mansur wept and confessed: 'My lord, I owe twenty thousand dinars to demanding creditors, and my household faces starvation.'

Yahya took a reed pen and wrote three letters: the first to the governor of Egypt, requesting him to grant Mansur a fertile estate; the second to the chief merchant of Damascus, directing him to clear all Mansur's debts; and the third to the imperial treasurer of Baghdad, granting Mansur a monthly pension of three hundred dinars.

Before Mansur could speak, Yahya handed him a heavy purse of five thousand gold dinars for travel expenses, saying with deep humility: 'Take this modest gift, my brother, and forgive me that my assistance is so small. It is we who are indebted to you for granting us the honor of serving an honorable man.'

Mansur walked out into the sunshine with tears of gratitude, marveling at how true nobility bestows charity with such grace that it elevates the receiver rather than humbling him.
moral: Nobility uses its influence to restore the dignity of the fallen without making them feel humiliated.

title: Ali Shar and Zumurrud
summary: Ali Shar was the generous son of an affluent merchant of Khorasan. Upon his father's death, false companions flattered him and squandered...
full_text:
Ali Shar was the generous son of an affluent merchant of Khorasan. Upon his father's death, false companions flattered him and squandered his fortune until he was left penniless. Abandoned by his summer friends, he wandered into the slave market, where an extraordinary maiden named Zumurrud was being auctioned.

Zumurrud was gifted not only with dazzling beauty, but with mastery of calligraphy, silk embroidery, and chess. Observing Ali Shar’s honest countenance, she insisted that he purchase her, giving him her own hidden purse of a thousand dinars to pay the price.

Through her exquisite embroidery, which Ali Shar sold at high profit, their fortunes were restored, and they lived in mutual affection and peace.

However, a treacherous neighbor who envied their happiness abducted Zumurrud while Ali Shar was away in the market. Escaping her captors by cutting her hair, dressing in the armor of a prince, and mounting a swift Arabian stallion, Zumurrud rode across the desert to an unknown kingdom.

Arriving at the capital just as the elderly king had died without an heir, the citizens, following an ancient oracle, proclaimed that the first horseman to pass through the city gates should be crowned monarch. Zumurrud, disguised as Prince Emerald, was crowned with the royal diadem!

She governed the kingdom with peerless justice, establishing grain storehouses, building hospitals, and protecting the poor. Remembering her beloved Ali Shar, she instituted a weekly public banquet where every traveler in the city was invited to dine in the royal presence.

Months later, Ali Shar, who had wandered across deserts searching for his bride, entered the hall in rags. Recognizing him beneath his dust, Queen Zumurrud descended from the throne, revealed her identity, and made Ali Shar king beside her, celebrating a reunion forged in unwavering fidelity.
moral: Steadfast fidelity, courage under trial, and resourceful intelligence reunite separated lovers.

summary: Jubayr bin Umayr, a wealthy young nobleman of Basra, had wed the peerless Lady Budur, daughter of the city’s chief judge. For a year, the...
keywords: the loves of jubayr bin umayr and lady budur
full_text:
Jubayr bin Umayr, a wealthy young nobleman of Basra, had wed the peerless Lady Budur, daughter of the city’s chief judge. For a year, their home was an arbor of joy, song, and poetry.

Yet in a moment of thoughtless haste, provoked by an idle remark during a banquet, Jubayr swore a rash oath that estranged them. Lady Budur, wounded by his pride, returned to her father’s palace, refusing to look upon his face or receive his letters.

Stricken with remorse, Jubayr realized that earthly wealth is cold ash when separated from the soul’s beloved. He abandoned his fine apparel, donned the patched robe of a penitent, and wandered along the banks of the Euphrates, reciting poems of lamentation and longing.

The wise vizier of Basra, observing Jubayr's sincere sorrow, resolved to act as an ambassador of peace. He arranged a literary gathering at his garden estate, inviting the chief judge and his daughter behind the embroidered silk screens.

The vizier invited Jubayr to recite his verses before the company. Jubayr stood before the assembly, his voice trembling with genuine remorse, reciting poems of how pride shatters the mirror of joy and how humble forgiveness is the greatest virtue of the soul.

Behind the screen, Lady Budur listened, her heart melting as she recognized the depth of his transformation. She sent forth an inscribed crystal cup filled with fragrant pomegranate sherbet, with a verse answering: 'The heart that repents in truth has already built a garden where love blossoms anew.'

The lovers were joyously reconciled before the assembly, having learned that forgiveness is a stronger cement for a home than any youthful vow.
moral: Patience, repentance, and mutual forgiveness heal the deepest rifts between loving hearts.

title: The Man of Al-Yaman and His Six Slave-Girls
summary: A wealthy and enlightened nobleman of Yemen had educated his six daughters in six distinct arts of the mind: the first in Astronomy, the ...
keywords: the man of al-yaman and his six slave-girls
full_text:
A wealthy and enlightened nobleman of Yemen had educated his six daughters in six distinct arts of the mind: the first in Astronomy, the second in Medicine, the third in Jurisprudence, the fourth in Poetry and Music, the fifth in Mathematics and Architecture, and the sixth in Philosophy and Ethics.

When business brought them to Baghdad, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid heard of this extraordinary assembly of intellect and summoned the family to his palace.

The Caliph challenged them to a friendly contest of wisdom: each scholar was to present an argument proving that her discipline was the foundation of human happiness and good governance.

The Astronomer spoke of the celestial spheres, the navigation of ships across trackless seas, and the majesty of the starry heavens. The Physician spoke of the preservation of life, the harmony of bodily humors, and the sacred relief of pain. The Jurist demonstrated how justice, fair laws, and the defense of the weak preserve peace in the commonwealth.

The Poet sang of how music and verse soften the human heart, inspiring empathy and courage. The Mathematician demonstrated how geometry builds bridges, aqueducts, and domes that endure through centuries. Finally, the Philosopher showed that without virtue, truth, and ethical conscience, all sciences become hollow instruments of vanity.

Harun al-Rashid listened with enraptured delight, applauding each discourse. He declared: 'None has surpassed the other, for wisdom is a single magnificent garden, and each of you tends a necessary blossom! No realm can stand on steel alone; it flourishes on science, art, and justice.' The Caliph bestowed royal gifts upon each of the six scholars and established a grand academy in Baghdad to teach their disciplines.
moral: Diverse branches of learning—science, art, and virtue—enrich human civilization like jewels in a single crown.

title: Harun al-Rashid and the Damsel and Abu Nowas
summary: The Caliph Harun al-Rashid was sitting in his garden pavilion beside a sparkling fountain, accompanied by an intelligent and witty court ...
keywords: harun al-rashid and the damsel and abu nowas
full_text:
The Caliph Harun al-Rashid was sitting in his garden pavilion beside a sparkling fountain, accompanied by an intelligent and witty court maiden named Zubayr. As the breeze ruffled the rosebushes, the Caliph resolved to test the famous court poet Abu Nowas, whose audacious humor was both the delight and exasperation of the court.

The Caliph challenged Zubayr to pose an impossible poetic riddle: 'When Abu Nowas enters, I shall recite the first half of an improbable verse; you shall recite the second; and if he cannot complete it on the spot with rhyme, meter, and brilliant wit, he shall pay twenty dinars to the gardeners!'

Presently, Abu Nowas entered the pavilion, bowing low with his usual whimsical grin.

The Caliph immediately cleared his throat and recited:
'The lion in his den bowed down before the mouse,'

Zubayr quickly added with a playful smile:
'And begged for mercy meekly outside his little house!'

Abu Nowas did not pause for the blink of an eye. Adjusting his embroidered turban, he declaimed with thunderous gravity:
'For though the lion's claw can tear the oak in twain,
A thorn within his paw was pulled by love again;
Thus power learns to kneel where gentle deeds abide,
And wisdom cures the hurt that steel could never hide!'

The Caliph and Zubayr stared in astonishment at how effortlessly the poet had turned their silly rhyme into a profound philosophical allegory.

Harun al-Rashid burst into hearty laughter, tossed a purse of fifty gold dinars into Abu Nowas’s hands, and exclaimed: 'By my ancestors, Abu Nowas, your tongue is quicker than an arrow in flight! Even when we set a snare for your wits, you weave our cords into a carpet of gold!'
moral: Spontaneous wit and poetic eloquence can defuse imperial wrath and bring laughter to solemn halls.

title: The Man Who Stole the Dish of Gold
summary: In Cairo lived an impoverished porter named Mansur who worked from dawn until dusk, yet could barely earn enough copper to buy bread for ...
keywords: the man who stole the dish of gold
full_text:
In Cairo lived an impoverished porter named Mansur who worked from dawn until dusk, yet could barely earn enough copper to buy bread for his sick wife and young daughter. One evening, after delivering a heavy load of cedar beams to the mansion of a wealthy nobleman, he found himself alone in a banquet hall.

Upon a silver side-table lay a magnificent golden dish studded with turquoises, left behind by careless servants. Mansur looked at the gleaming gold. Thoughts of his weeping wife and hungry child rushed into his mind. In a moment of overwhelming weakness, he slipped the heavy golden dish beneath his rough cloak and fled into the night.

Returning home, he hid the dish beneath the floorboards. But sleep deserted him completely. Every rustle of the wind sounded like the guards knocking at the gate. When he looked at his daughter eating bread bought with pawning a piece of his old coat, he thought: 'Shall I feed my pure child on the proceeds of theft?'

Conscience struck him with such agony that before dawn, Mansur dug up the golden dish, walked back to the grand mansion, and threw himself at the nobleman’s feet.

'My lord,' wept Mansur, 'hunger tempted me, and I took this golden dish last night. But my father’s memory and my own soul could not bear the weight of stolen gold. Here is your treasure. Hang me or beat me as the law decrees, but let my family know I returned it with clean hands.'

The nobleman looked at the heavy gold, and then at the shivering, honest porter. His heart was touched with deep admiration.

'Rise, brother,' said the nobleman gently. 'He who steals in hunger and returns his prize in tears is no criminal, but a man of pure honor tested by adversity. Keep the golden dish as a gift from my household, and come tomorrow to be the chief steward of my storehouses.' Mansur’s honesty transformed his despair into a lifetime of honorable abundance.
moral: Honesty and returning what was taken unjustly brings lasting peace and unexpected abundance.

title: The Sharper of Alexandria and the Chief of Police
summary: The Chief of Police of Alexandria was a pompous official who boasted at every public gathering that no thief, sharper, or pickpocket in a...
keywords: the sharper of alexandria and the chief of police
full_text:
The Chief of Police of Alexandria was a pompous official who boasted at every public gathering that no thief, sharper, or pickpocket in all of Egypt could outwit his guards or enter his fortified residence. 'My house is an iron fortress,' he proclaimed. 'My watchmen never sleep, my hounds never tire, and my locks are forged by the finest smiths in Cairo.'

A witty sharper of Alexandria heard these boasts and felt his professional pride challenged. He sent a polite message to the chief: 'Tomorrow night, O Chief, I shall steal your favorite horse from your stable and your personal silver basin from your bedroom, and I shall leave you a basket of onions in exchange!'

The police chief laughed in fury, doubled his guards, stationed ten armed watchmen around the stable, and placed four guards outside his bedroom door, sleeping with his naked sword upon the mattress.

At midnight, a cold, drizzling rain set in. A wandering peddler carrying a heavy earthen jar of warm spiced lentil soup and a skin of sweetened cordial knocked upon the courtyard gate, begging for shelter from the tempest. The shivering guards, freezing in the rain, gladly welcomed the peddler, who generously offered them bowls of hot soup and cups of sweet cordial.

Unknown to the guards, the cordial was steeped with a harmless herbal sleeping draught. Within an hour, every guard in the courtyard and corridor was snoring peacefully!

The sharper, throwing off his peddler's disguise, walked quietly into the stables, saddled the chief’s favorite grey mare, and tied a basket of fresh red onions to the manger. He then tiptoed into the bedroom, removed the silver washbasin from the stand beside the snoring chief, placed an onion in its center, and rode out through the open gates.

At dawn, the humiliated chief woke to the smell of onions and the silence of his guards. Realizing the sharper had fulfilled every word of his promise without shedding a drop of blood, the chief abandoned his haughty boasts, learning that true security is built on quiet diligence rather than loud arrogance.
moral: Vigilance requires constant humility; he who boasts of his security will be outsmarted by a watchful eye.

title: Al-Malik al-Nasir and the Three Chiefs of Police
summary: Sultan Al-Malik al-Nasir of Cairo sat upon his throne in the Citadel, holding council with the three chiefs of police who governed the qu...
keywords: al-malik al-nasir and the three chiefs of police
full_text:
Sultan Al-Malik al-Nasir of Cairo sat upon his throne in the Citadel, holding council with the three chiefs of police who governed the quarters of Cairo, Fustat, and Qus. Desiring to test their wisdom, the Sultan commanded: 'Let each of you recount the most remarkable case of justice you have ever administered, that I may see who among you truly understands the human heart.'

The Chief of Cairo spoke first: 'Sire, I once captured a man who broke into a bakery at midnight. When I examined him, I found he had stolen neither gold nor silver, but only three loaves of bread. His wife had given birth that night, and his three young children were starving. Instead of cutting off his hand, I paid the baker for the bread, secured the man employment in the public granaries, and saw him become an honest citizen. Justice must not punish hunger where industry can provide work.'

The Chief of Fustat spoke next: 'A merchant accused his neighbor of stealing a bag of pearls. The neighbor denied the theft, swearing by the sacred oaths. Observing the accuser’s servants, I noticed a young boy who turned pale whenever the pearls were mentioned. Taking the boy aside with gentle kindness, he confessed that he had hidden the pearls in the garden wall to buy toys. I restored the pearls to the merchant, saved the innocent neighbor from execution, and counseled the boy’s father. True justice protects the innocent by seeing through appearances.'

The Chief of Qus spoke third: 'Two brothers quarreled bitterly over their father’s inheritance of an orchard, ready to slay each other. I ordered the orchard divided equally, but commanded that neither brother could harvest his fruit until he had delivered one basket of his finest figs to his brother's door. Within a month, the daily exchange of gifts dissolved their anger, and they embraced as friends. Justice must heal severed families rather than merely divide property.'

The Sultan smiled with profound satisfaction, declaring: 'Blessed is the kingdom whose guardians rule with mercy, truth, and reconciliation rather than the naked blade.'
moral: Fair justice requires discernment, mercy, and understanding the root cause behind every human action.

title: The Thief and the Shroff
summary: A wealthy shroff—a currency banker—sat in his counting-house in the bazaar of Baghdad, weighing gold coins upon a brass balance and stori...
full_text:
A wealthy shroff—a currency banker—sat in his counting-house in the bazaar of Baghdad, weighing gold coins upon a brass balance and storing them in heavy leather bags. A nimble thief, having observed the banker’s movements for days, crept behind the wicker screen, waited until the shroff turned his back to consult a ledger, and swiftly snatched a heavy bag containing five hundred gold dinars.

However, as the thief backed away, the metal coins clinked against the screen. The shroff turned his head, saw the bag missing, and noticed the shadow behind the curtain.

Instead of shouting for the city watch or drawing his dagger, the wise banker spoke with gentle courtesy: 'Welcome, honored guest! It is unseemly that a visitor should depart from my counting-house without sharing a cup of sherbet and tasting my almonds.'

The trapped thief stood frozen in terror, clutching the heavy purse behind his back, expecting the guards to rush in with chains.

The shroff walked to the curtain, took the thief gently by the hand, led him to a comfortable cushioned seat, and poured him a goblet of iced rosewater.

'Brother,' said the banker softly, 'I noticed that you took my bag of five hundred dinars. Only a man driven by desperate hardship would risk his freedom in broad daylight. Tell me: what bitter sorrow brought you to this deed?'

Tears welled in the thief’s eyes, and he fell to his knees: 'My lord, my debts have overwhelmed me; my house is to be seized tomorrow, and my mother is dying without medicine. In my despair, I resolved to become a thief.'

The shroff placed his hand upon the young man's shoulder: 'Take these five hundred dinars, not as stolen loot, but as an honorable loan from my business. Go, heal your mother, pay your creditors, and when you have prospered in honest trade, return the sum to my balance.'

Overwhelmed by such saintly mercy, the youth wept, kissed the banker's hands, and renounced crime forever. Five years later, he returned to the counting-house, repaid every dinar with interest, and became the banker's most trusted partner.
moral: Generosity and gentle tact can turn a criminal toward repentance faster than chains and the whip.

title: The Chief of the Kus Police and the Sharper
summary: The Chief of Police of Qus in Upper Egypt had successfully captured many desert outlaws and river brigands, earning a reputation for unsh...
keywords: the chief of the kus police and the sharper
full_text:
The Chief of Police of Qus in Upper Egypt had successfully captured many desert outlaws and river brigands, earning a reputation for unshakeable firmness. However, this success caused pride to take root in his chest, and he began to boast that no criminal in Egypt could escape his net.

A famous sharper of Cairo, passing through Qus, resolved to administer a gentle lesson in humility. He donned the robes of an affluent Syrian silk merchant, rented a fine house near the river, and deposited a heavy iron-bound chest in the police headquarters for safekeeping, claiming it contained ten thousand gold pieces.

The police chief locked the chest in his private treasury with three keys and treated the merchant with supreme deference.

Two weeks later, the sharper approached the chief in great distress: 'O Chief, I have received urgent letters from Damascus; I must travel immediately. Grant me my chest, and send four of your most trusted guards to accompany me to the boat on the Nile.'

The chief opened the treasury, watched the heavy chest loaded onto a cart, and dispatched four armed guards to escort the merchant to the river barge. As the boat cast off into the current, the sharper stood on the deck, waved politely to the guards, and shouted: 'Farewell, brave protectors! Be so kind as to open the chest in your treasury tomorrow and read the parchment I have left for your master!'

The puzzled guards ran back to the chief, who opened his treasury—only to find another identical chest sitting in the corner! Breaking open the locks, the chief found the chest filled with broken river cobblestones and a letter:

'O Chief of Qus, remember that he who believes he knows all the tricks of men is already half-deceived. While your guards were loading the heavy chest of stones onto the cart, my companion quietly carried the real treasure chest out through your back gate. Farewell, and remember that vigilance is a continuous duty, not a crown to rest upon.'

The police chief buried his face in his hands, laughing at his own folly, and never again boasted of his infallibility.
moral: True security comes from constant vigilance and humility, not overconfidence in past victories.

title: Ibrahim bin al-Mahdi and the Merchant's Sister
summary: Prince Ibrahim bin al-Mahdi, the uncle of Caliph Al-Ma'mun, was celebrated not only for his royal lineage, but as the supreme melodist of...
keywords: ibrahim bin al-mahdi and the merchant's sister
full_text:
Prince Ibrahim bin al-Mahdi, the uncle of Caliph Al-Ma'mun, was celebrated not only for his royal lineage, but as the supreme melodist of Baghdad, whose voice upon the lute could make stones weep and bring peace to troubled minds.

One afternoon, visiting an affluent silk merchant who was his close friend, Ibrahim found the house wrapped in profound gloom. Servants walked on tiptoe, the fountains were silent, and the merchant sat in his courtyard with torn robes and downcast eyes.

'What sorrow has fallen upon your house, dear brother?' asked the prince.

The merchant sighed: 'My younger sister, the joy of our household, had a bitter quarrel with her betrothed over an idle misunderstanding. Words of pride were spoken, and in anger, they broke their engagement. For seven days she has sat in her room weeping, refusing food, while her betrothed wanders the streets in misery. No words of reason can bridge their pride.'

Ibrahim smiled gently: 'Where words of reason fail, music builds a bridge.'

The prince tuned his lute of cedarwood, sat beside the courtyard fountain, and began to play. His fingers moved across the silk strings like the whispering of spring rain. He sang verses describing the fragile dawn of love, how a stray wind can disturb the blossom, and how the noble heart finds its greatest triumph in stretching forth the hand of forgiveness.

His voice rose with such sublime sweetness, soulful purity, and heartfelt tenderness that the birds in the pomegranate trees fell silent to listen.

From the high latticed window above, a soft weeping was heard. The maiden opened her shutter, dropped an embroidered scarf of forgiveness into the courtyard, and sent her maid to summon her betrothed.

Before the stars appeared, the lovers met beside the fountain, embraced with tears of joy, and set aside their pride forever. The merchant embraced the prince, declaring that his music had saved an entire family from lifelong sorrow.
moral: Art and music have the divine power to heal domestic discord and soften wounded hearts.

title: The Woman whose Hands were Cut Off
summary: In a city of the Levant lived a virtuous and charitable young woman whose devotion to helping the poor was known to all. One bitter winte...

full_text:
In a city of the Levant lived a virtuous and charitable young woman whose devotion to helping the poor was known to all. One bitter winter day, a shivering beggar knocked at her door, starving and begging for a single morsel of bread in the name of the Creator. Having no bread baked, the maiden gave him two silver bracelets from her own arms, that he might purchase food and shelter.

However, her husband's envious sister observed the act and falsely accused the maiden before her brother, claiming she had squandered the household jewels on an impostor. In a fit of irrational fury, the suspicious husband drove the innocent maiden into the wilderness, where she suffered hardship and exposure.

Alone in the forest, the virtuous woman placed her trust in divine providence. She found shelter in an ancient hermitage where she tended sick animals and prayed for her family’s guidance.

Years passed, and a wealthy, just king of a neighboring realm, riding through the forest on a hunt, found the noble hermit woman. Struck by her saintly countenance and serene wisdom, the king inquired into her history. When she recounted her unjust suffering with neither bitterness nor desire for vengeance, the king’s heart was moved to profound reverence.

He brought her to his royal palace, treated her as his most honored guest, and ordered his judges to investigate the truth of her past.

The truth was brought to light: the envious sister-in-law, stricken with illness and remorse, confessed her wicked slander before the magistrates. The former husband, weeping in ashes and sackcloth, arrived at the court begging for forgiveness.

The noble woman harbored no wrath; she forgave her former husband and embraced her repentant sister-in-law, proving that patience and pure charity outlast the deepest winter of adversity and receive the highest rewards of peace.
moral: Divine justice and patient endurance overcome the darkest slanders and restore honor to the pure.

title: The Devout Israelite
summary: In an ancient city lived a poor weaver who was celebrated among his neighbors for his profound piety, contentment, and unwavering trust i...
full_text:
In an ancient city lived a poor weaver who was celebrated among his neighbors for his profound piety, contentment, and unwavering trust in divine providence. Though he laboured at his loom from dawn until dusk, he earned barely enough to purchase a small measure of barley meal for his wife and himself each day.

A severe famine struck the land. Grain prices soared, the mills stopped, and the streets were filled with starving people. The weaver and his wife had only a single small loaf of barley bread remaining in their clay jar, which they intended to share for their evening supper.

As they sat down to break the bread, a feeble knock was heard at the door. An elderly stranger, shivering with cold and leaning upon a staff, stood upon the threshold, saying: 'O people of the house! I have not tasted food for three days, and my soul is fainting within me. Give me a morsel, for the sake of the Merciful Creator!'

The weaver's wife looked at the single loaf, and then at her husband. The weaver smiled with radiant serenity, took the loaf, divided it in two, and placed the larger half in the beggar’s trembling hands.

The beggar ate with tears of relief, blessed the household with ancient words of abundance, and departed.

The weaver and his wife sat down to share the remaining crust, their hearts filled with peaceful contentment. When the wife went to wipe the crumbs from the clay flour-jar, she gasped in astonishment: the jar, which had been empty for weeks, was brimming over with finest white wheat flour!

Day after day, as long as the famine lasted, the jar never emptied. The weaver baked bread each morning, distributing loaves to all the starving families in his street without charging a single copper, proving that the hand that gives in the hour of need will never be empty of blessings.
moral: Sharing one's last bread in selfless charity multiplies blessings and banishes hunger forever.

title: Abu Hassan al-Ziyadi
summary: Abu Hassan al-Ziyadi was an eminent scholar and judge of Baghdad in the reign of the Caliph Al-Ma'mun. Known for his profound learning in...
full_text:
Abu Hassan al-Ziyadi was an eminent scholar and judge of Baghdad in the reign of the Caliph Al-Ma'mun. Known for his profound learning in jurisprudence and his generosity to students, he was also burdened by heavy debts, having borrowed money to support poor scholars who flocked to his lectures.

A day arrived when his creditors gathered before his gate, demanding payment of ten thousand dinars. Abu Hassan had not a single dirham in his house, and his larder was completely bare. He spent the entire day praying for deliverance and reflecting on his duties.

That night, as he sat in the dark reading by the light of a tiny oil wick, a knocking sounded at his door. A messenger from the imperial palace entered, saying: 'The Commander of the Faithful summons you immediately!'

Abu Hassan dressed in his patched cloak, believing that his creditors had complained to the Caliph and that imprisonment awaited him.

When he entered the imperial audience hall, Caliph Al-Ma'mun stepped down from his dais, took the scholar by the hand, and said: 'Peace be upon you, Abu Hassan! Know that tonight, as I slept, a vision appeared to me three times, commanding: "Deliver Abu Hassan al-Ziyadi from his affliction, for his prayers have reached the heavens!" Tell me, what distress has befallen you?'

Abu Hassan, with tears in his eyes, recounted the debts he had incurred to feed his poor scholars and sustain his academy of learning.

The Caliph embraced him with deep reverence, ordered thirty thousand gold dinars to be delivered to his home—ten thousand to pay his debts, ten thousand to expand his academy, and ten thousand for his household—and appointed him the Chief Justice of the eastern provinces.

Abu Hassan returned home at dawn, marveling at how sincere devotion and selfless dedication to truth are answered in the hour of greatest need.
moral: Trust in providence, faithful adherence to duty, and generous patience will turn the darkest midnight into a radiant dawn.

title: The Poor Man and His Friend in Need
summary: In Baghdad lived three devoted friends who had sworn a sacred bond of brotherhood in their youth. One was a bookbinder, the second a leat...
keywords: the poor man and his friend in need
full_text:
In Baghdad lived three devoted friends who had sworn a sacred bond of brotherhood in their youth. One was a bookbinder, the second a leather-worker, and the third a scribe. Each earned a modest living, and whenever one lacked bread, the others shared their earnings without keeping account.

One difficult year, the bookbinder was struck by severe misfortune: his workshop caught fire, destroying his tools and leather skins. Deeply indebted and having nothing to feed his children, he went to the leather-worker and confided his plight with tears.

The leather-worker had only one heavy purse containing a thousand silver dirhams, which he had saved over ten years to purchase new machinery. Without a moment's hesitation, the leather-worker placed the purse in his friend’s hands: 'Take this, brother! My machinery can wait; your children must not hunger.'

The bookbinder thanked him with tears of gratitude and returned home. But no sooner had he crossed his threshold than the third friend, the scribe, arrived at his door, pale and trembling. The scribe’s house had been seized by an oppressive landlord, and his family sat in the street.

The bookbinder looked at the purse of a thousand dirhams. Though he needed the money desperately himself, he thought: 'My friend's family is on the cobblestones; my children at least have a roof.' He handed the sealed purse directly to the scribe!

The scribe took the purse and ran immediately to the leather-worker to pay off his debt—for it was the leather-worker who had leased him his house!

When the leather-worker saw his own sealed purse returned to him, he was astonished. He summoned the bookbinder and the scribe, and the three friends stood together, each having placed the other's need before his own, the purse having traveled in a complete circle of selfless love!

The Caliph Harun al-Rashid, hearing of this sublime contest of selflessness, summoned the three friends, rewarded each with three thousand dinars from the royal treasury, and praised their brotherhood as the highest glory of Baghdad.
moral: True friendship puts the need of the companion above one's own comfort, creating an unbroken chain of love.

title: The Ruined Man Who Became Rich Again Through a Dream
summary: There was once in Baghdad a wealthy merchant who, through shipwrecks and misfortune, lost his entire fortune. Reduced to absolute poverty...
keywords: the ruined man who became rich again through a dream
full_text:
There was once in Baghdad a wealthy merchant who, through shipwrecks and misfortune, lost his entire fortune. Reduced to absolute poverty, he had to sell his furniture, his carpets, and his books, retaining only his small ancestral house with its overgrown courtyard garden.

One night, exhausted from a day of vain search for labor, he fell asleep with a heavy heart. In a dream, a venerable figure clothed in green appeared to him and said: 'Rise, O traveler! Your fortune awaits you in the city of Cairo; journey thither, and you shall find abundance!'

Believing the vision, the merchant packed a dry crust of bread, took his walking staff, and set forth on foot across the scorching Syrian desert and the Sinai. After weeks of exhausting travel and blistered feet, he arrived in Cairo, penniless and in rags.

Having no money for lodging, he took refuge in the courtyard of a neighborhood mosque to spend the night.

That very night, a band of thieves broke into the house adjacent to the mosque. The neighbors raised an outcry, and the Chief of Police rushed to the scene with his night watchmen. Finding the mosque empty save for the strange traveler sleeping upon the stones, the police seized him, assumed he was an accomplice, and gave him twenty lashes with a palm-cudgel before throwing him into a cell.

The next morning, the police captain questioned him: 'Who are you, and what brought you to Cairo?'

The merchant weeping recounted his dream: 'I was a wealthy merchant of Baghdad. A dream commanded me to travel to Cairo to find my fortune. I walked across deserts, only to find twenty lashes and an iron chain!'

The captain laughed uproariously, slapping his knee: 'O foolish man of little wit! Three times have I dreamed that in the city of Baghdad, in a quiet quarter, behind an old house with an overgrown courtyard, beneath an ancient fig tree beside a sun-dial, a great treasure of gold dinars is buried! Yet do you see me running to Baghdad on the word of a dream? Go back to your city, you credulous fool, and here are two dinars to buy bread for your journey!'

The merchant took the two dinars, smiled through his tears, and walked back to Baghdad. Arriving at his own house, he took a spade, went into his overgrown courtyard, and dug beneath the ancient fig tree beside the sundial. There he unearthed a brass chest filled with gold dinars and jewels, enough to restore his family to wealth for seven generations, thanking the heavens that a journey to Cairo was necessary to teach him to dig in his own garden.
moral: The treasure you seek across distant lands is often buried in your own home, waiting for patient eyes to see.

title: Caliph al-Mutawakkil and his Court Singer Mahbubah
summary: In the palace of Samarra, the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mutawakkil had in his court a singer of sublime talent and poetic sensitivity named Mahbu...
keywords: caliph al-mutawakkil and his court singer mahbubah
full_text:
In the palace of Samarra, the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mutawakkil had in his court a singer of sublime talent and poetic sensitivity named Mahbubah. She had been educated in all the refined arts of the golden age, and her compositions on the lute were celebrated for their emotional depth and delicate nuance.

Unlike many flatterers who courted royal favor for gold and estates, Mahbubah’s devotion to the Caliph was founded on sincere gratitude for his patronage of the arts and his generous protection of poets and scholars.

When courtly intrigue and political turbulence suddenly swept over the capital, Caliph Al-Mutawakkil perished, and a new regime seized power in Samarra. The fickle courtiers immediately pledged allegiance to the new rulers, casting aside their mourning garments and celebrating in the banqueting halls.

Mahbubah alone refused to sing songs of hollow praise for the usurpers. She retired to her private chambers, dressed in simple mourning garments, tuned her lute to the ancient elegiac modes, and composed moving verses lamenting the transience of worldly splendor and celebrating the generous spirit of the fallen monarch.

When the new sovereign summoned her to court, commanding her to perform celebratory melodies, Mahbubah stood with quiet dignity, touched the strings of her lute, and sang her elegies of faithful memory with such heartbreaking beauty, sincerity, and sorrow that the entire assembly—including the new ruler—wept openly in their robes.

Moved by her unshakeable fidelity, the new sovereign did not punish her; instead, he bowed before her artistic integrity, granted her complete freedom and a royal pension, and allowed her to retire to Baghdad in peace, where her verses were preserved for centuries as a monument to true loyalty that refuses to compromise with the changing winds of power.
moral: True loyalty and poetic fidelity outlive earthly power, honoring the memory of kindness with enduring art.

title: Wardan the Butcher; His Adventure With the Lady and the Bear
summary: In Cairo lived an honest and respected butcher named Wardan who kept a flourishing stall in the meat bazaar. Every morning for a month, a...
keywords: wardan the butcher; his adventure with the lady and the bear
full_text:
In Cairo lived an honest and respected butcher named Wardan who kept a flourishing stall in the meat bazaar. Every morning for a month, a wealthy, veiled lady accompanied by two servants arrived at his stall, purchased a whole fat sheep, paid with bright gold dinars without asking for change, and had the meat carried away in a wicker hamper.

Wardan was grateful for her generous custom, yet curious as to why a single household required an entire sheep each day. One morning, having packed the meat into the hamper, Wardan followed the servants at a discreet distance through winding alleys, across ancient aqueducts, until they entered a grand, isolated mansion outside the city walls.

Peering through a crack in the garden gate, Wardan beheld an extraordinary sight: the lady opened an iron trapdoor leading down into an underground vaulted cellar, where an enormous, gentle brown bear was chained to a stone pillar! The bear, which had been raised from a cub by her late father, was fed the fresh meat, while the lady tended its bedding with affectionate care.

Suddenly, two armed brigands who had scaled the back wall leaped into the courtyard, drawing their scimitars to rob the lady's mansion and seize her ancestral jewels!

Wardan did not hesitate. Drawing his heavy meat cleaver and shouting a loud battle-cry, the sturdy butcher leaped over the wall and charged the brigands with fearless valor. The bear, seeing his mistress threatened, snapped his chain with a mighty roar and joined the fray!

Terrified by the combined assault of a furious butcher and a roaring bear, the brigands threw down their weapons and begged for mercy. Wardan bound them securely with ropes and delivered them to the city magistrate.

The grateful lady rewarded Wardan with five hundred gold dinars and made his shop the exclusive supplier for her vast estates. Wardan returned to his stall with his head held high, having learned that true courage leaps to the defense of the innocent without calculating the danger.
moral: Curiosity must be balanced with prudence, and courage in uncovering truth delivers the innocent.

title: The King's Daughter and the Ape
summary: In the islands of the Indian Ocean ruled a wise and powerful monarch who had an only daughter named Princess Niloufar. The princess was c...
keywords: the king's daughter and the ape
full_text:
In the islands of the Indian Ocean ruled a wise and powerful monarch who had an only daughter named Princess Niloufar. The princess was celebrated not only for her beauty, but for her profound skill in healing, astronomy, and the decoding of ancient manuscripts.

One day, a foreign ship brought to the palace a rare creature: an ape of remarkable grace and intelligence that played the flute, played chess with the royal counselors, and showed astonishing understanding of human speech. While the court treated the beast as a comical curiosity, Princess Niloufar observed the profound sorrow in the creature’s amber eyes.

One evening, as the ape sat in the garden pavilion, Niloufar noticed that he was tracing Arabic letters in the damp sand with a reed. Reading the script, she was astonished to find verses of deep philosophy and royal lineage!

Speaking softly to the creature in the language of ancient Persia, she discovered the truth: the ape was Prince Bahram of Shiraz, who had been transformed by a jealous sorcerer whose unjust demands the prince had refused. The curse decreed that he must remain an ape until a maiden of royal blood recognized his noble mind without knowing his crown.

Niloufar resolved to break the enchantment. Consulting ancient scrolls of counter-sorcery in her father’s library, she discovered that the spell could only be dissolved by the water of the Mountain of Mirrors, guarded by three riddling sphinxes.

Without hesitation, Princess Niloufar embarked on the perilous journey. With her keen intellect and courageous heart, she solved the three riddles, gathered the crystal water, and returned to the palace.

Sprinkling the drops upon the creature's brow, the fur dissolved, and Prince Bahram stood restored in his full human majesty and princely grace! The king and the entire court cheered in wonder, celebrating a union founded on intellect, courage, and the discernment that sees the soul beyond the guise.
moral: Look beyond outward appearances, for true nobility and virtue are hidden beneath the humblest guises.

title: The Ebony Horse
summary: During the celebration of the spring festival of Nowruz in the ancient city of Shiraz, three brilliant inventors appeared before the King...
full_text:
During the celebration of the spring festival of Nowruz in the ancient city of Shiraz, three brilliant inventors appeared before the King of Persia, each presenting a masterpiece of mechanical craft. The first presented a peacock of gold that crowed the hours; the second, a brass trumpeter that sounded warnings; but the third, an artisan from India, presented a marvelous mechanical horse carved of polished ebony and ivory, decorated with gold harness.

'O King,' said the inventor, 'this horse requires neither barley nor water. By turning the golden peg upon his right shoulder, he leaps into the clouds, flying through the air to any city on earth with the speed of thought!'

Prince Kamar al-Akmar, the king’s daring son, leaped into the saddle to test the marvel. Turning the peg, the ebony horse shot like an arrow into the stratosphere, soaring above mountains and oceans! The prince was thrilled, but when he wished to descend, he searched frantically for the reverse mechanism. At last, he discovered a smaller silver peg behind the ear; turning it, the horse gently spiraled down through the night sky, landing upon the marble roof of an enchanted palace in the city of Sana'a in Yemen.

There, upon a moonlit terrace, the prince met Princess Shams al-Nahar, the daughter of the King of Yemen. A deep affection sprang between them, founded on mutual admiration of courage and intellect.

When the jealous Indian inventor, seeking revenge for his horse, abducted the princess by stealth and flew her to Greece, Prince Kamar al-Akmar pursued them across continents. Disguised as a master physician, the prince gained entrance to the palace of the King of Greece, who had imprisoned the princess, believing her delirious.

Prince Kamar approached the ebony horse in the courtyard under the guise of an exorcism, lifted the princess onto the saddle behind him, turned the golden peg, and soared triumphantly into the sky, returning safely to Shiraz amidst grand celebrations that united Persia and Yemen in lasting friendship.
moral: Technological marvels and human ingenuity must be guided by wisdom, honor, and noble purpose.

title: Uns al-Wujud and Rose-In-Hood
summary: Uns al-Wujud was a noble youth of Isfahan, renowned for his martial prowess, his gentle manners, and his mastery of verse. He loved Al-Wa...
full_text:
Uns al-Wujud was a noble youth of Isfahan, renowned for his martial prowess, his gentle manners, and his mastery of verse. He loved Al-Ward fi'l-Akmam—whose name meant 'Rose-in-Hood'—the daughter of the Grand Vizier. Their affection was celebrated across the city for its pure nobility, but the proud vizier, fearing court gossip, secretly transported his daughter to the Castle of the Mountain of Birds, an inaccessible fortress perched on a sea-girt island.

Devastated by her disappearance, Uns al-Wujud cast off his armor, donned a pilgrim’s cloak, and set forth alone into the wilderness to find his bride.

For months, he wandered through scorching deserts and rocky ravines, speaking only to the wild beasts and reciting poems of longing to the wind. Seeing his pure heart and unyielding devotion, the wild gazelles walked beside him, and a friendly hermit of the mountains gave him shelter, pointing him toward the Sea of Birds.

Reaching the rocky coast, an old boatman was so moved by the youth’s verses that he rowed him across the stormy straits to the island fortress.

Meanwhile, Rose-in-Hood sat upon the battlements, releasing carrier pigeons with inscribed verses of hope. One pigeon landed upon Uns al-Wujud's shoulder as he climbed the rocky crags.

Recognizing her beloved’s voice as he sang below the walls, Rose-in-Hood lowered silk cords from her balcony, and the lovers were joyfully reunited.

When the vizier arrived with armed troops to punish the intruder, he heard the young couple reciting their sublime poems of fidelity. His stern heart melted with remorse. He embraced Uns al-Wujud as his worthy son, gave them his blessing, and celebrated a magnificent wedding in Isfahan that became a legend of true love across the East.
moral: Enduring devotion, poetry, and compassionate friendship conquer deserts, mountains, and separation.

title: Abu Nowas With the Three Boys
summary: The celebrated poet Abu Nowas was walking through the academy quarter of Baghdad one sunny afternoon when he encountered three young scho...
keywords: abu nowas with the three boys
full_text:
The celebrated poet Abu Nowas was walking through the academy quarter of Baghdad one sunny afternoon when he encountered three young scholars sitting beside a fountain, wearing new student turbans and boasting loudly of their mastery of grammar, logic, and poetic rhetoric.

Seeing the famous poet approaching in his simple woollen robe, the three students resolved to test his reputation and mock his casual attire.

The first student bowed with exaggerated courtesy: 'Peace be upon you, venerable elder! We are testing the three branches of poetic eloquence. Can you tell us why the moon appears silver while the sun shines golden?'

Abu Nowas smiled with amusement and answered: 'The sun shines with the golden fire of active labor, which builds cities by day; while the moon reflects the silver peace of meditation, which rests the soul by night.'

The second student stepped forward, smirking: 'And tell us, O master, which is swifter: the flight of an arrow, the speed of lightning, or the tongue of a scholar?'

Abu Nowas replied without hesitation: 'None of these, my young friend. The swiftest thing in all creation is the thought of an honest man turning toward truth, for it spans the distance from earth to heaven in less than a heartbeat.'

The third student, frustrated by their failure to confound the poet, asked with haughty disdain: 'And what is the heaviest burden that an educated youth can carry upon his shoulders?'

Abu Nowas looked him gently in the eye, adjusted his mantle, and said with quiet authority: 'The heaviest burden a youth can bear is a head inflated with unearned pride, for it blinds his eyes to wisdom, deafens his ears to counsel, and makes his feet stumble on the smoothest road.'

The three scholars blushed with deep shame, recognized their foolish arrogance, and bowed low before the master poet, thanking him for the lesson in humility that no classroom could teach.
moral: A sharp mind must always be tempered by humility, for youthful arrogance will inevitably meet its master.

title: Abdallah bin Ma'amar
summary: Abdallah bin Ma'amar was the governor of Basra in the golden days of the Abbasid Caliphate, revered by his people as a ruler who combined...
full_text:
Abdallah bin Ma'amar was the governor of Basra in the golden days of the Abbasid Caliphate, revered by his people as a ruler who combined firm justice with the tenderest compassion for the poor and the troubled.

One evening, as Abdallah was returning from inspecting the public granaries, he heard the sounds of bitter lamentation coming from an ancient cemetery. Dismounting from his mule, he entered the quiet tombs and found a handsome young Bedouin weeping beside a freshly dug grave.

Abdallah approached gently, placed a hand upon his shoulder, and asked: 'What great sorrow has brought you to weep among the dead, my son?'

The young man wiped his tears and answered: 'O noble traveler, I am Utbah, son of a desert shaykh. For five years, my cousin Rayya and I have loved each other with pure affection. But her father, demanding an exorbitant dowry of fifty pedigree camels and a thousand gold dinars which my impoverished father could not provide, has betrothed her against her will to an affluent stranger from Damascus. Tomorrow she departs, and my soul is already dead.'

Abdallah’s heart was touched by the youth’s sincere devotion. He lifted Utbah to his feet and said: 'Do not despair, for hope is never dead while justice lives.'

The governor immediately dispatched messengers to the bride’s father and the Syrian suitor, inviting them to his palace.

Before the council, Abdallah spoke with eloquent passion on the sanctity of true love and the cruelty of treating children as merchandise. He then opened his own treasury, paid the full dowry of fifty fine camels and a thousand gold dinars on Utbah’s behalf, and compensated the Syrian suitor with rare silks and jewels from his personal stores.

The bride’s father, moved to tears and ashamed of his greed, joyfully bestowed his daughter upon Utbah. The happy union was celebrated across Basra with feasts that lasted three days, and Abdallah bin Ma'amar was blessed by all the people as the protector of faithful hearts.
moral: Generous intervention that reconciles estranged lovers and heals family rifts is the highest duty of a noble leader.

title: The Lovers of the Banu Ozrah
summary: Among the ancient tribes of Arabia, none was more renowned for the purity of their affection and the delicacy of their verses than the no...
keywords: the lovers of the banu ozrah
full_text:
Among the ancient tribes of Arabia, none was more renowned for the purity of their affection and the delicacy of their verses than the noble clan of Banu Ozrah. It was proverbial throughout the desert that when a youth of the Banu Ozrah loved, he loved with his whole soul, and if parted, his spirit would pine away in steadfast fidelity rather than compromise with fickle sentiment.

An elder traveler of Baghdad, journeying through the fertile valleys of the Hijaz, pitched his tent near a Bedouin encampment. At eventide, as the campfires flickered against the crimson dunes, he heard a young shepherd reciting verses of sublime beauty beside an ancient spring.

The youth sang of a maiden named Lubna, whose eyes were like the gazelles of the morning and whose character was purer than desert rain. When the traveler approached, the youth welcomed him with customary desert hospitality, sharing his bowl of fresh camel’s milk and dates.

'Why do you weep into the spring, young brother?' asked the traveler.

The youth sighed: 'Lubna and I were betrothed from our childhood, our hearts knit together by shared poetry and honor. But her kinsmen, demanding a great herd of red camels which my poor father does not possess, have decreed that she must be given to an affluent chieftain of the north. We have sworn an oath: though our bodies be separated by hundreds of leagues of sand, our hearts shall remain as pure and faithful as the stars that never wander from their course.'

Moved to tears by their noble devotion, the generous traveler rode immediately to the camp of Lubna’s father. He opened his leather pouches, weighed out fifty gold dinars, and purchased fifty fine red camels from the caravans of Mecca, presenting them to the bride’s father on the youth’s behalf.

The clan celebrated the union of Lubna and her faithful poet with ten days of joyous festivities, and the traveler departed with a peaceful heart, knowing that he had preserved the most sacred virtue of the Banu Ozrah.
moral: Pure love founded on spiritual nobility, chastity, and devotion transcends all earthly sorrow.
