title: The Wazir of al-Yaman and His Younger Brother
summary: In the ancient kingdom of Yemen, King As'ad had for his Grand Vizier a statesman of extraordinary wisdom named Mansur. Mansur governed th...
keywords: the wazir of al-yaman and his younger brother
full_text:
In the ancient kingdom of Yemen, King As'ad had for his Grand Vizier a statesman of extraordinary wisdom named Mansur. Mansur governed the kingdom with such equity, expanding agriculture, constructing cisterns, and establishing fair markets, that the realm flourished in unprecedented prosperity.

Mansur had a younger brother named Haydar, whom he loved with boundless affection. Rather than keeping all royal honors to himself, Mansur petitioned the king: 'Sire, power is a heavy mantle that bends the back of a single man. My brother Haydar is endowed with courage, intellect, and an upright heart. Let him share the vizierate with me, that two hands may uphold your throne.'

The king consented, and the two brothers sat side by side in the council hall, dividing the duties of state: Mansur directed the civil administration and the courts of justice, while Haydar organized the frontiers and commanded the armed defenses.

Jealous courtiers, unable to comprehend such fraternal unity, sought to sow discord between them. One courtier crept to Haydar, whispering: 'Your brother treats you as a subordinate; he keeps the royal treasury in his palace and gives you only the dusty labor of the camps.' Another courtier whispered to Mansur: 'Beware of Haydar; his soldiers revere him, and he plots to usurp your seat.'

The two brothers listened with serene composure, and that evening, met in their father’s ancestral garden.

Mansur embraced Haydar, and Haydar embraced Mansur. They recounted to each other every word the slanderers had whispered, laughing at the transparent malice of the courtiers.

The next morning before the assembled court, Mansur presented Haydar with the keys to the treasury, and Haydar placed the command sword into Mansur's hands, demonstrating before all men that fraternal trust is a citadel that slander cannot breach. The king banished the envious conspirators and ruled in peace for forty years, supported by the twin pillars of brotherhood.
moral: Fraternal love that shares power and wealth without envy creates an unshakeable fortress for an empire.

title: The Loves of the Boy and Girl at School
summary: In an ancient quarter of Baghdad stood a famous school where children of noble families were instructed in the Quran, Arabic grammar, the...

full_text:
In an ancient quarter of Baghdad stood a famous school where children of noble families were instructed in the Quran, Arabic grammar, the art of calligraphy, and the composition of classical poetry.

Among the pupils was a handsome boy named Qasim, son of a respected merchant, and a bright, graceful girl named Jamila, daughter of the Chief Scribe. Both excelled above all their companions in quickness of intellect and beauty of penmanship. While the other children struggled with ink-horns and reed pens, Qasim and Jamila composed spontaneous verses upon their polished wooden slates, passing them across the wooden benches with quiet smiles.

One morning, the strict schoolmaster noticed Qasim inscribing a poetic verse upon his slate instead of copying the day's grammar lesson:
'The ink upon this wooden slate shall fade with time away,
Yet honor, truth, and faithful hearts forever live and stay.'

The schoolmaster picked up Jamila's slate, and found that she had written in response:
'Like rivers flowing toward the sea that never part their course,
The soul that seeks the highest good drinks from an endless source.'

The master frowned, tapped his cane upon his desk, and declared: 'School is an academy of serious learning, not an exchange for poets!' He threatened to summon their parents and chastise them with his palm-switch.

However, the Chief Scribe happened to enter the classroom at that moment to inspect his daughter's progress. Reading the two slates, the scribe was struck by the moral maturity, elegance of meter, and exquisite calligraphy of the children.

'Hold your cane, master!' said the scribe with a proud smile. 'These two children have mastered grammar, meter, and virtue before their years! An affection founded upon mutual reverence for wisdom is a flower to be nurtured, not crushed.'

The families agreed that when the children attained maturity, their union should be celebrated. Years later, Qasim became a celebrated statesman and Jamila a renowned scholar, their lifelong companionship having sprouted from two polished wooden slates.
moral: Innocent affection, refined learning, and mutual respect in youth lay the foundation for enduring character.

title: The Caliph Harun al-Rashid and Queen Zubaydah in the Bath
summary: Queen Zubaydah, the celebrated consort of Caliph Harun al-Rashid, was renowned not only for her royal elegance, but for an architectural ...
keywords: the caliph harun al-rashid and queen zubaydah in the bath
full_text:
Queen Zubaydah, the celebrated consort of Caliph Harun al-Rashid, was renowned not only for her royal elegance, but for an architectural vision and public benevolence that outshone all the monarchs of her era.

During her pilgrimage to the holy city of Mecca, the queen was deeply moved by the hardships endured by the poor pilgrims. The desert heat was scorching, the mountain passes were treacherous, and water was so scarce that a single waterskin cost more than a poor traveler’s entire savings. Thousands of men, women, and children suffered agonizing thirst on the desert roads.

Standing upon the arid plains of Arafat, Queen Zubaydah summoned her chief engineers, geologists, and architects. She declared with royal resolve: 'I will not see the pilgrims of the earth thirst in this valley. I command you to cut through the solid granite mountains, divert the distant springs of the hills, and construct an aqueduct that shall bring fresh, sweet water to every corner of Mecca!'

Her chief treasurer stepped forward in alarm: 'My Queen, to cut through these mountains and build stone aqueducts across forty miles of desert will exhaust our imperial treasury; it will cost millions of gold dinars!'

Queen Zubaydah removed her pearl necklace and said with majestic calm: 'Build the aqueduct, even if every blow of the iron chisel costs a gold dinar! The gold of monarchs turns to dust, but the water that refreshes a thirsty traveler flows as a blessing before the throne of heaven forever.'

For ten years, thousands of stonemasons chiseled through stone, built underground qanats, vaulted reservoirs, and arched aqueducts. The waters of Ayn Zubaydah flowed in abundance, filling fountains, wells, and cisterns for over a thousand years, immortalizing the queen’s name as the mother of the pilgrims.
moral: True royal magnificence is measured by public works that relieve the suffering of millions of travelers.

title: Harun al-Rashid and the Three Poets
summary: One evening, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid sat in his imperial salon in Baghdad, surrounded by his vizier Ja'afar, his courtiers, and three ...
keywords: harun al-rashid and the three poets
full_text:
One evening, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid sat in his imperial salon in Baghdad, surrounded by his vizier Ja'afar, his courtiers, and three famous poets: Abu Nowas, Abu al-Atahiyah, and Al-Raqqashi. The hall was fragrant with ambergris, and crystal lamps illuminated the marble fountains.

The Caliph turned to the poets and commanded: 'Let each of you recite four lines describing the true condition of kings, that we may see whose verse touches the core of reality.'

Al-Raqqashi stepped forward, bowed low, and recited verses of lavish flattery:
'The world is yours, O King, from dawn to setting sun,
Thy sword commands the stars, thy will is ever done;
The nations bow their heads, thy glory shall not fade,
Eternal as the hills thy golden throne is made!'

Harun al-Rashid listened with a faint, weary smile, having heard such flattery a thousand times.

Abu Nowas stepped forward next, reciting with his customary sparkling wit:
'Enjoy the fragrant feast, the music of the lute,
Before the turning sphere makes every dancer mute;
Gather the rose of joy while youth and fortune smile,
For life is but a dream that lasts a little while!'

The Caliph nodded, pleased by the poet's merry elegance.

Finally, the ascetic poet Abu al-Atahiyah stepped forward, his eyes burning with moral conviction. He declaimed in a ringing voice:
'Rejoice within thy palace walls, O King of mighty power,
Yet know that death shall knock upon thy portal at its hour;
When all thy guards are sleeping and thy breath begins to fail,
Thy gold and armies shall not weigh a feather on the scale;
Only the justice thou hast wrought, the tears thou hast relieved,
Shall stand as witness for thy soul before the throne received!'

The entire court fell into dead silence. Harun al-Rashid covered his face with his mantle and wept bitterly, moved by the solemn truth.

The Caliph rewarded Abu al-Atahiyah with the highest prize, declaring: 'The first flattered my vanity; the second diverted my leisure; but the third was my true friend, for he reminded my soul of its eternal accountability.'
moral: True poetry speaks truth to power, reminding rulers that justice and humility are their only enduring shields.

title: The Miller and His Wife
summary: Beside a swift mountain brook in the province of Fars stood a watermill where an honest miller and his wife ground wheat into flour for t...
full_text:
Beside a swift mountain brook in the province of Fars stood a watermill where an honest miller and his wife ground wheat into flour for the surrounding villages. They lived in peace and modest comfort, waking with the song of the lark and sleeping soundly to the soothing rhythm of the turning millstone.

One evening, a wealthy caravan merchant, whose mule had gone lame, asked to lodge his goods in the mill for the night. In the miller’s presence, the merchant deposited a heavy iron-bound casket upon the grain bench, saying: 'Guard this casket with your life, for it contains ten thousand gold dinars.'

When the merchant fell asleep, the miller and his wife sat by their oil lamp, staring at the heavy casket. The simple miller whispered: 'Ten thousand dinars! With such a sum, a man could buy a palace in Shiraz, dress in silk, and never touch a dusty sack of flour again.'

His wife sighed: 'And we could have ten servants to bake our bread and wash our linen!'

For the first time in their lives, peace fled from their cottage. Every rustle of the wind sounded like thieves breaking the shutter. The miller paced the floor with a cudgel, terrified that someone would steal the box; his wife tossed on her bed, suspicious that the merchant would accuse them of tampering with the locks. All through the night, they were tormented by fear, greed, and suspicion, unable to close their eyes for a single heartbeat.

At dawn, the merchant arose, paid the miller two silver dirhams for his hospitality, strapped the casket onto his mule, and rode away into the morning mist.

The miller looked at his wife, saw her pale, exhausted face, and then looked at the turning millstone splash in the cool stream.

The miller laughed aloud and embraced her: 'Praise be to heaven! The golden monster has departed! One night under the same roof with ten thousand dinars brought us more misery than forty years of honest labor. Let us grind our wheat in peace, for sweet bread earned with clean hands is worth all the restless gold in the world.'
moral: Contentment with honest toil brings sweet sleep, while greed for unearned gold breeds sleepless suspicion.

title: The Simpleton and the Sharper
summary: A country simpleton was walking to the market of Baghdad, leading a handsome fat ram by a rope, hoping to sell it to buy new shoes and wi...
full_text:
A country simpleton was walking to the market of Baghdad, leading a handsome fat ram by a rope, hoping to sell it to buy new shoes and winter clothing.

A cunning sharper observed the simpleton and resolved to swindle him without using violence. The sharper enlisted two companions and positioned them at three successive crossroads along the country road.

When the simpleton reached the first crossroad, the first accomplice looked at the ram with astonished eyes and called out: 'Good day, brother! Why are you leading that dirty, mangy dog by a rope?'

The simpleton frowned and replied: 'Are you blind, friend? This is not a dog; this is a fat ram with horns and thick wool!' The stranger shook his head with pity and walked away.

At the second crossroad, the second accomplice stepped up and shouted: 'Ho, traveler! How much do you ask for that scrawny greyhound?'

The simpleton began to feel uneasy. He examined the ram, felt its wool and curved horns, and muttered: 'Surely it is a ram... or have my eyes been touched by an enchantment?'

At the third crossroad, the chief sharper stepped forward, raised his hands in horror, and scolded: 'O man of little sense! It is unlawful to lead such an unclean, mangy hound along the public highway! Let the beast go before the magistrate fines you!'

Overwhelmed by the agreement of three separate strangers, the simpleton abandoned all faith in his own senses. Believing that his prize ram had truly been transformed into an unclean dog by sorcery, he dropped the rope in terror and fled toward the city!

The three sharpers immediately gathered the fat ram, led it to the butcher's quarter, and sold it for twenty silver dirhams, laughing at how easily a man surrenders his truth when he allows false consensus to overrule his own eyes.
moral: Do not let deceptive consensus shake your confidence in what your own eyes clearly see.

title: The Kazi Abu Yusuf
summary: Abu Yusuf, the supreme Chief Justice of Baghdad during the reign of Harun al-Rashid, was celebrated as the greatest jurist of his age, po...
full_text:
Abu Yusuf, the supreme Chief Justice of Baghdad during the reign of Harun al-Rashid, was celebrated as the greatest jurist of his age, possessing an incomparable ability to untangle the most knotted disputes through keen intellect, encyclopedic knowledge of the law, and profound common sense.

One morning, two merchants appeared before his bench. The first merchant claimed that he had left a sealed jar of pure olive oil in the care of his neighbor five years ago before departing on a long journey to India. Upon his return, the neighbor returned the jar, but the merchant discovered that beneath a layer of oil at the top, the jar was filled with copper slugs instead of the thousand gold dinars he had secretly concealed within!

The neighbor indignantly denied the charge, swearing that he had never opened the jar, pointing to the original wax seal which remained intact.

The court was perplexed: how could gold turn to copper under an unbroken seal?

Abu Yusuf examined the jar closely. He summoned three expert oil-merchants of Baghdad and asked them to taste the oil floating at the top of the vessel.

The experts tasted the oil and declared unanimously: 'This oil is fresh, harvested from the olives of this very season; it cannot be more than two months old.'

Abu Yusuf turned his piercing gaze upon the neighbor: 'You swore by your honor that you never opened the jar during the five years of your friend’s absence! How then could oil harvested two months ago find its way beneath a seal five years old?'

Trapped by his own contradiction, the dishonest neighbor fell to his knees and confessed that he had broken the seal, stolen the gold, filled the jar with copper and fresh oil, and resealed it with counterfeit wax.

Abu Yusuf compelled the thief to return the thousand gold dinars, fined him heavily for his perjury, and restored the innocent merchant’s fortune, proving that true justice examines the evidence of nature rather than the empty oaths of liars.
moral: True legal wisdom combines strict justice with humane understanding and profound equity.

title: The Caliph al-Hakim and the Merchant
summary: The Fatimid Caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, who ruled Egypt from Cairo, was famous for his nightly tours through the city, riding a grey do...
keywords: the caliph al-hakim and the merchant
full_text:
The Fatimid Caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, who ruled Egypt from Cairo, was famous for his nightly tours through the city, riding a grey donkey through the bazaars in simple attire to inspect market weights and prices with relentless vigilance.

During a year of severe drought, when the Nile failed to flood its banks, the price of grain skyrocketed. Greedy merchants hoarded wheat in their warehouses, creating an artificial famine and selling flour at exorbitant prices to the starving citizens.

One evening, Al-Hakim stopped his donkey before the shop of an honest grain merchant named Abu Ali. While all the surrounding shops were demanding ten dinars for a measure of grain, Abu Ali continued to sell his wheat at the normal, fair price of two dinars, measuring each scoop with scrupulous accuracy.

Al-Hakim, disguised as a poor laborer, stepped forward and asked: 'O merchant, why do you not double your price like your neighbors? You could amass a fortune in gold before the week ends.'

Abu Ali looked at the customer with clear, honest eyes and answered: 'Brother, I purchased this wheat before the drought at fair cost. Shall I profit from the tears of hungry children and the misery of my neighbors? A single dirham gained by honest measure carries a blessing, while mountains of gold amassed through extortion are nothing but hot coals in the hand.'

Al-Hakim was deeply moved. The next morning, the Caliph summoned the merchants of Cairo to his palace.

Before the assembled assembly, the Caliph threw off his disguise, severely punished the hoarders, and appointed Abu Ali as the Grand Inspector of the Markets of Egypt, decreeing that only those who fear the heavens and love their fellow men are worthy to oversee the bread of the people.
moral: Honest commerce that refuses to exploit scarcity brings honor and royal protection.

title: King Kisra Anushirwan and the Village Damsel
summary: King Kisra Anushirwan, celebrated across the chronicles of Persia as 'The Just,' was hunting in a remote province of his empire when he b...
keywords: king kisra anushirwan and the village damsel
full_text:
King Kisra Anushirwan, celebrated across the chronicles of Persia as 'The Just,' was hunting in a remote province of his empire when he became separated from his retinue. Exhausted and parched with thirst, he rode into a modest village orchard where a young maiden was watering pomegranate trees.

The king dismounted and asked for a draught of water. The maiden smiled with graceful courtesy: 'Water is scarce, O traveler, but wait a moment, and I shall fetch you the sweet juice of our orchard.'

She went into the trees, plucked a single large, ruby-red pomegranate, and squeezed it into a clay bowl. To the king's astonishment, the single fruit yielded a full bowl of clear, deliciously sweet juice! Anushirwan drank with immense delight, finding his strength instantly restored.

Looking around the thriving village, a thought of greed entered the monarch’s mind: 'This orchard is extraordinarily fertile; when I return to the capital, I shall double the taxes on this district to enrich my royal treasury.'

He asked the maiden for a second bowl. She went into the orchard, plucked another pomegranate from the same bough, and squeezed it. But this time, she labored for a long time, and the fruit yielded only a few bitter drops of cloudy juice.

The king was amazed and asked: 'Why was the first fruit so abundant and sweet, while this second fruit from the same tree is so dry and bitter?'

The maiden looked at him with wise, untroubled eyes and replied: 'O traveler, know you not the ancient mystery of our land? When the king’s intention is just and benevolent, the heavens shower blessings, and the fruits overflow with sweetness. But when the king’s heart turns toward greed and oppression, the fertility departs from the earth, and the fruits wither in their rinds!'

Anushirwan’s heart was pierced with profound shame. He repented of his greedy intention, praised the maiden’s wisdom, and rewarded the village with tax exemptions, reaffirming his sacred vow that justice alone must be the crown of a king.
moral: The justice of a king sweetens the fruits of the land, while royal greed brings drought and bitterness.

title: The Water-Carrier and the Goldsmith's Wife
summary: In a quiet quarter of Baghdad lived an honest water-carrier named Salih who had served the same wealthy goldsmith’s household for thirty ...
keywords: the water-carrier and the goldsmith's wife
full_text:
In a quiet quarter of Baghdad lived an honest water-carrier named Salih who had served the same wealthy goldsmith’s household for thirty years. Every morning and evening, Salih carried heavy goat-skins of fresh river water into the courtyard, filling the kitchen jars and garden basins.

Throughout those thirty years, Salih had conducted himself with such impeccable modesty, lowering his gaze and respecting the privacy of the home, that the goldsmith trusted him as a member of his own family, allowing him to enter without announcing his arrival.

One afternoon, as Salih poured water into the basin, the goldsmith’s wife stepped onto the veranda to adjust the jasmine trellis, her golden bracelet catching the light. In that fleeting second, a sudden impulse of thoughtless indiscretion seized Salih's mind; he reached out and touched the maiden's hand before recovering his senses and fleeing the courtyard in burning shame.

The wife stood stunned, deeply offended by the unexpected breach of trust. When her husband returned from the bazaar that evening, she noticed that he looked unusually somber.

The goldsmith embraced his wife and sighed: 'A strange and shameful thing befell me today in the bazaar. A noble lady came to my shop to purchase a golden ring. As I slid the ring upon her finger, a sudden thoughtless impulse overcame my discipline, and I squeezed her hand! I instantly repented, but my soul has been tormented by remorse all afternoon.'

His wife looked at him with wide, knowing eyes and replied: 'Now I understand! Today, after thirty years of flawless courtesy, our water-carrier touched my hand in the courtyard! Your thoughtless action in the bazaar was reflected back upon your own house.'

The goldsmith wept in realization that one’s conduct in public returns to one’s own hearth.

The next morning, the water-carrier arrived with ashes on his head, begging for forgiveness with sincere tears. The goldsmith embraced him, both having learned that integrity requires unceasing vigilance in every thought, word, and deed.
moral: A momentary lapse in discipline can tarnish thirty years of honor; constant vigilance preserves integrity.

title: Khusrau and Shirin and the Fisherman
summary: King Khusrau of ancient Persia sat in his summer pavilion beside a cool lake, accompanied by his beloved queen, the fair Shirin. An hones...
keywords: khusrau and shirin and the fisherman
full_text:
King Khusrau of ancient Persia sat in his summer pavilion beside a cool lake, accompanied by his beloved queen, the fair Shirin. An honest fisherman approached the royal pavilion and presented the monarch with a magnificent, glistening fish of enormous size, freshly caught from the mountain waters.

Khusrau was so delighted by the splendid gift that he commanded his treasurer to reward the fisherman with four thousand silver dirhams!

Queen Shirin, who possessed a sharp financial mind, whispered to the king: 'My lord, you have acted with excessive haste. If you bestow four thousand dirhams for a single fish, whenever you reward your generals and viziers with such a sum, they will grumble, saying: "The king values our services no more than a fisherman’s catch!"'

Khusrau frowned: 'It is unseemly for a monarch to withdraw a gift once granted. What can be done?'

Shirin smiled cleverly: 'Summon the fisherman and ask him: "Is this fish male or female?" If he says male, say: "We required a female fish," and if he says female, say: "We required a male fish!" Thus you may lawfully revoke the reward.'

The fisherman was called back before the throne. Khusrau asked with royal gravity: 'Tell me, fisherman: is this splendid fish male or female?'

The fisherman, perceiving the trap with lightning wit, bowed low and answered: 'May heaven preserve the king! This fish is neither male nor female; it is an extraordinary creature that partakes of the nature of both, created by the heavens especially for the royal table of Khusrau!'

Khusrau laughed heartily at the fisherman’s brilliant reply and immediately ordered another four thousand dirhams to be added to his purse!

As the fisherman departed carrying the heavy bag of eight thousand dirhams, a single silver coin slipped through a hole and fell into the dust. The fisherman bent down, picked it up, and wiped it upon his sleeve.

Shirin exclaimed: 'Look at the miser! Even with eight thousand dirhams, he cannot leave a single coin for the palace servants!'

Khusrau demanded: 'Why did you grudge a single coin to the earth?'

The fisherman bowed: 'Heaven forbid that I should be a miser, sire! But upon that coin is stamped the sacred image of the King; I could not bear that the feet of men should trample upon the likeness of my sovereign!'

Enchanted by his incomparable tact, Khusrau commanded a third reward of four thousand dirhams, proving that a quick tongue and courteous mind can conquer all the subtleties of courts.
moral: Sharp wit, polite presence of mind, and eloquent speech can turn a king's test into double fortune.

title: Yahya bin Khalid and the Poor Man
summary: Yahya bin Khalid the Barmecide, renowned throughout Baghdad for his courtly refinement, was approached one afternoon by a modest, elderly...
keywords: yahya bin khalid and the poor man
full_text:
Yahya bin Khalid the Barmecide, renowned throughout Baghdad for his courtly refinement, was approached one afternoon by a modest, elderly scholar named Al-Hasan. The scholar was deeply versed in ancient poetry, philosophy, and history, but was so impoverished that his patched cloak barely concealed his frayed tunic.

Al-Hasan handed Yahya a sheet of parchment on which he had inscribed an elegant petition:
'My poverty is known to the heavens, yet my dignity forbids me to beg;
I knock upon the gate of Barmak, where generosity is the ancient law.'

Yahya read the verse with moist eyes. Instead of sending a servant with a purse of coins, which might have made the proud scholar feel like a common mendicant, Yahya stood from his divan, kissed the scholar’s forehead, and said: 'Welcome, venerable master! For months I have sought a scholar of your profound learning to catalog the rare manuscripts in my private library. Will you accept this office and honor my house with your presence?'

The scholar’s eyes filled with tears of gratitude; he had been offered not a humiliating handout, but an honorable office worthy of his intellect.

Yahya ordered a sum of two thousand gold dinars to be paid to Al-Hasan as his 'advance salary,' furnished him with a carriage, fine silk robes, and a comfortable house adjacent to the library.

For ten years, the scholar cataloged manuscripts, instructed Yahya’s sons, and lived in honored comfort.

Yahya’s companions marveled at his conduct, and Yahya replied: 'To give gold to a poor man while bruising his soul is cruelty disguised as charity. True generosity honors the mind and preserves the dignity of the receiver, so that both the giver and the recipient stand as brothers before the truth.'
moral: The highest charity preserves the self-respect of the recipient, treating him as an equal partner.

title: The Woman's Trick Against Her Husband
summary: In the city of Basra lived an affluent linen-draper named Abu Bakr whose excessive jealousy was the talk of the entire quarter. Though hi...
keywords: the woman's trick against her husband
full_text:
In the city of Basra lived an affluent linen-draper named Abu Bakr whose excessive jealousy was the talk of the entire quarter. Though his wife was a model of virtue, modesty, and domestic care, Abu Bakr locked the courtyard gates with three heavy bolts whenever he left for the market, refusing to allow even the old water-carrier or the bread-woman to enter.

Weary of being treated like a prisoner, the witty wife resolved to cure his ridiculous jealousy through an innocent comedy.

One morning, having observed that Abu Bakr was returning home early from the bazaar, she purchased a large, empty cedar shipping crate from a passing carpenter. She placed the crate in the center of the courtyard, left the lid half-open, and threw an old pair of men’s yellow slippers beside it on the tiles.

When Abu Bakr unlocked the three bolts and stepped into the courtyard, his eyes fell upon the yellow slippers. He turned purple with rage: 'Whose slippers are these? Who is hiding in my house?'

His wife ran out from the kitchen, feigning extreme panic, threw her arms across the crate, and cried: 'O husband, do not open that chest! By all that is sacred, do not look inside!'

Blinded by fury, Abu Bakr pushed her aside, shouting: 'Aha! The traitor is concealed within! I shall lock the crate, carry it directly to the Chief Justice, and have you both banished from Basra!'

He slammed down the heavy lid, padlocked it with an iron chain, hoisted the heavy wooden crate upon his back, and staggered through the crowded streets beneath the blazing sun!

A crowd of neighbors, merchants, and schoolboys followed the puffing linen-draper as he marched up to the tribunal of the Chief Judge.

'Justice, O Judge!' gasped Abu Bakr, dropping the crate with a crash before the bench. 'Open this crate and behold the deceiver who has violated my domestic honor!'

The judge ordered the locksmiths to break the chain. The lid was thrown open. The entire courtroom leaned forward with breathless suspense—only to find the crate completely empty, save for a large round turnip and a folded parchment inscribed with a verse:

'He who locks out the sun in fear of shadows
Will carry a turnip to court on his own shoulders!'

The courtroom erupted into roaring laughter. The judge laughed until tears rolled down his cheeks, reprimanded Abu Bakr for his foolish suspicion, and sent him home to beg his wife’s pardon, having cured his jealousy forever.
moral: Unreasonable jealousy and suspicion make a man a fool, easily cured by clever good humor.

title: The Devout Woman and the Two Wicked Elders
summary: In an ancient city lived a noble and devout woman named Sarah, whose beauty of character, modesty, and devotion to charity were revered b...
keywords: the devout woman and the two wicked elders
full_text:
In an ancient city lived a noble and devout woman named Sarah, whose beauty of character, modesty, and devotion to charity were revered by all the citizens. Two elderly judges of the high court, whose hearts were secretly corrupt, sought to force her to compromise her honor. When Sarah rejected their corrupt advances with righteous indignation, the wicked elders conspired to destroy her.

They appeared before the King’s supreme council, tearing their robes and claiming they had witnessed Sarah violating the sacred laws of the realm in her garden. Because the accusers were venerable judges with long white beards, the king and the populace believed their testimony, and the innocent woman was condemned to be cast from the city precipice.

As the guards led Sarah through the public square, a clever young youth named Daniel stepped forward and shouted to the crowd: 'Hold your hands! Will you shed innocent blood upon the word of two corrupt witnesses without testing their testimony?'

The king, observing the youth’s extraordinary confidence, halted the procession: 'How would you test them, young man?'

Daniel said: 'Separate the two judges so that neither can hear the other speak, and let me examine them one by one.'

The judges were led to opposite sides of the square. Daniel approached the first elder and asked: 'You swore you saw this deed committed in her garden. Tell the court: beneath which tree did it take place?'

The first elder answered without hesitation: 'Beneath the spreading boughs of the great mastic tree!'

Daniel recorded the answer, walked across the square to the second elder, and asked: 'Under which tree in the garden did you witness this deed?'

The second elder replied confidently: 'Beneath the tall, leafy green oak tree!'

Daniel turned to the King and the crowd: 'Behold the falsehood of their conspiracy! One claims a mastic tree, and the other an oak! Their own tongues have exposed the web of their deceit!'

The crowd cheered in triumph for the truth. The king exonerated the virtuous Sarah with royal honors, stripped the corrupt elders of their robes, and appointed young Daniel to his council of justice, demonstrating that the light of truth pierces the darkest deceptions.
moral: Innocence is protected by truth, and corrupt judges will be exposed by the sharp light of inquiry.

full_text:
Ja'afar the Barmecide, while riding through the desert outside Baghdad with a company of courtiers, met an elderly Bedouin riding a shaggy camel, carrying a hunting falcon upon his wrist and a patched leather waterskin across his saddle.

Desiring to enjoy the legendary wit of the desert nomads, Ja'afar halted his steed and called out: 'From whence come you, O father of the desert?'

The old Bedouin looked down from his saddle and replied with calm dignity: 'From the vast earth of heaven, young master.'

Ja'afar smiled: 'And whither are you traveling?'

'Whither my camel carries me and destiny directs my steps,' answered the Bedouin.

Ja'afar chuckled: 'And what is the name of your famous tribe?'

'A tribe that feeds the guest in famine, strikes down the oppressor in battle, and holds its head higher than the mountain crags!' replied the nomad proudly.

Ja'afar, delighted by his fearless answers, took off his gold signet ring and said: 'If you can tell me three things that are identical, three that are opposites, and three that never change, I shall give you this ring of gold and a hundred dinars.'

The old Bedouin answered without a moment's pause:
'Three things are identical: the breath of the desert, the soul of a free man, and the flight of an arrow.
Three things are opposites: truth and falsehood, light and darkness, the generous hand and the clenched fist.
And three things never change: the turning of the heavens, the debt of mortality, and the honor of a noble heart!'

Ja'afar was enchanted by the depth and poetic elegance of the nomad's words. He handed him the gold ring, ordered a hundred gold dinars to be weighed into his saddlebags, and invited him to his palace in Baghdad.

The Bedouin thanked him with royal courtesy, rode into the sunset, leaving Ja'afar to reflect that wisdom dwells not in palaces, but in the open sands where freedom sharpens the mind.
moral: Desert wit, poetic pride, and quick banter earn the admiration and generosity of princes.

title: The Caliph Omar bin al-Khattab and the Young Badawi
summary: In the reign of the Caliph Omar bin al-Khattab, two young brothers brought a handsome young Bedouin before the council in Medina, saying:...
keywords: the caliph omar bin al-khattab and the young badawi
full_text:
In the reign of the Caliph Omar bin al-Khattab, two young brothers brought a handsome young Bedouin before the council in Medina, saying: 'O Commander of the Faithful, this man’s camel entered our orchard and destroyed our fruit trees. When our father threw a stone at the camel, this youth struck back in anger, and our father perished. We demand justice according to the law.'

The young Bedouin stood tall, with clear, untroubled eyes, and confessed: 'It is true, O Caliph. The stone our father threw killed my prize mare; in my youthful anger, I struck him with my staff, and his spirit departed. I do not deny the deed, and I submit to the law. But I have one prayer: my father died leaving a great treasure of gold entrusted to me for my younger orphan brother, buried in a secret place in the desert. Grant me a reprieve of three days, that I may dig up the gold, place it in the hands of a guardian, and return to face judgment.'

Omar asked: 'Who among this assembly will stand as your surety with his own life if you fail to return?'

The youth looked around the hall, but he was a stranger, and no man knew him. Suddenly, Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, the venerable companion of the Prophet, stood forward and said: 'I will stand as his surety, O Caliph.'

The court was filled with awe; if the stranger did not return, the revered Abu Dharr would face execution!

Two days passed, and the third day arrived. As the sun began to sink toward the horizon, the youth had not appeared. The crowd began to weep for Abu Dharr.

Just as the sun touched the rim of the desert, a lone figure appeared running across the sands, covered in dust and drenched in sweat! It was the young Bedouin. He fell exhausted at Omar’s feet, gasping: 'I have secured my brother’s inheritance! Here is my life; execute your law!'

Omar wept and asked: 'Why did you return, when you could have fled into the vast desert where none could find you?'

The youth answered: 'I returned so that no man should ever say: "Honor and faith have vanished from among men!"'

Omar turned to Abu Dharr: 'And why did you vouch for a stranger?' Abu Dharr replied: 'So that no man should say: "Trust and brotherhood have perished from the world!"'

The two brothers, weeping in profound realization, stepped forward and said: 'We forgive him! We remit his blood-debt freely, so that no man should ever say: "Mercy and forgiveness have died in the human heart!"' The entire assembly cheered in joy, celebrating the triumph of honor.
moral: Keeping one's sacred word in the face of death inspires universal mercy and reconciles enemies.

title: The Caliph al-Maamun and the Pyramids
summary: The Abbasid Caliph Al-Ma'mun, famous for his passion for mathematics, astronomy, and the translation of ancient Greek and Persian manuscr...
keywords: the caliph al-maamun and the pyramids
full_text:
The Abbasid Caliph Al-Ma'mun, famous for his passion for mathematics, astronomy, and the translation of ancient Greek and Persian manuscripts, arrived in Egypt with a great retinue of engineers, scholars, and masons. Standing before the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Caliph looked upon its colossal limestone bulk, rising like a mountain against the azure desert sky.

Legend claimed that within the pyramid rested the secret scrolls of ancient sciences, celestial charts of forgotten astrologers, and immense treasures of gold accumulated by the pharaohs before the great flood.

Determined to unlock its mysteries, Al-Ma'mun ordered his stonemasons to breach the northern face of the monument. For six months, hundreds of workmen heated the hard stone with roaring fires of wood and cracked the boiling limestone with cold vinegar, tunneling fifty yards into the solid rock.

At last, their iron chisels broke through into a dark, echoing ascending passage paved with polished granite.

Al-Ma'mun and his chief scholars crawled through the narrow passage, their torches illuminating immense vaulted galleries, until they entered the King’s Chamber in the heart of the pyramid. The air was cold and ancient. In the center stood a single, plain sarcophagus carved of solid dark granite, completely empty!

There were neither heaps of gold nor chests of rubies, only the silent, unyielding stone that had defied four thousand years of human storms.

Perceiving the disappointment of his exhausted workmen, Al-Ma'mun secretly ordered his treasurer to bury a purse of three hundred gold dinars in the floor of the passage. When the masons unearthed the purse, they rejoiced, finding that the gold exactly equaled the wages of their six months of labor!

Al-Ma'mun looked upon the colossal monument and smiled with philosophical humility: 'The ancients did not build this mountain of stone to hoard gold; they built it to teach the conquerors of the future that the monuments of pride endure longer than the empires that raised them.'
moral: Human ambition that seeks to conquer ancient stone learns that true greatness lies in preserving wisdom.

title: The Thief and the Merchant
summary: In the city of Isfahan lived an affluent silk merchant named Kamal, celebrated for his tranquil temperament and generous charity. One nig...
full_text:
In the city of Isfahan lived an affluent silk merchant named Kamal, celebrated for his tranquil temperament and generous charity. One night, while reading ledgers late in his inner counting-house, Kamal heard a soft rustling sound from the ceiling rafters.

Looking up calmly, he saw a young thief descending by a silk cord, clutching an iron pry-bar. The thief slipped into the room, only to find the master sitting at his desk, watching him with gentle curiosity.

The trapped burglar turned pale, raised his pry-bar, and snarled: 'Do not cry out for the watch, old man, or I shall strike you down!'

Kamal did not flinch. He set down his reed pen, gestured toward a cushioned stool, and said in a soothing voice: 'Peace be upon you, young friend. Sit down and catch your breath; climbing down rafters in the dark is weary work. It is cold tonight; let me pour you a cup of hot spiced tea.'

The thief stood dumbfounded, his weapon lowering in confusion. No victim had ever offered him tea before.

Kamal poured the hot beverage, handed the youth a bowl of sweet almonds, and asked gently: 'What bitter distress has forced a strong, intelligent young man like you to risk his life and honor in the dark alleys?'

The youth hung his head in shame, weeping: 'My father was an honest weaver who died leaving great debts. My mother and little sisters are starving, and no merchant will give employment to a penniless lad.'

Kamal opened his iron cash-box, counted out one hundred silver dirhams, and placed them in the youth’s hands: 'Take this sum to pay your father’s debts and buy flour for your mother. Tomorrow morning at sunrise, come to my silk shop in the central bazaar; I need a trustworthy assistant to manage my caravans.'

The young man fell to the floor, kissing Kamal’s sandals, swearing to renounce crime forever. He served the merchant with heroic fidelity for thirty years, eventually inheriting the business and continuing the tradition of turning compassion into honest opportunity.
moral: Repaying theft with kindness and practical opportunity converts a criminal into a lifelong ally.

title: Masrur the Eunuch and Ibn al-Karibi
summary: Masrur, the chief palace attendant of Caliph Harun al-Rashid, was often charged with finding novel amusements when the Caliph suffered fr...
keywords: masrur the eunuch and ibn al-karibi
full_text:
Masrur, the chief palace attendant of Caliph Harun al-Rashid, was often charged with finding novel amusements when the Caliph suffered from insomnia and melancholy. One evening, finding the monarch in deep dejection, Masrur remembered Ibn al-Karibi, a famous jester and mimic in Baghdad whose witty impersonations could make a stone statue laugh.

Masrur slipped out to the bazaar, found the jester, and whispered: 'The Commander of the Faithful is melancholic. If you can make him laugh tonight, he will reward you with a hundred gold dinars. But hear my condition: you must swear to give me two-thirds of whatever reward the Caliph bestows upon you, or I will not let you enter the palace gates!'

The jester agreed to the bargain and entered the imperial presence.

Ibn al-Karibi began his performance, mimicking the pompous legal debates of the city judges, the boasting of the camel-drivers, and the flattery of the courtiers with such razor-sharp wit and comical gestures that Harun al-Rashid forgot his sorrow, laughing until his sides ached and his crown slipped!

Delighted by the entertainment, the Caliph smiled and said: 'You have cured my melancholy, jester! In return, ask whatever reward you desire!'

The jester bowed low and said: 'Sire, I ask for only one reward: that you command your guards to administer thirty strokes of the willow wand upon my back!'

The Caliph was astonished: 'Why do you ask for thirty lashes instead of gold?' The jester insisted: 'It is the only reward my heart desires.'

The Caliph, amused by the strange request, ordered the guard to strike lightly. After receiving ten gentle strokes, the jester shouted: 'Hold! The first third of the reward is mine, but the remaining twenty strokes belong to Masrur, who made me swear an oath to give him two-thirds of whatever the Caliph bestowed!'

Harun al-Rashid burst into thunderous laughter, summoned the blushing attendant, and commanded the remaining twenty strokes to be administered to Masrur’s back! The Caliph then rewarded the witty jester with a thousand gold dinars, teaching the greedy attendant that he who bargains for another's reward must be prepared to share the whip.
moral: Greed that tries to exploit another's art gets paid in the exact coin it bargained for.

title: The Devotee Prince
summary: Prince Harun, a royal prince of the Abbasid dynasty, grew weary of the luxury, flattering courtiers, and political intrigues of the Baghd...
full_text:
Prince Harun, a royal prince of the Abbasid dynasty, grew weary of the luxury, flattering courtiers, and political intrigues of the Baghdad court. Realizing that worldly crowns cannot satisfy the longing of the soul, he abandoned his palace by night, donned a coarse woollen tunic, and traveled down the river to the bustling port city of Basra.

There, among the docks and brickyards, he hired himself out as a simple day-laborer, working every Saturday as a mason’s assistant, carrying heavy mortar and bricks up high scaffolds.

He had one peculiar rule: he worked only on Saturdays, earned exactly one dirham and a single copper fals, and refused to labor for the rest of the week, spending his days in contemplation, study, and prayer in the great mosque. The one dirham he spent on barley bread and water, and the copper coin he gave to the poor.

The master builder of Basra marveled at his worker: 'This young laborer works with such quiet diligence and flawless honesty that he accomplishes in one day what three ordinary men cannot finish in a week, yet he refuses to take a single coin more than his simple need.'

After several years, the young prince fell ill of a fever. Lying upon a simple palm mat in a modest hut, he sent for the master builder and handed him a sealed ring bearing the royal crest of the Caliph of Baghdad.

'When I depart,' whispered the youth, 'take this ring to the Commander of the Faithful, and tell him: "Your brother has returned to his Creator, possessing nothing of this world save a clear conscience and the joy of honest labor."'

When the Caliph received the ring, he wept bitterly, acknowledging that his humble brother had conquered a greater kingdom with his mason’s trowel than all the armies of Baghdad could ever subdue with the sword.
moral: Inner peace earned by honest manual labor is more noble than all the gilded trappings of royal palaces.

title: The Unwise Schoolmaster
summary: In a village near Damascus lived a schoolmaster who was deeply versed in ancient grammatical rules, archaic vocabulary, and obsolete lega...
full_text:
In a village near Damascus lived a schoolmaster who was deeply versed in ancient grammatical rules, archaic vocabulary, and obsolete legal commentaries, but who possessed not a single grain of ordinary common sense. He insisted on speaking in ancient rhetorical verses even when ordering onions in the marketplace, causing confusion wherever he went.

One afternoon, the schoolmaster was riding his donkey along a narrow canal path, engrossed in reading a massive leather-bound dictionary held before his nose. The donkey, left to its own judgment, wandered off the path, and both beast and master tumbled into a deep ditch filled with black mud.

A passing farmer saw the mishap, ran up with a long willow pole, and shouted: 'Catch hold of the pole, master, and I will pull you out of the ditch!'

The schoolmaster, covered in black slime up to his chin, looked up haughtily and replied in high classical rhetoric: 'O rustic agriculturalist! Thou hast addressed me with a grammatical solecism! Thou shouldst have exclaimed: "Grasp thou the extremity of the arboreal branch, that I may extract thy physical vessel from the alluvial mire!" Correct thy syntax immediately, before I deign to accept thy assistance!'

The farmer blinked in astonishment, shrugged his shoulders, and said: 'If you prefer grammar to dry clothes, master, stay in the mud and conjugate your verbs!' The farmer picked up his pole and walked away.

The schoolmaster spent three hours struggling in the slimy ditch, ruining his precious dictionary and catching a severe chill, before a passing cart driver hauled him out without asking for his grammatical approval.

The drenched pedagogue returned home shivering, having learned that in the hour of difficulty, a plain word spoken with practical sense is worth more than ten thousand archaic dictionaries.
moral: Pedantic knowledge that lacks practical common sense makes a man a laughingstock to his neighbors.

title: The Foolish Dominie
summary: In a crowded schoolroom in Cairo, twenty mischievous boys sat upon palm mats on a hot summer afternoon, weary of memorizing long lists of...
full_text:
In a crowded schoolroom in Cairo, twenty mischievous boys sat upon palm mats on a hot summer afternoon, weary of memorizing long lists of irregular verbs under the watchful eye of their strict dominie.

The cleverest boy in the class whispered a daring plot to his companions: 'Our master is a hypochondriac who fears illness above all things. If we all play our parts with solemn faces, we shall have a holiday before the hour of noon!'

As the master sat upon his chair, the first boy stepped forward to recite his lesson, looked at the master’s face with theatrical horror, and gasped: 'O master! May heaven preserve you! Why are your cheeks so pale, and why do your eyes look so glassy?'

The dominie frowned: 'Silence, boy! I am perfectly well; recite your lesson!'

A few minutes later, the second boy approached with his slate, dropped it in alarm, and cried: 'Alas, master! You are shivering! Your lips are blue, and a dreadful fever has seized your countenance!'

The dominie began to feel a strange chill down his spine. He touched his forehead: was it truly hot?

One by one, all twenty boys approached, each wailing with louder lamentation, begging the master to lie down before he collapsed from the terrible contagion!

Overcome by the power of suggestion, the healthy schoolmaster’s knees began to shake; his head throbbed, his vision blurred, and he groaned in genuine agony!

'Help me home, my children!' moaned the dominie. 'A pestilence has struck down your poor master!'

The boys helped him to his house, tucked him beneath five heavy woollen blankets, closed the shutters, and ran shouting into the sunshine to enjoy three days of joyful holiday, while the poor dominie drank bitter herbal broths, completely cured of his health by twenty determined schoolboys.
moral: Power of suggestion and hypochondria can convince even a healthy man of imaginary illness.

title: The Illiterate Who Set Up For a Schoolmaster
summary: An unemployed laborer in a remote mountain village in Syria noticed that the local school had been closed since the death of the old teac...
keywords: the illiterate who set up for a schoolmaster
full_text:
An unemployed laborer in a remote mountain village in Syria noticed that the local school had been closed since the death of the old teacher. Desiring to earn an easy living without turning the heavy spade, the clever fellow purchased an enormous pair of silver spectacles, donned an imposing turban of scholar’s muslin, carried a thick manuscript of ancient parchment under his arm, and opened a schoolroom in the public square.

The villagers, illiterate themselves, marveled at his dignified appearance and entrusted thirty children to his care, paying him with bread, honey, and silver coins.

The fake teacher had a simple system: he distributed wooden slates, had the children copy arbitrary squiggles on the boards, and spent his days smoking his clay pipe and nodding with solemn authority.

One morning, an old peasant woman received a letter from her son who was a soldier in Baghdad. Unable to read, she rushed to the schoolroom, handed the letter to the master, and wept: 'O learned master, read me what my beloved son has written!'

The impostor took the letter, opened it, and stared at the Arabic script in absolute panic—for he could not read a single letter of the alphabet!

Holding the paper before his nose, he began to beat his breast, wail aloud, and tear his turban, shedding dramatic tears!

The poor mother shrieked in terror: 'Alas! Is my son dead? Has he fallen in battle?'

The impostor wept louder, nodding mournfully.

At that moment, the village magistrate, who was a literate scholar, entered the room. Seeing the woman weeping, he took the letter from the schoolmaster’s hands.

The magistrate looked at the letter, and then at the schoolmaster with a sarcastic smile: 'Woman, your son is in splendid health; he has been promoted to captain and has sent you fifty gold dinars with the royal courier! But tell me, master: why were you holding the letter upside down, and why did you invent his death?'

The exposed charlatan fell to his knees, confessing his fraud amidst the laughter and fury of the villagers. He was driven from the village, having learned that true teaching requires real knowledge, not an oversized turban and silver spectacles.
moral: Deceitful pretension in teaching will inevitably be exposed by the simplest test of truth.

title: The King and the Virtuous Wife
summary: A powerful king of ancient Persia, while riding through his capital, caught sight of an exceptionally beautiful lady sitting upon the wal...
keywords: the king and the virtuous wife
full_text:
A powerful king of ancient Persia, while riding through his capital, caught sight of an exceptionally beautiful lady sitting upon the walled balcony of a modest mansion. Enamored by her grace, the king dispatched her husband, who was an officer in the royal guard, on a distant diplomatic mission to the borders of China.

The following evening, the king visited the mansion unattended, intending to use his royal authority to win her favor.

The lady, perceiving the king’s intention, welcomed him with serene composure and royal hospitality. She invited him into the salon, seated him upon the sofa of honor, and served him a banquet consisting of twelve distinct dishes, each arranged in delicate porcelain bowls.

The king tasted the first dish; it was delicious. He tasted the second, third, and fourth dishes; each was seasoned differently with saffron, cinnamon, and rosewater, yet all possessed the same foundational texture.

'O fair lady,' asked the king, 'what are these twelve dishes you have prepared with such subtle art?'

The lady smiled with modest dignity and replied: 'Sire, though one is colored with yellow saffron, another with green herbs, and a third with pomegranate seeds, all twelve dishes are prepared from the exact same common fowl. In taste, nature, and nourishment, they are identical.'

The king, possessing a sharp intellect, perceived the profound allegory immediately: she was telling him that in the eyes of honor, one woman is like another, and that an honorable man does not leave his own table to rob the modest dish of his loyal soldier.

Ashamed of his unworthy impulse, the king rose from the sofa, slipped his royal signet ring beneath the cushion as a token of respect, and departed into the night without having uttered a single improper word.

When the husband returned, he noticed the royal ring and was troubled by suspicion. The king summoned the officer to court, promoted him to general of the imperial guard, and declared before all the emirs: 'Your garden was visited by the king, but its roses were guarded by a wall of virtue that no monarch could ever cross.' The household lived in honored prosperity, having conquered temptation with wit and moral majesty.
moral: Dignity, moral courage, and delicate wit can awaken the conscience of the most powerful ruler.

title: Abd al-Rahman the Maghribi's Story of the Rukh
summary: Abd al-Rahman the Maghribi, an intrepid mariner from the shores of North Africa, appeared before the court of Harun al-Rashid carrying an...
keywords: abd al-rahman the maghribi's story of the rukh
full_text:
Abd al-Rahman the Maghribi, an intrepid mariner from the shores of North Africa, appeared before the court of Harun al-Rashid carrying an astonishing curiosity: a translucent pipe or trough carved from a single bird’s quill, large enough to hold two skins of water!

When the Caliph marveled at the object, Abd al-Rahman related the perilous voyage on which he had obtained it:

'In my youth, our merchant vessel was blown off course by a furious hurricane into the uncharted southern waters of the Sea of China. After weeks of drift, we sighted a mountainous island rising from the azure waves. In the center of the island stood an enormous white dome, shining like polished alabaster, spanning fifty paces across and rising into the clouds.

Thinking it was the tomb of an ancient titan, my companions and I climbed the grassy slope. When we struck the dome with our pickaxes, it cracked, and we discovered with awe and dread that it was not stone at all, but the colossal egg of the legendary Rukh—the monstrous bird of the heavens that preys upon elephants!

Presently, the sky darkened as if a black thunderhead had blotted out the midday sun. Looking up, we beheld wings that spanned the horizon, each feather like a ship's sail, and eyes that burned like twin beacons. It was the parent Rukh returning to its nest!

Terrified, we scrambled back to our ship, hoisted all sail, and pulled with our oars. The giant bird circled the island, let out a cry that shook the sea, and flew toward the mountains. From the abandoned nest, I snatched this single quill fragment that had fallen from the egg’s down.

The Caliph held the massive quill in his hands, marveling at how frail human knowledge is before the infinite mysteries of the unexplored earth.'
moral: The boundless wonders of creation surpass human imagination, inspiring awe and humility.

title: Adi bin Zayd and the Princess Hind
summary: Adi bin Zayd was an illustrious Christian Arab poet and diplomat of the kingdom of Al-Hirah on the Euphrates, renowned across Arabia and ...
keywords: adi bin zayd and the princess hind
full_text:
Adi bin Zayd was an illustrious Christian Arab poet and diplomat of the kingdom of Al-Hirah on the Euphrates, renowned across Arabia and Persia for his handsome countenance, his courtly manners, and his mastery of verse.

During the spring festival of the Palm-Boughs, Adi visited the grand church of Al-Hirah, carrying a branch of flowering myrtle. Standing near the marble colonnade, his eyes met those of Princess Hind, the daughter of King Al-Nu'man. Hind was celebrated for her sharp intellect, her pride, and her refusal of all royal suitors who courted her with mere gold.

When Adi saw the princess, he recited an impromptu verse describing the sunrise over the river and how the purest blossom grows not in the king’s conservatory, but in the garden of the soul.

Hind listened, her heart stirred by the profound sincerity and spiritual elevation of his poetry. Rather than exchanging clandestine messages, Adi approached King Al-Nu'man openly, seeking her hand with dignity and honor.

Though political rivals sought to poison the king’s mind with false suspicions, Adi’s unblemished record as an ambassador to Constantinople and his unwavering fidelity won the monarch’s esteem.

King Al-Nu'man granted his consent, celebrating a wedding that united the desert tribes and the royal court in forty days of music and poetry. Their union became a proverb of enduring affection throughout Arabia, proving that verse spoken from the heart builds palaces that outlast earthly thrones.
moral: True love founded on poetic nobility, mutual respect, and patience creates a bond that bridges kingdoms.

title: Isaac of Mosul and the Merchant
summary: Isaac of Mosul, the chief musician of Harun al-Rashid, was dining at the mansion of a wealthy textile merchant in Baghdad. While all the ...
keywords: isaac of mosul and the merchant
full_text:
Isaac of Mosul, the chief musician of Harun al-Rashid, was dining at the mansion of a wealthy textile merchant in Baghdad. While all the guests praised Isaac’s fame, an elderly, austere merchant named Abu Salih sat with crossed arms, declaring with contempt: 'Music is a frivolous waste of time; it is nothing but the scraping of gut strings against wood. It can neither weave cloth, nor build houses, nor soften a hard heart!'

The other guests were scandalized by the insult, but Isaac smiled with serene confidence. 'Brother,' said Isaac gently, 'will you grant me five minutes of your ear before you condemn my art?'

The old merchant grumbled: 'Play if you must; you will not stir a single hair on my beard.'

Isaac took his cedarwood lute, tightened the silk pegs, and touched the strings. At first, he played a brisk, martial rhythm with sharp chords; the old merchant’s foot tapped unconsciously upon the carpet.

Next, Isaac modulated into a playful, lively dance melody; the merchant’s stern lips twitched, and a faint smile appeared in his eyes.

Finally, Isaac tuned the lowest string to the ancient mode of Iraq, singing a soft, soulful ballad of the Euphrates orchards, of childhood homes left behind, and of mothers singing by the cradle in the dusk of summer. His voice was like a gentle river of pure memory and sorrow.

The guests held their breath. Isaac glanced up and saw tears streaming down Abu Salih's wrinkled cheeks! The old merchant threw his arms around the musician, weeping: 'Forgive me, master! You have not played upon wood; you have opened the locked chamber of my childhood memories and brought my mother’s voice back to my ears.'

The merchant gifted Isaac a robe of gold brocade, learning that art is not a frivolous diversion, but the key that unlocks the deepest sanctuary of the human soul.
moral: The true power of music is a universal language that can unlock the most stubborn and guarded heart.

title: The Three Unfortunate Lovers
summary: In the city of Basra lived three noble young companions: a poet, a physician, and a merchant. All three fell deeply in love with the fair...
full_text:
In the city of Basra lived three noble young companions: a poet, a physician, and a merchant. All three fell deeply in love with the fair Salma, the daughter of a venerable judge. Each suitor was endowed with virtue, intellect, and honor, and the maiden respected all three, unable to choose among them without breaking the hearts of the others.

One afternoon, Salma was stricken with an unprecedented and mysterious fever that baffled all the doctors of Basra. Her breath grew faint, and her father wept in despair.

The three young men met at the city gates, casting aside all rivalry to save the maiden they adored.

The merchant opened his vault and purchased a rare dried medicinal flower brought from the Himalayas at the cost of his entire inheritance. The physician applied his deepest scientific skill, distilling the flower into an exquisite life-saving elixir. The poet rode day and night across dangerous mountains to fetch fresh snow from the peaks to cool her burning brow.

Working together with selfless devotion, the three youths administered the medicine. The fever broke, Salma opened her radiant eyes, and color returned to her cheeks!

When her father, overjoyed, asked: 'Which of you shall claim her hand, for each of you has saved her life?' the three companions looked at each other with noble selflessness.

The poet said: 'The merchant gave all his wealth.' The merchant said: 'The physician gave his science.' The physician said: 'The poet gave his breath.'

Salma spoke softly from her divan: 'He who loves truly does not demand a reward for mercy. Let us remain four lifelong friends bound by a covenant of honor and mutual support.' The three suitors agreed with joyous reverence, having learned that true love is proven by selfless sacrifice rather than jealous possession.
moral: Noble love seeks the well-being and freedom of the beloved, refusing to turn affection into an instrument of possession.

title: How Abu Hasan Brake Wind
summary: Abu Hasan was a wealthy and popular young merchant of Yemen who celebrated his lavish wedding feast surrounded by all the emirs, judges, ...
full_text:
Abu Hasan was a wealthy and popular young merchant of Yemen who celebrated his lavish wedding feast surrounded by all the emirs, judges, and dignitaries of the city. The banquet was sumptuous, with roasted sheep, almond pastries, and fragrant sherbets flowing in abundance.

When the feast concluded and Abu Hasan arose to greet his guests at the threshold, he made an awkward, noisy slip upon the polished floor tiles, stumbling and tearing his fine silk trousers with a loud rip!

Paralyzed by agonizing embarrassment and imagining that the entire city would mock him forever, the sensitive youth did not even enter his bridal chamber. He slipped out through the garden gate, mounted his swiftest mare, and galloped into the desert!

He boarded a merchant vessel in the port, sailed to India, and settled in the distant city of Calicut. For ten long years he lived in exile, amassing a second fortune in the spice trade, yet tormented every single day by the bitter memory of his wedding night mishap.

At last, overwhelmed by homesickness, Abu Hasan returned to Yemen in disguise. As he approached his native village, he sat beside a well outside the walls to listen to the talk of the town.

An old woman was speaking to her young daughter: 'Daughter, when were you born?' The girl replied: 'I was born, mother, on the tenth day of the spring festival, the year of the great locust harvest.' The mother nodded: 'Ah yes, the year of the locusts, five years after the great flood.'

Abu Hasan listened closely, expecting to hear someone mention 'the year Abu Hasan ripped his trousers at his wedding.' He asked the elders at the coffee shop, the market vendors, and the guards at the gate: not a single soul remembered his blunder! Everyone remembered his generosity, his honest father, and his abandoned mansion.

Abu Hasan laughed aloud at his own foolish vanity: 'For ten years I lived in exile over a trifle that everyone forgot in ten days!' He returned to his home, embraced his family, and lived in honored joy, having learned that the world is far too busy with its own affairs to remember our minor embarrassments.
moral: Do not let social embarrassment drive you into exile; time washes away minor blunders, and life moves on.

title: The Lovers of the Banu Tayy
summary: In the rugged mountains of the Shammar desert dwelt the noble nomadic tribe of Tayy, famed for their chivalry and proud traditions. A val...
keywords: the lovers of the banu tayy
full_text:
In the rugged mountains of the Shammar desert dwelt the noble nomadic tribe of Tayy, famed for their chivalry and proud traditions. A valiant young warrior named Wasim loved his cousin Rayhana, a maiden whose beauty was matched only by her wisdom and skill with the bow.

A feud broke out between their respective clans over the grazing rights to a mountain spring. Rayhana’s father, seeking to sever the lovers, moved his tents forty leagues to the south, declaring that no warrior of Wasim’s branch should ever approach his campfire.

Wasim did not succumb to despair. Rather than seeking violent confrontation, he rode alone to the neutral assembly of the tribal elders during the sacred truce month. Standing before the council of the Banu Tayy, Wasim challenged the rival clan to a contest of chivalry:

'Let the feud be judged not by shedding the blood of kin, but by three trials of desert virtue: a trial of horsemanship, a trial of archery, and a trial of poetic generosity!'

Rayhana’s brothers accepted the challenge. In horsemanship, Wasim rode bareback across the rocky ridges with peerless balance; in archery, he split a willow wand at eighty paces; and in poetry, he recited an ode celebrating the ancient unity and valor of the entire tribe of Tayy, bringing tears to the eyes of the fiercest warriors.

Rayhana stepped forward before the elders, testifying with modest courage that her heart belonged to Wasim and that his valor had healed the tribal rift.

The chief of the council embraced both families, wiped away the boundary lines of the spring, and blessed their wedding amidst the singing of the entire tribe, proving that chivalric honor and patience can dissolve decades of tribal strife.
moral: Steadfast courage and chaste fidelity overcome the harshest desert trials, uniting noble hearts.

title: The Mad Lover
summary: In Damascus lived an eminent scholar and poet named Al-Muntajib, celebrated for his profound learning in philosophy and his unyielding de...
full_text:
In Damascus lived an eminent scholar and poet named Al-Muntajib, celebrated for his profound learning in philosophy and his unyielding defense of the rights of the common people. When a tyrannical governor was appointed over the province, who extorted heavy taxes and imprisoned all who criticized his decrees, Al-Muntajib’s friends warned him that his life was in immediate peril.

To save his life without compromising his principles, Al-Muntajib chose a daring path: he donned a ragged tunic decorated with peacock feathers, walked through the streets carrying a hobby-horse made of a palm reed, and began reciting strange, whimsical verses in the marketplace. The citizens whispered: 'Alas! The great philosopher has lost his wits through excessive study!'

The suspicious governor summoned the 'mad poet' to the citadel to interrogate him.

'Why do you ride a stick of palm wood, O philosopher?' asked the governor with mocking laughter.

Al-Muntajib bowed with comical reverence: 'My lord, my palm-reed steed has many virtues over your Arabian stallions: he requires no oats, never kicks his groom, carries me directly toward the truth, and never participates in the robbery of the poor!'

The governor frowned, unsettled: 'And what say you of my royal government?'

The poet chanted with brilliant madness:
'The shepherd who devours his flock shall find his shears grow dull,
The palace built on tears and blood is nothing but a skull;
The crown upon a tyrant's head is fashioned out of glass,
And through the gates of history his shadow soon shall pass!'

The courtiers gasped, but the governor, believing the man was genuinely insane, merely laughed in contempt and ordered him released: 'He is a harmless lunatic; let him ride his palm-stick in the streets!'

Al-Muntajib preserved his life and freedom, continuing to guide the oppressed citizens with allegorical verses until the tyrant was deposed, proving that the guise of folly can be the sharpest sword of wisdom.
moral: Apparent madness is often the shield of wisdom, protecting truth from the wrath of oppressive tyrants.

title: The Prior Who Became a Moslem
summary: Upon the cool, cedar-crested heights of Mount Lebanon stood an ancient monastery celebrated throughout the Levant for the medicinal garde...
keywords: the prior who became a moslem
full_text:
Upon the cool, cedar-crested heights of Mount Lebanon stood an ancient monastery celebrated throughout the Levant for the medicinal gardens of its venerable prior, Father Paul. The prior had spent forty years studying ancient manuscripts in Greek, Syriac, and Hebrew, tending to sick pilgrims of every faith who knocked upon the oak portal.

One autumn afternoon, a caravan of Muslim merchants traveling from Damascus to Beirut was caught in a furious blizzard on the mountain pass. Freezing and exhausted, fifty men and their animals sought refuge at the monastery gates.

Father Paul threw open the portals, welcomed the frozen travelers into the great stone refectory, built roaring fires of cedar logs, and shared his bread, cheese, and hot herb broths without inquiring into their creed.

Among the merchants was a venerable jurist of Baghdad, Shaykh Abdallah. As the storm raged for three days, the prior and the jurist sat by the hearth, engaging in deep and respectful dialogue on theology, the teachings of the prophets, the nature of divine mercy, and the universal moral duties of humankind.

Father Paul was profoundly moved by the moral clarity, philosophical depth, and spiritual universality of the Quranic teachings presented by the jurist. He realized that the essence of all divine revelation is one: to love the Creator, to act with righteous justice, and to serve humanity with compassionate charity.

When the storm cleared, Father Paul accompanied the caravan to Damascus, embraced the faith of Islam, and spent the remainder of his days teaching the harmony of the scriptures in the great Umayyad Academy, demonstrating that an open heart finds truth wherever its light shines.
moral: Sincere spiritual inquiry that seeks truth with an open heart discovers unity across all traditions.

title: The Loves of Abu Isa and Kurrat al-Ayn
summary: Prince Abu Isa, son of the Caliph Al-Rashid, was walking through the palace gardens of his brother, Caliph Al-Ma'mun, when he heard a voi...
keywords: the loves of abu isa and kurrat al-ayn
full_text:
Prince Abu Isa, son of the Caliph Al-Rashid, was walking through the palace gardens of his brother, Caliph Al-Ma'mun, when he heard a voice of peerless purity singing classical verses to the accompaniment of an ivory lute from behind a jasmine trellis.

The singer was Kurrat al-Ayn, a maiden of noble education and sublime artistic mastery, who was the favorite singer of Al-Ma'mun’s court. Abu Isa stood enchanted, his heart pierced by the beauty of her melody and the refined intellect expressed in her improvisation.

Rather than using his royal rank to demand her presence, Prince Abu Isa composed an elegant poetic petition in the classic meter, expressing his sincere admiration for her artistry and seeking permission to court her with honorable intentions.

Caliph Al-Ma'mun, discovering the correspondence, summoned both the prince and the maiden to the grand audience chamber. 'Abu Isa,' said the Caliph with imperial gravity, 'Kurrat al-Ayn is the pride of my court. If you wish to claim her hand, you must prove that your mind matches her artistry. She shall compose three musical verses on the theme of royal justice, and you must answer each on the spot with equal rhyme and philosophical depth.'

Kurrat al-Ayn struck her lute and sang of the balance of the scales, the defense of the weak, and the light of knowledge. Abu Isa answered each stanza with spontaneous verses of such brilliance, humility, and chivalric grace that the entire assembly applauded in delight.

Al-Ma'mun smiled with deep fraternal joy, bestowed upon them a magnificent palace on the Tigris, and celebrated a wedding that became an enduring model of courtly refinement and mutual respect.
moral: Courtly refinement, poetic eloquence, and respectful conduct win the highest favors of monarchs.

title: The Angel of Death With the Proud King and the Devout Man
summary: In ancient times reigned a mighty monarch who possessed an army of a hundred thousand armored horsemen, treasuries filled with rubies, an...
keywords: the angel of death with the proud king and the devout man
full_text:
In ancient times reigned a mighty monarch who possessed an army of a hundred thousand armored horsemen, treasuries filled with rubies, and palaces of polished jasper. One morning, the king mounted his proudest war-steed, caparisoned in gold-embroidered velvet, and rode out to review his troops, his chest swollen with pride as his heralds blew silver trumpets and the soldiers prostrated themselves before him.

As he rode through the city gates, an elderly traveler dressed in tattered rags stepped into his path, seized the horse’s bridle, and called out: 'Hold, O King! I have a secret word to deliver unto your ear.'

The king frowned in fury, his eyes flashing: 'How dare you touch the royal bridle, insolent beggar? Wait until I return to my palace!'

The stranger answered with calm, terrifying authority: 'My errand cannot wait; it touches your very breath.' He whispered his identity into the king's ear: 'I am the Angel of Death, sent to take your soul this very hour!'

The king turned pale as ashes; his knees shook, his pride vanished like mist, and he stammered: 'Grant me but one hour! Let me return to my palace, bid farewell to my children, and distribute my hoarded gold to the poor!'

The Angel replied: 'Your days were numbered, yet you spent them in pride and oppression, ignoring the cries of the needy. The hour has struck, and not a single breath can be added.' The king collapsed from his saddle, lifeless upon the stones, his gold and armies powerless to save him.

The Angel then traveled to a modest hut outside the city where an honest water-carrier lay dying. The humble man had spent his life distributing water to travelers and sharing his crust with the hungry.

When the Angel appeared, the humble man smiled with peaceful joy: 'Welcome, gentle messenger! I have longed for this hour, for I have lived with clean hands and a loving heart.' His spirit departed gently as a sigh of spring, proving that righteousness alone provides safe passage to eternity.
moral: Earthly pomp and iron armies cannot halt the appointed hour; only a life of justice and humble charity endures.
