title: Of Trust in Allah
summary: On the sixth day, the Sixth Wazir addressed King Azadbakht on the role of human effort and divine destiny. Bakhtiyar stood before the thr...
full_text:
On the sixth day, the Sixth Wazir addressed King Azadbakht on the role of human effort and divine destiny. Bakhtiyar stood before the throne, his countenance shining with spiritual serenity:

'O King! Human intellect and honest endeavor are necessary duties; we must till the soil, build the ship, and steer with the oar. But he who relies entirely upon his own frail cunning, imagining that his intellect alone commands the universe, is like an ant that thinks it moves the mountain!

True trust in providence is not passive sloth; it is the courage to do what is right, just, and honorable, and then leave the outcome peacefully in the hands of the Creator of all things.

When the storm is fierce and all earthly instruments fail, the soul that trusts in providence remains serene, knowing that behind the darkest cloud shines the sun of divine wisdom.

This unshakeable trust removes fear from the heart, delivers a man from the temptation to compromise his honor for temporary gain, and opens doors of deliverance where human eyes see only sheer stone walls, as the chronicle of King Bakhtzaman illustrates.'
moral: Trust in divine guidance provides peace of soul and delivers the righteous in the hour of trial.

title: Story of King Bakhtzaman
summary: Bakhtiyar recounted the history of King Bakhtzaman of Yemen:
full_text:
Bakhtiyar recounted the history of King Bakhtzaman of Yemen:

'A military rebellion led by an ambitious general overthrew King Bakhtzaman, driving the righteous monarch into the desert with his queen and young infant. Wandering across trackless dunes, the king lost his camel, his water, and was captured by desert brigands who separated him from his family.

In his darkest hour, chained in a foreign port, Bakhtzaman did not curse heaven or surrender to despair. He said: "The heavens that gave me a crown can take it away, and the providence that sustains the sparrow in the storm can restore the wanderer. I place my soul in the hands of the Merciful."

He worked as an honest porter in the docks for seven years, conducting himself with such integrity that the city merchants appointed him guardian of the harbor storehouses.

When the tyrannical usurper in Yemen died, leaving the kingdom in civil strife, the people rose in revolt, demanding the return of their beloved King Bakhtzaman.

Envoys were dispatched to search the ports of the East. They discovered their former monarch working in the harbor, his hands calloused by labor and his spirit purified by faith!

Bakhtzaman was escorted back to Yemen, joyfully reunited with his queen and son who had been preserved in safety, and restored to his throne amidst national celebrations, proving that trust in providence outlasts the darkest exile.'
moral: Unwavering faith and adherence to justice restore the rightful ruler to his throne.

title: Of Clemency
summary: On the seventh day, the Seventh Wazir demanded the execution of all who challenge royal authority. Bakhtiyar stepped forward and delivere...
full_text:
On the seventh day, the Seventh Wazir demanded the execution of all who challenge royal authority. Bakhtiyar stepped forward and delivered an eloquent defense of clemency:

'Sire! Any barbarian can draw a sword and take the life of a fallen enemy; brute force requires neither wisdom nor greatness of soul. But to stay the hand when the sword is raised, to forgive when you have the absolute power to destroy, is the divine attribute of true kingship!

Vengeance only perpetuates the cycle of bitterness: the son of the slain man will harbor hatred, and his grandson will sharpen a dagger. Blood cannot wash away blood; only the sweet water of mercy cleanses the stain of enmity.

Clemency turns an enemy into a devoted defender, softens the hardest heart, and wins a victory that steel can never achieve.

The conqueror who slays his captives rules over corpses and slaves; but the monarch who pardons with magnanimity rules over the grateful hearts of free men, as shown in the history of King Bihkard.'
moral: Pardoning an adversary when you have the power to destroy him is the highest victory of a monarch.

title: Story of King Bihkard
summary: Bakhtiyar related the story of King Bihkard of ancient Persia:
full_text:
Bakhtiyar related the story of King Bihkard of ancient Persia:

'King Bihkard defeated a formidable rebel chieftain named Ardashir, who had led an insurrection in the northern mountains for ten years. Captured in the final battle, Ardashir was brought into the royal palace in chains, bruised, defiant, and expecting the scaffold.

The king’s viziers shouted unanimously: "Off with his head! Strike him down, sire, as a warning to all rebels!"

King Bihkard looked upon the captive chieftain, stepped down from his golden throne, and with his own hands struck the iron chains from Ardashir’s wrists!

The king said with noble serenity: "Ardashir, you are a valiant warrior of ancient blood. We fought for ten years because we misunderstood each other’s hearts. Today, victory is mine; and my victory is to grant you life, honor, and complete pardon. Return to your mountains in peace, or remain as my brother."

Ardashir stood dumbfounded, tears streaming down his scarred cheeks. He fell at the king’s feet, kissed his sandals, and wept:

"O King! For ten years I hated your crown, but today your clemency has conquered my soul! By the heavens, the blade that sought your throne shall henceforth be your truest shield."

Ardashir became King Bihkard’s most faithful general, defending the frontiers of the empire against all invaders for thirty years, proving that mercy builds fortresses that no army can overthrow.'
moral: Magnanimous clemency transforms a mortal enemy into the most faithful defender of the realm.

title: Of Envy and Malice
summary: On the eighth day, the Eighth Wazir argued before King Azadbakht. Bakhtiyar stood before the throne and delivered his discourse on the de...
full_text:
On the eighth day, the Eighth Wazir argued before King Azadbakht. Bakhtiyar stood before the throne and delivered his discourse on the destructive nature of envy:

'O King! Envy is the most venomous serpent that crawls within the human breast. The thief steals for hunger or gain, the angry man strikes for a perceived injury; but the envious man suffers agony simply because his neighbor prospers!

The envious man looks upon another’s happiness as his own personal calamity; the sun that warms the earth burns his eyes, and the rain that fertilizes the fields chokes his throat.

He does not seek to elevate his own condition through labor; he desires only to pull down the noble to his own mire. Yet look upon the end of all envious schemers: they consume their own flesh with bitter bile, while the righteous man continues to shine like the sun above the clouds.

Malice is a boomerang that returns with double force upon the hand that threw it, as the chronicle of King Aylan Shah and Abu Tammam demonstrates.'
moral: Envy consumes the heart of the envious man, destroying his own peace while leaving the good unharmed.

title: Story of Aylan Shah and Abu Tammam
summary: Bakhtiyar recounted the story of King Aylan Shah of Khwarazm:
keywords: story of aylan shah and abu tammam
full_text:
Bakhtiyar recounted the story of King Aylan Shah of Khwarazm:

'King Aylan Shah had a wise and virtuous counselor named Abu Tammam, whose learning, honesty, and charity won the love of the entire nation. A jealous courtier named Qasim, burning with envy at Abu Tammam’s favor, resolved to destroy him.

Qasim approached the king and whispered falsely: "Sire, Abu Tammam boasts in private that your breath is foul and offensive; observe tomorrow when he approaches your throne: he will cover his mouth with his sleeve!"

Qasim then invited Abu Tammam to his home for dinner and served him a dish heavily seasoned with raw garlic.

The next morning, when Abu Tammam approached the throne to deliver state papers, he discreetly placed his sleeve before his mouth so that the smell of garlic would not offend the monarch.

The king, believing the slanderer’s accusation, wrote a royal order to the captain of the city fortress: "Strike off the head of the bearer of this letter immediately!" The king handed the sealed parchment to Abu Tammam, saying: "Deliver this to the captain."

As Abu Tammam left the palace, Qasim met him in the courtyard, saw the royal letter, and thinking it was an order for a rich gift of gold, seized it from Abu Tammam’s hand: "I will deliver it for you, brother!"

Qasim ran to the fortress, handed the letter to the captain, and was immediately seized and executed according to the royal decree!

When Abu Tammam appeared before the king the next day, the truth was brought to light. King Aylan Shah marveled at the divine justice that had made the slanderer carry his own death sentence, praising the virtue that shields the innocent.'
moral: The slanderer falls into the very trap he dug for the innocent, while truth is vindicated.

'Sire, men often blame destiny for the disasters that their own folly, greed, and recklessness have created!

Destiny provides the circumstances of our birth, the climate of our lands, and the turns of the seasons; but how we respond to those circumstances is the sacred trust of human character.

Two men may suffer the same shipwreck: one weeps in the mud and perishes; the other builds a raft of driftwood, navigates the stars, and discovers an empire! It was not destiny that differentiated them; it was the courage and virtue within their souls.

A noble character turns adversity into an academy of wisdom, and transforms modest bread into a feast of honor. He who cultivates justice, truth, and benevolence within himself will find that destiny aligns with his footsteps, as shown in the history of King Ibrahim and His Son.'
moral: Destiny provides the canvas of life, but our character, virtue, and choices paint the masterpiece.

title: Story of King Ibrahim and His Son
summary: Bakhtiyar related the story of King Ibrahim of Balkh:
keywords: story of king ibrahim and his son
full_text:
Bakhtiyar related the story of King Ibrahim of Balkh:

'King Ibrahim had an only son, Prince Ismail, whom he wished to train in the highest virtues of statecraft. When the prince reached eighteen years of age, the king sent him disguised as a common student to live in the provincial cities for two years.

Prince Ismail lived in student hostels, ate barley bread with poor weavers, helped farmers harvest wheat, and sat among the litigating peasants in the courts of justice.

He saw how corrupt magistrates favored the wealthy, how oppressive tax-collectors seized the milk-goats of widows, and how the honest poor suffered in silence.

When he returned to the palace, his father seated him upon the throne and asked: "What did you learn of your royal destiny, my son?"

Prince Ismail answered with tears in his eyes: "Father, I learned that a king is not a master to be served, but the chief servant of the realm! His palace exists to shelter the helpless, his army to defend the peaceful, and his treasury to feed the hungry. If a single orphan cries in the night from injustice, the king’s crown is stained with blood."

King Ibrahim embraced his son, weeping with joyful pride, and crowned him king before the assembled nation, and Prince Ismail governed for fifty years as the most beloved monarch of the East.'
moral: A prince’s true destiny is to serve his people with justice, empathy, and humble dedication.

title: Of the Appointed Term
summary: On the tenth and final day, the Tenth Wazir demanded that the execution proceed without delay. Bakhtiyar stepped forward and delivered hi...
full_text:
On the tenth and final day, the Tenth Wazir demanded that the execution proceed without delay. Bakhtiyar stepped forward and delivered his final, crowning discourse before King Azadbakht:

'O King! Every mortal creature has an appointed term upon this earth. The mightiest conqueror whose armies shook the continents, and the humble beggar who slept upon the doorstep, both step down into the same narrow earthen bed.

Neither gold, nor ivory palaces, nor armies of iron can delay the hour by a single heartbeat.

What then remains of a king when his body is laid beneath the marble?

His gold is plundered by strangers, his palaces crumble into dust, and his armies are scattered by time. Only one treasure outlasts the grave: the memory of the tears he wiped away, the justice he established, the schools he built, and the mercy he showed to the weak!

He who lives for his own selfish vanity dies completely; but he who lives for the welfare of his fellow men achieves an immortality that shines brighter than the stars, as the chronicle of King Sulayman Shah demonstrates.'
moral: Earthly life is a passing journey; only the enduring memory of justice and charity outlives the grave.

full_text:
Bakhtiyar recounted the story of King Sulayman Shah of ancient Fars:

'King Sulayman Shah was on the brink of waging a devastating war against the King of Khorasan over a disputed border province. His generals urged immediate invasion, sharpening their swords and mobilizing sixty thousand horsemen.

The king’s niece, Princess Shahzanan, an educated statesman who had mastered jurisprudence, philosophy, and history, stepped boldly into the royal council.

She presented an economic and diplomatic audit demonstrating that the war would cost twenty times the value of the disputed province, exhaust the treasury, and invite barbarian invasions from the north.

With her uncle’s permission, Shahzanan rode as the imperial ambassador to the court of the King of Khorasan.

Before the foreign monarch, she delivered an oration of sublime diplomatic eloquence, presenting a compromise: the disputed province was established as a shared commercial emporium, with a joint court of arbitration to govern fair trade.

The King of Khorasan was so impressed by her brilliant intellect, dignity, and statesmanship that he ratified the treaty on the spot, celebrating thirty years of peace.

King Sulayman Shah proclaimed before his council: "A wise woman’s word has saved sixty thousand lives and preserved two empires from ruin!"'
moral: Feminine wisdom, diplomatic skill, and moral courage save an entire nation from catastrophic war.

title: Of the Speedy Relief of Allah
summary: Concluding his ten days of philosophical defense, Bakhtiyar addressed King Azadbakht:
keywords: of the speedy relief of allah
full_text:
In the golden audience hall of King Azadbakht, where the ten viziers stood in solemn array, the noble prisoner Bakhtiyar stood before the royal throne. For ten successive days, he had faced the shadow of the executioner's sword, meeting every accusation not with anger or despair, but with calm tales of wisdom and unwavering faith in the justice of heaven. As the final hour arrived and the assembly leaned forward in breathless silence, Bakhtiyar raised his eyes to the King.

"Sire," spoke Bakhtiyar in a voice clear and untrembling, "the darkest hour of the night is ever that fleeting watch that immediately precedes the dawn. When a traveler feels that every earthly pass is blocked, when iron walls close upon his spirit and despair knocks with heavy fists at the portal of the heart, that is the very instant when the swift relief of Providence arrives with miraculous power! Deliverance does not require the marching of ten thousand horsemen; it enters through the quiet whisper of a witness, the sudden falling of a mask, or the turning of a lock in the dead of night."

"He who perseveres in honor," continued the sage, "keeping his conscience pure and his tongue anchored in truth, will witness the scaffold of persecution transform into the throne of vindication. Truth is an unquenchable flame; men may throw dust upon it, yet it rises to illuminate the world." King Azadbakht was moved to tears by the young man's serene fortitude, ordered his heavy chains struck off, and restored him to the highest seat of honor in the realm.
moral: When human difficulties reach their absolute limit, divine relief arrives with miraculous swiftness.

title: Story of the Prisoner and How Allah Gave Him Relief

full_text:
Bakhtiyar concluded his ten days of storytelling with this history:

'In the kingdom of Sind, an honest treasurer was falsely accused by corrupt courtiers of embezzling forty thousand dinars. He was thrown into a deep, subterranean dungeon, bound with heavy iron chains, and condemned to execution at dawn.

The treasurer sat in the darkness, praying with calm serenity: "O Creator, You know that my hands are clean; into Your care I commit my breath."

That very night, an earthquake shook the citadel! A heavy stone fell from the dungeon ceiling, striking the iron chains and shattering the master link, freeing the prisoner’s hands!

At that same hour, the chief conspirator, stricken with terror by the earthquake, believed that celestial judgment had arrived. He ran into the palace square, confessed his forgery before the king, and produced the stolen gold!

The king rushed to the dungeon with torches, embraced the innocent treasurer, and appointed him Grand Vizier of the empire!'

At that moment, the royal couriers burst into King Azadbakht’s audience hall, carrying letters that fully exposed the conspiracy of the Ten Wazirs against Bakhtiyar!

King Azadbakht threw off his crown, embraced Bakhtiyar with tears of joy, and made him King beside him, while the Ten Wazirs were dismissed in shame, proving that truth and patience conquer all.
moral: Integrity under false persecution is delivered by truth, transforming the dungeon into royal honor.

full_text:
Abd al-Malik, an elderly, respected former governor of Egypt, fell into political disgrace through false court intrigues and had his property confiscated, living in poverty in Baghdad, avoided by all his former colleagues.

Knowing the legendary chivalry of the Barmecide family, Abd al-Malik visited Ja'afar the Barmecide late at night, recounting his unjust humiliation.

Ja'afar did not merely offer him gold. The next morning, during the grand imperial audience of Caliph Harun al-Rashid, Ja'afar took Abd al-Malik by the hand and presented him before the throne.

Ja'afar spoke with magnificent eloquence on Abd al-Malik’s forty years of unblemished service, his honesty in managing the Nile granaries, and the malice of the slanderers who had engineered his fall.

Harun al-Rashid, enlightened by his vizier's courageous defense of an innocent elder, ordered the full restitution of Abd al-Malik’s estates, granted him an imperial pension, and appointed him Counselor of the realm.

Abd al-Malik embraced Ja'afar with tears of gratitude, saying: 'You did not merely save my livelihood, O Barmecide; you restored my honor, which is dearer to me than life itself.'
moral: Generous intercession that restores the honor of a disgraced official earns eternal gratitude.

title: Al-Rashid and the Barmecides
summary: Following the downfall of the Barmecide viziers in Baghdad, Caliph Harun al-Rashid rode through the provinces of Iraq, accompanied by his...
full_text:
Following the downfall of the Barmecide viziers in Baghdad, Caliph Harun al-Rashid rode through the provinces of Iraq, accompanied by his courtiers.

Passing through the agricultural district of Nahrawan, the Caliph stopped to admire a colossal stone bridge spanning the river, surrounded by clean irrigation canals and thriving date orchards.

The Caliph asked an elderly farmer: 'Who constructed this magnificent bridge and these canals that bring such fertility to your fields?'

The old farmer lifted his hands with tears of gratitude: 'May heaven shower blessings upon the noble house of Barmak! It was Yahya and his sons Ja'afar and Al-Fadl who built this bridge, dug these canals, and distributed seeds to the poor without demanding taxes.'

A courtier frowned and whispered sternly: 'Old man, do you not know that the Caliph has forbidden the praise of the Barmecides?'

The old farmer looked at the courtier with fearless dignity: 'You can forbid the tongues of flatterers in the palace, but can you forbid the river to flow beneath this bridge? Can you forbid the date palms to yield their sweet fruit? Every drop of water that irrigates these fields is a tongue that praises their generosity!'

Harun al-Rashid covered his eyes, wept with deep remorse, and said to his escort: 'Leave the old man in peace. He speaks truth. We had the power to destroy their palaces, but their good deeds have built a monument in the hearts of the people that will outlive our dynasty.'
moral: True statesmen who serve with benevolence leave a fragrance that royal edicts cannot erase.

The Caliph Harun al-Rashid sat in his golden audience hall on a sweltering summer day, attended by emirs, viziers, and guards. The Caliph called for a drink, and a cupbearer brought him a crystal goblet filled with iced water scented with rose petals.

As the Caliph raised the goblet to his lips, an elderly, austere scholar named Ibn al-Sammak stepped forward and said: 'Hold, O Commander of the Faithful! Before you drink, permit me to ask you a single question.'

The Caliph paused and said: 'Speak, Ibn al-Sammak.'

The sage asked: 'If you were lost in the scorching wilderness of the desert, dying of thirst, and no man possessed water save one traveler with this single cup, what portion of your imperial kingdom would you give to obtain it?'

Harun al-Rashid replied without hesitation: 'By heavens, I would give half of my entire empire!'

The sage said: 'Drink, O Caliph, and may it be pleasant to your health.'

When the Caliph had drained the crystal goblet, the sage asked a second question: 'And if, through an affliction of the body, this water could not pass from your veins, causing you agonizing pain and threatening your life, what portion of your kingdom would you give to be relieved?'

The Caliph answered: 'I would give the remaining half of my empire!'

Ibn al-Sammak smiled with gentle philosophical authority: 'Then, O Commander of the Faithful, why do you boast of an empire whose total value in the balance of life is worth no more than a single cup of water and its release?'

Harun al-Rashid wept bitter tears of humility, recognized the fragility of earthly splendor, and treated the sage as his closest spiritual counselor.
moral: An entire empire of gold is worth less than a single cup of clear water in the hour of desperate thirst.

full_text:
Following the civil war in Baghdad that brought Caliph Al-Ma'mun to the throne, a lingering shadow of sorrow lay between the young monarch and his stepmother, Queen Zubaydah. The palace was quiet, and courtiers feared that political grudges would sever the royal family forever.

Caliph Al-Ma'mun, who possessed a profound intellect and revered wisdom above martial triumph, visited Queen Zubaydah in her private garden pavilion.

Instead of approaching with imperial haughtiness, the Caliph knelt before her, kissed her hands, and said: 'Mother, the storms of politics have passed, but the sacred bond of family remains. Forgive whatever sorrow the turns of destiny have brought upon your heart.'

Queen Zubaydah looked upon the young ruler with tears in her eyes. Perceiving the absolute sincerity of his humility, her heart melted.

She engaged him in an intellectual dialogue on the governance of the Abbasid empire, discussing the translation of Greek and Persian sciences, the construction of universities, and the expansion of the public aqueducts she had established in Mecca.

Al-Ma'mun listened with deep reverence, adopting her counsels and granting her complete authority over the imperial charitable endowments.

Their reconciliation brought radiant peace to Baghdad, demonstrating that when intellect and family love unite, the deepest political wounds are transformed into fountains of enduring progress.
moral: Intellectual discourse, mutual forgiveness, and family harmony heal the bitterest political rifts.

title: Al-Nu'uman and the Arab of the Banu Tay
summary: King Al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir of Al-Hirah had instituted two ceremonial days in his court: a Day of Grace, on which he enriched whoever a...
keywords: al-nu'uman and the arab of the banu tay
full_text:
King Al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir of Al-Hirah had instituted two ceremonial days in his court: a Day of Grace, on which he enriched whoever appeared before him, and a Day of Wrath, on which the first stranger to cross his path was condemned to death.

On a Day of Wrath, an honest, impoverished Bedouin of the Banu Tayy, who knew nothing of the royal decree, walked into the palace grounds carrying two dead partridges to sell to the royal kitchens.

The king frowned with sorrow, for he had sworn an oath: 'Stranger, the law of my Day of Wrath condemns you to the scaffold! Ask whatever favor you desire before you perish.'

The Bedouin stood with calm dignity: 'O King, I have three infant daughters and an aged mother starving in the desert; I have debts unpaid. Grant me a reprieve of one single year to settle my affairs, and by the Creator of the heavens, I swear to return on this exact day to face your sword.'

The king asked: 'Who will stand as your surety with his life if you fail to return?'

A noble courtier named Qarad stood forward: 'I will be his surety, sire.'

A year passed. On the appointed Day of Wrath, the scaffold was prepared, and Qarad was led out to be executed in place of the absent Bedouin.

Just as the sword was raised, a horseman appeared running across the plain—it was the Bedouin, covered in dust, arriving on the exact hour!

Al-Nu'man was struck with awe: 'Why did you return to death?' The Bedouin replied: 'So that no man should ever say that fidelity has perished among the Arabs!'

The king turned to Qarad: 'And why did you vouch for him?' Qarad replied: 'So that none should say generosity has died!'

The king wept, threw down his sword, abolished the cruel Day of Wrath forever, and rewarded both noble men with royal honors.
moral: Desert fidelity to one’s sacred word inspires universal mercy and turns execution into celebration.

title: Firuz and His Wife

full_text:
Firuz was an honorable and trusted minister of state in ancient Persia, whose wife was celebrated across the capital for her peerless beauty, modest dignity, and intelligence.

One afternoon, the King, while riding through the city, stopped before Firuz’s mansion and asked for a cup of water. Firuz’s wife received her monarch with serene composure, served him cool water from behind the lattice, and spoke with such refined elegance that the King was tempted by selfish desire.

However, the noble lady smiled with dignified gravity and said: 'Sire, if an imperial lion enters a humble gazelle’s garden, will he trample the delicate lilies, or will his royal majesty protect the flowers from the wild beasts?'

The King was struck to his soul by the delicate reprimand. Filled with shame, he left his royal ring upon the divan as a token of reverence and departed with clean hands.

When Firuz returned, he found the King’s ring, and dark suspicions troubled his mind; he withdrew from his wife in silence.

The lady brought the matter before the King’s public tribunal in an allegorical petition: 'O King! I possessed a fertile garden which I tended with honor. A lion entered my garden and departed without breaking a single reed; yet my husband refuses to enter his orchard in fear of the lion’s paw!'

The King stood before the court and declared: 'The lion entered your garden, O lady, and found it guarded by angels of virtue; he departed with bowed head! Let your husband return with joyous pride.'

Firuz understood the truth, embraced his virtuous wife, and praised the wisdom that had preserved their domestic honor.
moral: Delicate allegories of honor and mutual respect preserve the sanctity of the home.

Following the King's public proclamation in the tribunal, Firuz and his wife returned to their garden mansion, their bond of affection and trust strengthened tenfold by the trial they had endured.

Firuz took his wife’s hands and asked with sincere humility: 'Forgive me, dear companion! Why did you bring the matter before the public tribunal rather than speaking to me in private?'

His wife smiled with profound wisdom and replied: 'O husband, a private whisper in the bedchamber might have left a lingering shadow of doubt in your heart, and slanderous tongues in the bazaar would have whispered that the King’s visit had compromised our honor.

By bringing our cause before the open assembly in the language of noble allegory, the King himself was compelled to stand as witness to my virtue, your honor was vindicated before all the ministers, and the sanctity of our household was established as a fortress of light.'

Firuz bowed before her extraordinary intellect and discernment. He realized that a wife endowed with moral courage and sharp wit is a greater treasure than all the jewels in the royal treasury.

The King appointed Firuz Grand Chancellor of the realm, and their home became a celebrated sanctuary where young couples came to learn that mutual respect, open truth, and moral dignity are the true foundations of enduring joy.
moral: A household founded on mutual trust and moral courage cannot be shaken by the greatest powers.

title: King Shah Bakht and his Wazir Al-Rahwan
summary: King Shah Bakht of Persia was an energetic and valiant monarch, but his fiery temper often led him to issue hasty decrees of punishment. ...
keywords: king shah bakht and his wazir al-rahwan
full_text:
King Shah Bakht of Persia was an energetic and valiant monarch, but his fiery temper often led him to issue hasty decrees of punishment. In his court served a Grand Vizier of sublime philosophical learning named Al-Rahwan, who had resolved to train the monarch’s mind in the virtues of deliberation.

Whenever an urgent or controversial case was brought before the royal tribunal, Al-Rahwan would step forward and say: 'Sire, before the sword of judgment is drawn, listen to an ancient history of how past rulers resolved this exact dilemma with wisdom.'

For months, Al-Rahwan related a cycle of philosophical tales—tales of merchants, judges, travelers, and kings—illustrating how hasty wrath brings lifelong regret, while patient investigation reveals hidden truth.

King Shah Bakht listened with fascinated delight, finding his hasty impulses calmed and his understanding deepened with every passing narrative.

He realized that an empire cannot be sustained by the sword alone; it requires the balance of equity, the testing of evidence, and the gentle touch of mercy.

The king established a supreme council of appeal, revoked unjust decrees, and ruled for forty years in unbroken prosperity, proclaiming that his vizier Al-Rahwan’s tales had transformed a fiery conqueror into a father of his people.
moral: A wise minister uses parables of justice to guide his monarch away from hasty decisions.

title: Tale of the Man of Khorasan His Son and His Tutor
summary: An affluent merchant of Khorasan entrusted his only son, Farhad, to an eminent tutor, saying: 'Instruct my son in all the sciences of the...
keywords: tale of the man of khorasan his son and his tutor
full_text:
An affluent merchant of Khorasan entrusted his only son, Farhad, to an eminent tutor, saying: 'Instruct my son in all the sciences of the world, and spare no expense.'

For seven years, the tutor instructed the youth in astronomy, Greek logic, mathematics, and classical rhetoric. At the end of that time, the tutor brought the young man back to his father, boasting: 'Behold, your son is a master of all knowledge! He can debate philosophers and calculate the orbits of the stars.'

The father smiled, placed a simple brass ring in his closed fist, and said to his son: 'You who understand the stars, tell me what is hidden within my hand.'

The son closed his eyes, calculated the astrological alignments, and declared: 'Father, it is round, it has a hole in the center, and it is made of metal.'

The father marveled: 'Flawless! And what is the object?'

The youth thought for a moment and said: 'It must be a stone water-mill for grinding wheat!'

The father looked at his small closed fist, and then at the pedantic tutor with a sorrowful smile: 'Your logic can deduce that it is round and made of metal, yet your common sense fails to see that a water-mill cannot fit inside a human hand!

You have filled my son’s head with abstract formulas, but you have left him devoid of practical sense, observation, and humble reality.'

The father took his son to the agricultural fields, apprenticing him to honest builders and farmers, having learned that true education begins where abstract vanity ends.
moral: True education trains the heart in empathy and honor, not merely the head in theoretical vanity.

title: Tale of the Singer and the Druggist
summary: In a quiet quarter of Cairo lived an impoverished young musician named Tariq, whose voice upon the lute was sweet as running water, and a...

full_text:
In a quiet quarter of Cairo lived an impoverished young musician named Tariq, whose voice upon the lute was sweet as running water, and an honest herbal druggist named Abu Ahmad, whose shop was filled with fragrant jars of camphor, myrrh, and dried chamomile.

Whenever Tariq was penniless, the kind druggist fed him warm bread and lentils, never demanding payment, saying: 'Sing me a verse of your homeland, brother; your melody is a medicine for my soul richer than all the balsams of Arabia.'

One winter, a royal courier from Baghdad arrived in Cairo, seeking the finest musician in Egypt for the court of the Caliph. Tariq was chosen, taken to the Abbasid palace, and rewarded with robes of honor and three thousand gold dinars.

Instead of forgetting his humble beginnings, Tariq’s first thought was of the honest druggist who had shared his bread.

He returned to Cairo with four mules laden with silks, porcelain, and two thousand gold dinars, presenting them to Abu Ahmad before all the merchants of the bazaar:

'Ten years ago, you gave me medicine for my body and belief in my art; today, I return to repay your bread with gold!'

Abu Ahmad embraced the young master with tears of joy. Together, they established a free clinic and music conservatory for the poor youth of Cairo, proving that true friendship and gratitude are the highest virtues of civilization.
moral: Kindness and mutual support between humble artisans create a bond that outlasts fortune.

title: Tale of the King Who Kenned the Quintessence
summary: A wise King of ancient Persia possessed an extraordinary gift of natural discernment: he could examine any object or person and determine...
keywords: tale of the king who kenned the quintessence
full_text:
A wise King of ancient Persia possessed an extraordinary gift of natural discernment: he could examine any object or person and determine its essential inner quality, whether genuine or counterfeit.

Three gifts were presented before his throne: a magnificent diamond, a fiery Arabian war-steed, and a brilliant foreign scholar who sought the office of Grand Vizier.

The king examined the diamond, which sparkled like a star: 'This stone appears pure, but in its center rests an invisible worm that gnaws the mineral.' When the stone was split, a tiny fossilized insect was discovered in the core!

The king examined the war-steed: 'This stallion is swift as the wind, but he was nourished on the milk of a cow, and in the heat of battle, he will look for pasture rather than charging the enemy.' The royal grooms investigated and confirmed that the colt’s mother had died at birth and he had been raised on cow’s milk!

Finally, the king looked at the brilliant foreign scholar, whose rhetoric was dazzling: 'This man has memorized ten thousand books, but his inner essence is corrupt; he values gold above truth, and will betray the state when temptation arises.'

The king’s ministers were astonished and asked: 'Sire, how did you perceive his essence?'

The king answered: 'When I offered him a robe of honor, his eyes did not look at the embroidery; they looked at the weight of the gold threads! A man who calculates coin while discussing justice has a soul of brass, no matter how silver his tongue may be.'

The king appointed only those whose character was pure, ruling his realm with peerless equity.
moral: True discernment looks past outward pedigree and appearances to judge the inner reality of character.

title: Tale of the Richard Who Married His Beautiful Daughter to the Poor Old Man
summary: An affluent merchant of Baghdad had an only daughter named Salma, whose beauty was matched by her profound learning in literature, mathem...
keywords: tale of the richard who married his beautiful daughter to the poor old man
full_text:
An affluent merchant of Baghdad had an only daughter named Salma, whose beauty was matched by her profound learning in literature, mathematics, and ethics. Wealthy young emirs and boastful merchants courted her with gifts of pearls and golden carriages, but Salma rejected them all, seeking a husband whose character was steadfast and pure.

Her father, sharing her wisdom, visited the Great Academy of Baghdad and observed an elderly, modest scholar named Abu Bakr, who taught the poor without fee and lived in quiet contentment.

The merchant invited the scholar to his mansion and offered him his daughter’s hand in marriage with a handsome dowry!

The neighbors were astonished, mocking the merchant: 'Why do you bestow your radiant young daughter upon a poor, gray-bearded scholar, when wealthy young emirs knock upon your gate?'

The merchant replied with calm authority: 'I looked upon the young emirs, and I saw men whose wealth was inherited, whose minds were empty, and whose pride would bring domestic tyranny into my home.

I looked upon this scholar, and I saw a man of unshakeable integrity, gentle speech, and profound wisdom. If my daughter weeps, he will comfort her with philosophy; if misfortune strikes, his faith will sustain her; and in his house, she will be an honored queen, not a gilded toy.'

Salma and the scholar lived in radiant intellectual and domestic harmony for thirty years, proving that a marriage founded on character and wisdom outlasts all the fleeting illusions of youth and gold.
moral: Choose character, wisdom, and moral integrity over mere youth and fleeting gold.

title: Tale of the Sage and His Three Sons
summary: A venerable sage of Shiraz, feeling his earthly life drawing to its close, called his three sons to his bedside. He pointed to three lock...
keywords: tale of the sage and his three sons
full_text:
A venerable sage of Shiraz, feeling his earthly life drawing to its close, called his three sons to his bedside. He pointed to three locked cedarwood chests standing in the corner of his library, and said:

'My sons, I leave you neither gold mines nor estates, for earthly wealth vanishes like smoke. In these three chests, I leave you the three treasures that sustained my soul through eighty seasons of life. Take each his chest, and open them only when I am laid beneath the cypress trees.'

When the sage was buried, the three sons opened the chests.

The eldest son opened the first chest: inside rested a master carpenter’s bronze compass and drawing instruments, with a scroll inscribed: 'Build for others; honest labor with your hands is an armor against poverty.'

The second son opened the second chest: inside lay a balance scale of brass with twenty-four standard weights, with a scroll inscribed: 'Measure with absolute justice; equity in commerce wins the trust of nations.'

The youngest son opened the third chest: inside lay a mirror of polished silver and a blank leather-bound book, with a scroll inscribed: 'Examine your own soul daily before you judge your brother; and write in this book only those deeds of charity that make the world sweeter.'

The three brothers embraced, took their treasures, and built three thriving, honorable lives: the first as a master builder, the second as a fair merchant, and the third as a beloved philosopher, demonstrating that true inheritance is the cultivation of the soul.
moral: The greatest inheritance a parent can bestow is the legacy of ethical wisdom, compassion, and honest labor.

title: Tale of the Prince who Fell in Love With the Picture
summary: Prince Farhad of Persia discovered in an ancient ivory cabinet an exquisitely painted miniature portrait of a maiden of breathtaking beau...

full_text:
Prince Farhad of Persia discovered in an ancient ivory cabinet an exquisitely painted miniature portrait of a maiden of breathtaking beauty. Captivated by the painted eyes, the prince neglected his studies, refused food, and vowed to travel the ends of the earth to find the living original.

After two years of wandering through India and China, he arrived at the court of the King of the White Isles, where he discovered that the original of the portrait was Princess Niloufar.

However, when he entered her presence, he was bitterly disappointed: the princess was proud, vain, spoke with cruel sarcasm to her servants, and cared only for her own reflection in mirrors!

Disillusioned and grieving, Farhad left the palace and walked through the city gardens. There he met Princess Niloufar’s younger sister, Princess Parisa, who was not portrayed in royal miniatures, but who spent her days reading books, nursing wounded birds, and managing schools for orphan children.

As they spoke, Farhad discovered a soul of sublime intelligence, gentle wit, and radiant compassion.

He realized his youthful folly: 'I chased a painted phantom of vanity, while the true pearl of the kingdom was walking quietly in the garden!'

Farhad sought Princess Parisa’s hand in marriage, celebrating a union founded on genuine character, proving that real beauty resides in the living virtues of the heart, not on painted parchment.
moral: Do not fall in love with a painted shadow; seek the living reality of character and virtue.

title: Tale of the Fuller and His Wife and the Trooper
summary: Beside the river Barada in Damascus lived an honest cloth-washer and his witty wife, who earned their living washing carpets and linens. ...
keywords: tale of the fuller and his wife and the trooper
full_text:
Beside the river Barada in Damascus lived an honest cloth-washer and his witty wife, who earned their living washing carpets and linens. One afternoon, a boastful cavalry trooper rode his horse into their drying meadow, trampling their clean white linens and threatening to strike the fuller with his scabbard if he did not wash his muddy saddlecloth immediately without pay.

The fuller was intimidated by the soldier’s sword, but his wife stepped forward with a cheerful smile:

'Welcome, valiant warrior! A hero of your martial renown deserves to have his saddlecloth washed in our special imperial soap-vat, which preserves the leather forever. But our vat is deep; if you will hold this willow pole and stir the boiling suds, the honor will be completed in an instant!'

The vain trooper, flattered by her praise, dismounted, leaned over the stone soap-vat, and began to stir the foam.

Quick as lightning, the fuller’s wife gave the soldier’s heavy boots a sudden shove! The boastful trooper plunged headfirst into the warm soapy suds, spluttering, soaked in foam from head to toe, his iron helmet clattering like an empty pot!

The fuller seized the soldier’s horse by the bridle, while his wife called for the city watchmen.

When the magistrate arrived, he laughed heartily at the dripping 'hero' who had been conquered by a bucket of soap, fined the trooper twenty dinars for damaging the clean linens, and awarded the money to the fuller, teaching the arrogant soldier that bullying working folk brings slippery consequences.
moral: Quiet common sense and presence of mind can outsmart the most arrogant bully.

title: Tale of the Merchant The Crone and the King
summary: A wealthy merchant of Cairo entrusted a sealed leather pouch containing a magnificent ruby worth twenty thousand dinars to an old woman w...

full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Cairo entrusted a sealed leather pouch containing a magnificent ruby worth twenty thousand dinars to an old woman who lived near the Great Mosque, believing her to be an ascetic saint.

Upon his return from Mecca, he asked for his pouch; the old woman returned the leather bag, but when the merchant opened the seal, he found only a polished red glass bead in place of his ruby!

The old woman wept and shrieked, accusing the merchant of slandering a pious widow. The citizens took her part, and the merchant was driven away.

The merchant brought his suit before the Sultan. The Sultan summoned the old woman, but rather than threatening her with torture, he engaged her in pleasant conversation, offering her sweetmeats and a cup of mint tea.

While she drank, the Sultan quietly observed her hands: her fingernails were stained with green lapidary wax, and in her sleeve rested a jeweler’s brass file!

The Sultan suddenly said: 'O mother, my royal jeweler has lost his finest cutting tool; will you lend me that file in your sleeve to trim my signet ring?'

The old woman turned pale as ashes, realizing that her trade as a counterfeit gem-cutter was exposed!

The Sultan sent guards to search her cellar, where they unearthed the merchant’s real ruby, along with fifty counterfeit glass stones.

The ruby was restored to the merchant, the old woman was sentenced to repay all her victims, and the city praised the Sultan’s keen observation, which had seen through the guise of false piety.
moral: Keen judicial observation and testing subtle habits expose the craftiest thief.

title: Tale of the Simpleton Husband
summary: In a village near Baghdad lived a simple, credulous farmer named Abu Bakr, whose gullibility was legendary across the district: if someon...
full_text:
In a village near Baghdad lived a simple, credulous farmer named Abu Bakr, whose gullibility was legendary across the district: if someone told him that donkeys laid golden eggs, he would spend three days checking the stables with a basket.

One morning, two mischievous youths resolved to test his credulity to the uttermost. One climbed into the hollow trunk of an ancient hollow oak tree, while the other waited beside the road.

When Abu Bakr passed with his mule, the youth shouted: 'Halt, Abu Bakr! The ancient Tree of Whispers is speaking your name!'

From within the hollow trunk, a deep, ghostly voice echoed: 'O Abu Bakr! Listen to the voice of destiny! Climb onto the highest branch of this oak, tie your ears together with your woollen turban, and crow like a rooster three times, and a pot of gold shall rain down from the sky!'

Abu Bakr did not pause for a second’s reflection. He tied his mule, scrambled up the oak tree, tied his turban around his ears, flapped his elbows, and began crowing with all his might: 'Cock-a-doodle-doo!'

A crowd of villagers, returning from the market, gathered beneath the tree in utter astonishment, laughing until tears rolled down their cheeks!

The village elder walked up and called: 'Abu Bakr! Are you laying an egg, or has the midday sun boiled your wits?'

Abu Bakr looked down, saw the two laughing youths running away with his mule’s pack-saddle, and realized with burning shame that he had been made the fool of the district.

He climbed down from the tree, embraced the laughter of his neighbors, and resolved never again to believe voices from trees before consulting his own common sense.
moral: Gullibility that believes every absurd tale makes a man a laughingstock; test rumors with reason.

title: Tale of the Simpleton Husband
summary: In an isolated mountain village where polished glass was unknown, an honest peasant named Mansur visited the city of Aleppo for the first...
full_text:
In an isolated mountain village where polished glass was unknown, an honest peasant named Mansur visited the city of Aleppo for the first time. In the bazaar, he found a small silver pocket mirror dropped by a traveling merchant.

Mansur picked up the mirror, looked into the polished surface, and gasped in astonishment: 'Praise be to heaven! It is a portrait of my beloved late father, looking young and handsome as in his youth!'

He kissed the glass with filial devotion, wrapped it in silk, and hid it in a cedar chest beneath his bed, visiting it secretly every evening to speak to 'his father.'

His wife, noticing his secretive visits to the chest, waited until Mansur went to the fields, unlocked the coffer, and looked into the mirror!

She shrieked in horror: 'Aha! The traitor has hidden the portrait of an ugly, scowling rival woman inside my chest!'

She ran weeping to the village judge, demanding a divorce!

The judge took the silver mirror, looked into the surface, stroked his long white beard, and frowned with solemn authority: 'Woman, your jealousy has blinded your eyes! This is neither a rival woman nor his father; this is a sacred portrait of the Chief Judge of Aleppo, wearing a splendid scholar’s turban!'

The village schoolmaster entered the courtroom, saw the dispute, laughed heartily, and explained the scientific mystery of reflection.

He held the mirror before the husband, wife, and judge together, showing them their own faces laughing in the glass!

The couple embraced in joyful relief, learning that ignorance creates monsters out of shadows, while knowledge brings light and peace.
moral: Ignorance creates imaginary rivals out of ordinary objects; knowledge dispels baseless fears.

title: Tale of the Unjust King and the Tither
summary: An oppressive King of ancient Yemen appointed an unscrupulous tax-collector named Kardan, with orders to collect a tithe of one-tenth of ...

full_text:
An oppressive King of ancient Yemen appointed an unscrupulous tax-collector named Kardan, with orders to collect a tithe of one-tenth of every harvest, herd, and catch of fish across the realm.

Kardan, seeking to enrich himself, increased the tithes to one-third, then one-half, seizing the milk-cows of farmers, the nets of fishermen, and the looms of weavers. Within three years, the farmers ceased to plow, the fishermen abandoned their boats, and the markets of Yemen were deserted.

Famine struck the capital, and the royal treasury ran dry.

One morning, an honest old farmer entered the royal audience hall carrying an empty wooden basket. He placed the basket before the throne and said:

'O King! Look upon this basket. Three years ago, it was filled with sweet figs, and your tither took two figs, leaving eighteen for my children; we ate, prospered, and planted ten new trees.

Last year, your tither took fifteen figs, leaving five; my children hungered, and we could not buy water.

This year, your tither came to seize all the figs, but finding my trees dead of drought, he cut down the wood for his hearth! Now my orchard is dead, your basket is empty, and both you and I must starve together!'

The words struck the King like an iron hammer. He looked at his empty treasury, looked at the ruined countryside, and realized that by destroying the producers, he had destroyed his own crown.

The King dismissed the greedy tither, abolished the oppressive taxes, and distributed free seeds from the royal granaries, learning that a kingdom flourishes only when its producers are allowed to thrive.
moral: Oppressive taxation that bleeds the productive laborer destroys the prosperity of the commonwealth.

title: Story of David and Solomon
summary: Two men appeared before King David in Jerusalem to settle a bitter dispute. The first was an honest farmer whose lush vineyard was heavy ...
full_text:
Two men appeared before King David in Jerusalem to settle a bitter dispute. The first was an honest farmer whose lush vineyard was heavy with ripening purple grapes; the second was a shepherd whose flock of sheep had broken into the vineyard at night, trampling the vines and devouring the entire crop.

King David, hearing that the damage equaled the value of the sheep, judged according to strict law: 'Let the flock of sheep be forfeited and given to the vineyard owner to compensate for his lost harvest.'

Young Solomon, who sat beside the throne, bowed respectfully and said: 'O father, with your royal leave, may I suggest a judgment that contains both justice and mercy?'

David smiled: 'Speak, Solomon.'

Solomon said: 'Let the vineyard owner take the sheep for one year: he shall enjoy their milk, their wool, and their newborn lambs to nourish his family. Meanwhile, let the shepherd take the ruined vineyard: he shall water the soil, prune the vines, and cultivate the land with his own labor until the vines bear purple grapes once more!

At the end of the year, let the vineyard be returned to the farmer, and let the flock of sheep be returned to the shepherd!'

King David marveled at his son’s profound equity: 'Your judgment is greater than mine, Solomon! Strict law merely transfers property, but your wisdom restores the loss while teaching the offender to repair his wrong with honest labor.'

The two men embraced with joyful gratitude, and the judgment of Solomon became an eternal model of restorative justice across all nations.
moral: True justice repairs the injury of the victim while preserving the livelihood of the offender.

keywords: tale of the robber and the woman
full_text:
A hardened burglar in Baghdad scaled the wall of an isolated house at midnight, intending to steal gold and silver. Slipping through the courtyard, he entered a modest chamber where a single oil wick illuminated a bed.

Upon the bed lay a sick child, pale with fever, while beside the couch knelt a young mother, weeping as she prayed in the darkness:

'O Merciful Creator! You who nourish the birds in the winter storm, look upon my child! I have no medicine, no coin for the physician, and no bread in the larder; yet I trust in Your boundless compassion to deliver my little one.'

The burglar stood in the shadows, his hand resting upon his iron pry-bar. His heart was struck with an agonizing pang of conscience: 'Shall I rob a house where hunger and disease have already entered? Shall I be worse than the wolves of the wilderness?'

Tears welled in the robber’s eyes. He took off his heavy leather purse containing fifty silver dirhams—the fruit of his previous thefts—and placed it gently upon the table beside the medicine bottle.

He slipped out into the courtyard, leaving his purse behind, and climbed down into the street.

The next morning, the mother found the silver, bought medicine and nourishment, and her child was healed!

The burglar, transformed by the power of that midnight prayer, renounced crime forever, took service with an honest blacksmith, and dedicated his life to protecting the vulnerable, proving that conscience can awaken in the darkest hour.
moral: The sincere prayer of an innocent soul can melt the hardest heart and inspire genuine repentance.

title: Tale of the Three Men and Our Lord Isa

keywords: tale of the three men and our lord isa
full_text:
Three travelers walking along an ancient desert trail discovered a heavy earthenware jar buried in the sand, overflowing with sparkling gold coins left behind by a forgotten caravan.

Overjoyed, they agreed to divide the gold equally among themselves. But having traveled all day in the heat, they were starving.

They sent the youngest traveler to the neighboring village to purchase bread, meat, and sweet cordials, while the two elder travelers guarded the treasure.

As the youth walked to the village, greed entered his soul: 'Why should I share this gold with two old men? If I put poison in their bread, all the treasure will be mine alone!' He purchased food, and mixed a potent, tasteless poison into the meat.

Meanwhile, sitting beside the gold jar, the two elder companions whispered together: 'Why should we divide the gold three ways? When the youth returns, let us strike him down with our staves, and divide the gold between the two of us!'

When the young traveler returned carrying the food, the two elders sprang upon him, struck him down, and buried his body in the sand.

They then sat down upon the treasure, laughed at their cleverness, and devoured the roasted meat and bread with greedy relish.

Within an hour, the poison took effect! The two elder companions collapsed upon the heap of gold, writhing in agony, perishing beside the treasure they had murdered to possess.

A venerable sage passing by saw the three lifeless bodies lying around the jar of gold, and said: 'Behold the bitter harvest of greed! The gold remains upon the sand, untouched and worthless, while the souls of those who coveted it have perished in their own snares.'
moral: Greed turns companions into murderers; he who schemes to hoard gold for himself brings his own ruin.

title: The Disciple's Story
summary: A young student who had studied for ten years in the universities of Cairo traveled to the desert hermitage of an ancient master of wisdo...
full_text:
A young student who had studied for ten years in the universities of Cairo traveled to the desert hermitage of an ancient master of wisdom, boasting: 'Master, I have read all the commentaries, mastered the seventy philosophical systems, and memorized twenty thousand traditions! Teach me now the final secret of wisdom.'

The master looked upon the proud youth with gentle eyes, and handed him a heavy earthen water jar and a broom: 'The well is half a league away in the rocky gorge. Fetch water for the travelers, sweep the courtyard every morning, and wash the sandals of the pilgrims who enter our gate.'

The student was indignant: 'I came to debate the mysteries of the cosmos, not to sweep floors like a common servant!'

The master smiled serenely: 'He whose vessel is already brimming over with the muddy water of pride cannot receive the pure wine of wisdom. Empty your cup, and then it may be filled.'

For three years, the student carried water and swept the courtyard. As his calloused hands laboured and his pride melted away, he observed the silent patience of nature, the gratitude of weary travelers, and the peace of humble service.

At the end of three years, the master called him and said: 'Now, my son, you are ready to speak.'

The student bowed with genuine humility: 'Master, I have learned that true wisdom is not a crown of words to be worn for the praise of men, but a towel of service to wipe away the tears of the world.'
moral: True spiritual understanding is found in practicing humility, not in the intellectual pride of books.

title: Tale of the Dethroned Ruler
summary: A powerful King of Persia was deposed in a military coup and forced to flee his capital in disguise. Having escaped with his life, he pur...
full_text:
A powerful King of Persia was deposed in a military coup and forced to flee his capital in disguise. Having escaped with his life, he purchased a small, secluded orchard of apricot and olive trees in a distant province, earning his bread by his own manual labor.

For ten years, he pruned his trees, channeled mountain spring water to the roots, harvested the fruit, and sold it in the local village market.

One afternoon, an old courtier who had served in his former palace passed through the orchard and recognized the former monarch, dressed in a coarse linen tunic and wooden clogs.

The courtier wept with pity: 'Alas, my royal master! What a tragic fate! You who once sat upon a golden throne and commanded armies now shovel earth around apricot trees!'

The former king smiled with radiant serenity, wiped the sweat from his brow, and offered his old courtier a basket of sweet, ripe apricots:

'Do not weep for me, old friend! When I wore that golden crown, I slept with a naked sword beneath my pillow, terrified of assassins; every courtier was a flatterer, every feast was poisoned by suspicion, and my soul was a prisoner of anxiety.

Today, my bread is earned with clean hands; my sleep is as sweet as childhood, the birds in my trees sing without flattery, and my heart knows peace.

I did not lose a kingdom; I was delivered from a gilded prison to become the sovereign of my own soul.'
moral: The true kingdom is peace of soul; earthly crowns bring anxiety, while honest labor brings sweet sleep.

title: Talk of the Man Whose Caution Slew Him
summary: In Damascus lived an affluent gentleman named Abu Bakr, whose terror of illness, accidents, and death grew into a ridiculous, debilitatin...
keywords: talk of the man whose caution slew him
full_text:
In Damascus lived an affluent gentleman named Abu Bakr, whose terror of illness, accidents, and death grew into a ridiculous, debilitating mania. He refused to walk in the bazaar for fear of falling roof-tiles; he refused to eat fruit for fear of insects; and he refused to drink water unless it had been boiled seven times and filtered through silk!

One winter, fearing that the drafty winds would give him a fatal chill, Abu Bakr constructed an airtight chamber of polished cedar inside his mansion. He sealed every window with wax, caulked every seam of the doors with felt, built a roaring charcoal furnace in the center, and shut himself within!

'Here at last,' chuckled the paranoid man, 'no draft can touch me, no cold air can reach my chest, and I am completely safe from all the perils of nature!'

However, because the chamber was completely airtight and the charcoal furnace burned without ventilation, the air was depleted of life within two hours!

When his servants finally forced open the cedar door, they found Abu Bakr lying unconscious upon his cushions, having nearly suffocated himself in his desperate attempt to avoid a common breeze!

The physician revived him with cold water and fresh air, saying: 'O Abu Bakr! Prudence is a virtue, but excessive fear is a sickness that creates the very disaster it dreads. Walk in the open sunshine, breathe the clean air, and trust the heavens, for a life lived in a box is not life at all.'
moral: Excessive, paranoid anxiety destroys life in the very effort to preserve it; live with balanced faith.

title: Tale of the Man Who Was Lavish

full_text:
In the city of Basra lived an affluent merchant named Mansur who was celebrated for his open-handed hospitality. For thirty years, his doors stood open to travelers, he paid the debts of bankrupt craftsmen, and provided dowries for the daughters of impoverished widows, never asking for repayment.

A disastrous fire swept through the harbor, destroying Mansur’s warehouses, his ships, and his home, leaving the noble elder without a single silver dirham.

Mansur sat upon the steps of the Great Mosque, his head bowed, preparing to endure his poverty with silent dignity.

Word of his misfortune spread through the bazaars of Basra.

Within three hours, an extraordinary sight was seen: hundreds of citizens—bakers, carpenters, weavers, fishermen, and wealthy merchants—gathered in the square!

Each brought what he could: the wealthy merchants brought bags of gold; the weavers brought bolts of cloth; the carpenters brought timber and tools; and the poor laborers brought their copper coins, saying: 'When we were in despair, Mansur’s hand lifted us up; today, the city shall rebuild Mansur’s house!'

Before sunset, Mansur stood surrounded by thirty thousand dinars, his warehouses were rebuilt by volunteer labor, and his ships were restored by the shipbuilders guild!

Mansur wept with joyful gratitude, learning that the gold you hoard in iron vaults is lost in an hour, but the generosity you invest in the hearts of your community is an eternal fortress that no fire can ever destroy.
moral: Bread cast upon the waters of hospitality returns as an unbreakable fortress of community support.

title: Tale of the Melancholist and the Sharper
summary: In the city of Basra lived an affluent merchant named Abu Ali, who fell into such a deep and persistent melancholy that he ceased to smil...
keywords: tale of the melancholist and the sharper
full_text:
In the city of Basra lived an affluent merchant named Abu Ali, who fell into such a deep and persistent melancholy that he ceased to smile, closed his shop, and sat in his courtyard wrapped in black wool, weeping for no reason whatsoever. All the physicians of Basra prescribed bitter herb broths and bloodletting, but Abu Ali’s gloom only deepened.

A merry, traveling sharper from Cairo named Juha arrived in the city, heard of the merchant’s condition, and knocked upon his gate, claiming: 'I am a master physician who cures grief with a single word!'

Juha sat before the melancholic merchant, took out a polished brass whistle, and began to recount a series of the most preposterous, whimsical, and comical misadventures: of a donkey that sued his master for back wages, of a baker who baked a loaf of bread so large it had to be delivered on a four-wheeled cart with a team of oxen, and of a pompous magistrate who sat upon a basket of eggs!

Juha acted out every role with hilarious gestures, mimicking the voices with such razor-sharp timing and absurd dignity that Abu Ali’s lips twitched.

Suddenly, Abu Ali burst into a roaring, uncontrollable shout of laughter! He laughed until his turban slipped, tears of joy streamed down his cheeks, and his chest felt light as the morning breeze.

The black cloud of gloom evaporated from his spirit forever.

Abu Ali rewarded Juha with five hundred gold dinars, reopened his business, and declared that a spoonful of genuine laughter is worth ten thousand apothecary jars of bitter medicine.
moral: Laughter, good humor, and shared human sympathy are the truest medicines for melancholy.

title: Tale of Khalbas and his Wife and the Learned Man
summary: In Damascus lived an honest weaver named Khalbas, whose wife was celebrated for her sharp practical wit and domestic management. A self-i...

full_text:
In Damascus lived an honest weaver named Khalbas, whose wife was celebrated for her sharp practical wit and domestic management. A self-important traveling scholar visited their home, boasting loudly at the supper table of his supreme erudition in logic and philosophy, treating the weaver and his wife as ignorant peasants.

The scholar pontificated: 'Through logic, I can prove that the two roasted pigeons upon this platter are actually three!'

The wife smiled pleasantly: 'Show us your demonstration, learned master.'

The scholar declared: 'Here is the first pigeon, and here is the second pigeon; and one added to two equals three! Therefore, there are three pigeons upon the platter!'

The wife immediately took the first pigeon and placed it on her husband’s plate, saying: 'Khalbas, take the first pigeon.' She then took the second pigeon and placed it upon her own plate: 'And I shall take the second pigeon.'

She then turned to the astonished scholar with a courteous smile: 'And you, learned master, may feast upon the third pigeon that your logic has created!'

The scholar sat before his empty plate, blushing with profound shame amidst the hearty laughter of the household.

He apologized for his pedantic arrogance, and the wife generously shared her meal with him, having taught him that philosophical logic must never lose touch with practical reality and humble manners.
moral: A household thrives on mutual respect and shared intellect, not arrogant displays of pedantry.

full_text:
An elderly hermit who had spent forty years tending a mountain shrine in Syria was framed by a corrupt tax-collector who had stolen a jeweled gold chalice from the municipal sanctuary. The tax-collector hid the chalice in the hermit’s cave, brought the guards, and accused the saintly elder of theft!

The mob gathered, ready to stone the hermit.

The old man stood with serene composure, looking at his accuser: 'If I am guilty, let the earth swallow me; but if I am innocent, let the chalice itself speak before this assembly!'

At that moment, the governor’s young son, who was playing with a hunting falcon nearby, stepped forward. The boy testified: 'Yesterday at sunset, while searching for my falcon, I saw this tax-collector climb the mountain path carrying a heavy sack under his cloak and enter the cave alone!'

The guards searched the tax-collector’s mule-bags and discovered the melted silver and jewels of other plundered shrines!

The corrupt official fell to his knees in terror, confessing his conspiracy.

The governor exonerated the saintly hermit with royal honors, punished the corrupt official, and rebuilt the mountain shrine, proving that an innocent life lived in truth is guarded by providence.
moral: Divine truth protects the innocent, and false accusations are dissolved by the light of evidence.

title: Tale of the Hireling and the Girl
summary: In a village near Aleppo, a wealthy landowner hired a young orphan laborer named Tariq to tend his olive groves and harvest the fruit. Wh...
keywords: tale of the hireling and the girl
full_text:
In a village near Aleppo, a wealthy landowner hired a young orphan laborer named Tariq to tend his olive groves and harvest the fruit. While the other laborers worked only when the overseer was watching, Tariq pruned every branch with dedicated skill, gathered every fallen olive, and watered the roots as if the orchard belonged to his own father.

The landowner, observing his quiet diligence from his terrace, resolved to test his integrity.

He placed an unsealed purse containing thirty gold dinars among the roots of an ancient olive tree where Tariq was digging an irrigation trench.

Tariq struck the leather pouch with his spade, picked it up, and saw the gleaming gold within. Without a second’s hesitation, he carried the purse immediately to the landowner’s mansion: 'Master, I found this purse buried beneath the third tree; someone has lost his treasure!'

The landowner smiled with tears of admiration: 'Tariq, that gold was placed there by my own hand to test your soul! A man who is faithful in the dust is worthy to manage an empire.'

The landowner adopted the honest orphan as his partner, gave him his virtuous daughter in marriage, and bequeathed him the vast olive estates, demonstrating that honest labor is the truest foundation of nobility.
moral: Conscientious labor performed with integrity in small matters earns the highest crown of trust.

title: Tale of the Weaver Who Became a Leach

full_text:
In Cairo lived an idle weaver named Abu Ali, who grew weary of his handloom. Seeing that the royal physician received hundred-dinar fees and rode a white mule caparisoned in velvet, Abu Ali threw away his shuttle, purchased a brass mortar, filled fifty glass vials with colored water and powdered chalk, and put up a sign: 'Master Physician of Ancient Sciences!'

His first patient was an elderly woman suffering from a common cold; Abu Ali prescribed warm chamomile tea and honey, and she recovered, spreading his fame!

Emboldened by accidental success, Abu Ali was summoned to the palace of the Grand Vizier to diagnose a mysterious ailment affecting the minister’s prize Arabian stallion.

Abu Ali examined the horse, pretended to read the stars, and declared with theatrical gravity: 'This stallion has a cold in his liver! He must be rubbed with hot mustard and fed thirty raw onions!'

The stallion ate the onions, sneezed with a mighty blast that knocked Abu Ali flat into the horse-trough, broke his halter, and galloped around the courtyard in a frenzy!

The chief royal veterinary surgeon arrived, examined the horse, and pulled a sharp thorn from the beast’s gum, instantly restoring the animal to peace.

The surgeon exposed Abu Ali’s fraudulent herbs before the entire court.

The vizier gave Abu Ali twenty lashes for his dangerous charlatanry and sent him back to his handloom, warning: 'Weave linen, fool, and leave medicine to those who have studied the anatomy of living creatures!'
moral: True medicine and science require disciplined study; ignorant pretension endangers human life.

title: Tale of the Two Sharpers Who Each Cozened His Compeer
summary: Two celebrated confidence tricksters—one from Cairo and the other from Damascus—met by chance at a roadside caravanserai near the Dead Se...
keywords: tale of the two sharpers who each cozened his compeer
full_text:
Two celebrated confidence tricksters—one from Cairo and the other from Damascus—met by chance at a roadside caravanserai near the Dead Sea. Each perceived that his companion was a master of the trade, and each resolved to swindle the other before sunset.

The Cairene sharper displayed a heavy leather bag filled with copper slugs coated in gold leaf, offering to sell it as a purse of pure dinars at a discount.

The Syrian sharper displayed an exquisite silk pouch supposedly filled with rare musk and ambergris, which was actually common clay perfumed with a drop of rosewater.

After an elaborate negotiation of solemn oaths, complimentary flattery, and mutual embraces, the trade was completed: the Cairene took the 'musk,' and the Syrian took the 'gold,' and both parted with immense secret satisfaction, each gloating over his victory.

At the next oasis, the Cairene opened his pouch and smelled common clay! At that exact same moment, the Syrian opened his bag and scratched the copper slugs!

Both burst into roaring laughter across the desert.

They turned their mules around, met again at the caravanserai, embraced with genuine professional admiration, and swore an oath of honest partnership: 'If we can deceive each other with such peerless art, let us abandon swindling and establish an honest import guild!' They became prosperous legitimate merchants, having met their match in wit.
moral: When two cunning tricksters meet, their mutual deception ends in a fair draw and an alliance of wit.

title: Tale of the Sharpers With the Shroff and the Ass
summary: Three clever sharpers in Baghdad resolved to swindle an affluent currency banker—a shroff—named Abu Mansur, who was renowned for his scru...
keywords: tale of the sharpers with the shroff and the ass
full_text:
Three clever sharpers in Baghdad resolved to swindle an affluent currency banker—a shroff—named Abu Mansur, who was renowned for his scrupulous bookkeeping.

The sharpers purchased an old donkey, dyed its ears white with chalk, and led it to the banker’s counting-house, claiming: 'O shroff, this is an extraordinary royal donkey that was trained in the palace of the Emperor of Hind to detect counterfeit coin; whenever a false coin is placed upon the counter, the beast brays!'

The banker looked at the chalk-eared donkey with a sarcastic smile: 'Indeed? Let us test this wondrous beast!'

The first sharper secretly pressed a pebble into the donkey’s ear, causing the animal to bray loudly as a false coin was laid down!

The sharpers demanded two hundred gold dinars for the magical beast.

The banker nodded: 'I will buy the donkey on one business condition: sign this legal ledger receipt with your full names, addresses, and finger-prints, guaranteeing that if the beast fails to bray at a false coin tomorrow in the presence of the Chief Magistrate, you will repay four hundred dinars!'

The sharpers, terrified of signing their real names before the law, hesitated, glanced at each other, and tried to stammer excuses.

The banker called out: 'Watchmen! Seize these horse-dyers!'

The three sharpers abandoned the donkey and fled down the alley, leaving the banker to laugh at how easily a simple ledger receipt disperses the most elaborate fraud.
moral: Rigid adherence to verified receipts and careful accounting defeats the most elaborate fraud.

title: Tale of the Chear and the Merchants
summary: A smooth-tongued swindler arrived in the spice bazaar of Cairo, dressed in the luxurious brocades of an imperial merchant of Samarkand. H...
keywords: tale of the chear and the merchants
full_text:
A smooth-tongued swindler arrived in the spice bazaar of Cairo, dressed in the luxurious brocades of an imperial merchant of Samarkand. He approached three prominent spice dealers, offering to purchase their entire inventory of cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg on credit, promising to pay thirty thousand dinars upon the arrival of his caravan next morning.

Two of the younger merchants were dazzled by the prospect of enormous profit, but the third, an experienced elder named Abu Bakr, noticed that the stranger’s hands were soft as a child’s, without the calluses of a merchant who managed camel caravans, and that his servants looked like hired street loafers.

Abu Bakr gathered his two colleagues in secret: 'Do not release a single ounce of spice on promises! Let us demand that he deposit a commercial bond in the guild treasury, as the law of Cairo requires.'

When the three merchants stood together and insisted on the lawful bond, the impostor began to bluster and threaten to take his business elsewhere.

Abu Bakr summoned the guild inspector, who checked the imperial merchant registry: the stranger’s name was completely unknown, and his 'caravan' was a phantom of air!

The exposed swindler was expelled from Cairo.

The three merchants embraced in mutual gratitude, having learned that collective guild solidarity and adherence to verified rules protect the community from the most glittering deceptions.
moral: Commercial solidarity and shared vigilance protect honest traders from fraudulent impostors.

title: Story of the Falcon and the Locust
summary: A royal hunting falcon, resting upon an olive branch in the heat of midday, saw a green locust struggling to free its wing from a sticky ...
keywords: story of the falcon and the locust
full_text:
A royal hunting falcon, resting upon an olive branch in the heat of midday, saw a green locust struggling to free its wing from a sticky spiderweb upon the bark. The falcon could easily have snapped up the insect for a morsel, but moved by a gentle impulse of mercy, he carefully snipped the web with the tip of his beak, allowing the locust to hop freely into the grass.

The little locust looked up: 'Thank you, noble monarch of the sky! A day may come when a humble locust may repay your grace.' The falcon laughed gently at the thought of a locust helping a falcon, and took wing.

A week later, the falcon was flying low across a meadow, watching for a field mouse. A fowler had concealed a broad net of fine green silk among the clover, perfectly disguised to trap birds of prey. The falcon was about to land directly in the center of the trap!

The little locust saw the peril. With all its might, it leaped into the air, landed squarely upon the falcon’s eye, and gave a sharp, vibrating buzz!

Startled by the sudden obstacle, the falcon checked his flight, veered sharply to the right, and landed upon a fence post, looking down just in time to see the fowler pull the net cords tight over the empty grass!

The falcon shuddered, realizing that the tiny locust had saved him from a lifetime of captivity in an iron cage. He lowered his head before the insect, having learned that kindness to the humblest creature returns as an angel of deliverance.
moral: No creature is too small to render assistance; kindness shown to the humble is repaid in the hour of peril.
