title: The Cure for the King's Cold
summary: King Krishnadevaraya was struck by a severe head cold and throat congestion. He lay in his royal bedchamber, wrapped in heavy woolen shaw...
keywords: the cure for the king's cold
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya was struck by a severe head cold and throat congestion. He lay in his royal bedchamber, wrapped in heavy woolen shawls, his nose red, his eyes watering, coughing and grumbling in foul humor.
The royal physicians prepared bitter herbal decoctions of black pepper, neem, and ginger, but the King spat them out, refusing to drink the foul-tasting draughts, shouting at his ministers and threatening to banish his doctors.

The royal household walked on tiptoe, terrified of provoking the irritable monarch.
Tenali Raman entered the bedchamber carrying no medicine bowls or herbs, but wearing an absurd, oversized turban made of a braided straw floor mat, balanced precariously with a giant yellow pumpkin tied to its peak!

The King blinked his watery eyes, glared at Tenali, and croaked:
'Tenali! What is that ridiculous monstrosity on your head? Have you come to mock your suffering Emperor?'

Tenali bowed with exaggerated solemnity, wobbling the heavy pumpkin:
'Maharaj! I have consulted the greatest veterinarian of the royal elephant stables! He assured me that your cold was caused by an excess of heavy thoughts weighing down your royal head.
To balance the cosmic humors, I have worn this pumpkin hat, and I have brought the imperial royal decree of elephant etiquette!'

Tenali pulled out an enormous palm leaf and began reading fabricated royal rules in an absurd, nasal, high-pitched voice:
'Rule Number One: Any elephant that sneezes in the presence of the King must bow thrice, wipe its trunk with a silk handkerchief measuring forty cubits, and recite a poem in praise of mangoes!
Rule Number Two: Any physician who prepares bitter neem soup must first drink three buckets of his own potion in the public square while balancing a goose on his forehead!'

The mental image of the dignified court physicians balancing geese while drinking buckets of neem soup was so overwhelmingly hilarious that King Krishnadevaraya could no longer contain himself.
A snort escaped his nose, followed by a chuckle, and then the Emperor burst into roaring, body-shaking, tearful laughter:
'Ha-ha-ha! Ho-ho-ho! Stop, Tenali, stop! My ribs are aching!'

As the King laughed uproariously, his chest opened, he sneezed three tremendous sneezes that cleared his blocked nasal passages completely, and his heavy headache vanished!
He wiped his eyes, breathed deeply without coughing, and realized with astonishment that his throat was clear and his fever was broken!

The King sat up in bed, energized and refreshed:
'Tenali, your absurd pumpkin hat and witty prescription have done what forty bowls of bitter medicine could not! Laughter is indeed the sovereign remedy of nature!'
The King rewarded Tenali with a basket of sweet apples, proving that joy and humor possess genuine healing power.
moral: Hearty laughter and joyful spirits are the most potent medicine for both bodily ailments and mental gloom.

title: Tenali and the Persian Scholar
summary: A proud linguist and ambassador from the court of the Shah of Persia, named Mirza Baig, visited Vijayanagara. He was fluent in several Mi...
full_text:
A proud linguist and ambassador from the court of the Shah of Persia, named Mirza Baig, visited Vijayanagara. He was fluent in several Middle Eastern languages, but spoke only classical Persian at the court, refusing to speak a single word of the local Telugu or Kannada languages.
Through his interpreter, Mirza boasted:
'Your Majesty, Persian is the language of angels, kings, and refined poetry. None in your southern kingdom possesses the intellectual refinement to understand its profound cadences or converse with me!'

The court scholars were embarrassed, having studied primarily Sanskrit and regional tongues.
King Krishnadevaraya, unwilling to let his court appear uncultured, looked anxiously toward Tenali Raman.

Tenali stepped forward, smiled warmly at the Persian scholar, and bowed with grand courtly gestures.
Tenali cleared his throat and addressed Mirza Baig in a rapid, energetic stream of words that sounded remarkably like Persian:
'Khuda-ba-khud, nishast-o-barkhast, qalami-kalam, mirza-salam!
Tungabhadra-paani, mirza-hairaani!
Katori-mein-shakar, mirza-chakkar!'

Mirza Baig listened intently, his eyes widening in shock. The rhythm, the nasal cadences, and the rhyming inflections were delivered with such majestic confidence and perfect Persian inflection that Mirza assumed Tenali was reciting an obscure, highly philosophical Persian proverb on hospitality and river currents!

Mirza bowed low with deep respect:
'Masha'Allah! What profound philosophical synthesis! You have encapsulated the essence of friendship and the flow of rivers in four sublime lines!'
Mirza presented Tenali with an expensive embroidered Persian shawl and a silver pen-case, praising the scholarly depth of Vijayanagara before departing in awe.

When the Persian ambassador was safely outside the city, King Krishnadevaraya turned to Tenali in astonishment:
'Tenali! When did you learn classical Persian? What did those verses mean?'

Tenali burst into laughter, wrapping the Persian shawl around his shoulders:
'Maharaj, I know not a single word of real Persian!
I merely took five common Hindustani bazaar words—"Kalam" (pen), "Shakar" (sugar), "Paani" (water), and "Salam" (greeting)—and mixed them with our local river Tungabhadra, rhyming them with "Mirza's dizziness" (Mirza-chakkar)!
The Persian scholar was so eager to find profound poetry that his own imagination translated my nonsensical bazaar rhymes into celestial wisdom!'

The King and the courtiers roared with laughter, marveling at how Tenali’s linguistic audacity and understanding of human nature had outsmarted foreign arrogance.
moral: True mastery of language lies in mutual understanding and situational wit, not in showing off foreign vocabulary.

title: The Donkey and the Washerman
summary: In a neighborhood along the riverbanks of Vijayanagara lived a harsh washerman named Devappa, who owned an old, faithful grey donkey. Alt...
full_text:
In a neighborhood along the riverbanks of Vijayanagara lived a harsh washerman named Devappa, who owned an old, faithful grey donkey. Although the beast had carried mountainous bundles of wet clothes for fifteen years, Devappa beat it mercilessly with an iron-tipped stick and gave it only dry thistle scraps to eat.
One evening, bruised and starving, the donkey slipped its tether and wandered into the forest.

The next morning, Devappa came weeping to Tenali Raman, begging for help:
'Master Tenali, my donkey is gone! Without him, I cannot deliver laundry to the palace courtiers! Help me find him!'

Tenali, who had long observed Devappa’s cruelty to the beast, resolved to teach the washerman an unforgettable lesson.
Tenali went into the forest, found the gentle donkey grazing peacefully near a pond, and led it to an empty stable behind his house.
Using non-toxic yellow turmeric paste and black charcoal soot, Tenali painted bold, ferocious tiger stripes across the donkey’s grey coat!
He then tied a large brass cowbell inside a burlap bag around its neck.

That evening, Tenali told Devappa:
'Devappa, a ferocious striped mountain beast with a booming bell has taken shelter in the rocky ravine near thy house. Go and capture it!'

Devappa approached the ravine with a wooden cudgel.
Suddenly, out trotted the striped donkey, shaking its brass bell.
In the moonlight, the beast appeared like a monstrous, demon-striped tiger!
Devappa threw down his cudgel, screaming in terror:
'Help! A man-eating tiger has come to devour me!'
He fell onto his knees, trembling, weeping, and begging the heavens for mercy:
'I have been a cruel wretch! I beat my poor donkey! Spare my life, O tiger king!'

At that moment, the donkey looked at its trembling master, opened its mouth, and let out a familiar, resounding bray:
*‘HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW! HAW-HAW!’*

Tenali Raman stepped out from behind the trees with a lantern:
'Look closely, Devappa! Is this a man-eating tiger, or the gentle friend who carried thy laundry for fifteen years?'

Devappa wiped his eyes, recognizing his donkey beneath the yellow turmeric stripes.
He was overcome with profound shame and relief.
He embraced the donkey, fed it sweet jaggery and fresh grass, and swore never again to raise a stick against the faithful beast, having learned that those who serve us deserve compassion and respect.
moral: Cruelty and neglect toward faithful working beasts invite poetic justice that teaches gratitude.

title: Tenali and the Dream Merchant
summary: A traveling trickster named Mayan arrived in the bustling market of Vijayanagara, setting up an opulent velvet tent adorned with colored ...
full_text:
A traveling trickster named Mayan arrived in the bustling market of Vijayanagara, setting up an opulent velvet tent adorned with colored glass lanterns. He proclaimed to the curious townspeople:
'I am the Master Dream Merchant! For a single gold coin, I will sell you a fragrant herbal incense that will grant you whatever dream you desire—to be an emperor, to discover mountains of emeralds, or to fly across the stars!'

Many foolish youths and gullible citizens paid gold coins, burned the incense, dreamed extravagant dreams, and woke up to find their purses empty and their daily chores neglected.

Tenali Raman decided to bring an end to this deceptive trade.
He walked into the tent, paid one gold coin, and said:
'Master Mayan, sell me a dream of becoming the sole sovereign of Vijayanagara, seated upon the Golden Throne, commanding all the treasuries and armies.'

Mayan handed Tenali a pinch of scented sandalwood powder: 'Burn this tonight, and thy dream is guaranteed!'

The next morning, Tenali arrived at the tent accompanied by four royal guards with drawn swords!
Tenali pointed at Mayan: 'Arrest this man for high treason!'

Mayan trembled in terror: 'Treason? What have I done, Master Tenali?'
Tenali declared in a booming, authoritative voice:
'Last night, I burned thy incense. In my dream, I became the absolute Emperor of Vijayanagara! As Emperor, I reviewed the royal accounts and discovered that thou hast been operating an illegal lottery within my empire without paying the imperial license fee of five thousand gold dinars!
Pay the five thousand gold dinars to the imperial guards immediately, or be marched to the citadel dungeon!'

Mayan cried out in despair:
'Master Tenali! It was only a dream! How can you arrest a real man for a decree issued in a dream?'

Tenali smiled with razor-sharp irony:
'Why, Master Merchant? If thy dreams are real enough to demand real gold coins from innocent citizens, then the imperial decrees issued inside those dreams are real enough to demand real fines!
Confess that dreams are illusions of no commercial value, return every stolen coin to the people, and leave Vijayanagara forever!'

Terrified, the Dream Merchant unlocked his iron cashbox, returned every single gold coin to the cheated townspeople, packed his tent, and fled the empire.
The citizens cheered Tenali, realizing that those who profit from illusions must be defeated with their own phantoms.
moral: Deceptive peddlers who sell imaginary illusions must be paid with mirror reflections.

title: The Price of Buttermilk
summary: On a scorching summer afternoon, an elderly village woman named Gangamma walked three miles carrying a heavy earthen pot of fresh, cool b...
full_text:
On a scorching summer afternoon, an elderly village woman named Gangamma walked three miles carrying a heavy earthen pot of fresh, cool buttermilk seasoned with curry leaves and ginger to the royal plaza. She sold cups of buttermilk for a single copper coin to parched porters and travelers.

An arrogant and haughty courtier named Somappa, dressed in lavish silk robes, strutted past. He demanded a large brass cup of cold buttermilk, drank it in one thirsty gulp, and tossed the cup back without paying.
When Gangamma asked for her copper coin, Somappa sneered:
'Old hag! Thou shouldst be honored that an imperial courtier drank from thy dirty earthen pot! Away from my path before I have my servants overturn thy stall!'

Gangamma began to weep. Tenali Raman, who was walking across the plaza, witnessed the injustice.
Tenali gently wiped the old woman's tears: 'Mother, sit in the shade. Somappa shall pay for thy buttermilk with interest.'

Tenali hurried to the palace and entered King Krishnadevaraya's audience hall, where Somappa was boasting of his lineage.
Tenali bowed:
'Maharaj, today I observed a miraculous demonstration of ancient culinary alchemy in the marketplace! Courtier Somappa has mastered the secret art of churning buttermilk so efficiently that a single cup can generate the strength of ten elephants!
He claims that churning butter is so effortless that he can churn an entire barrel of thick cream within two hours without breaking a sweat!'

The King, intrigued, looked at Somappa: 'Is this true, Somappa?'
Somappa, too proud to contradict Tenali in the presence of the Emperor, puffed out his chest: 'Of course, Your Majesty! For an aristocrat of my vigor, manual churning is child's play!'

Tenali smiled: 'Splendid! The palace kitchen has four barrels of thick buffalo curd waiting to be churned for tonight’s banquet. Let Somappa demonstrate his prowess before the court!'

A massive wooden churn and heavy rope were set up in the hot palace courtyard.
Somappa was forced to take off his fine silk coat and grip the rough hemp ropes.
For two grueling hours under the blazing afternoon sun, Somappa pulled and hauled, back and forth, back and forth!
His soft, unaccustomed hands blistered, his silk dhoti was splattered with sour cream, his breath came in ragged wheezes, and sweat poured like rain into his eyes!
Whenever he stopped, Tenali called out cheerfully:
'Keep pulling, noble courtier! The King is watching from the balcony!'

By the time the golden butter finally separated, Somappa collapsed onto the stone floor, completely exhausted, clutching his blistered palms.
Tenali handed him a cup of cold water and said softly:
'Now, Somappa, thou knowest what sweat, toil, and blistered hands go into making a single pot of buttermilk.
When poor old Gangamma walks three miles in the sun carrying her pot, a single copper coin is not just money; it is her very life and dignity.'

Somappa, humiliated and genuinely remorseful, reached into his purse and handed Gangamma ten gold coins for her cup of buttermilk.
The King praised Tenali’s lesson in the dignity of labor, decreeing that working artisans and vendors must be treated with unwavering courtesy throughout the empire.
moral: Arrogant nobility who despise the hard labor of working women are humbled when forced to sweat at the churn.

title: Tenali and the Elephant and the Mouse
summary: The Commander-in-Chief of the Vijayanagara army, General Veerabhadra, was excessively proud of the royal war elephant, Airavata. The beas...
keywords: tenali and the elephant and the mouse
full_text:
The Commander-in-Chief of the Vijayanagara army, General Veerabhadra, was excessively proud of the royal war elephant, Airavata. The beast was an immense tusker standing twelve feet tall, armored in steel plates, and trained to shatter fortress gates.
The General boasted:
'Airavata is invincible! Nothing on earth can make him turn back or tremble! He fears neither fire, nor arrows, nor lions!'

Tenali Raman smiled quietly from the pavilion:
'General, the universe is full of mysteries. The largest mountain can be moved by a hidden fault, and the mightiest giant often trembles before the smallest creature. I can make your invincible Airavata flee in terror using a creature no larger than a betel nut!'

The General laughed scornfully:
'Tenali, thou art a jester who talks nonsense! If thou canst make Airavata take a single step backward with a creature the size of a betel nut, I will surrender my jeweled sword to thee!'

The wager was accepted before King Krishnadevaraya.
The next morning, the immense war elephant was brought to the parade grounds, trumpeting fiercely, surrounded by armored cavalry.

Tenali Raman walked into the arena carrying a tiny, woven wicker box.
He walked directly in front of the towering tusker.
The elephant raised its trunk, preparing to crush the tiny man.
Tenali opened the wicker box and released a tiny, energetic grey field mouse onto the sand!

The little mouse, terrified by the thundering noise, scurried straight toward the elephant's massive front foot, seeking shelter near the shadow of its toenails.
The moment Airavata’s sensitive eyes saw the tiny creature darting toward its feet, the elephant’s ancient equine and pachyderm instinct took over:
Elephants possess an intense, instinctual terror that small creatures might crawl up their sensitive, nerve-packed trunks!

Airavata let out a shrill, panic-stricken squeal:
*‘TRUMP-EEEET!’*
The colossal beast scrambled backward, trampled the decorative flags, knocked over the commander's reviewing canopy, and bolted out of the arena at top speed, splashing into the river shallows to get away from the tiny mouse!

The entire audience erupted in roaring laughter.
General Veerabhadra stood frozen in utter mortification.
Tenali picked up the tiny mouse, placed it safely back into its wicker box, and bowed to the King:
'Maharaj, nature has designed the world with perfect balance. The mighty must never despise the weak, nor should size be mistaken for absolute invulnerability. A tiny thorn can bring down a champion, and a little mouse can rout an armored tusker!'

The King rewarded Tenali with a gold medal, and the General learned a lifelong lesson in humility.
moral: True strength does not lie in colossal size; even the mightiest fear the smallest unexpected danger.

title: The Two Brothers and the Field
summary: Two farmer brothers, Somanna and Bhimanna, came before King Krishnadevaraya’s court, arguing furiously over the inheritance of a fertile ...
keywords: the two brothers and the field
full_text:
Two farmer brothers, Somanna and Bhimanna, came before King Krishnadevaraya’s court, arguing furiously over the inheritance of a fertile five-acre agricultural field left by their late father.
Somanna shouted: 'The eastern half has the canal water; it belongs to me by birthright!'
Bhimanna yelled: 'The western half has rich black soil; our father promised it to me on his deathbed!'

They produced contradictory witnesses, spent their savings on dishonest lawyers, and neglected the land completely, until the once-blooming field became overgrown with thorny weeds and scrub.

The King, exhausted by their endless bickering, turned to Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, settle this dispute equitably, for they have disrupted the court for three months.'

Tenali had both brothers brought before him. He asked:
'Brothers, have you asked the field itself to whom it wishes to belong?'
The brothers stared: 'Can a patch of dirt speak?'
Tenali replied solemnly:
'The Earth is a living mother; she speaks to those who listen. Let us go to the field at sunset.'

At the field, Tenali knelt upon the soil, placed his ear against the dry ground, and listened intently for ten minutes while the brothers watched in silence.

Tenali stood up, brushing dirt from his knees, with a sorrowful expression:
'Brothers, I heard the field speaking clearly.'
Somanna asked eagerly: 'What did she say? Did she award the land to me?'
Bhimanna asked: 'Did she name me her owner?'

Tenali answered:
'The field was laughing aloud with bitter mockery!
She said: "Behold these two foolish brothers! For ten generations, their ancestors claimed they owned me; each man died, turned to dust, and became part of my soil, while I remained here eternal and unchanged!
Today, these two sons fight and bleed over who owns me, yet neither of them has planted a single seed of corn or given me a drop of water for a whole year!
Tell them: I belong not to the man who waves a stamped paper of ownership, but to the hands that till my soil, plant seeds with love, and feed the hungry with honest sweat!"'

The two brothers stood in stunned silence.
Tenali’s profound words pierced through their selfish arrogance like an arrow of light.
They looked at the neglected, weed-choked field that had fed their ancestors for centuries, and tears of shame filled their eyes.

Somanna embraced Bhimanna, dropping their lawsuits on the spot.
They agreed to divide the work equally, sharing water and soil as partners. Within a season, the field was green with bumper crops of golden paddy, proving that true ownership is earned through loving care, not angry contention.
moral: Earth yields its treasure not to legal squabbles, but to honest labor that nurtures it with love.

title: Tenali and the Envious Courtiers
summary: Three senior ministers of Vijayanagara, consumed by jealousy over King Krishnadevaraya’s high regard for Tenali Raman, hatched a petty pl...
full_text:
Three senior ministers of Vijayanagara, consumed by jealousy over King Krishnadevaraya’s high regard for Tenali Raman, hatched a petty plot to humiliate him during the royal Diwali celebrations.

Before the court assembled, they secretly scattered long, sharp *babul* acacia thorns across the cushions of Tenali’s customary silk seat in the second row of the audience hall, covering them with a thin layer of rose petals so the trap was invisible.
They whispered: 'When the jester sits, he will scream like a stuck pig, jump in the air, and disgrace himself before the Emperor!'

Tenali Raman entered the hall, dressed in festive white silks. As he approached his seat, his sharp eyes noticed two thorns poking through the rose petals and caught the guilty, expectant smirks on the three ministers' faces.

Instead of sitting immediately, Tenali bowed with immense grace to the three plotters. He then carefully placed his heavy palm-leaf manuscript upon the cushion to flatten the thorns safely, and sat down gently with complete composure.
He closed his eyes and exclaimed in a loud voice of ecstasy:
'Aha! Ah! What exquisite heavenly bliss! What transcendent fragrance!'

King Krishnadevaraya looked over from his throne, curious:
'Tenali, what brings such sudden ecstasy to thy countenance?'

Tenali stood up, holding a handful of the rose petals mixed with the acacia thorns, and proclaimed:
'Jahanpanah! Look at the noble generosity of my dear ministerial colleagues!
Knowing that a courtier's mind must remain sharp and vigilant, they have arranged a sublime spiritual seat for me! The fragrant rose petals symbolize the Emperor's loving grace, while these sharp thorns symbolize the rigorous vigilance required to defend our borders!
They honored me with this special seat of wisdom!'

The King was deeply touched by what he assumed was a profound philosophical gesture by the ministers:
'Marvelous! What noble fraternal affection!
Since these three ministers conceived such a sublime spiritual seat, it is only fitting that they receive the highest honor of their own invention!'

The King commanded the royal guards:
'Bring three large sacks of fresh babul acacia thorns! Scatter them thickly across the velvet thrones of these three noble ministers, and let them sit upon them for the remainder of today’s four-hour assembly to share Tenali’s spiritual bliss!'

The three ministers turned green with horror. Under the Emperor’s watchful eyes, they were forced to sit on their thorn-covered cushions, squirming, grimacing in agony, their teeth clenched, unable to cry out lest they offend the King!

Tenali smiled cheerfully from his safe seat, proving that those who dig pits of malice inevitably tumble into their own traps.
moral: Those who plant thorns for others find their own schemes transformed into blessings for the righteous.

title: The Tale of the Talking Parrot and the Thief
summary: In a quiet lane of Vijayanagara lived an elderly scholar named Shastriji, who lived alone with an intelligent green parrot named Mithu. T...
keywords: the tale of the talking parrot and the thief
full_text:
In a quiet lane of Vijayanagara lived an elderly scholar named Shastriji, who lived alone with an intelligent green parrot named Mithu. The parrot had learned several short phrases from listening to the old man’s evening studies.
One night, Shastriji fell ill and was taken to the hospital, leaving his modest house empty.
Tenali Raman, being a caring neighbor, promised to watch over Shastriji’s home.

That midnight, a seasoned housebreaker named Gangu, knowing the owner was away, jimmied open the kitchen window and slipped silently into the dark house, carrying a sack to loot the brass vessels.

Tenali Raman, who was sitting quietly in the veranda shadows reading by the moonlight, heard the window creak.
Instead of rushing in with a stick, Tenali crept to the side window where the parrot’s covered cage hung near the hallway.
Tenali lightly tapped the cage and whispered in a harsh voice:
'Who is that?'

The green parrot, startled awake in the dark, immediately repeated its favorite phrase in a loud, piercing, human-like screech:
*‘WHO IS THERE? WHO GOES THERE? HALT OR I SHOOT!’*

The burglar froze in the dark kitchen, his heart leaping into his throat!
Believing an armed palace guard was standing in the shadows, Gangu whispered frantically:
'Only a poor traveler, sir! Do not shoot!'

Tenali, standing outside the lattice, rattled a heavy brass poker against an iron bucket, imitating the cocking of a musket, and whispered in a deep, menacing baritone:
'Cock the gun, brother! Take aim at his legs!'

The parrot squawked again with delight:
*‘SHOOT HIM! SHOOT HIM! FIRE!’*

Gangu dropped his loot, shrieked in absolute terror, dove out of the kitchen window, leaped over the garden wall, and ran three miles without stopping, abandoning his shoes and his burglar tools in the mud!

The next morning, Shastriji returned home to find his house intact, his brass vessels safe, and a set of valuable iron tools left behind by the fleeing thief.
Tenali Raman fed sweet figs to the green parrot, laughing at how easily a simple bird's voice and a handful of wit can defend a home better than a company of soldiers.
moral: A clear presence of mind and unexpected noise can disarm burglars without physical combat.

title: Tenali and the Golden Bath
summary: King Krishnadevaraya, influenced by flatterers who urged him to rival the legendary opulence of Persian emperors, commissioned an extrava...
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, influenced by flatterers who urged him to rival the legendary opulence of Persian emperors, commissioned an extravagant private bathhouse in the palace.
The walls were lined with mirrors of polished silver, the tubs were carved from white marble inlaid with lapis lazuli, and the faucets were cast in solid gold.
The project cost fifty thousand gold dinars from the royal treasury.

The King invited his ministers to inspect the finished palace:
'Behold! Was there ever a bathhouse so divine in all the history of Bharatavarsha? Does it not elevate the majesty of the Emperor to bathe in pure gold?'

All the courtiers praised the extravagance with extravagant flattery.
Tenali Raman remained silent, observing the display.

The next morning, an extraordinary spectacle unfolded in the palace courtyard.
Tenali Raman arrived leading an ancient, mangy street donkey whose coat was caked in dried street mud and coal soot.
Tenali led the donkey straight into the new golden bathhouse!
He turned on the gold faucets, poured warm scented rosewater over the donkey’s back, lathered its fur with imported almond soap, and began rubbing the beast's ears with a silk towel!

The King, arriving for his morning bath, stood frozen in stunned outrage:
'Tenali! What unspeakable sacrilege is this? You are washing a filthy street donkey in the royal golden bathhouse?'

Tenali looked up with innocent sincerity:
'Maharaj, pardon my humble efforts! I noticed that this poor donkey was dirty, weary, and despised by all the horses in the city.
Remembering your royal words yesterday—that bathing in pure gold and scented rosewater elevates the majesty of the bather—I thought: "If gold can elevate a man into a glorious sovereign, surely an hour in this golden bath will transform this common donkey into a celestial white stallion!"'

The King stared at Tenali, then at the donkey, which was contentedly chewing on a garland of tuberoses.
Tenali added softly:
'Alas, Your Majesty! I have washed him for two hours, but he remains an ordinary donkey.
External gold cannot transform the nature of an animal, nor can extravagant marble baths add a single cubit to the true majesty of a monarch. While fifty thousand gold coins were spent on golden taps, three villages on our northern border lack clean drinking water wells.'

King Krishnadevaraya felt a deep pang of conscience. The biting truth of Tenali’s satire pierced through his vanity.
The King embraced Tenali:
'Thou hast opened my eyes, Tenali. A king’s true bath is the clean stream of justice.'
The King halted all further ostentatious construction, diverted royal funds to build irrigation tanks across the province, and gifted the donkey to an honest farmer with a supply of oats.
moral: A ruler’s true glory is not measured by ostentatious luxury, but by the clean prosperity of his humblest subjects.

title: The Well That Drank Water
summary: An honest vegetable farmer named Chennappa purchased a plot of land with an ancient stone well from a cunning landholder named Raghava. T...
full_text:
An honest vegetable farmer named Chennappa purchased a plot of land with an ancient stone well from a cunning landholder named Raghava. The sale deed clearly stated that the land and the well were transferred unconditionally.

However, two days after the sale, when Chennappa brought bullocks to pump water for his thirsty cabbage crops, the well was completely dry!
When Chennappa complained, Raghava laughed slyly:
'My good man, I sold you the well, but I never promised the water would stay! This well is an enchanted "Thirsty Well"; it drinks all water that enters it! If you want water, you must pay me a monthly fee of twenty silver coins to channel water from my neighboring tank!'

Chennappa, ruined by the sudden loss of water, appealed to Tenali Raman.
Tenali inspected the well. He dropped a heavy stone into the depths: it hit stone with a hollow, echoing thud.
Tenali took a small boat and rowed along the nearby canal belonging to Raghava’s estate, which ran twenty yards below the level of the well.
He noticed that the water in Raghava’s canal was unusually fresh, clear, and bubbling from a submerged stone archway.

Tenali returned to the dry well carrying five large bags of red powdered ochre dye.
In the presence of the village council, Tenali poured the red dye into the bottom of the dry well, followed by ten large barrels of water.
The water disappeared quickly down a fissure.

Tenali then led the council to Raghava’s canal:
Within twenty minutes, bright crimson-red water came gushing out of the submerged stone conduit into Raghava’s private canal!

Tenali pointed to the red water:
'Behold the "Thirsty Well"! Raghava had secretly chiseled an underground drainage pipe from the bottom of Chennappa’s well into his own lower canal! Whenever water accumulated in the well, it drained straight into Raghava’s private reservoir, stealing Chennappa’s water while Raghava demanded extortionate monthly fees!'

The village council was outraged by the deceit.
Raghava was ordered to seal the illegal drainage pipe with solid granite masonry, pay Chennappa fifty silver coins in restitution, and provide free irrigation for two seasons.
Chennappa’s well filled to the brim with sweet, abundant water, proving that deceitful schemes cannot hide from thorough investigation.
moral: Greedy landlords who construct deceitful deceptions to void legal sales are defeated by scientific investigation.

title: Tenali and the Challenge of Counting Crows
summary: On a pleasant spring morning, King Krishnadevaraya was walking in the imperial palace gardens with his courtiers. Looking up at the tall ...
keywords: tenali and the challenge of counting crows
full_text:
On a pleasant spring morning, King Krishnadevaraya was walking in the imperial palace gardens with his courtiers. Looking up at the tall banyan trees, the King noticed hundreds of black crows cawing and fluttering among the branches.

In a whimsical mood, the King turned to his ministers and posed an impossible challenge:
'Tell me, noble counselors: how many crows reside in our imperial capital of Vijayanagara?
Whosoever provides the exact count by tomorrow morning shall receive a thousand gold dinars; whosoever fails shall be fined fifty silver coins!'

The courtiers looked at each other in panic. Counting flying crows across an entire metropolis of three hundred thousand citizens was completely impossible! They spent the day wandering through streets, staring at roofs, getting dizzy, and counting in vain.

Only Tenali Raman sat comfortably in his garden veranda, sipping sweet mango sherbet and reading poetry.

The next morning, the court assembled. The courtiers hung their heads, confessing their failure.
Then Tenali Raman stepped forward, bowed with supreme elegance, and declared:
'Jahanpanah! I have completed the census of the crow population of Vijayanagara!'

The King sat forward, amazed: 'Indeed, Tenali? What is the exact number?'

Tenali answered without a moment's hesitation:
'There are precisely **ninety-nine thousand, five hundred and forty-three** crows residing in Vijayanagara, Maharaj!'

King Krishnadevaraya raised an eyebrow, smiling skeptically:
'Ninety-nine thousand, five hundred and forty-three? How canst thou be so certain, Tenali? What if there are more?'

Tenali smiled with dazzling composure:
'If there are more crows, Your Majesty, it simply means that their cousins and relatives from neighboring kingdoms have arrived to visit them for the spring harvest holidays!'

The King chuckled: 'And what if there are fewer crows upon counting?'

Tenali replied with effortless wit:
'If there are fewer crows, Maharaj, it means that our local crows have flown to visit their relatives in the Sultanates of the Deccan for the weekend!'

The entire court erupted in roaring laughter.
King Krishnadevaraya slapped his knees with delight:
'Only Tenali could answer an unanswerable question with an unassailable explanation!'
The King awarded Tenali the thousand gold dinars, demonstrating that when confronted with arbitrary demands, wit and humor are the wisest defenses.
moral: Absurd, unanswerable royal whims are best met with witty, unverifiable logic.

title: The King and the Dull Minister
summary: In the court of Vijayanagara served a senior minister named Chandrashekar, whose only strategy for political survival was absolute, unque...
keywords: the king and the dull minister
full_text:
In the court of Vijayanagara served a senior minister named Chandrashekar, whose only strategy for political survival was absolute, unquestioning flattery. Whatever King Krishnadevaraya said, Chandrashekar would nod vigorously and exclaim:
'Yes, Your Majesty! Absolutely, Maharaj! Your royal wisdom is incomparable!'

One morning, the King grew weary of this sycophancy.
Tenali Raman noticed the King’s irritation and whispered:
'Maharaj, allow me to demonstrate the danger of a minister who has lost the ability to say "No".'

Tenali stepped before the throne and said:
'Maharaj, I have conceived a brilliant municipal reform. To celebrate the coming festival, let us issue an imperial decree commanding that all citizens of Vijayanagara walk on their hands instead of their feet from dawn until noon!'

King Krishnadevaraya played along, nodding solemnly:
'A remarkable idea, Tenali! Minister Chandrashekar, what is your opinion of this royal reform?'

Chandrashekar, terrified of disagreeing with what seemed like a royal preference, bowed low:
'Yes, Your Majesty! A magnificent, divine decree! Walking on hands will strengthen the arms of our soldiers and elevate our subjects above common mortals!'

Tenali continued:
'And furthermore, Maharaj, to ensure public hygiene, let us decree that all cooks in the city must boil their rice in seawater and season it exclusively with powdered chalk!'

The King turned to the minister: 'Chandrashekar, what say you?'
Chandrashekar nodded enthusiastically:
'Yes, Maharaj! A masterstroke of culinary medicine! Chalk will whiten the teeth of the people, and seawater will preserve their health!'

Tenali then delivered the masterstroke:
'And finally, Maharaj, since Minister Chandrashekar agrees so passionately with every single measure, let us decree that he shall be the first to demonstrate them!
Let him walk on his hands three times around the palace outer moat, while eating a bowl of rice boiled in seawater and seasoned with chalk!'

Chandrashekar’s eyes bulged in horror!
He fell prostrate upon the carpet, sweating, waving his hands frantically:
'No, no, no! Mercy, Your Majesty! I cannot walk on my hands! Seawater and chalk will poison my stomach!'

The King and the entire court burst into thunderous laughter!
King Krishnadevaraya looked down sternly at the trembling flatterer:
'Chandrashekar, thou didst find thy "No" only when thine own stomach was in peril!
A ruler who is surrounded by men who say "Yes" to every folly is a blind man walking toward a precipice. The state needs ministers with the courage to say "No" when an idea is harmful to the people.'

Chandrashekar was demoted, while Tenali showed that honest disagreement in council is the truest pillar of good governance.
moral: Flattery that agrees blindly with every word of power is dangerous to an empire; true loyalty exercises independent judgment.

title: Tenali and the Sword of the King
summary: The ceremonial Sword of State—a magnificent damascene steel blade encrusted with rubies, gifted to King Krishnadevaraya by the King of Ka...
keywords: tenali and the sword of the king
full_text:
The ceremonial Sword of State—a magnificent damascene steel blade encrusted with rubies, gifted to King Krishnadevaraya by the King of Kalinga—disappeared overnight from the secure armory inside the citadel.
The iron door showed no signs of forced entry, indicating that one of the four night sentries on duty had committed the theft.

All four guards—Ramu, Somu, Bheemu, and Deva—swore upon their sacred daggers that they had seen nothing.
The King was on the verge of ordering them tortured when Tenali Raman intervened:
'Maharaj, violence only forces innocent men to confess falsehoods. Allow me to test the sentries using the ancient Turmeric Test of Kalinga.'

Tenali had the four guards assembled in a courtyard.
He brought forth a large stone basin filled with pure water mixed with crushed fresh turmeric roots, turning the water bright, radiant yellow.
Tenali announced:
'The ceremonial steel of Kalinga has a secret metallurgical property: it reacts with the human sweat of whoever touched it within forty-eight hours.
Wash your hands thoroughly in this yellow turmeric water. The innocent will see no change. But whoever touched the stolen blade will find that his hands turn bright crimson-red within five minutes!'

The four guards dipped their hands into the yellow water, washing vigorously.
Tenali then handed each man a clean linen towel to dry his hands.
Three of the towels showed only yellow turmeric stains.

However, Tenali noticed that the fourth guard, Bheemu, was repeatedly rubbing his palms against his woolen trousers, nervously checking his fingers.
Tenali suddenly stepped forward and touched Bheemu’s wet hands with a piece of wet alkaline lime paste (*chunam*), used for betel leaves!
The chemical reaction between the alkaline lime and the turmeric immediately turned Bheemu’s wet hands bright, blood-red!

Bheemu shrieked in horror, falling to his knees:
'The blade has cursed me! I confess! I hid the Sword of State inside the hollow stone cannon on the north rampart!'

The guards ran to the rampart and recovered the precious sword undamaged.
The King marveled at Tenali’s demonstration.
Tenali smiled:
'Maharaj, turmeric naturally turns red when touched with alkaline lime; the only magic was in the thief's own panic, which revealed his guilt!'
Bheemu was punished, the innocent sentries were exonerated, and Tenali’s forensic wit preserved justice.
moral: A thief cannot hide physical evidence when confronted with chemical truth.

title: The Tale of the Stolen Necklace
summary: Queen Tirumala Devi, while bathing in the royal pleasure pavilion on the palace grounds, left her priceless necklace of five strands of B...
keywords: the tale of the stolen necklace
full_text:
Queen Tirumala Devi, while bathing in the royal pleasure pavilion on the palace grounds, left her priceless necklace of five strands of Basra pearls upon an open silver tray by the veranda window.
When she emerged from her bath, the necklace had vanished!
The palace guards searched the rooms in panic. Suspicion immediately fell upon the three young maidservants who had attended the Queen.
The Chief Chamberlain was preparing to throw the weeping maidens into prison when Tenali Raman arrived.

Tenali inspected the open window.
He examined the stone sill: there were no human footprints, but on the polished ledge he found two small, distinctive scratch marks, and on the grass below lay a single bitten neem fruit.
Looking up, Tenali saw an ancient gulmohar tree whose branches overhung the window, where a troop of wild rhesus monkeys frequently played.

Tenali said: 'Chamberlain, release the maidservants. The thief is not human.'

Tenali knew that if guards climbed the tree with sticks, the frightened monkeys would scatter across the city roofs and the necklace would be lost forever in the river or bushes.

Tenali devised a clever, peaceful strategy.
He brought twenty strings of cheap, glittering glass bead necklaces from the market and a large basket of ripe yellow bananas.
He walked beneath the gulmohar tree and began tossing bananas and glass necklaces onto the grass, wearing one glass necklace around his own neck, dancing and making joyful sounds.

The curious monkeys descended to the lower branches.
One large male monkey was sitting on a high bough, proudly holding the Queen's pearl necklace around its neck!
Seeing the other monkeys picking up bananas and wearing the shiny glass beads, the monkey grew jealous.
Tenali took off his own glass necklace, made a dramatic flourish, and tossed it into the soft grass, walking away.

The monkey on the bough immediately mimicked Tenali's motion:
It took off the heavy pearl necklace, tossed it down into the grass to grab a shiny glass necklace and two bananas!

Tenali’s attendants immediately scooped up the pearl necklace undamaged!
The Queen wept with joy upon receiving her heirloom, the innocent maidens were rewarded with gold coins for their distress, and King Krishnadevaraya praised Tenali’s patient understanding of animal behavior.
moral: Patience and understanding the habits of nature recover lost treasures where brute force fails.

title: Tenali and the Ghost in the Palace
summary: A chilling rumor spread through the imperial citadel of Vijayanagara: the eastern wing of the palace was haunted by a glowing, wailing ph...
keywords: tenali and the ghost in the palace
full_text:
A chilling rumor spread through the imperial citadel of Vijayanagara: the eastern wing of the palace was haunted by a glowing, wailing phantom!
Several night sentries swore they had seen a luminous white figure floating across the high parapets at midnight, accompanied by strange rattling sounds and hollow groans.
The sentries abandoned their posts in panic, and the King’s younger brother refused to sleep in the eastern pavilion.

King Krishnadevaraya summoned the court priests to perform expensive exorcism rituals, but the glowing phantom continued to appear.

Tenali Raman suspected a political plot to leave the eastern armory unguarded.
He resolved to confront the ghost himself.
Arming himself not with holy ash, but with a stout bamboo staff, a lantern, and a bag of sticky bird-lime, Tenali hid behind the stone pillars of the eastern gallery at midnight.

At the stroke of midnight, a chilling moan echoed through the corridor.
A tall, luminous white figure with glowing green eyes began gliding slowly along the parapet wall, rattling a chain.

Instead of running away, Tenali leaped out from the shadows, swung his bamboo staff with formidable precision, and swept the ghost off its feet!
*WHACK!*
The phantom hit the stone floor with a thoroughly mortal grunt: 'Oof! My ribs!'

Tenali sat upon the struggling specter, blew his whistle for the guards, and lit his lantern.
He stripped off the white sheet:
It was an ordinary white linen bedsheet, coated with luminous phosphorescent powder made from crushed sea fireflies and sulfur!
Tied to the sheet was a terrified tomcat in a wire basket, whose frantic clawing had created the rattling sounds!

Beneath the sheet was a disgruntled former armory clerk named Shankara, who had been fired for drunkenness. He had been paid by a rival merchant to stage the 'haunting' so that arms could be smuggled out of the unguarded eastern gate!

The King and the courtiers arrived, staring in amazement at the shivering 'ghost'.
Tenali laughed:
'Maharaj, ghosts exist only in the dark corners of superstitious minds. Whenever a phantom appears, look for the thief who benefits from the darkness!'

The conspirators were arrested, the armory was secured, and Tenali’s fearless logic was celebrated across Vijayanagara.
moral: Superstition is the cloak worn by cowards and schemers; fearless inquiry dispels the darkest specters.

title: The Farmer and the Seeds
summary: A hardworking farmer named Mallappa saved two bags of rare, high-yielding black mustard seeds to sow his fields after the monsoon rains. ...
full_text:
A hardworking farmer named Mallappa saved two bags of rare, high-yielding black mustard seeds to sow his fields after the monsoon rains. One night, the two bags were stolen from his barn.
Mallappa suspected his neighbor, a shifty farmer named Lingappa, whose fields bordered his own.
However, Lingappa swore before the village council:
'I bought my own mustard seeds from a traveling merchant in Bellary! These are my seeds!'

Because mustard seeds appear identical to the naked eye, the village headman could not determine ownership and brought the dispute to Tenali Raman.

Tenali looked at the disputed bags of seeds. He said:
'Since both men claim these seeds, we shall perform the Trial of the Fertile Soil.
Let Mallappa plant half an acre with seeds from the bag, and let Lingappa plant half an acre with seeds from the bag.
Within forty days, the harvest will reveal the truth.'

The two men sowed their fields.
Tenali, however, had privately visited Mallappa’s home before the planting and asked:
'Mallappa, what secret method did thy late father use when drying his prized seed crop?'
Mallappa whispered:
'My father always mixed dried leaves of wild basil with the seeds to protect them from weevils, leaving a subtle fragrance of basil on the leaves.'

Forty days later, the fields blossomed into brilliant yellow flowers.
Tenali brought the King, the ministers, and the two farmers to inspect the crops.
Tenali plucked a handful of mustard leaves from the harvested plants and handed them to Lingappa:
'Lingappa, smell these leaves. What rare herb’s fragrance is infused into their sap?'

Lingappa, eager to prove his superior knowledge of the seeds, boasted:
'Why, it smells of crushed mountain wild basil, which I carefully dried with the seeds in my barn!'

Tenali smiled with cold triumph:
'Aha, Lingappa! Only the man who stole Mallappa’s family seeds could know that secret!
For Mallappa’s father was the only farmer in the entire province who seasoned his seed bags with wild basil! If you had bought common seeds from a Bellary merchant as you claimed, you would have had no idea that basil was present!'

Lingappa realized he had convicted himself through his own boastful tongue.
He fell to the ground, confessed the theft, and surrendered his entire harvest to Mallappa.
The King praised Tenali’s razor-sharp deduction, proving that truth always blossoms from the earth.
moral: Guilt betrays itself through unnatural knowledge; truth sprouts from the soil.

title: Tenali and the Language of Animals
summary: A pompous scholar named Pandit Shastrakavi arrived at King Krishnadevaraya's court, claiming he had attained supernatural enlightenment i...
keywords: tenali and the language of animals
full_text:
A pompous scholar named Pandit Shastrakavi arrived at King Krishnadevaraya's court, claiming he had attained supernatural enlightenment in the Nilgiri hills and had mastered the 'Universal Language of Birds and Beasts'.
'I understand every chirp of the sparrow, every bark of the hound, and every moo of the cow!' he boasted, demanding a monthly royal pension of two hundred gold dinars for his services as the Emperor’s Animal Ambassador.

King Krishnadevaraya, always fascinated by natural lore, was ready to grant the pension when Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, before we disburse royal gold, let us test the Pandit’s fluency before the court.'

Tenali sent a servant to the palace kitchens. The servant returned holding two animals: a hungry street dog and an aggressive alley cat, each secured in a separate wire basket.

Tenali placed the two baskets facing each other in the center of the hall, and pulled the wire latches.
The moment the cat saw the dog, its fur stood on end, its tail puffed up like a bottle-brush, and it let out a ferocious, spitting hiss:
*‘HIIISSS-FFFT-MREOOOWW!’*
The dog lunged forward, barking furiously:
*‘WOOF! WOOF! BOW-WOW-GRRR!’*

Tenali turned to the animal linguist:
'Learned Pandit! Translate their dialogue for His Majesty! What did the cat say to the dog, and what was the dog’s philosophical reply?'

The pretender began to stammer, sweating beneath his high turban:
'Ah... the cat said: "Peace be upon thee, noble canine brother, the weather is pleasant today!" And the dog replied: "Indeed, sister feline, may the gods grant thee good health!"'

Tenali burst into body-shaking laughter:
'Maharaj, hear the Pandit’s translation!
Any child in Vijayanagara knows that the cat said: "Keep away from me, you ugly hound, or I will claw your nose off!" And the dog replied: "Come down here, you spitting hairball, and I will chew your tail!"'

The King and the entire court erupted in uncontrollable laughter.
The pretender hung his head in humiliation, unable to utter another word.
King Krishnadevaraya dismissed the charlatan, warning him that in Vijayanagara, nature speaks for itself without the need of fraudulent translators.
moral: Pretenders who claim secret, unverifiable knowledge are quickly unmasked when tested with reality.

title: The Tale of the Three Suitors
summary: A wealthy and cultured nobleman of the court, Lord Somasundaram, had an accomplished, intelligent daughter named Madhavi. Three eligible ...
keywords: the tale of the three suitors
full_text:
A wealthy and cultured nobleman of the court, Lord Somasundaram, had an accomplished, intelligent daughter named Madhavi.
Three eligible young noblemen sought her hand in marriage:
Prince Jayadeva, a handsome warrior;
Lord Haridasa, a wealthy merchant;
And Master Ananda, a modest scholar and musician.

Unable to choose among them without causing factional discord, the nobleman appealed to King Krishnadevaraya, who referred the matter to Tenali Raman.

Tenali arranged a private trial in the palace garden pavilion.
Lady Madhavi sat behind a translucent silk screen that completely obscured her facial features, allowing only her voice and silhouette to be perceived.

Tenali called the three suitors into the garden one by one.
To Prince Jayadeva, Tenali said:
'Describe the maiden behind the screen, and tell us why you desire to marry her.'
Jayadeva puffed out his chest: 'She must possess the radiance of the morning sun! I will dress her in gold armor, conquer kingdoms for her glory, and she shall be admired by all men as the most beautiful queen of my palace!'

Next came Lord Haridasa, the merchant. He said:
'Her father is wealthy and connected to the spice guilds. I will shower her with pearls, diamonds from Golconda, and seven palaces of marble. Her beauty will be the crowning jewel of my commercial empire!'

Finally came Master Ananda, the scholar.
He sat upon the grass, looked at the quiet silhouette behind the screen, and spoke softly:
'I do not know whether her face is fair as the lotus or humble as the field flower. But I have heard her speak of compassion for the sick; I have heard her verses honoring truth; and I have heard the music of her gentle kindness.
I seek to marry not a trophy of glory or an ornament of wealth, but a kindred soul with whom to share life’s sorrows and joys, reading books, cultivating a garden, and walking together in mutual reverence.'

Behind the silk screen, Lady Madhavi wept tears of profound joy.
Tenali smiled and turned to Lord Somasundaram:
'The first man loves his own pride; the second loves his own gold; but the third loves your daughter’s soul. A marriage of pride crumbles in defeat, a marriage of gold shatters in poverty, but a marriage of true hearts endures through all seasons.'

Lady Madhavi was wed to Master Ananda, living in deep harmony and love, celebrated as a union blessed by true wisdom.
moral: True love perceives the inner character and spirit of a person, while superficial passion sees only outward form.

title: Tenali and the Pot of Ghee
summary: Tenali Raman’s cousin, a good-natured but notoriously lazy youth named Subbanna, had a bad habit of daydreaming extravagant fantasies ins...
keywords: tenali and the pot of ghee
full_text:
Tenali Raman’s cousin, a good-natured but notoriously lazy youth named Subbanna, had a bad habit of daydreaming extravagant fantasies instead of doing honest work.
One festival morning, Tenali gifted Subbanna a large earthenware pot filled with ten pounds of pure, fragrant cow's ghee, saying:
'Subbanna, carry this pot carefully to the market. Sell it for five silver coins, and use the money to buy seeds to plant your vegetable patch.'

Subbanna placed the heavy pot of ghee carefully upon his head, wrapped in a cloth ring, and began walking toward the bazaar.
As he walked down the dusty road, his mind began to spin an extravagant web of daydreaming:

'Ah!' thought Subbanna, smiling at the sky. 'I shall sell this ghee for five silver coins.
With the five silver coins, I will not buy common seeds; I will buy five pairs of fine hens!
The hens will lay hundreds of eggs, which will hatch into thousands of chickens!
I shall sell the chickens and buy ten she-goats!
The goats will multiply into a herd of a hundred!
I shall sell the goats and buy twenty fine milk cows!
I will become the wealthiest dairy lord in Vijayanagara!
I will build a three-story mansion with fountains of rosewater!
I will marry the wealthiest merchant’s daughter, and when she asks me to fetch water from the well, I will turn to her with supreme aristocratic disdain, shake my head proudly, and shout:
"NO! NOT AT ALL!"'

Lost completely in his imaginary glory, Subbanna made a violent, haughty gesture, shaking his head violently from side to side!
*CRASH!*

The heavy earthenware pot slipped from his head, slammed onto the hard cobblestones, and shattered into a hundred jagged fragments!
The ten pounds of rich, golden ghee spilled across the dirt road, soaking into the dust, where stray dogs and crows immediately descended to feast!

Subbanna sat on the roadside stones, clutching his empty head, weeping bitterly:
'Woe is me! My chickens are gone! My goats have vanished! My cows have died! My three-story mansion is ruined!'

Tenali Raman, who was walking behind, tapped him on the shoulder with his walking cane:
'Subbanna, dry your tears. Your chickens and cows were never born, and your mansion was built of smoke.
He who builds castles in the clouds trips over the stones of reality. Get up, take this broom, sweep the road, and earn a real copper with your hands. For a single real drop of milk earned by honest toil is worth ten thousand imaginary oceans of ghee!'

Subbanna learned the lesson of mindfulness, abandoned his idle fantasies, and learned to focus his mind upon the reality before him.
moral: Building imaginary castles in the air while neglecting the task at hand leads to the loss of real blessings.

title: The King and the Beard
summary: King Krishnadevaraya was intensely proud of his full, majestic, jet-black imperial beard, which he groomed daily with scented oils and co...
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya was intensely proud of his full, majestic, jet-black imperial beard, which he groomed daily with scented oils and comb.
One morning, the royal barber, an elderly, loyal craftsman named Ramdas whose hands had begun to tremble with age, accidentally slipped with his sharp steel shears.
*SNIP!*
A massive chunk of the King's beard on the left cheek was sliced away completely, leaving an awkward, bare patch!

The King looked into his silver hand mirror and let out a roar of thunderous fury:
'Incompetent fool! Thou hast mutilated the Emperor's royal countenance!
Guards! Take this wretch to the courtyard and have his hands bound for banishment!'

Poor Ramdas fell to the marble floor, trembling, weeping, clutching the King's feet in despair.
Tenali Raman, who was entering the chamber for morning consultation, took in the scene at a glance.

Tenali did not argue with the King or make excuses for the barber.
Instead, he walked up to King Krishnadevaraya, looked intently at the King's newly shortened beard, and clapped his hands in theatrical admiration:
'Jahanpanah! Congratulations! What a magnificent, youthful transformation!
I had heard that the emperors of Persia and Rome trim their beards closely to reveal the chiseled jawlines of warrior-heroes, but I never dreamed our own Emperor would adopt this heroic fashion!'

The King paused, his hand halfway to his scabbard, looking confused:
'Youthful transformation? Heroic fashion?'

Tenali continued with enthusiastic praise:
'Indeed, Maharaj! For ten years, your full beard made you look like a venerable, sixty-year-old grandfather sage!
Now, with your jawline exposed by this modern trim, you look barely twenty-five years old—a dashing, invincible general ready to lead cavalry charges into battle!
Your enemies will tremble at the sight of your fierce, youthful vigor!
In fact, Maharaj, order the barber to trim the right side to match immediately, so the entire court may celebrate your youthful majesty!'

The King looked back into the silver mirror.
He tilted his head, imagined himself as a dashing twenty-five-year-old warrior, and a broad smile broke across his face.
The King chuckled, then burst into hearty laughter:
'Ha-ha! Tenali, thou art right! A heavy beard makes a man look old before his time!'

The King turned to the trembling barber:
'Ramdas, rise! Trim the other side to match, and take this gold coin for thy service, but keep thy hands steady henceforth!'

Ramdas wept tears of gratitude, kissing Tenali’s feet.
Tenali smiled, having turned an execution into a celebration through the sovereign magic of tactful wit.
moral: A skillful word of witty reassurance can turn sudden anger into pleasant laughter and pardon.

title: Tenali and the Blind Donation
summary: A wealthy merchant of Vijayanagara named Dhanpal boasted throughout the city of his boundless religious charity. To prove that his philan...
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Vijayanagara named Dhanpal boasted throughout the city of his boundless religious charity. To prove that his philanthropy was 'pure, selfless, and untainted by favoritism', he announced an extraordinary ritual:
Every Friday morning, he sat on a raised platform outside the main city gates, tied a thick black silk blindfold over his eyes, and distributed silver coins from a large copper bowl to anyone who touched his hands.
He boasted: 'My charity is truly blind! I give without looking, asking no questions of caste, merit, or need!'

Tenali Raman observed that this theatrical spectacle was being shamelessly exploited:
A gang of robust, lazy gamblers and healthy tricksters stood in line repeatedly, changing their voices, receiving dozens of coins each, while truly blind orphans, crippled elders, and sick widows were pushed into the gutters by the aggressive mob.

Tenali resolved to cure Dhanpal of his vain, foolish ritual.

The following Friday, Tenali arrived at the distribution platform carrying an enormous basket filled with coarse river pebbles and jagged pottery shards.
As Dhanpal reached into his bowl to hand out silver coins blindly, Tenali stepped onto the platform, took Dhanpal’s hand, placed a large, jagged, sharp granite stone into the merchant’s palm, and closed his fingers over it!

Dhanpal yelped in pain:
'Ouch! What is this? Who has placed a sharp, jagged stone in my hand?'
He ripped off his black silk blindfold, glaring in furious anger:
'Who dared do this to a noble benefactor?'

Tenali stood before him, smiling calmly:
'Why, noble Dhanpal! Why did you remove your blindfold?
You proudly boast that your charity is blind, and that you give without looking.
If your charity is blind, why should your hands complain when they receive stones instead of gold?
Look around you!'

Tenali pointed to the crowd:
'Look at these twenty strong, able-bodied young gamblers laughing behind the trees with bags of your silver, while yonder crippled grandmother and blind orphan weep in the ditch with empty hands!
Heaven gave you eyes not to blindfold them for public applause, but to seek out genuine suffering and wipe away real tears.
Blind charity is not virtue; it is lazy vanity that feeds parasites and starves the truly needy!'

Dhanpal looked at the sharp stone in his hand, then looked at the suffering poor in the gutters.
His heart filled with profound remorse.
He threw away his blindfold, apologized to Tenali, and restructured his philanthropy, visiting the homes of the disabled, funding orphanages, and ensuring that his charity was guided by open eyes, discernment, and genuine love.
moral: Charity done for theatrical vanity without discernment feeds frauds while true need goes unassisted.

title: The Trick of the Palm Leaf
summary: During an anxious dry spell before the arrival of the monsoon, a self-proclaimed 'Supreme Imperial Astrologer' named Varahamitra set up c...
keywords: the trick of the palm leaf
full_text:
During an anxious dry spell before the arrival of the monsoon, a self-proclaimed 'Supreme Imperial Astrologer' named Varahamitra set up camp near Vijayanagara. He held up a dried palm leaf covered in mysterious astrological diagrams and declared:
'According to my celestial calculations, an evil planetary conjunction has blocked the rain clouds over Vijayanagara!
Unless the Emperor and the farming guilds pay five thousand gold coins to perform a seven-day Celestial Cloud Sacrifice, not a single drop of rain will fall, and the entire empire will perish in famine!'

Terrified farmers sold their cattle to contribute to the sacrifice fund.
King Krishnadevaraya was on the verge of handing over the gold when Tenali Raman intervened:
'Maharaj, let me examine the astrologer’s palm leaf. If his celestial calculations are infallible, he should be able to predict today’s local atmospheric events with absolute precision.'

Tenali approached the astrologer and asked:
'Revered Astrologer, does your palm leaf reveal what the sky will drop upon your own head before this afternoon’s audience concludes?'
The astrologer puffed out his chest:
'The stars reveal only celestial truths! The sky will drop nothing upon my head today, for the atmosphere is dry as bone!'

Tenali nodded. He stepped to the palace balcony, gave a prearranged signal to his servants waiting on the roof directly above the assembly terrace.
Within three seconds, a massive, fifty-gallon leather fire bucket filled with cold, muddy river water was dumped straight down upon the astrologer's head!
*SPLAAASH!*

The astrologer was knocked to his knees, his tall silk turban crushed, his face dripping with muddy slime, his astrology palm leaf soaked into pulp!
He spluttered and shrieked in fury:
'Treason! Outrage! Who dumped this filthy water on my head?'

Tenali Raman folded his hands with innocent courtesy:
'Alas, great Astrologer! You claimed to know the movements of clouds across ten thousand leagues of heaven, yet you could not predict a local rainstorm occurring three feet above your own head!
If your stars cannot warn you of a simple bucket of river water, how can you demand five thousand gold coins to predict the monsoon?'

The King and the entire court erupted in laughter.
King Krishnadevaraya ordered the charlatan to return every coin to the farmers and banished him from the empire.
Three days later, natural monsoon clouds gathered over the Western Ghats, bringing torrential, life-giving rain to the fertile fields of Vijayanagara, proving that nature follows its eternal laws, not the greed of false prophets.
moral: Superstitious prophecies designed to fleece anxious farmers crumble before empirical observation.

title: The Tale of the Lazy Servant
summary: Tenali Raman’s neighbor, a wealthy but frustrated merchant named Jagannath, had a servant named Somappa who was afflicted with incurable ...
keywords: the tale of the lazy servant
full_text:
Tenali Raman’s neighbor, a wealthy but frustrated merchant named Jagannath, had a servant named Somappa who was afflicted with incurable laziness. Somappa could fall asleep anywhere: leaning against a doorpost, sweeping the courtyard, or holding a horse's reins.
Whenever Jagannath scolded him, Somappa would yawn and say:
'Master, sleep is a sacred divine gift; why should I fight nature?'

Jagannath complained to Tenali: 'I pay him three silver coins a month, but he sleeps eighteen hours a day! If I fire him, his poor mother will starve. How can I make him work?'

Tenali smiled: 'Leave Somappa to me for one week. I will cure his passion for sleep.'

Tenali hired Somappa to work at his house, offering an extraordinary employment contract:
'Somappa, I have heard of your deep dedication to sleep.
In my house, you do not need to sweep, cook, or carry water.
Your only job is to sleep continuously upon this comfortable cot on my front veranda from sunrise to sunset!
For every hour you sleep without moving, I will pay you one silver coin!
However, if you open your eyes, sit up, or take a single step off the cot before the sunset gong, you must pay me a fine of five silver coins!'

Somappa could not believe his good fortune:
'To be paid in silver just for sleeping? This is paradise!'

On the first morning, Somappa lay down upon the soft cot, grinning, and fell asleep.
He slept for three hours. But by noon, his back began to ache from lying flat.
He wanted to stretch, but Tenali sat on a stool beside the cot with a notebook, saying:
'Keep sleeping, Somappa! If you move a toe, you owe me five silver coins!'

By afternoon, Somappa was desperately bored, thirsty, and restless. Outside the veranda, boys were playing games, vendors were shouting interesting wares, and life was bustling.
Somappa wanted to get up, but Tenali ordered:
'Sleep, Somappa! Close your eyes! Sleeping is your royal duty!'
By evening, Somappa felt as though the comfortable cot had become an iron torture rack!

On the second morning, when Tenali called him to the cot, Somappa trembled:
'Master Tenali, please, I beg of you! Do not make me sleep!
Let me sweep the courtyard! Let me carry twenty buckets of water from the river! Let me chop five bundles of firewood!
I never realized that forced idleness is worse than the hardest labor!'

Tenali laughed and released him from the contract.
Somappa returned to Merchant Jagannath’s house as the most energetic, industrious worker in the neighborhood, having learned that purposeful work gives sweetness to rest, while forced indolence is a prison.
moral: Ingenious psychological motivation cures chronic indolence better than angry reprimands.

title: Tenali and the Woodcutter's Axe
summary: On the outskirts of Vijayanagara, a poor, honest woodcutter named Kariappa was chopping firewood along the steep, rocky banks of the Tung...
full_text:
On the outskirts of Vijayanagara, a poor, honest woodcutter named Kariappa was chopping firewood along the steep, rocky banks of the Tungabhadra River. His old iron axe slipped from his sweaty hands and plummeted into the deep, swirling water.
Having no money to buy another tool to feed his hungry family, Kariappa sat upon the riverbank and wept with bitter sorrow.

Tenali Raman, who was walking along the river path, heard his weeping.
Learning of his plight, Tenali dove into the deep pool.
A moment later, Tenali surfaced holding an axe forged of glittering, solid gold!
'Is this thy axe, good man?' asked Tenali.

Kariappa looked at the dazzling gold, shook his head honestly, and said:
'No, noble sir. That axe is made of gold; it belongs to a king. My axe was an ordinary tool of rusted iron with a worn neem-wood handle.'

Tenali dove a second time, surfacing with an axe crafted of pure, polished silver with an ebony handle:
'Is this thy axe?'
Kariappa replied:
'No, master. That is of silver; I cannot claim what is not mine.'

Tenali dove a third time, bringing up Kariappa’s old, rusted iron axe.
Kariappa leaped with joy, tears of relief in his eyes:
'Yes! That is my axe! That is the breadwinner of my family!'

Tenali, moved by the woodcutter's rare, incorruptible honesty, presented him with all three axes—the gold, the silver, and the iron—along with a bag of grain, saying:
'Honesty like thine is worth more than all the gold in the river.'

Kariappa returned to his village, prosperous and happy.
Hearing of his fortune, an envious, greedy neighbor named Somanna took his own iron axe, ran to the same riverbank, threw his axe into the water, and sat down to weep fake tears.

Tenali Raman, watching from behind a tree, dove into the water and brought out a magnificent golden axe:
'Is this thy axe, friend?'
Somanna snatched greedily at the golden tool, shouting:
'Yes, yes! That is my axe! Give it to me!'

Tenali pulled the golden axe back, his eyes flashing with righteous disdain:
'Thou art a liar and a cheat! This gold belongs to the river, and since thou hast lied, thou shalt not even have thine own iron axe back!'

Tenali threw the golden axe back into the deep current, leaving the greedy cheat with empty hands, weeping real tears of regret over his lost tool, proving that greed reaps only loss, while honesty inherits the earth.
moral: Uncompromising honesty receives lasting honor, while greedy imitation reaps only empty hands.

title: The Tale of the Two Doors
summary: King Krishnadevaraya, desiring to test the intellectual acumen of his court councilors, constructed a grand philosophical maze in the sub...
keywords: the tale of the two doors
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, desiring to test the intellectual acumen of his court councilors, constructed a grand philosophical maze in the subterranean vaults beneath the palace.
At the end of the corridor stood two identical heavy iron doors:
One door led to the Royal Treasure Garden of Freedom;
The other door led to the Pit of Banishment.

Before the two doors stood two identical guards:
One guard always spoke the absolute truth;
The other guard always told a deliberate lie.
Neither guard wore any distinguishing badge, and the King gave each councilor permission to ask only **one single question** to **one single guard** to determine which door led to freedom.

Several ministers tried:
One asked: 'Art thou the truth-teller?' Both guards answered 'Yes!'
Another asked: 'Is this the door to freedom?' Both gave contradictory answers, leaving the ministers baffled and trapped in the maze.

Finally, Tenali Raman walked into the vault.
He looked at the two guards calmly. He walked up to the guard on the left and asked his single question:

'Tell me, guard: if I were to ask the other guard which door leads to the Royal Treasure Garden of Freedom, which door would he point to?'

The left guard pointed his spear toward the Door on the Left!

Tenali Raman smiled with supreme confidence.
Without hesitation, Tenali walked over and opened the **Door on the Right**!

The heavy iron door swung open, revealing the sunlit Royal Treasure Garden of Freedom, with King Krishnadevaraya standing there applauding with delight!

The King embraced Tenali:
'Tenali, how didst thou deduce the correct door with absolute certainty using only one question?'

Tenali explained his brilliant logical deduction:
'Maharaj, consider the two possibilities:
If the guard I asked was the Truth-Teller, he would truthfully tell me what the Liar would say. Since the Liar always points to the wrong door, the Truth-Teller would point to the Door of Banishment!
On the other hand, if the guard I asked was the Liar, he would lie about what the Truth-Teller would say. Since the Truth-Teller would point to the Door of Freedom, the Liar would also point to the Door of Banishment!
Therefore, in either case, the answer was guaranteed to point to the wrong door!
By simply choosing the opposite door, I was mathematically guaranteed to step into freedom!'

The King and the scholars marvelled at Tenali’s peerless logical brilliance, celebrating that true reason can navigate through any maze of deception.
moral: Logic and strategic questioning penetrate through deceit to reveal the path of safety.

title: Tenali and the King's Portrait with One Eye
summary: Following the historical battle of Raichur, King Krishnadevaraya carried a glorious battle scar: an enemy arrow had grazed his left cheek...
keywords: tenali and the king's portrait with one eye
full_text:
Following the historical battle of Raichur, King Krishnadevaraya carried a glorious battle scar: an enemy arrow had grazed his left cheek, leaving him partially blind in that eye. While the Emperor was proud of his martial courage, the court flatterers and nervous portrait artists struggled with how to paint his imperial likeness.

One courtier suggested covering the King's left eye with an embroidered silk patch like a pirate; another suggested painting him only from behind!
The King was disgusted by their cowardice:
'Am I a monster to be hidden? Or an emperor to be painted with truth?'

Tenali Raman stepped forward with a fresh wooden board and charcoal:
'Maharaj, your scars are the medals of our empire's freedom. An artist must paint not merely a face, but the soul of a warrior.'

Tenali requested the King to take up his golden recurve hunting bow and pose upon the palace terrace overlooking the distant blue hills.
Tenali painted for five days with natural earth pigments, lapis lazuli, and gold leaf.

When the canvas was unveiled, the entire assembly was awestruck.
Tenali had depicted King Krishnadevaraya standing upon a mountain crest at sunrise, drawing his golden bowstring taut to his ear.
The King was shown in a majestic right-side profile: his commanding right eye was open, focused with fierce, eagle-like concentration upon a distant target in the clouds, while his scarred left eye was naturally angled away in the dynamic posture of a master marksman!

The portrait did not hide the King's wound with false flattery, nor did it insult him with clumsy exposure; it placed the monarch in his natural element as the Supreme Archer and Defender of the Realm!

King Krishnadevaraya stepped down from his throne, gazing upon the canvas with profound emotion:
'Tenali, other painters saw only a blemish on my face. Thou hast seen the warrior in my heart. This portrait shall hang in the Grand Hall of Victory for centuries!'

The King awarded Tenali a hereditary jagir of land and a diamond ring, demonstrating that true respect honors reality with noble grace.
moral: Honoring human reality with dignity and heroic grace is the highest expression of art.

title: The Challenge of Making a Rope from Ashes
summary: An ambassador from a rival northern sultanate arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, presenting an extraordinary challenge from his sovere...
keywords: the challenge of making a rope from ashes
full_text:
An ambassador from a rival northern sultanate arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, presenting an extraordinary challenge from his sovereign:
'O Emperor Krishnadevaraya! My Sultan desires to test whether your famed courtiers possess true philosophical magic.
You must deliver to our capital within seven days a rope twenty cubits long woven entirely of pure ash!
If your court fails, Vijayanagara must pay a tribute of five thousand gold coins!'

The King and his ministers were in despair. Ash is powdery, crumbly, and has no fiber; as soon as one touches it, it dissolves into dust.
'How can anyone weave a rope out of ash?' groaned the Prime Minister.

Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, weaving a rope of ash is simple. Permit me to prepare it tonight.'

Tenali took a sturdy, well-twisted hemp rope measuring precisely twenty cubits in length.
He laid the rope flat in a straight, neat line upon a wide, flat granite slab in the palace courtyard.
He soaked the rope lightly in sesame oil and camphor, and then set fire to one end.
The flame burned steadily down the length of the rope without disturbing its woven twists.
When the fire burned out and the smoke cleared, the charred remains lay upon the granite slab completely undisturbed:
Every twist, braid, and fiber was preserved perfectly—yet the entire rope was made of solid, pure white and grey ash!

The next morning, Tenali invited the foreign ambassador and King Krishnadevaraya to the courtyard.
Pointing to the granite slab, Tenali said:
'Behold, noble ambassador! Here is your rope of pure ash, precisely twenty cubits long, woven with flawless braids!
Now, I pray thee: pick it up gently with your own hands and carry it to your Sultan!'

The ambassador reached down eagerly to pick it up—but the moment his fingers touched the fragile ash, the braid crumbled into powder between his fingers!

The ambassador gasped in embarrassment: 'I cannot lift it! It falls apart!'

Tenali smiled with dazzling triumph:
'Ah, noble envoy! My Emperor commanded me to make the rope of ash, and I have made it.
If your Sultan wishes to possess it, he must provide servants who know how to lift a rope of ash without breaking it!
Bring your carrying cases of cloud and wind to pack it, or acknowledge the superiority of Vijayanagara!'

The ambassador blushed, bowed low, and withdrew his challenge with profound apologies.
King Krishnadevaraya rewarded Tenali with a diamond armlet, celebrating that wit can answer any impossible puzzle.
moral: Impossible demands are best answered by demanding the impossible conditions necessary to receive them.
