title: Tenali Raman Tale 109
summary: A notoriously stingy landlord named Kuberappa was embarrassed by his reputation as a miser. To improve his social standing, he invited al...
full_text:
A notoriously stingy landlord named Kuberappa was embarrassed by his reputation as a miser. To improve his social standing, he invited all the scholars, poets, and councilors of Vijayanagara, including Tenali Raman, to an 'Imperial Eight-Course Banquet' at his grand mansion.

The guests arrived, their mouths watering in anticipation.
They were seated upon silk cushions around an empty dining hall.
Kuberappa entered, clapped his hands with theatrical enthusiasm, and said:
'Welcome, noble guests! Let the feast begin!
Imagine, my friends! Look at the imaginary silver platters before you!
Behold this celestial saffron rice cooked in pure ghee! Inhale its divine aroma!
Taste these imaginary almond laddus, crisp samosas, and roasted partridges!
Eat, my friends, eat of the feast of imagination!'

The bewildered guests sat in stunned silence with empty plates.
While the other scholars frowned in angry disgust, Tenali Raman smiled with supreme enthusiasm!
Tenali pretended to scoop up imaginary rice with his fingers, smacking his lips with loud relish:
'Ah! Divine! Magnificent! Kuberappa, your imaginary samosas are crispy, and your imaginary payasam is sweeter than nectar!'
Tenali chewed the empty air, swallowed imaginary sweets, and rubbed his stomach with theatrical joy:
'I have never eaten so well in all my life!'

Kuberappa was delighted, thinking Tenali was supporting his cheap trick.

As the gathering concluded, Kuberappa accompanied the guests to the front gate.
Tenali Raman turned to Kuberappa, bowed low, and reached into his pocket.
Tenali pulled out an empty fist, held it over Kuberappa’s open palm, and pantomimed dropping fifty heavy gold coins into the landlord's hand:
'Here, noble Kuberappa! Take this generous tip of fifty imaginary gold coins for your magnificent feast!
Feel their heavy, glittering weight! Buy yourself fifty imaginary cows and an imaginary palace of marble!'

Kuberappa stared at his completely empty hand:
'Tenali! My hand is empty! You have given me nothing!'

Tenali laughed with booming joy:
'Why, noble host! If an imaginary saffron banquet can fill the bellies of twenty hungry scholars, surely fifty imaginary gold coins will fill your treasury to overflowing!
You fed us on empty air, and I have paid you with phantom gold!
The account is balanced to the last coin!'

The entire gathering burst into roaring laughter, while Kuberappa turned red as a beet.
Humiliated by the lesson, Kuberappa rushed to his kitchen, ordered his cooks to light the fires, and served the guests an actual, lavish feast of real rice, ghee, and sweets, learning that hospitality must be real to earn real honor.
moral: Miserly hosts who promise grand banquets but serve empty airs deserve to feast on imaginary fragrances.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 110
summary: The King’s chief royal falconer, an arrogant man named Shaukat, boasted that his prize hunting falcon, Toofan, was the fiercest, fastest ...
full_text:
The King’s chief royal falconer, an arrogant man named Shaukat, boasted that his prize hunting falcon, Toofan, was the fiercest, fastest predator in the skies. He trained his birds through starvation and harsh whipping, mocking the palace pigeon-keepers who raised gentle homing doves.
Shaukat boasted:
'Gentle birds are cowards! Only beasts ruled by fear and hunger possess true skill!
My falcon can intercept and bring down any bird in Vijayanagara within two minutes of release!'

Tenali Raman smiled:
'Shaukat, love and gentle patience build stronger wings than cruelty and starvation.
I wager that a simple, gentle homing dove raised with affection can outfly your fiercest falcon!'

The wager was accepted before King Krishnadevaraya on the palace terraces.
Shaukat brought forward his fierce falcon, hooded, talons sharpened, screeching hungrily.
Tenali brought a modest, snow-white homing dove named Shanti, which perched calmly upon his wrist, cooing affectionately and pecking sweet millet from his palm.

The signal was given!
Tenali released the white dove into the sky.
Shaukat unhooded his fierce falcon, shouting: 'Strike, Toofan! Slay the dove!'
The falcon soared into the air with lightning speed, its talons extended, diving directly at the white dove!

Any ordinary bird would have panicked and fluttered into the open air to be shredded.
However, Tenali had trained the dove through patient love: whenever danger appeared, the dove knew that safety lay in diving straight into the deep, thorny bougainvillea trellis on the palace terrace!
The dove folded its wings, plummeted like a white stone, and darted safely into the dense, maze-like thorns of the thick bougainvillea bush!

The fierce falcon, blinded by aggressive hunger and flying too fast to pull up, crashed headlong into the dense, thorny brambles!
Its wings were tangled, its feathers plucked, and it struggled helplessly among the thorns, squawking in panic!

Tenali gently reached his hand into the safe inner hollow of the bush:
The little white dove hopped calmly onto his fingers, completely unhurt, cooing softly!

Tenali freed the tangled falcon, smoothed its bruised feathers, and handed it back to the humiliated falconer:
'Look, Shaukat! Thy falcon was driven by blind, starving fury, and crashed into ruin.
My dove was guided by calm trust and loving intelligence, finding safe refuge in an instant!
Cruelty blinds the eyes, but patience and gentle affection conquer the skies.'

The King praised Tenali’s gentle wisdom, awarded him the prize, and ordered the royal falconry to abandon harsh training methods in favor of humane care.
moral: Cruelty and arrogance toward gentle creatures are defeated by patient training and natural devotion.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 111
summary: A wealthy silk importer named Dhananjaya was burgled overnight of three heavy bolts of imported Chinese gold-woven damask, each bolt weig...
full_text:
A wealthy silk importer named Dhananjaya was burgled overnight of three heavy bolts of imported Chinese gold-woven damask, each bolt weighing thirty pounds.
The theft occurred during a brief monsoon shower that had softened the red clay pathway outside the warehouse.
The city police were baffled: the thief had covered his face and worn no distinctive shoes.

Tenali Raman was invited to inspect the crime scene.
Tenali examined the red clay path.
In the soft mud, there was a single set of bare human footprints leading away from the warehouse door toward the northern highway.
Tenali knelt, measured the footprints with a bamboo ruler, and examined their depth:

'Notice three things,' Tenali said to the King and the police captain:
'First: The footprint shows that the left foot is pressed far deeper into the mud than the right foot. A man who carries an uneven load over his left shoulder naturally presses harder with his left foot to maintain balance.
Second: The toes of the left foot are turned outwards at an angle of thirty degrees, while the heel is unusually narrow, indicating that the carrier walks with a slight habitual limp in his left hip.
Third: Along the path, every fifty paces, the walker stopped and leaned against a tree, leaving the distinctive circular indentation of a heavy round iron-shod walking stick!'

The police captain scratched his head: 'There are thousands of men in Vijayanagara, Tenali; how does this help us?'

Tenali smiled: 'We need not search the city; we need only check the palace porter registry for a man who limps in his left hip, uses an iron-shod staff, and has broad shoulders capable of carrying ninety pounds of fabric!'

The registry revealed only one match: a former palace porter named Somanna, who had retired with a hip injury.
Tenali and the guards marched to Somanna’s cottage.
Behind the stable, buried under dry hay, were the three stolen bolts of Chinese gold-woven damask!
Somanna’s iron-shod staff stood beside the door, matching the circular indentations in the mud with millimeter precision!

Somanna fell to his knees, confessing that a rival merchant had paid him to steal the cloth.
The silk was returned to Dhananjaya, and the King marveled at Tenali’s extraordinary forensic deduction:
'Tenali, while others saw only mud, thou didst read a complete portrait of the thief from his footprints!'
moral: Forensic observation of gait, depth, and weight solves crimes that leave no eyewitnesses.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 112
summary: The Chief Accountant of the Royal Treasury, an arrogant official named Govindaswamy, presented his audited annual revenue ledger to King ...
full_text:
The Chief Accountant of the Royal Treasury, an arrogant official named Govindaswamy, presented his audited annual revenue ledger to King Krishnadevaraya.
The King noticed that the tax collection from the wealthy diamond district of Bellary was listed as only ten thousand gold coins, whereas the district usually generated fifty thousand gold coins!
When questioned, Govindaswamy insisted:
'Maharaj, drought and poor yields reduced the tax collection. The ledger is written in indelible royal oak-gall ink and stamped with the district seal; it has not been altered by a single stroke!'

The King suspected embezzlement, but the calligraphy appeared smooth, uniform, and untouched to the naked eye.
Tenali Raman was summoned to examine the parchment.

Tenali held the palm leaf ledger up against the bright morning sunlight.
He examined the fibers of the paper beneath a high-magnification quartz lens:
Around the number '10,000', the surface of the parchment was noticeably thinner and slightly rougher than the surrounding paper, indicating that the original ink had been carefully scraped away with a fine razor!

Tenali smiled: 'Maharaj, the ink may be erased, but the chemical memory of the paper remains.'

Tenali procured a small vial of diluted tincture of gallic acid mixed with iron sulfate solution, and a soft camel-hair brush.
In the presence of the King and the trembling accountant, Tenali gently brushed the clear liquid across the scraped area of the ledger.

Within three minutes, a miraculous reaction occurred:
The chemical solution reacted with the invisible iron residues that had soaked deep into the parchment fibers from the original ink!
Right beneath the newly painted '10,000', the original, dark, indelible numbers reappeared with absolute clarity:
**50,000 Gold Coins**!

And right beside it, the original signature of the Bellary tax officer became legible!
Govindaswamy had pocketed forty thousand gold coins and scraped the '5' into a '1'!

The accountant shrieked, fell to his knees on the marble floor, and confessed his crime, revealing the hidden gold buried in his garden cellar.
King Krishnadevaraya was awestruck by Tenali’s brilliant forensic chemistry:
'Tenali, thou hast made invisible truth speak through chemical magic!'
The King restored the forty thousand gold coins to the public works fund, dismissed the corrupt accountant, and rewarded Tenali with a gold-embroidered robe of honor.
moral: Criminals who alter official accounts leave physical traces that chemical science easily exposes.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 113
summary: Outside the southern gates of Vijayanagara, a cunning ascetic named Swami Prakashananda set up an altar around an ordinary black basalt s...
full_text:
Outside the southern gates of Vijayanagara, a cunning ascetic named Swami Prakashananda set up an altar around an ordinary black basalt stone.
He proclaimed to gathering crowds of pilgrims:
'Behold the Miraculous Weeping Stone of Agastya!
Whenever I chant my sacred morning mantras, this holy stone miraculously weeps fragrant sesame oil from its pores!
Whoever donates a gold coin shall receive a drop of this miraculous oil to cure all diseases!'

Hundreds of sick pilgrims and poor villagers donated their hard-earned coins, and indeed, every morning at sunrise, glistening drops of golden oil seeped from the crevices of the black basalt rock!
The municipal councilors were awed, urging the King to build a grand gold-plated temple over the stone.

Tenali Raman visited the site at dusk after the pilgrims had departed.
He observed that the stone was black basalt—a dense, non-porous volcanic rock that cannot absorb or weep oil naturally.
Tenali examined the earthen hillock directly behind the stone altar:
He noticed that the grass was recently planted, and an ancient hollow tamarind tree stood ten paces behind the rock.

That night, accompanied by two trusted guards with spades, Tenali dug into the hillock behind the basalt stone.
Just two feet beneath the surface, they uncovered a hidden lead pipe running from the hollow trunk of the tamarind tree directly into a concealed drilled hole in the back of the basalt stone!
Tenali climbed the tamarind tree:
Inside the hollow trunk was a large copper tank filled with thirty gallons of sesame oil, fitted with a brass valve that could be turned on from behind the tree!

Tenali smiled. He did not break the pipe.
Instead, he poured a bottle of dark, foul-smelling fish oil and crushed bitter neem juice into the copper tank!

The next morning, Swami Prakashananda assembled hundreds of pilgrims, King Krishnadevaraya, and the ministers.
The ascetic began chanting loudly, while his hidden disciple turned the valve behind the tree!
The stone began to 'weep' oil!

The ascetic proudly caught the first drops in a silver spoon and offered it to the King:
'Taste the celestial nectar, Your Majesty!'
The moment the King smelled the spoon, a nauseating stench of rotten fish and bitter neem filled the air!
The King gagged in disgust:
'Ugh! What foul devil's stench is this?'

Tenali Raman stepped out from behind the tamarind tree, holding the severed lead pipe and the copper tank:
'Behold the source of the miracle, Maharaj!
The ascetic’s stone weeps whatever oil is poured into his secret tank!
Yesterday it wept sweet sesame oil to fleece the poor; today it weeps rotten fish to reveal the stench of his fraud!'

The crowd gasped in outrage.
The King ordered the charlatan arrested and sentenced to clean the public sewage canals for a year, while Tenali showed that superstitious miracles dissolve when their plumbing is exposed.
moral: Supernatural hoaxes that fake divine miracles to extract donations are demolished by simple inspection.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 114
summary: In the food bazaar of Vijayanagara, a notoriously dishonest sweetmaker named Mithai Ram operated a thriving shop. He was famous for using...
full_text:
In the food bazaar of Vijayanagara, a notoriously dishonest sweetmaker named Mithai Ram operated a thriving shop. He was famous for using two sets of brass weights: a lighter, hollowed-out set when selling sweets, and a heavier set when buying raw sugar, cheating poor customers on every transaction.
When poor mothers complained that their bag of laddus felt unusually light, Mithai Ram would sneer:
'My scales are blessed by the goddess of fortune! If the sweets feel light, it is because my sugar is as airy and delicate as celestial clouds!'

Tenali Raman decided to cure the dishonest merchant.

Tenali went to his friend, a skilled coppersmith, and had ten special coins crafted:
They were brass coins cast with a thin gold-gilded foil surface, but hollow inside, filled with light elder-pith, so that while they looked identical to heavy gold dinars, each coin weighed barely a fraction of a feather!

Tenali walked into Mithai Ram’s shop:
'Master Mithai Ram, I desire to purchase ten pounds of your finest saffron almond halwa for a royal banquet.'

Mithai Ram’s eyes gleamed with greed. He used his hollowed-out, fraudulent weights, scooped out barely seven pounds of halwa, packed it into a box, and placed it upon the scale:
'Ten pounds exactly, Master Tenali! That will be ten gold dinars!'

Tenali nodded with a pleasant smile.
He reached into his purse and counted out the ten hollow, lightweight gold coins, placing them in Mithai Ram’s palm.

Mithai Ram lifted the coins: they felt unnaturally light, like dry husks!
Mithai Ram shouted in outrage:
'Tenali! What trickery is this? These gold coins are completely hollow and weightless! They are not worth five coppers!'

Tenali Raman looked at him with innocent, wide eyes:
'Why, Master Mithai Ram! Did you not proclaim just moments ago that your sweets feel light because your sugar is as airy and delicate as celestial clouds?
My gold coins were forged in the exact same celestial cloud!
They are delicate, airy, spiritual coins!
A light box of halwa deserves a light purse of gold!
When your scale becomes honest, my coins will regain their weight!'

The surrounding crowd of customers burst into deafening cheers and laughter!
Mithai Ram turned crimson with shame, realizing that his own excuse had been turned into a weapon against him.
He fell to his knees, smashed his fraudulent weights with an iron hammer before the crowd, and swore to use only certified imperial balances henceforth.
Tenali smiled, paid him with real silver for the actual weight, and distributed the halwa to the poor children of the bazaar.
moral: Cheating the public with hollow weights invites a sharp-witted customer who pays with hollow coins.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 115
summary: Two foreign weavers named Jalal and Bilal arrived at the imperial court of Vijayanagara, claiming they were masters of the 'Mystical Ethe...
full_text:
Two foreign weavers named Jalal and Bilal arrived at the imperial court of Vijayanagara, claiming they were masters of the 'Mystical Ethereal Loom'.
They told King Krishnadevaraya:
'Your Majesty! We can weave an imperial coronation mantle so fine, so delicate, and so magical that it is completely invisible to anyone who is incompetent, corrupt, or born of dishonorable lineage! Only the pure of heart and truly wise can perceive its golden patterns!'

The King and his courtiers were captivated by the concept.
The weavers were given a private palace suite, fifty pounds of pure gold thread, fifty pounds of silk, and a generous advance of two thousand gold coins.
For three weeks, the two scoundrels sat at empty wooden looms, clicking their shuttles in empty air, pretending to weave with invisible threads!

The King sent his Prime Minister to inspect the progress.
The Prime Minister entered the room, looked at the empty looms, and saw nothing!
He panicked inwardly: 'Heavens! If I admit I see nothing, the King will declare me incompetent and corrupt!'
So the Prime Minister praised the weavers: 'Magnificent! What exquisite golden peacocks! What radiant azure flowers!'

Next went the Chief General: he, too, saw nothing, but terrified of appearing unfit for command, praised the 'invisible embroidery' with extravagant flattery!

Finally, the weavers announced the mantle was finished.
King Krishnadevaraya entered the room. The weavers pantomimed lifting an enormous, heavy garment:
'Behold, Your Majesty! Feel its feather lightness! Slip your royal arms into the sleeves!'
The King looked, saw only empty air, and broke into a cold sweat: 'Am I a fool? Am I unfit to be Emperor?'
Terrified of public disgrace, the King pretended to put on the invisible cloak, admiring himself before an empty mirror!

The King announced an imperial grand procession through the city, marching down the main boulevard dressed only in his white undergarments, pretending to wear the magnificent invisible mantle!
The courtiers walked behind, holding up empty hands as if carrying an invisible train, shouting:
'Look at the Emperor's glorious cloak! Long live the Emperor!'
The terrified citizens, afraid of being labeled corrupt, cheered and applauded the empty air!

Tenali Raman was standing along the procession route with his six-year-old son, Vittal.
Little Vittal looked at the King, blinked his round eyes in utter confusion, and suddenly shouted in a clear, ringing, innocent voice:
'Father! Look! The King has no clothes on! He is walking in his underwear!'

A dead silence fell across the boulevard.
Then a giggle broke out among the weavers, followed by a chuckle from a shopkeeper, and suddenly the entire crowd of thirty thousand citizens erupted into roaring, uncontrollable laughter!
*‘THE KING HAS NO CLOTHES ON! HE IS IN HIS UNDERWEAR!’*

King Krishnadevaraya stopped in his tracks, feeling the cool morning breeze against his bare shoulders.
The veil of vanity and fear was instantly shattered!
The King realized the monstrous absurdity of his pride.
He turned back to the palace, laughing heartily at his own folly.

The two swindlers were captured trying to flee with the gold and were sentenced to hard labor, while Tenali Raman and his son were rewarded for proving that honest innocence is the truest eye of an empire.
moral: Cowardly courtiers who pretend to see what does not exist out of fear are unmasked by a child's honest laughter.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 116
summary: In a wealthy merchant’s house in Vijayanagara, a skinny and agile cat-burglar named Somu climbed down the wide kitchen chimney flue at mi...
full_text:
In a wealthy merchant’s house in Vijayanagara, a skinny and agile cat-burglar named Somu climbed down the wide kitchen chimney flue at midnight to rob the brass and silverware.
However, during the previous day, the kitchen masons had narrowed the lower hearth with new bricks to improve the draft!
Halfway down the chimney, Somu got wedged tightly between the soot-covered bricks!
He could not move forward, nor could he pull himself back up to the roof!
He was trapped like an iron cork in a bottle!

Hearing muffled groans and soot dropping into the empty fireplace, the terrified merchant ran to Tenali Raman’s house next door, shouting that a demon was dwelling in his chimney!

Tenali arrived carrying no weapons or ladders.
He peered into the fireplace and saw two human legs dangling three feet above the hearth grate, kicking frantically.

Tenali smiled: 'Merchant, do not call the soldiers with sledgehammers; they will ruin your expensive chimney.
Let us prepare a midnight meal to welcome our guest!'

Tenali instructed the servants to bring a small bundle of dry chili peppers, a handful of bitter sulfur powder, and a bundle of damp green coconut husks.
Tenali placed the materials on the hearth grate directly beneath the dangling feet, and lit a small, smoldering fire.
Thick, pungent, white acrid smoke—infused with concentrated red chili fumes—began billowing up the chimney shaft!

Within five seconds, a frantic, coughing, tearful screaming exploded from inside the chimney:
*‘COUGH! ACHO0! MERCY! I AM NOT A DEMON!
I AM SOMU THE BURGLAR! I AM SUFFOCATING!
PULL ME DOWN! CALL THE POLICE! DO ANYTHING, BUT PUT OUT THE CHILIES!’*

Tenali poured a cup of water onto the fire, and called up:
'Somu, if we pull your legs down, will you confess all your burglaries to the magistrate?'
'YES! YES! I SWEAR UPON MY MOTHER’S HEAD!' shrieked the weeping thief.

Tenali and the servants gripped the dangling feet, gave a coordinated heave, and pulled Somu down through the brick opening!
Somu tumbled onto the hearth floor, completely black with soot from head to toe, coughing, sneezing, tears streaming down his face, looking like a chimney demon!

The guards arrived and took the thief into custody.
Somu led them to his hideout, where thirty stolen silver platters were recovered.
The merchant thanked Tenali with a basket of sweets, laughing at how easily a handful of dried chilies and a bit of smoke can disarm the craftiest housebreaker.
moral: A trapped burglar cannot escape the smoke of his own crime; patience outwaits violence.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 117
summary: Two celebrated vina virtuosos arrived at King Krishnadevaraya's court: Master Madhava, known for his dazzling, furious speed, and Master ...
full_text:
Two celebrated vina virtuosos arrived at King Krishnadevaraya's court: Master Madhava, known for his dazzling, furious speed, and Master Govinda, known for his deep, meditative melodies.
They engaged in a four-hour musical contest.
Master Madhava played with blistering rapidity, his fingers flying across the frets like lightning, producing ten thousand notes a minute!
Master Govinda played with profound, slow grace, letting each note resonate like a temple bell, pausing between phrases to let the music linger in the air.

The court was divided:
The younger courtiers favored Madhava’s astonishing speed;
The older scholars favored Govinda’s emotional depth.
King Krishnadevaraya could not decide who was the greater master, and turned to Tenali Raman.

Tenali stood up and said:
'Maharaj, music is not merely the striking of strings; music is the divine architecture of sound and silence.
To test who is the true master, I ask each musician to play one final composition:
The Hymn of the Sacred Pause!'

Master Madhava stepped forward. He plucked his vina strings furiously, playing at breakneck speed, but whenever he tried to pause, his nervous fingers twitched and kept plucking notes, unable to remain silent for even two seconds without breaking the rhythm!
His music was continuous noise without rest.

Then Master Govinda took up his vina.
He struck a single, pure, resonant bass note that vibrated through the marble hall like the sacred syllable OM.
Then Govinda closed his eyes, held his hands suspended above the strings, and remained completely, motionless in serene silence for one full minute!
The silence was so profound, so peaceful, and so heavy with spiritual presence that the entire audience held their breath, feeling the sublime echo of the music inside their own hearts!
Then Govinda struck the concluding harmonic chord with gentle perfection.

Tenali Raman smiled and turned to the King:
'Maharaj, any craftsman can train his fingers to run fast across strings like a spider, but only a true master of the soul knows how to honor the silence between the notes!
Without silence, music is only a clamor of noise; but with silence, a single note becomes an ocean of peace.
Master Govinda is the true master!'

King Krishnadevaraya and the court were moved to tears by Tenali’s profound aesthetic insight.
The King awarded the Golden Vina to Master Govinda, while Madhava bowed with humble respect, learning that the highest art is the mastery of stillness.
moral: True musical mastery knows that silence between notes is as sacred as the sound itself.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 118
summary: Three magnificent royal white peacocks, gifted to Queen Tirumala Devi by the King of Ceylon, disappeared from the royal aviary inside the...
full_text:
Three magnificent royal white peacocks, gifted to Queen Tirumala Devi by the King of Ceylon, disappeared from the royal aviary inside the palace gardens. The peacocks were pure white, with magnificent snow-colored plumage and blue eyes.
A rumor spread that a corrupt animal dealer named Bhima had stolen them and concealed them in his private farm outside the city.

The royal guards raided Bhima’s farm, but found only thirty common, mottled grey-and-green farm geese and brown turkeys in the pens.
Bhima laughed: 'Look around! I have no white peacocks! The guards are harassing an honest farmer!'

The captain was about to leave when Tenali Raman arrived at the farm.
Tenali looked at a large, windowless wooden barn in the center of the compound, locked with three iron padlocks.
Bhima said: 'That barn holds only sacks of dry onions and garlic; opening it will spoil the crop!'

Tenali did not break the locks.
He knew that peacocks possess an intense, instinctual reaction to the arrival of rain and thunder, spreading their plumage and emitting their distinctive, loud, ringing trumpet call: *‘MAY-AWE! MAY-AWE!’*

Tenali instructed two royal drummers, who had accompanied the guards, to set up two massive war drums (*nagaras*) outside the closed barn.
Tenali signaled the drummers:
The drummers struck the heavy drumheads with furious, rhythmic power, producing a deep, reverberating rumble that shook the ground, perfectly imitating the thunderclaps of a monsoon thunderstorm!
At the same time, Tenali’s servants tossed buckets of water onto the barn's tin roof to mimic torrential rain!

The moment the rhythmic thunder and rain sound echoed inside the dark barn, the birds inside responded to their nature!
From inside the locked barn came three unmistakable, loud, piercing, trumpet calls:
*‘MAY-AWE! MAY-AWE! MAY-AWE!’*
And the distinct, heavy rustling of massive white feathers fanning against the wooden walls was heard by everyone present!

Tenali turned to the police captain:
'Break down the doors! The onions are singing royal peacock hymns!'

The guards smashed open the doors:
There, standing inside a hidden straw pen, were the Queen's three pure-white peacocks, their magnificent snow-white tails fully fanned in response to the false thunder!

Bhima collapsed in terror, confessing his theft.
The white peacocks were returned safely to the Queen’s aviary, Bhima was imprisoned, and the King marveled at Tenali’s ingenious use of animal psychology to make the victims announce their own rescue.
moral: Nature's distinct calls and habits cannot be concealed; truth sounds its own fanfare.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 119
summary: A pretentious court astrologer named Pandit Vidyadhar boasted before King Krishnadevaraya: 'Maharaj, with this astrological slate and cha...
full_text:
A pretentious court astrologer named Pandit Vidyadhar boasted before King Krishnadevaraya:
'Maharaj, with this astrological slate and chalk, I hold the past, present, and future of every soul in the palm of my hand!
No event occurs in this palace without my slate recording it beforehand!'

Tenali Raman walked into the council hall, holding his closed right hand behind his back.
Tenali bowed to the astrologer:
'Revered Pandit, since your slate records all events beforehand, write upon your slate right now:
What is currently held in my right hand behind my back?
Is it dead, or is it alive?'

The astrologer’s mind raced in a frantic dilemma:
If he wrote 'It is alive', Tenali could instantly squeeze his hand, kill the small sparrow or insect inside, and show it dead!
If he wrote 'It is dead', Tenali could simply open his hand and let the living creature fly away!
Believing he had discovered the trap, the astrologer wrote with a smug smile upon his slate:
**'It is in your own hands whether it lives or dies!'**

The astrologer showed the slate to the King, boasting: 'Behold my unassailable wisdom!'

Tenali Raman laughed with boundless amusement!
He brought his right hand out from behind his back, opened his fingers, and revealed:
Inside his palm was a common, small, polished round river pebble!

Tenali tapped the stone:
'Master Astrologer! A river pebble was never alive, nor can it ever die!
Your profound philosophical answer about living and dying was an evasive trick to cover your ignorance!
If your slate cannot tell the difference between a bird and a stone, how can you claim to guide the destiny of an empire?'

The entire court erupted in roaring laughter!
The astrologer dropped his chalk, hid his slate beneath his shawl, and shrank into the background.
King Krishnadevaraya smiled, acknowledging that Tenali’s simple stone had shattered a mountain of pretentious claims.
moral: Those who claim to read the secrets of heaven are blinded by the simplest earthly surprises.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 120
summary: During a severe drought that impoverished thousands of cattle herders in the countryside, the chief court priests persuaded King Krishnad...
full_text:
During a severe drought that impoverished thousands of cattle herders in the countryside, the chief court priests persuaded King Krishnadevaraya to perform a lavish expiation ritual:
'Maharaj, to bring rain and cleanse the sins of the realm, you must cast a life-size sacred cow in solid gold, weighing one hundred tolas, and donate it exclusively to the senior priests of the council!'

The King, in his devout anxiety, was preparing to melt treasury gold when Tenali Raman arrived.
Tenali said: 'Maharaj, donating a golden cow is a noble thought. But let us invite the poorest cowherds of the kingdom to witness the sacred donation.'

On the day of the ceremony, the magnificent golden cow stood upon the altar, gleaming with fifty thousand gold coins' worth of precious metal.
The priests stood ready with silver platters to claim the treasure.

Tenali Raman entered the temple leading an emaciated, starving, living mother cow and her hungry little calf, whose ribs were poking through their hides.
Tenali led the starving animals straight up to the altar.

The priests shouted in disgust:
'Tenali! What sacrilege is this? Taking a filthy, starving cow onto the sacred altar of the Golden Cow?'

Tenali turned to the King and the priests with fierce, righteous moral clarity:
'Sacrilege?
Look at these two cows!
This living cow was created by heaven; she gave milk to nourish your children, and her bullocks plowed your fields for twenty years!
Today, because of the drought, she and her calf are starving to death, while her owner weeps without bread!
And here you stand, casting one hundred tolas of pure gold into a cold, dead, metal idol that cannot eat, cannot produce a single drop of milk, and cannot plow a field, merely to divide the gold among yourselves!

Tell me, O priests: which cow is truly sacred to heaven?
The living cow whose stomach cries for grass, or the dead metal cow that feeds only your greed?
If you melt this golden cow, its gold could buy grain and fodder to feed ten thousand starving cattle and poor farmers across the entire province for an entire year!'

Tenali’s profound, prophetic words struck the assembly like a thunderbolt.
Worshippers wept openly, and the priests lowered their heads in utter shame.
King Krishnadevaraya stood up, his eyes filled with tears of awakening:
'Tenali has spoken the truth of heaven!'

The King canceled the golden donation on the spot.
He ordered the gold melted and converted into emergency fodder banks, grain subsidies, and drinking water tanks for the drought-stricken pastoral communities.
The living cow and calf were adopted into the royal dairy, and Tenali was blessed by thousands of grateful farmers as the true protector of life.
moral: Religious charity is fulfilled by feeding living mouths, not by casting golden idols to enrich priests.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 121
summary: Two forest dwellers, a humble tribal honey-gatherer named Kanna and a wealthy, smooth-talking village trader named Somappa, appeared befo...
full_text:
Two forest dwellers, a humble tribal honey-gatherer named Kanna and a wealthy, smooth-talking village trader named Somappa, appeared before King Krishnadevaraya's court disputing ownership of an enormous, thirty-pound wild forest honeycomb harvested from the cliff face of Mount Matanga.
The honey was rare, fragrant with wild mountain lotus, and worth fifty silver coins.

Somappa swore: 'I found the hive, climbed the cliff, and harvested the honey with my own hands! Kanna stole the basket from my cart!'
Kanna wept: 'Maharaj, climbing the cliff is the hereditary trade of my people! I gathered it at midnight!'

The King was perplexed, as both men described the mountain cliff accurately.
He asked Tenali Raman to resolve the dispute.

Tenali said: 'Maharaj, the proof is not in the honey, but in the hands that gathered it.'

Tenali commanded both men to step forward and hold out their bare arms and palms before the court.
Tenali inspected Somappa’s hands:
Somappa’s hands were soft, smooth, fair, with trimmed fingernails, completely unblemished by thorns or stings.

Tenali then inspected Kanna’s arms and hands:
Kanna’s palms were rough, calloused, and hardened like tree bark from climbing granite cliffs.
More importantly, across Kanna’s forearms and neck were dozens of fresh, swollen red bee stings, and small cuts from mountain brambles!

Tenali smiled and said to the court:
'Wild mountain cliff bees are fierce defenders of their hives; no human can harvest thirty pounds of wild comb without receiving dozens of stings and scratches!
Somappa’s hands are as smooth as a baby’s cheek; he never climbed a cliff or faced a bee in his life!
Kanna’s body carries the honorable scars of his dangerous labor!'

Faced with the undeniable evidence of his own unblemished palms, Somappa confessed that he had stolen the basket while Kanna was washing his stings in the mountain stream.
The King awarded the honeycomb to Kanna, along with a purse of silver, and fined Somappa fifty coins for false testimony.
The people cheered Tenali Raman, who proved that the scars of honest toil are the truest title deeds of labor.
moral: The true creator of wealth is proven by the scars of labor, not by the smooth palms of claimants.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 122
summary: King Krishnadevaraya was troubled by sleepless nights and anxious political worries. He called Tenali Raman to his garden pavilion and as...
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya was troubled by sleepless nights and anxious political worries. He called Tenali Raman to his garden pavilion and asked:
'Tenali, what is the lightest thing in the universe, and what is the heaviest?'

The court scholars answered with textbook physics:
'A swan’s down feather is the lightest, Maharaj! And a boulder of solid iron is the heaviest!'

Tenali Raman shook his head gently:
'No, Maharaj. The scholars measure with brass balances, but life is measured by the soul.
A swan’s down feather is heavy compared to a **Clear Conscience**!
A man who has wronged no soul, spoken no slander, and stolen no copper sleeps upon a bed of stones as lightly as a bird floating upon the morning breeze! No anxiety weighs upon his heart, and his spirit is completely weightless!'

The King sighed, touched by the words: 'And what is the heaviest thing, Tenali?'

Tenali answered with penetrating moral depth:
'The heaviest thing in the universe, Maharaj, is **Guilt**!
A man who has taken an unlawful bribe, betrayed a faithful friend, or oppressed a poor subject may sleep upon cushions of velvet stuffed with swan feathers, yet his heart feels as though a mountain of molten lead were resting upon his chest!
Every creak of the floor terrifies him; every whisper sounds like an accusation; and no wealth on earth can lift the crushing weight of a guilty soul!'

King Krishnadevaraya sat in silence for a long time, absorbing the profound wisdom of Tenali’s counsel.
The Emperor stood up, took Tenali’s hand, and said:
'Tenali, thou hast diagnosed the true ailment of kings.
We worry about defending fortresses, yet the only fortress that truly preserves peace is an unblemished conscience.'

The King reviewed all pending prison petitions that afternoon, pardoned those unjustly detained, lowered taxes on struggling weavers, and that night, the Emperor slept with the peaceful lightness of a clear conscience.
moral: A clear conscience rests lighter than a feather; ill-gotten wealth weighs heavier than lead upon the soul.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 123
summary: In the newly renovated council chamber of the palace, King Krishnadevaraya had an ornate granite pillar installed, carved with images of ...
full_text:
In the newly renovated council chamber of the palace, King Krishnadevaraya had an ornate granite pillar installed, carved with images of celestial guardians.
A few weeks later, a chilling rumor spread among the ministers:
Whenever the King sat alone in the evening near the pillar, a faint, eerie, supernatural whisper echoed from the stone:
*‘Beware the Prime Minister... Trust only the Chief Treasurer...’*

King Krishnadevaraya, disturbed by the ghostly warnings, began to treat his faithful Prime Minister Appaji with cold suspicion, while promoting the dishonest Chief Treasurer, Devaraya.

Tenali Raman knew Prime Minister Appaji was incorruptible and suspected a treacherous conspiracy.
Tenali resolved to examine the whispering pillar.

Tenali waited until midnight, when the palace was quiet.
He entered the council chamber, lit a small oil lamp, and tapped the stone pillar with a small brass mallet from top to bottom.
At the height of six feet, the stone produced a slightly hollow, resonant ring!
Tenali examined the intricate stone carvings with a magnifying glass:
Beneath the carved ear of a celestial guardian, there was an almost invisible, paper-thin slit in the granite!

Tenali traced the direction of the pillar up to the ceiling.
Directly above the pillar was an ornamental false ceiling made of carved teakwood panels, leading to an attic storage gallery.

Tenali climbed into the dark attic above the chamber.
There, hidden beneath old rolls of carpets, Tenali found a long, hollow copper acoustic pipe, running from the attic floor straight down through the hollow core of the granite pillar to the tiny ear slit below!
Sitting on a stool beside the pipe, holding a speaking horn and waiting for the King’s evening prayer, was the Chief Treasurer’s confidential secretary!

Tenali gripped the secretary by his collar and marched him straight to the King’s private quarters!
Tenali brought the acoustic horn and exposed the mechanism before the Emperor:
'Maharaj! Behold your "celestial stone guardian"!
The pillar had no supernatural wisdom; it was merely an iron pipe through which a treacherous thief whispered poison to destroy an honest Prime Minister and seize control of the empire!'

King Krishnadevaraya was horrified and furious at his own gullibility.
He immediately restored Prime Minister Appaji to his full royal confidence, arrested the corrupt Chief Treasurer and his secretary, and had the hollow pipe dismantled.
The Emperor thanked Tenali Raman for preserving the integrity of the state against insidious deception.
moral: Supernatural whispers that manipulate royal decisions are traced to human conspirators hiding in the masonry.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 124
summary: A celebrated archery master from the northern borders, Drona Sen, arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that none in the souther...
full_text:
A celebrated archery master from the northern borders, Drona Sen, arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that none in the southern empire possessed true mastery of the bow.
He challenged the court archers:
'I can split an apple on a boy’s head at one hundred paces!
I challenge any courtier to shoot an arrow through a suspended iron ring at fifty paces while completely blindfolded!'

The royal archers failed, missing the ring completely.
King Krishnadevaraya turned to Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, canst thou shoot an arrow through the ring while blindfolded?'

Tenali smiled: 'Maharaj, I am a poet, not a warrior. But the mind has eyes that see clearer than physical vision. I accept the challenge!'

Tenali asked that the iron ring be suspended from a rope in the center of the archery range.
He tied a small brass bell to the top of the iron ring.
Tenali then tied a thick black silk cloth over his own eyes, ensuring total blindness.
He took up a royal recurve bow and notched a feathered arrow.

Tenali said: 'Let the wind blow, or let a courtier strike the brass bell once!'
A courtier gently tapped the bell: *‘TING!’*

The clear, ringing tone echoed across the silent courtyard.
Tenali stood motionless for three seconds, his ears attuned to the vibration, calculating the distance, the angle, and the height of the sound with complete, meditative concentration.
He drew the bowstring taut to his cheek, breathed out smoothly, and released the arrow:
*TWANG!*

The arrow whistled through the air!
*CLINK-THWACK!*
The arrow passed cleanly through the center of the suspended iron ring, striking the center of the wooden target post behind it with flawless accuracy!

The entire court erupted in thunderous, deafening cheers!
The northern archery master took off his hat, bowed low, and confessed:
'Tenali Raman, thou hast mastered the ancient secret of *Shabdavedhi*—striking a target purely by sound! Thou art a master of focus!'

The King embraced Tenali: 'Tenali, how didst thou shoot so accurately without eyes?'
Tenali smiled gently:
'Maharaj, physical eyes are easily distracted by the crowd, the flags, and self-doubt.
When the eyes are closed in calm discipline, the mind hears truth without distortion.
A clear mind sees through the ears and strikes true every time!'
moral: True vision is not merely in the eyes, but in the focused discipline of the concentrated mind.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 125
summary: During the celebration of his military triumph at Raichur, an exuberant King Krishnadevaraya promised an impoverished, elderly court poet...
full_text:
During the celebration of his military triumph at Raichur, an exuberant King Krishnadevaraya promised an impoverished, elderly court poet named Somadeva a royal reward of one thousand gold coins and a fertile orchard for his victory ode.
However, in the busy months of administrative reorganization that followed, the King completely forgot his promise.
Whenever poor Somadeva approached the palace, the royal chamberlains turned him away.
Somadeva came weeping to Tenali Raman: 'The Emperor’s promise was my family's only hope, but power forgets the poor.'

Tenali comforted him: 'King Krishnadevaraya is an honorable king; he has merely forgotten. Tomorrow, his memory shall be refreshed.'

The next morning, while King Krishnadevaraya was walking through the royal menagerie with Tenali Raman, they stopped before the enclosure of a newly arrived Bactrian camel.
The King looked at the camel’s large, curved, awkward hump and remarked with amusement:
'Tenali, look at that beast! Why has nature given the camel such an ugly, crooked, bent hump upon its back?'

Tenali Raman looked at the camel, sighed with deep, theatrical sorrow, and said:
'Alas, Your Majesty! That camel was once a great emperor in its past life!'

The King blinked in surprise: 'An emperor? Why is its back crooked then?'

Tenali replied with razor-sharp, devastating wit:
'Because in its past life, Maharaj, that emperor made a solemn promise to a poor poet to give him one thousand gold coins and an orchard, and then completely forgot his royal word!
Every time a king makes a solemn promise to a humble subject and forgets to honor it, heaven bends his spine a little further!
That poor camel’s back is crooked because it is weighed down by the heavy, unfulfilled promises of its past reign!'

King Krishnadevaraya froze.
The words hit the Emperor’s conscience like a thunderbolt!
He remembered his unfulfilled coronation promise to poor poet Somadeva!
The King blushed crimson with shame and profound realization.

The King turned to his chamberlain and commanded in a booming voice:
'Summon poet Somadeva to the palace immediately!
Deliver to him two thousand gold coins—double the promised reward—and the deeds to the finest mango orchard in the province!'

Somadeva was brought to court and showered with royal honors.
King Krishnadevaraya embraced Tenali Raman with tears of gratitude:
'Tenali, thou hast saved my spine from bending like a camel’s back!
A king who forgets his promises to the poor forgets his honor before heaven.'

The court celebrated Tenali’s brilliant, compassionate wit, which held power accountable to truth.
moral: A ruler who makes promises to the poor must fulfill his sacred word; a camel's hump serves as an unforgettable reminder.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 126
summary: Following an unexpected spike in municipal lamp-oil taxes, poor artisans and weavers in Vijayanagara could no longer afford oil for eveni...
full_text:
Following an unexpected spike in municipal lamp-oil taxes, poor artisans and weavers in Vijayanagara could no longer afford oil for evening lamps, forcing their families to eat dinner and work in total darkness.
When Tenali Raman raised the issue in council, King Krishnadevaraya dismissed it lightly:
'What difference does a little darkness make? One eats with one’s mouth, not with one’s eyes! A sensible man can find his rice in the dark without complaining!'

Tenali Raman smiled politely and said nothing.
Two days later, Tenali invited King Krishnadevaraya and five senior ministers to an 'Exclusive Imperial Royal Banquet' at his house at nightfall.

The King and ministers arrived dressed in fine silks.
They were seated around a low table upon velvet floor cushions.
Before the food was brought in, Tenali quietly extinguished every single oil lamp and candle in the house, shuttered all windows, and bolted the doors, plunging the room into pitch-black, absolute darkness!

The King blinked in confusion: 'Tenali! Why hast thou extinguished the lamps? It is pitch black!'

Tenali’s voice echoed from the shadows:
'Maharaj! Remember your royal wisdom spoken in council: "One eats with one’s mouth, not with one’s eyes!"
To honor your philosophy, tonight’s royal feast is served in total darkness!'

Servants placed large banana leaves before each guest in the dark, laden with hot, spicy curries, sticky rice, rasam, and sweet, runny payasam.
The hungry King and ministers attempted to eat:
In the pitch-black room, chaos immediately ensued!
The King tried to scoop up rice, but plunged his fingers directly into a bowl of burning hot, spicy rasam: 'Ouch! My fingers!'
Minister Chandrashekar reached for a sweet laddu, but grabbed the Prime Minister’s knee instead!
Another minister brought his hand up to eat, missed his mouth completely, and shoved a handful of sticky, sweet payasam straight into his own left eye and mustache!
Curry spilled onto silk dhotis, water jugs were overturned, and courtiers bumped heads in the dark, groaning and grumbling!

King Krishnadevaraya shouted in exasperation:
'Tenali! Light the lamps this instant! We cannot eat a single bite without smearing curry across our faces!'

Tenali struck a flint and lit a row of bright brass lamps.
The sight revealed was hilarious:
The King’s mustache was dripping with sweet pudding, the ministers were splattered with yellow dal and red chili curry, looking like bruised circus clowns!

The King looked around at his stained ministers, then looked at Tenali standing with folded hands.
The Emperor felt a deep, humble realization.
Tenali spoke softly:
'Maharaj, if the greatest Emperor in India and his noble ministers cannot eat dinner in the dark for ten minutes without burning their fingers and spilling their food, imagine the misery of thousands of poor weavers, potters, and children forced to spend their nights in darkness because of an unjust tax on lamp oil.'

King Krishnadevaraya wiped the pudding from his face, embraced Tenali, and immediately abolished the lamp-oil tax, ordering free oil distributed to poor artisans.
The people blessed Tenali Raman for bringing light to their homes through the magic of a darkened feast.
moral: A ruler must understand the daily hardships of his subjects; tasting darkness teaches empathy.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 127
summary: A cunning textile merchant named Haridas arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, claiming he possessed a shawl woven of 'Spiritual Lotus Mi...
full_text:
A cunning textile merchant named Haridas arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, claiming he possessed a shawl woven of 'Spiritual Lotus Mist'.
He brought an empty, ornate velvet-lined wooden box, opened it before King Krishnadevaraya, and pantomimed unfolding a delicate garment:
'Jahanpanah! Behold this celestial shawl! It is woven from the spiritual mists of Mount Kailash!
It has no physical weight, but its magical threads keep the wearer cool in summer and warm in winter!
However, only a monarch of pure divine intellect can see its subtle celestial blue threads; to fools and incompetents, it appears like empty air!'

The King and the courtiers stared at the empty box.
Terrified of being considered foolish, King Krishnadevaraya nodded vigorously:
'Ah! Yes, indeed! What exquisite azure embroidery! What celestial lightness!'
The courtiers chimed in with competitive flattery:
'Remarkable! The flowers look alive! What peerless weaving!'

The merchant bowed: 'The price for this celestial shawl is only one thousand gold coins!'
The King was on the verge of paying when Tenali Raman stepped forward with an expression of ecstatic admiration:
'Maharaj! The merchant’s shawl is sublime!
Allow me the honor of draping this celestial shawl around Your Majesty’s shoulders right now!'

Tenali reached into the empty box with careful, delicate fingers, pretended to lift the invisible shawl, and draped the empty air across the King's shoulders!
Tenali smoothed the invisible folds over the King’s chest:
'Look at Your Majesty! What divine majesty!
Now, Maharaj, to complete this spiritual transaction, let us pay the merchant in the exact same celestial currency!'

Tenali pulled out his leather purse, held his empty hand over the merchant’s palm, and mimed dropping heavy gold coins into the merchant's hand:
*‘Clink! Clink! Clink!’*
Tenali said:
'Here, Master Haridas! Take these one thousand Celestial Spiritual Gold Coins forged from the golden clouds of heaven!
Like your shawl, these coins have no physical weight, and can only be seen and spent by merchants of pure divine intellect!
Feel their heavy celestial radiance in your purse!'

The merchant stared at his empty hand in frozen horror:
'Tenali! My hand is completely empty! You have paid me with nothing!'

Tenali replied with razor-sharp irony:
'Why, Master Haridas? If an invisible shawl of empty air can be sold to a King for real gold, surely invisible celestial gold coins are the only proper payment for such an ethereal garment!
When you bring a real shawl woven of real silk by real human hands, the King will pay you in real gold!'

The King and the entire court burst into thunderous, body-shaking laughter!
The swindler snatched his empty box and fled from Vijayanagara, while King Krishnadevaraya praised Tenali’s presence of mind, which protected the treasury from vanity.
moral: Pretentious vanity that boasts of appreciating non-existent subtleties is cured by holding an empty mirror.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 128
summary: In a quiet ward of Vijayanagara lived an old scholar named Somayaji, who had accumulated two thousand gold coins through a lifetime of ex...
full_text:
In a quiet ward of Vijayanagara lived an old scholar named Somayaji, who had accumulated two thousand gold coins through a lifetime of extreme frugality. He wore threadbare rags, ate only dry rice crusts, starved his family, and refused to spend a single copper on doctor's medicine when sick.
Every midnight, he would unearth an iron pot buried beneath his bedroom floor, count his gold coins, weep with greedy joy, and bury them again.

One night, a clever burglar observed him through a window crack, dug up the iron pot while Somayaji was asleep, and vanished with all the gold!

The next morning, when Somayaji found the empty hole in the floor, he collapsed in agonizing despair. He tore his hair, beat his chest, and screamed so loudly that the entire neighborhood gathered:
'My gold is gone! My life is over! I will drown myself in the well!'

Tenali Raman arrived at the scene.
He looked at the empty pit, picked up a large, heavy granite river stone from the courtyard, and dropped it into the hole:
*THUD!*

Tenali turned to the weeping miser:
'Somayaji, dry your tears. Cover this stone with earth, and pretend it is your pot of gold!'

Somayaji yelled in fury:
'Tenali, art thou mocking my ruin? A granite stone is not a pot of gold! I cannot spend a stone!'

Tenali Raman looked at him with profound philosophical clarity:
'Didst thou ever spend a single copper of thy gold while it was buried in that hole?
Didst thou buy clothes to warm thy shivering back?
Didst thou buy medicine to heal thy cough?
Didst thou share a grain of rice with a starving child?
No!
Thou didst only look at it in the dark, touch it, and bury it in the dirt!
For twenty years, thy gold was nothing more than heavy stones resting in the mud!
Cover this stone with earth, look at the spot every midnight, and imagine thy gold is still there!
For gold that is never spent, never shared, and never used to relieve human suffering has no more value than common granite dirt!'

The crowd murmured in deep approval of Tenali’s profound words.
Somayaji stood transfixed. The truth pierced through his hardened heart of avarice like an arrow of light.
He realized that his greed had made him a penniless beggar while sitting upon a fortune.
When the police recovered half his stolen gold a week later, Somayaji was a transformed man: he built a hospital ward for the poor, bought warm clothes for his family, and lived with generous peace, cured of his miserly blindness forever.
moral: A hoarder who loves money more than life discovers that unspent gold buried in dirt is no different from common stones.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 129
summary: For the grand festival of Vijaya Dashami, King Krishnadevaraya commissioned a magnificent Navaratna (Nine Gems) royal diadem from the gui...
full_text:
For the grand festival of Vijaya Dashami, King Krishnadevaraya commissioned a magnificent Navaratna (Nine Gems) royal diadem from the guild of imperial jewelers.
When the crown was delivered, it was a dazzling spectacle: diamonds, rubies, emeralds, sapphires, pearls, corals, topaz, cat’s eyes, and garnets blazed in golden filigree.
The Chief Goldsmith swore: 'Every gem is of first-water purity, tested by fire and stone!'

However, an anonymous note reached Tenali Raman, warning that the central ruby—a stone valued at ten thousand gold coins—was an imitation made of red Bohemian crystal foil!

Tenali examined the crown in the presence of the King and the jewelers.
To the naked eye, the red gem sparkled with intense fire.
The jewelers scoffed: 'Tenali is a poet; what does he know of lapidary arts?'

Tenali asked for a common unglazed terracotta brick and a bowl of fresh lemon juice.
Tenali explained:
'A genuine Burmese ruby possesses a hardness of nine on the mineral scale; it cannot be scratched by hardened steel, nor does natural sunlight alter its inner refraction when immersed in acid.
Foil-backed crystal, on the other hand, relies upon a thin layer of silver-mercury amalgam painted on its rear facets to reflect light.'

Tenali placed the central red gem gently into the warm lemon juice.
He then took an unglazed terracotta tile and rubbed the surface of the gem firmly against the rough clay.
Within thirty seconds, a fine grey powder began to rub off the stone, and the bright crimson fire inside the gem suddenly dissolved into a dull, pale, scratched piece of common red glass!
The acid had dissolved the false silver foil backing, exposing the cheap crystal underneath!

The Chief Goldsmith turned white as chalk, falling to his knees on the marble floor:
'Mercy, Maharaj! I substituted the real ruby and hid it in my workshop safe!'

The real Burmese ruby was recovered, the dishonest jeweler was dismissed and fined, and King Krishnadevaraya embraced Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, thy simple lemon juice and clay brick have defended the honor of the imperial crown!'
Tenali smiled, reminding the court that genuine truth fears no friction, while false brilliance dissolves under testing.
moral: Flawless integrity shines without fear; true gems need no painted foils to prove their brilliance.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 130
summary: In the fruit market of Vijayanagara, two fruit vendors, Govind and Balaram, engaged in a violent physical scuffle over an enormous wicker...
full_text:
In the fruit market of Vijayanagara, two fruit vendors, Govind and Balaram, engaged in a violent physical scuffle over an enormous wicker basket containing eighty prize Neelam mangoes.
Govind shouted: 'I picked these mangoes from my own orchard at dawn! Balaram grabbed the basket from my cart while I was parking!'
Balaram yelled: 'A lie! My son and I harvested them yesterday afternoon; it is my basket!'

Because both men were recognized fruit vendors, the market guards brought them before Tenali Raman.

Tenali looked at the basket of mangoes.
He called each vendor forward separately to question them away from the other’s hearing.
Tenali asked Balaram:
'How many mangoes are in the basket?'
Balaram replied: 'About eighty or ninety, master.'
'What is lining the bottom of the basket?'
Balaram guessed: 'Ordinary dry rice straw, master.'

Tenali then called Govind forward:
'Govind, how many mangoes are in the basket?'
Govind answered without hesitation:
'Exactly eighty-four mangoes, master. My daughter counted them three times.'
'And what is lining the bottom of the basket beneath the fruit?'
Govind replied:
'Because the basket was rough, I lined the bottom with three broad, green jackfruit leaves, and beneath the leaves lies a small, folded piece of red cotton cloth where my daughter tied a small sprig of fresh tulsi for auspiciousness.'

Tenali had the basket brought to the center of the court.
He removed the top layers of mangoes:
Count: Exactly **eighty-four** mangoes!
At the bottom lay three broad green jackfruit leaves, and beneath them lay the folded piece of red cotton cloth containing the fresh sprig of tulsi!

Tenali turned to Balaram:
'A thief sees only the prize on top, but the owner knows every leaf and cloth placed by his own family’s hands!'

Balaram fell to his knees, confessing the theft.
The fruit was returned to honest Govind, Balaram was fined twenty silver coins to be given to Govind's daughter, and the market merchants applauded Tenali Raman’s sharp forensic inquiry.
moral: Truth speaks through the natural details of memory, while thieves stumble over fabricated stories.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 131
summary: A wholesale oil merchant named Chennappa was robbed of two large leather casks containing fifty gallons of pure, expensive pungent black ...
full_text:
A wholesale oil merchant named Chennappa was robbed of two large leather casks containing fifty gallons of pure, expensive pungent black mustard oil from his warehouse.
The next day, Chennappa discovered that a rival merchant named Shankara was suddenly selling large quantities of fresh black mustard oil at half the market price.
Shankara claimed: 'I pressed this oil from my own mustard harvest in my private mill!'

Chennappa appealed to the court.
Shankara produced witnesses who swore they had seen his oil mill turning.
The magistrate was ready to dismiss the case when Tenali Raman stepped forward.

Tenali inspected the disputed oil in Shankara’s shop.
Tenali asked Chennappa:
'Chennappa, what unique traditional method did your family use when pressing your famous mustard oil?'
Chennappa whispered privately to Tenali:
'Master Tenali, my late grandfather always added crushed dried cloves and wild cinnamon bark into the pressing mortar to give our oil its distinctive preservative aroma and golden-amber hue.'

Tenali took a sample of the disputed oil, poured it into a shallow porcelain bowl, and heated it gently over an oil lamp.
As the oil warmed, a subtle, unmistakable, fragrant aroma of toasted cloves and cinnamon rose into the air!

Tenali then took a second bowl containing pure, unadulterated mustard oil pressed that morning in the public market, and heated it.
It smelled purely of raw, acrid mustard, with no trace of cloves or cinnamon!

Tenali turned to Shankara:
'Shankara, you claimed you pressed this oil from ordinary seeds in your private mill.
Why does your oil emit the sweet fragrance of toasted cloves and cinnamon—a secret recipe used exclusively by Chennappa’s family for four generations?
Can common mustard seeds magically sprout cloves in your mill?'

Shankara’s face blanched. He was completely trapped by the aromatic evidence.
He dropped to his knees, confessed the burglary, and led the guards to his cellar where the remaining oil casks were recovered.
King Krishnadevaraya praised Tenali’s sharp sensory observation, which used culinary science to deliver justice.
moral: Nature leaves invisible signatures that chemical reaction reveals with certainty.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 132
summary: A secret treaty document outlining military defenses on the northern border disappeared from King Krishnadevaraya’s private study inside ...
full_text:
A secret treaty document outlining military defenses on the northern border disappeared from King Krishnadevaraya’s private study inside the royal apartments.
Only three senior officials had access to the study: Minister Timmappa, General Veeranna, and Secretary Raghavan.
The King was in agony: 'One of my closest confidants is an enemy spy!'

Tenali Raman entered the private study.
He looked around the room:
In the corner, perched on a brass ring, was the Queen’s favorite grey African parrot, a gift from an Egyptian ambassador, known for repeating human phrases.
Tenali asked: 'Maharaj, was the parrot in this room when the document was stolen?'
'Yes,' replied the King, 'the bird has lived here for three months.'

Tenali sat quietly beside the parrot’s cage, feeding it pomegranate seeds and gently whistling.
For two hours, Tenali waited patiently.
Suddenly, as the palace bells chimed three o'clock, the parrot cocked its head, fluttered its wings, and began speaking in a low, conspiratorial human whisper:
*‘Quick, hide it under the saddlecloth... Meet at the Bellary crossroads at midnight...’*

Tenali listened intently: the parrot’s mimicry was extraordinary!
It did not merely repeat words; it imitated the exact nasal timbre, cadence, and breathy whisper of **Secretary Raghavan**!

Tenali immediately alerted the King.
A troop of royal cavalry was dispatched to the Bellary highway.
At the fourth milestone, they intercepted Secretary Raghavan riding a fast mare:
Hidden beneath the quilted leather saddlecloth was the secret military defense treaty, ready to be delivered to enemy envoys!

Raghavan was arrested and confessed his treason.
King Krishnadevaraya was awestruck:
'Tenali, while my spies searched the city, thou didst listen to a bird!'
Tenali smiled:
'Maharaj, conspirators speak in whispers believing walls cannot hear, but nature places sentinels where human eyes forget to look.'
The loyal parrot was granted a lifetime supply of royal pomegranates, and Tenali’s vigilance was celebrated across the empire.
moral: Truth cannot be suppressed by walls; innocent creatures echo the words spoken in shadows.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 133
summary: An eccentric visiting mathematician from Ujjain, Master Aryabhatta II, challenged the scholars of Vijayanagara with a culinary puzzle: 'I...
full_text:
An eccentric visiting mathematician from Ujjain, Master Aryabhatta II, challenged the scholars of Vijayanagara with a culinary puzzle:
'I place five dried black peppercorns upon this table.
I challenge any mathematician in this court to divide these five peppercorns equally among three scholars, so that each scholar receives an identical whole number of peppercorns, without cutting, grinding, crushing, or breaking a single peppercorn, and without leaving any peppercorns on the table!'

The court mathematicians argued for two hours:
'Five cannot be divided by three without fractions! Five divided by three is one and two-thirds! It is mathematically impossible without cutting the peppercorns!'

Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, the division is simple and mathematically flawless!'

Tenali called the three scholars forward to the table: Scholar A, Scholar B, and Scholar C.
Tenali picked up the five peppercorns.
He handed **one peppercorn** to Scholar A.
He handed **one peppercorn** to Scholar B.
He handed **one peppercorn** to Scholar C.

Tenali then picked up the remaining two peppercorns, looked at Scholar A, Scholar B, and Scholar C, and said:
'Now, brothers, look at the table:
Has each of you received an identical whole number of peppercorns?'
The three scholars answered: 'Yes! Each of us has received exactly one whole peppercorn!'
Tenali asked: 'Was any peppercorn cut, crushed, or broken?'
'No, all are whole!'
Tenali asked: 'And are there any peppercorns left on the table?'
'No, the table is clean!'

Tenali then popped the remaining two peppercorns straight into his own mouth, chewed them with a loud crunch, and swallowed them with a smile!
'And these two peppercorns are the mathematician’s consulting fee paid to Tenali Raman for resolving the dispute!'

The entire court erupted in roaring laughter!
The visiting mathematician stared in utter bewilderment, then broke into appreciative applause:
'Brilliant! The puzzle stated that each scholar must receive an identical whole number without breaking any, and that none remain on the table!
Tenali fulfilled every single condition with practical wit!'
King Krishnadevaraya rewarded Tenali with a purse of silver, celebrating that practical wisdom outshines theoretical rigidities.
moral: Simplicity and sharp wit solve riddles where complex mathematics creates confusion.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 134
summary: Two cloth merchants, Madhav and Keshav, formed a business partnership to buy and sell fine silks. After a year of trading, they had accum...
full_text:
Two cloth merchants, Madhav and Keshav, formed a business partnership to buy and sell fine silks. After a year of trading, they had accumulated fifty bolts of silk of varying quality and twenty bags of silver.
However, mutual greed corrupted their partnership:
Madhav claimed the finest twenty-five bolts of gold-embroidered silk, offering Keshav only the coarse dyed cotton;
Keshav claimed all twenty bags of silver, offering Madhav only the damaged goods.
They appeared before King Krishnadevaraya, accusing each other of embezzlement and perjury.

The King, exhausted by their shouting, asked Tenali Raman to divide the assets equitably.

Tenali smiled:
'Maharaj, ancient law provides the perfect, incorruptible method of equitable division:
**The Rule of the Cake: One Divides, the Other Chooses!**'

Tenali brought all fifty bolts of silk and the twenty bags of silver into the center of the hall.
He turned to Madhav:
'Madhav, since you claim to be the senior partner, you shall divide all the silk and silver into two separate piles upon this floor.
Divide them however you see fit!'

Madhav’s eyes gleamed with greed. He thought:
'I will put the forty finest silk bolts and fifteen bags of silver into Pile One, and put the ten cheap bolts and five bags into Pile Two, so I can claim Pile One!'
Madhav arranged the piles accordingly.

When Madhav finished, he puffed out his chest: 'The division is complete!'

Tenali Raman smiled with devastating brilliance and turned to **Keshav**:
'Now, Keshav! As the junior partner, you have the absolute legal right to choose whichever pile you desire for yourself!'

Keshav leaped forward with a joyous shout and seized **Pile One** containing forty finest silks and fifteen bags of silver!
Madhav was left staring in frozen, horrified despair at **Pile Two**, containing only ten cheap bolts and five bags!

Madhav shrieked: 'Wait! That is unfair! I made Pile One for myself!'

Tenali looked at him with stern moral justice:
'If you had divided the property with absolute fairness and equal honesty, you would have been completely satisfied with whichever pile was left!
Your own greed designed the trap, and justice has closed the door upon you!'

King Krishnadevaraya and the court cheered Tenali’s timeless demonstration of fair division.
Madhav was forced to accept his share, learning that selfish cunning always defeats its own author.
moral: Partners who conspire to cheat each other are easily exposed by requiring one to divide and the other to choose.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 135
summary: A corrupt provincial governor named Jagannatha Rao sent a magnificent 'ceremonial tribute' to King Krishnadevaraya: A miniature, life-siz...
full_text:
A corrupt provincial governor named Jagannatha Rao sent a magnificent 'ceremonial tribute' to King Krishnadevaraya:
A miniature, life-size bullock cart crafted entirely of teakwood overlaid with embossed gold foil, pulled by two wooden bullocks with horns of pure silver.
Accompanying the cart was a letter from the governor:
'A humble token of my infinite loyalty, funded entirely from my modest ancestral savings!'

In reality, the governor had embezzled twenty thousand gold coins from the provincial road maintenance budget, leaving bridges broken and trade routes impassable.
The King was dazzled by the golden cart, preparing to promote the governor.

Tenali Raman inspected the golden cart.
He noticed that beneath the thin gold foil, the teakwood base was stamped with the official government insignia of the **Provincial Public Works Department**!

Tenali stepped before the King:
'Maharaj, Governor Jagannatha Rao’s loyalty is so extraordinary that he has offered to demonstrate the practical utility of his golden bullock cart today!'

Tenali had the golden cart hitched to two real, powerful palace oxen in the courtyard.
Tenali loaded the cart with fifty bags of heavy stone gravel from the broken city road.
Tenali then turned to Governor Jagannatha Rao, who was present in court:
'Noble Governor! Since you built this magnificent cart from your road budget, mount the driver’s seat and drive it across the main highway to Bellary to deliver these gravel bags to repair the broken bridges!'

The governor broke into a cold sweat:
'Master Tenali! This is a decorative ceremonial cart! Its axles are made of soft gold foil; if it carries heavy gravel across rough roads, the wheels will snap!'

Tenali replied with thunderous moral authority:
'Aha! The golden cart snaps under real gravel, just as your provincial roads collapsed because you spent the public road maintenance budget on gold foil to flatter the Emperor!
While you built gold carts for the palace, common bullock carts belonging to poor farmers are breaking their axles in muddy potholes on your neglected highways!'

An immediate imperial audit of the governor's province revealed that twenty thousand gold coins allocated for bridge repairs had been stolen.
The King stripped the corrupt governor of his post, melted down the golden cart to finance real road and bridge construction, and praised Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, thou hast turned a corrupt ornament into real roads for my people!'
moral: Public servants who accept lavish bribes disguised as ceremonial gifts find their graft exposed by fiscal reality.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 136
summary: During an afternoon hunting expedition in the rocky crags of Anegundi, King Krishnadevaraya’s prized northern hunting hawk, Garud, slippe...
full_text:
During an afternoon hunting expedition in the rocky crags of Anegundi, King Krishnadevaraya’s prized northern hunting hawk, Garud, slipped its jesses and flew into the dense mountain forest.
The King was heartbroken: the bird was loyal, had saved the King from a poisonous cobra years before, and responded only to a silver whistle.
Three companies of soldiers beat the bushes for two days, blowing horns and shouting, but the hawk was nowhere to be found.

The King fell into deep gloom, refusing to hold court.
Tenali Raman volunteered: 'Maharaj, hawks do not respond to beating drums and shouting soldiers; noise drives them higher into the peaks. Allow me to bring Garud back before sunset.'

Tenali did not take soldiers or drums.
He took a small wicker basket containing three fat, live field quail—a hawk’s favorite prey—and a small brass pan of fresh sheep’s liver seasoned with aromatic oil.
Tenali also took the King’s silver hunting whistle.

Tenali climbed to a high, rocky plateau overlooking the forested valley where the bird was lost.
He observed the afternoon sky:
High above the thermal updrafts, circling gracefully on mountain winds, was a solitary raptor with a distinctive white wing-band. It was Garud!

Tenali did not shout or wave.
He placed the fragrant liver on a flat, sun-warmed granite boulder where the rising thermals would carry its scent upward.
Then Tenali tied one live quail by its leg to a peg in the soft grass, allowing it to flutter its wings gently.
Tenali hid beneath a camouflaged screen of wild fern branches, held the silver whistle to his lips, and blew the King’s exact three-note hunting call:
*‘TWEET... TWEET-TWEEE!’*

High in the sky, the hawk heard the familiar silver whistle and caught the scent of warm meat!
Seeing the fluttering quail below, Garud folded its wings and executed a breathtaking, vertical dive from the clouds!
*WHOOOOSH!*

The hawk landed gracefully upon the granite boulder, digging its talons into the meat.
Tenali emerged slowly from the ferns, speaking gentle, soothing words in the falconer's dialect, and extended his leather-gloved arm:
The magnificent bird recognized the gentle voice, hopped calmly onto Tenali’s wrist, and allowed the leather jesses to be fastened!

Tenali carried the hawk back to the palace.
When King Krishnadevaraya saw his beloved hunting companion perched safely on Tenali’s wrist, tears of joy filled the Emperor's eyes!
The King rewarded Tenali with a diamond armlet, celebrating that understanding the nature of living creatures accomplishes what an army cannot.
moral: Careful inquiry into natural habits recovers lost companions where blind searching fails.
