title: Tenali Raman Tale 137
summary: A charismatic traveling charlatan named Hakim Dhanvantari arrived in Vijayanagara, selling bottles of a cloudy, foul-smelling dark liquid...
full_text:
A charismatic traveling charlatan named Hakim Dhanvantari arrived in Vijayanagara, selling bottles of a cloudy, foul-smelling dark liquid he called the 'Universal Elixir of Ten Thousand Herbs'.
He claimed: 'A single spoonful of this elixir cures blindness, baldness, rheumatism, asthma, broken bones, and guarantees a life of one hundred and fifty years!'
He charged ten silver coins per bottle, fleecing hundreds of poor, sick villagers.

Tenali Raman resolved to expose the fraud before the public.

Tenali dressed in the ragged clothes of a crippled beggar, limping heavily with two crutches, his face smeared with ash, groaning piteously as he dragged himself to the Hakim’s booth in the central bazaar.
A large crowd gathered.

Tenali groaned:
'O Great Hakim! I have been crippled in both legs for twenty years! I cannot take a single step without these crutches!
Can your miraculous elixir heal my legs right now?'

The Hakim, eager to demonstrate a theatrical 'miracle' before hundreds of paying customers, boasted loudly:
'Drink this bottle, brother! In one minute, thy legs will run like a mountain gazelle!'

Tenali drank the bottle, smacked his lips, and blinked.
Then Tenali looked at the Hakim with an expression of sudden, intense demonic fury!
Tenali raised his heavy wooden crutches in the air, shouted at the top of his lungs:
'Help! This man has given me demon’s poison! It has turned me into a wild madman!'
Tenali began swinging his heavy crutches like war clubs directly at the Hakim’s head!
*SWISH! CRACK!*

The terrified Hakim shrieked in terror, leaped over his display table, dropped his bottles, and began running for his life down the crowded bazaar!
Tenali ran right behind him, sprinting with the speed of an Olympic athlete, brandishing his crutches, shouting:
'Halt, Hakim! Let me thank thee with my crutches!'

The Hakim ran three laps around the temple square, gasping for breath, dodging cows and carts, before diving headfirst into an open mud ditch, screaming:
'Help! Police! Save me from this madman!'

Tenali stopped at the edge of the ditch, tossed aside his crutches, and laughed heartily before the cheering crowd:
'Look at the great Hakim!
He promised his medicine would make a crippled man run like a gazelle—and indeed, it made the Hakim himself run like a gazelle through the mud!'

Tenali then revealed the contents of the bottles: common pond water mixed with bitter neem juice, molasses, and dirt!
The charlatan was marched out of the city gates, and Tenali was hailed as the protector of public health and common sense.
moral: Quack doctors who sell fake cures for profit are silenced when forced to drink their own concoctions.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 138
summary: A spiteful and jealous neighbor named Lingaiah sought to ruin an honest vegetable farmer named Somu. Somu owned a piece of fertile land b...
full_text:
A spiteful and jealous neighbor named Lingaiah sought to ruin an honest vegetable farmer named Somu.
Somu owned a piece of fertile land bordering the dry summer riverbed of the Tungabhadra. During the dry season, Somu dug a shallow sand well in the dry riverbed to water his gourds.
Lingaiah brought a lawsuit before King Krishnadevaraya:
'Maharaj! The riverbed belongs to the crown! Somu has dug a well on imperial river territory!
I demand that Somu be ordered to remove his well immediately and take it away from the riverbed, or be imprisoned!'

The King, in a hasty mood, accepted the literal argument and ordered:
'Somu, within twenty-four hours, remove thy well from the riverbed!'

Poor Somu came weeping to Tenali Raman:
'How can I remove a well? A well is a hole in the ground! If I dig it up, it is only dirt!'

Tenali smiled: 'Fear not, Somu. Tomorrow morning, Lingaiah shall help thee remove it.'

The next morning, Tenali Raman, Somu, and twenty village laborers arrived at the dry riverbed with spades, ropes, and baskets.
King Krishnadevaraya and Lingaiah arrived to inspect the removal.

Tenali bowed to Lingaiah:
'Master Lingaiah, we are ready to remove the well!
We have brought spades and bullocks to haul the well away to Somu’s private field.
However, according to the King’s royal decree, Somu must remove **only the well itself**, and not a single grain of the surrounding imperial river sand!
Therefore, Master Lingaiah, step forward with your measuring tools, hold back all the river sand, and separate the water-hole from the surrounding earth, so we can lift the hole into our carts!'

Lingaiah stared in utter bewilderment:
'Separate the hole from the sand? Art thou insane, Tenali? A well is an empty space inside the ground! How can anyone hold back the sand and lift empty space into a cart?'

Tenali Raman smiled with devastating logic:
'Precisely, Master Lingaiah!
A well is simply the space where water gathers. It removes nothing from the river, and when the monsoon rains arrive, the river will fill it and flow over it harmlessly!
Thou didst demand an impossible decree merely out of jealous spite to ruin an honest neighbor who waters vegetables for the city!'

King Krishnadevaraya saw through Lingaiah’s petty malice.
The King revoked the order, permitted Somu to use the water freely, and fined Lingaiah fifty silver coins for filing frivolous and vindictive lawsuits.
Somu’s gourds flourished, and Tenali’s wit once again shielded the humble from bureaucratic cruelty.
moral: Demands born of arbitrary malice are defeated by claiming the natural boundaries that define them.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 139
summary: A wealthy, litigious merchant named Varadappa filed an extraordinary lawsuit before King Krishnadevaraya against a poor woodcutter named ...
full_text:
A wealthy, litigious merchant named Varadappa filed an extraordinary lawsuit before King Krishnadevaraya against a poor woodcutter named Kaliappa:
'Maharaj! Last night, I had an extraordinarily vivid and sacred dream!
In my dream, woodcutter Kaliappa broke into my stables, stole my prize riding elephant, and sold it in the market for five hundred gold coins!
Our ancient dream treatises state that dreams reveal real spiritual debts. I demand that Kaliappa pay me five hundred gold coins in restitution!'

Poor Kaliappa, who earned barely three coppers a day cutting firewood, wept in terror: 'Maharaj, I never saw an elephant in my life!'
The King was amused, but puzzled over how to dismiss the traditional dream argument without offending the religious scholars.

Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, Varadappa’s dream claim is completely valid according to the ancient Code of Dreams!
I shall settle the debt immediately on Kaliappa’s behalf!'

Tenali had an enormous bronze mirror placed upon a table in the center of the audience hall.
Tenali then brought out a large leather bag containing five hundred gold dinars from the royal treasury.
Tenali placed the open bag of gold directly in front of the mirror, so that five hundred gleaming gold coins were reflected with dazzling brilliance in the glass!

Tenali turned to Merchant Varadappa:
'Master Varadappa, step forward and collect your restitution!'

Varadappa reached out his hands eagerly toward the real leather bag of gold.
Tenali smacked his hand away with a fan:
'No, no, Master Varadappa! Do not touch the real gold!
Your elephant was stolen in an imaginary dream; therefore, you cannot touch real physical coins!
Look into the mirror!
Behold the five hundred gleaming gold coins reflected in the glass!
Reach out your hands, scoop up the reflected gold coins from inside the mirror, and take them home to your treasury!
A dream elephant has been paid for with mirror gold! The account is settled!'

The entire court erupted in roaring, body-shaking laughter!
Varadappa stood frozen in utter mortification, realizing how thoroughly his greed had been rebuked.
King Krishnadevaraya laughed until tears ran down his cheeks, dismissed the absurd lawsuit, and fined Varadappa twenty silver coins to be given to the poor woodcutter.
Tenali was hailed as the master of poetic justice.
moral: Claims based upon dreams have no legal standing in the waking world of justice.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 140
summary: Two neighboring householders, Somu and Ramu, were locked in a bitter feud over a massive coconut palm tree. The trunk of the tree grew in...
full_text:
Two neighboring householders, Somu and Ramu, were locked in a bitter feud over a massive coconut palm tree.
The trunk of the tree grew in Somu’s garden, but its top branches leaned over the wall, hanging directly above Ramu’s tiled roof.
Whenever ripe coconuts fell, they smashed Ramu’s roof tiles; but whenever Ramu picked the fallen coconuts, Somu accused him of theft!
Somu claimed: 'The roots are in my soil; every coconut belongs to me!'
Ramu claimed: 'The nuts fall on my roof and break my tiles; they belong to me!'

They brought the dispute to King Krishnadevaraya, demanding that the tree either be chopped down or the other neighbor imprisoned.
The King referred the case to Tenali Raman.

Tenali inspected the coconut tree.
He said to both men:
'The law must divide the tree according to natural equity!
Since Somu owns the trunk and roots in his soil, Somu shall be the sole owner of the **lower half** of the tree from the roots up to the branches!
And since Ramu owns the airspace and suffers the broken tiles, Ramu shall be the sole owner of the **upper half** of the tree where the coconuts grow!'

Both men were delighted:
Ramu smiled, thinking he would get all the coconuts;
Somu smiled, thinking he owned the base.

Then Tenali announced the operational rules:
'Now, hear the law:
Somu, as owner of the lower trunk, must water the roots, fertilize the soil, and protect the trunk every single day! But he is strictly forbidden from climbing into Ramu’s upper half to touch a single coconut!
And Ramu, as owner of the upper half, may harvest all the coconuts! But he is strictly forbidden from touching Somu’s trunk with a ladder or stepping upon Somu’s bark to climb up!'

The two neighbors stared at each other in stunned silence.
Somu realized: 'If I water the tree, Ramu gets all the coconuts, and I get only hard labor!'
Ramu realized: 'If I cannot touch the trunk or lean a ladder against it, I cannot reach the coconuts at all!'

Tenali looked at them with a warm, gentle smile:
'Do you see the folly of your stubborn selfishness?
Nature created a tree as a single, harmonious living blessing. You cannot divide a living tree with anger without rendering it useless to both!
Now, shake hands:
Let Somu water the tree, let Ramu harvest the coconuts, and let both families share the sweet fruit equally, dividing the coconuts and sharing the cost of repairing the roof tiles!'

The two neighbors were deeply moved by Tenali’s wise counsel.
They embraced, dropped their lawsuits, and shared the harvests for decades in harmony and peace.
moral: Generosity and neighborly compromise yield sweet fruit; selfish litigation bears only legal thorns.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 141
summary: An elderly, impoverished court copyist named Shastriji dropped his worn, ancient iron writing stylus (*ghantam*) into the deep palace wat...
full_text:
An elderly, impoverished court copyist named Shastriji dropped his worn, ancient iron writing stylus (*ghantam*) into the deep palace water reservoir.
The stylus was thirty years old, its wooden grip worn smooth by decades of copying sacred scriptures and imperial decrees.
Shastriji sat on the stone steps of the reservoir, weeping bitterly, unable to earn his daily bread without his writing tool.

Tenali Raman saw the old scholar weeping and dove into the clear, deep water.
Tenali surfaced holding a magnificent stylus crafted of solid, gleaming twenty-four-karat gold, encrusted with rubies!
'Is this thy writing stylus, Shastriji?' asked Tenali.

Old Shastriji looked at the dazzling golden tool, blinked through his tears, and shook his head with simple honesty:
'No, noble Tenali. That golden stylus belongs to a king or an emperor.
Gold is too soft and slippery to carve fine letters upon dry palm leaves; my fingers would slip.
My stylus was a plain tool of hardened iron, with a humble handle of neem wood smoothed by thirty years of honest ink.'

Tenali dove a second time, surfacing with an ornate stylus of pure, polished silver with an ivory handle:
'Is this thine?'
Shastriji replied: 'No, master. Silver tarnishes, and its tip is too blunt for my delicate script. That is not mine.'

Tenali dove a third time, bringing up Shastriji’s old, blackened iron stylus with its worn neem handle.
The old scribe let out a cry of pure, joyous relief, clutching the iron tool to his chest as though it were his own child:
'Yes! That is my stylus! That is the breadwinner of my family! With this iron tip, I have copied ten thousand pages of poetry!'

Tenali Raman was moved to tears by the old scribe’s profound, incorruptible honesty and love for his craft.
Tenali presented Shastriji with his old iron stylus, and then handed him the gold and silver styluses as gifts, along with a purse of fifty gold coins from King Krishnadevaraya:
'Shastriji, an honest craftsman who honors the humble tools of his labor is greater than an emperor.
Take the gold to secure thy family’s comfort, and use thine iron stylus to continue copying the wisdom of our ancestors!'

The old scribe blessed Tenali with a full heart, proving that true wealth resides in honest devotion to one’s work.
moral: Honest tools used with devotion are the true wealth of a craftsman; false pride seeks only golden toys.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 142
summary: A sudden panic struck the northern agricultural district of Anegundi: A rumor spread that an ancient curse had turned the communal irriga...
full_text:
A sudden panic struck the northern agricultural district of Anegundi:
A rumor spread that an ancient curse had turned the communal irrigation lake completely salty!
Farmers tasted the water at the southern weir and spat it out in horror: it was intensely salty, threatening to kill their rice crops!
A corrupt grain speculator named Bhupati immediately offered to buy all the farmers’ lands at pennies on the dollar, claiming the valley was ruined forever.

King Krishnadevaraya sent Tenali Raman to investigate the catastrophe.

Tenali rode to the lake.
He tasted the water at the southern weir: indeed, it was intensely salty.
However, Tenali rowed a small wooden boat across to the northern inlet where the mountain mountain stream entered the lake:
He dipped his cup into the water:
The northern inlet water was completely, delightfully sweet, fresh, and cold!

Tenali reasoned:
'If a curse had salted the lake, the entire body of water would be uniformly saline.
Why is the water fresh at the northern inlet, but salty only at the southern weir?'

Tenali inspected the stone masonry of the southern weir.
Beneath the water line, Tenali’s boat paddle struck something soft.
He dove into the shallows:
Submerged behind the stone sluice gate were thirty enormous burlap sacks of coarse sea salt, slowly dissolving into the outflow current!
Tied to the sacks was an iron tag stamped with the warehouse seal of none other than **Grain Speculator Bhupati**!

Bhupati had dumped thirty cartloads of cheap sea salt into the weir to create a temporary panic, hoping to buy the fertile lands for nothing!

Tenali hauled the salt sacks out of the water, arrested Bhupati on the spot, and had the sluice gate flushed with fresh mountain water.
Within two hours, the outflow ran completely sweet and fresh again!
The farmers cheered, their lands were saved, and Bhupati’s entire grain empire was confiscated to fund free agricultural schools.
King Krishnadevaraya praised Tenali Raman’s sharp scientific logic, which saw through speculative fraud to protect the innocent.
moral: False rumors designed to spark speculative panics are extinguished by scientific investigation.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 143
summary: A wealthy merchant of Vijayanagara named Somadatta was murdered and robbed of five hundred gold coins in an alley behind the Great Shiva ...
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Vijayanagara named Somadatta was murdered and robbed of five hundred gold coins in an alley behind the Great Shiva Temple.
A notorious rogue named Shankara was arrested as the primary suspect, having been seen near the temple.
However, Shankara produced a sworn witness, an astrologer named Keshava, who swore an oath before the court:
'Shankara is innocent! At the exact hour of the murder—precisely two hours after sunrise on Friday morning—Shankara was sitting with me on the eastern steps of the temple, resting in the cool shadow of the temple spire, studying his horoscope!'

Because the alibi was supported by a respected astrologer, the court was on the verge of releasing Shankara.
Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, let us examine the astrologer’s astronomical testimony.'

Tenali turned to Keshava:
'Revered Astrologer, you swear that you and Shankara were resting in the shadow of the great temple spire on the **eastern steps** two hours after sunrise?'
Keshava puffed out his chest: 'I swear it upon the sacred scriptures! The shadow was cool and dark upon our heads!'

Tenali Raman burst into laughter:
'Maharaj! The alibi is a fabricated, perjured lie!'
The King demanded: 'How dost thou know, Tenali?'

Tenali explained the basic laws of solar geometry:
'The sun rises in the **East**!
Two hours after sunrise, the morning sun is climbing high in the eastern sky!
Therefore, the shadow of any building, pillar, or temple spire falls toward the **WEST**!
The eastern steps of the temple were bathed in blazing, direct morning sunlight!
The shadow of the temple spire could not possibly fall upon the eastern steps; it fell upon the western garden!
Only a liar who was never there would claim to sit in a western shadow on an eastern staircase!'

The astrologer’s knees buckled in terror. He confessed that Shankara had bribed him with fifty gold coins to fabricate the alibi.
Shankara broke down, confessed the murder, and led the guards to the stolen gold.
King Krishnadevaraya embraced Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, while lawyers argue words, thou dost call upon the sun itself to testify to the truth!'
Justice was delivered, and Tenali’s astronomical deduction was hailed throughout the empire.
moral: A liar who invents a false alibi is trapped by the immutable physics of the sun.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 144
summary: An elderly scholar named Ramakrishna Shastri purchased a fine, hand-woven Benares silk turban dyed with rare vegetable indigo, embroidere...
full_text:
An elderly scholar named Ramakrishna Shastri purchased a fine, hand-woven Benares silk turban dyed with rare vegetable indigo, embroidered with tiny silver lotus motifs along the border.
While taking a bath at the public river ghat, he left the turban on a flat stone.
A haughty courtier named Somappa snatched the turban and wrapped it around his own head.
When the poor scholar confronted him, Somappa sneered:
'Old beggar! This turban is an ancestral heirloom of my noble family! How dare a threadbare scholar claim my silk?'

The dispute was brought before Tenali Raman.
Somappa produced three friends who swore the turban had belonged to his family for years.
The poor scholar wept, having no witnesses.

Tenali Raman looked at the disputed silk turban.
He asked Somappa: 'What thread was used to stitch the inner lining of this turban?'
Somappa guessed: 'Fine silver thread, of course!'
Tenali asked the scholar: 'What thread was used?'
The scholar answered:
'Because I am poor, my wife stitched the inner headband with coarse, blue cotton thread, and inside the seam she placed a small dried jasmine leaf for fragrance.'

Tenali carefully snipped two stitches of the inner lining before the court:
Inside was coarse blue cotton thread, and between the silk folds lay a single, dried, fragrant jasmine leaf!

Tenali smiled:
'Somappa, you know the price of silk, but only the poor scholar’s wife knows the humble thread that binds it!'

Somappa was fined fifty gold coins for theft and perjury, which were awarded to the scholar, and the silk turban was restored to its rightful owner.
The court praised Tenali Raman’s gentle, observant justice.
moral: Careful examination of the smallest details exposes the claims of arrogant thieves.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 145
summary: An envoy from the Chola kingdom of the south arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, presenting three deep philosophical questions from his...
full_text:
An envoy from the Chola kingdom of the south arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, presenting three deep philosophical questions from his king:
'First: Who is the richest man in the world?
Second: Who is the poorest man in the world?
Third: Who is the most invincible warrior in the universe?'

The court ministers gave conventional answers:
'The richest is the Emperor with the most gold; the poorest is the beggar in rags; the most invincible is the general with the largest army!'
The Chola envoy shook his head: 'Those are common answers of common minds.'

Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, allow me to answer the Chola King’s inquiry.'

Tenali addressed the envoy:
'First: The **richest man in the world** is he who is completely content with what he has, who desires no more than what honest labor provides, and whose heart is free from envy! A contented man possesses the wealth of the universe!'

The envoy smiled: 'And who is the poorest?'
Tenali continued:
'Second: The **poorest man in the world** is the greedy king or miser who owns mountains of gold, yet tosses awake at night tormented by the craving for more! His soul is a bottomless pit of starvation, and no wealth can ever satisfy his spiritual poverty!'

The envoy nodded with deep reverence: 'And who is the most invincible warrior?'
Tenali concluded:
'Third: The **most invincible warrior in the universe** is not he who conquers ten thousand enemies with sword and lance, but he who conquers his own anger, his own pride, and his own selfish desires!
He who has conquered himself can never be defeated by any earthly foe!'

The Chola envoy was moved to tears by the sublime spiritual depth of Tenali’s answers.
He bowed low, presented Tenali with a golden medallion of honor, and declared:
'Emperor Krishnadevaraya, your empire is truly invincible, for it is guided by the wisdom of Tenali Raman!'
The King embraced Tenali, celebrating that moral truth outshines all earthly power.
moral: True royalty is defined by benevolence, true wisdom by humility, and true strength by self-mastery.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 146
summary: A cunning alchemist named Siddha Ramanand set up a laboratory in Vijayanagara, claiming he had perfected a secret clay crucible that coul...
full_text:
A cunning alchemist named Siddha Ramanand set up a laboratory in Vijayanagara, claiming he had perfected a secret clay crucible that could turn common river sand into pure silver.
Before a gathering of wealthy merchants, he put sand into the crucible, sealed it with wax, heated it in a charcoal furnace, and opened it:
Inside were ten bright, solid silver beads!
The merchants were dazzled, offering thousands of gold coins to buy the 'miraculous crucible'.

Tenali Raman attended the demonstration.
He examined the crucible: it was an ordinary earthenware pot coated with dark red clay slip.
Tenali smiled: 'Master Siddha, your alchemy is magnificent!
Let us perform the trial once more before King Krishnadevaraya in the royal palace, using clay and sand provided by the crown!'

The alchemist, unable to refuse without admitting fraud, arrived at the royal audience hall.
Tenali provided an ordinary clay pot, filled it with river sand from the Tungabhadra, and said:
'Now, Master Siddha, seal this pot with your secret wax and heat it in our furnace!'

The alchemist hesitated, sweating profusely:
'Master Tenali, my alchemy works only in my own consecrated laboratory with my own ancestral crucibles!'

Tenali picked up the alchemist’s original 'miraculous crucible' from the table:
'Then let us examine your ancestral vessel!'
Tenali picked up an iron hammer and cleanly cracked the crucible in two!

He held up the broken pieces before the King:
The clay crucible had a **false bottom**!
Between the double layers of clay, the alchemist had concealed ten real silver beads, sealed with wax that melted when heated, allowing the silver to drop into the sand!

The court erupted in outrage!
King Krishnadevaraya ordered the charlatan arrested and his ill-gotten wealth distributed to the cheated merchants.
Tenali laughed:
'Maharaj, those who promise silver from dirt always have their silver hidden in the false bottoms of their own greed!'
The King rewarded Tenali, once again defending public reason against fraud.
moral: Charlatans who claim secret transmutation cannot withstand the bright light of independent testing.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 147
summary: A corrupt, ambitious courtier named Mallikarjuna sought to remove honest ministers from King Krishnadevaraya’s council. He approached the...
full_text:
A corrupt, ambitious courtier named Mallikarjuna sought to remove honest ministers from King Krishnadevaraya’s council. He approached the King with an ornate signet ring set with a black onyx stone, whispering:
'Maharaj, this is an ancient sacred talisman.
When you wear it on your thumb, it vibrates and whispers warnings whenever a minister in your presence harbors treacherous thoughts!
Yesterday, when Prime Minister Appaji spoke, the ring vibrated fiercely, proving his disloyalty!'

The King, though skeptical, was unsettled by the claim.
Tenali Raman noticed the King’s troubled brow and asked to examine the ring.

Tenali took the ring, slipped it onto his own thumb, and walked up to King Krishnadevaraya.
Tenali closed his eyes, frowned with deep concentration, and suddenly began shaking his hand violently!
'Maharaj! The ring! It is vibrating with furious, uncontrollable intensity! It is buzzing like a hornet’s nest!'

The King stared in alarm: 'What does it whisper, Tenali?'

Tenali shouted in theatrical terror:
'The ring whispers: "Beware! The courtier Mallikarjuna is an insidious traitor who is planning to poison the royal elephant and steal the crown jewels tomorrow midnight!"'

Mallikarjuna turned pale as death, dropping to his knees, screaming:
'Lies! Treason! I never planned such things! The ring is lying!'

Tenali laughed with booming joy, pulling the ring from his thumb:
'Aha, Mallikarjuna! If the ring was telling the truth yesterday about the loyal Prime Minister, why is it lying today about you?
And if it is lying today, it was a fraudulent trick yesterday!'

Tenali examined the inner band of the ring before the King:
Inside the hollow bezel was a tiny, coiled steel spring attached to a minute sliding peg, which the wearer could press with his forefinger to make the stone click and vibrate!

King Krishnadevaraya was furious at the deception.
He stripped Mallikarjuna of all titles, banished him from court, and restored full confidence to his loyal ministers.
The King embraced Tenali:
'Tenali, thy quick wit has broken another insidious chain of courtly intrigue!'
moral: Flattery that claims supernatural signs to influence policy is exposed by silence.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 148
summary: Two traveling grain merchants, Shankara and Ramadas, appeared before the royal magistrate of Vijayanagara, both claiming ownership of a s...
full_text:
Two traveling grain merchants, Shankara and Ramadas, appeared before the royal magistrate of Vijayanagara, both claiming ownership of a sturdy, red wooden bullock cart pulled by two white Kangayam oxen.
Shankara swore: 'I bought the cart in Bellary two months ago; Ramadas stole it while I was eating at an inn!'
Ramadas yelled: 'A lie! I had the cart built by my village carpenter; it is mine!'

Both men produced receipts from different carpenters, and the magistrate was baffled.
Tenali Raman was invited to resolve the dispute.

Tenali inspected the cart and the two white bullocks.
He said: 'Maharaj, paper receipts can be forged, but the memory of animals cannot be bribed.
Let us take the cart to the Great Crossroads outside the city, where four highways branch off to four different provinces.'

The court retinue rode to the four-way crossroads.
Tenali had both merchants stand in the center of the road, fifty paces away from the cart.
Tenali ordered the driver to step down, loosened the reins completely, and placed them loosely upon the oxen's backs.
Tenali clapped his hands: 'Go home, brothers!'

The two white oxen turned their heads, sniffed the air, and without hesitation, turned down the southern road leading toward Ramadas’s village!
The cart trotted for two miles down the highway, turned into a narrow country lane, entered an open village farmhouse courtyard, and walked straight up to the feeding trough, where two young children ran out shouting:
'Father's cart is home!'

Tenali turned to the King and the assembly:
'An animal knows its own stable, its own trough, and the voices of its master's children!
Nature has delivered the verdict!'

Shankara hung his head in shame, confessing that he had stolen the cart from an inn.
The cart and oxen were restored to honest Ramadas, Shankara was fined thirty silver coins, and the people celebrated Tenali Raman’s reliance on the incorruptible truth of nature.
moral: Animals know their own homes; releasing the reins reveals the true master.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 149
summary: A brilliant actor and linguist named Bahurupi Govinda arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that he was an absolute master of di...
full_text:
A brilliant actor and linguist named Bahurupi Govinda arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that he was an absolute master of disguise.
He challenged King Krishnadevaraya:
'Your Majesty! For seven days, I will walk through your court and city in seven different disguises—as a beggar, a merchant, an astrologer, a soldier, a monk, a physician, and a woman.
If your famous wit Tenali Raman cannot unmask me on any day, you must award me five hundred gold coins!'

Tenali accepted the wager.
On the first day, a beggar asked for alms; Tenali looked into his eyes and said: 'Greetings, Govinda!'
On the second day, a physician offered herbs; Tenali unmasked him immediately by his gait.
On the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days, Tenali penetrated every disguise through careful observation.

On the seventh day, a dignified scholar from Kashmir arrived, speaking impeccable classical Kashmiri, wearing authentic northern furs, debating Sanskrit with profound erudition.
The King was convinced this was a real northern scholar, and even Tenali could find no flaw in his accent, clothing, or behavior!
The sun was setting, and the court prepared to declare Govinda victorious.

As the Kashmiri scholar bowed low to the King to conclude the audience, Tenali Raman quietly slipped behind him, holding a small brass vessel of ice-cold mountain spring water.
Without warning, Tenali dumped the freezing water down the back of the scholar’s neck!

The scholar leaped into the air like a scalded cat, clutching his wet neck, and shouted in fluent, unvarnished, colloquial local **Telugu**:
*‘AYYO! AMMA! WHO POURED COLD WATER DOWN MY SHIRT?’*

The entire court erupted in roaring laughter!
Govinda stood soaked and sheepish, realizing that his native tongue had betrayed him!

Tenali smiled with dazzling triumph:
'Maharaj, a man may master ten foreign languages and practice seventy disguises, but when struck by sudden pain or cold water, he always cries out in his mother tongue!'

The actor bowed low, laughing in admiration:
'Tenali Raman, thou art truly invincible! No disguise can deceive thy understanding of human nature!'
The King rewarded both Tenali and the actor for an unforgettable demonstration of psychology and wit.
moral: An actor may change his costume and accent, but his native tongue betrays him in moments of sudden surprise.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 150
summary: King Krishnadevaraya, feeling restless and weary of courtly flattery, summoned Tenali Raman to his private chamber at midnight: 'Tenali, ...
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, feeling restless and weary of courtly flattery, summoned Tenali Raman to his private chamber at midnight:
'Tenali, put on the coarse wool cloak of an ordinary night watchman. We shall walk through the sleeping quarters of Vijayanagara to see how our subjects fare when they believe no Emperor watches them.'

The King and Tenali slipped through a secret postern gate into the quiet city.
They walked through the weavers' quarter, where loom lamps burned late as tired mothers finished fabric for the morning market.
In the bakers' lane, they smelled fresh bread being prepared for the hungry porters.
At the city hospital, they observed selfless physicians tending the sick by candlelight without asking for pay.

In a dark alley near the grain market, they encountered a municipal patrol captain shaking down an elderly vegetable vendor, demanding bribes.
Before the King could draw his sword in wrath, Tenali stepped forward in the shadows, raised his heavy wooden night watchman's staff, and shouted in the voice of the Chief Constable:
'Halt! Inspection by the Royal Guard!'
The corrupt captain dropped his loot, took to his heels, and fled into the night!

The grateful vegetable vendor bowed to the two disguised watchmen, handing them two fresh, sweet mangoes:
'Take these, honest brothers; you have protected my family's bread tonight.'

The King accepted the mango with deep reverence, tears glistening in his eyes.
As dawn broke over the Tungabhadra River, King Krishnadevaraya turned to Tenali on the palace balcony:
'Tenali, tonight I saw the true soul of my empire.
I saw the toil of the weaver, the charity of the physician, the vulnerability of the poor vendor, and the corruption that hides in dark corners.
A ruler who sits only on a golden throne sees only what flatterers want him to see; but he who walks the night with an honest companion sees the living heart of his people.'

The King promoted the selfless physicians, dismissed the corrupt patrol officers, lowered taxes on working weavers, and thanked Tenali Raman for being his eternal compass of truth.
moral: A sovereign who walks among his people learns their real needs, guided by the lantern of honest counsel.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 151
summary: On the twentieth anniversary of King Krishnadevaraya’s coronation, an imperial assembly of poets, scholars, and monarchs from across Bhar...
full_text:
On the twentieth anniversary of King Krishnadevaraya’s coronation, an imperial assembly of poets, scholars, and monarchs from across Bharatavarsha gathered in the Grand Hall of Victory at Vijayanagara.
The royal court poet laureate, Allasani Peddana, stood before the assembly and presented a gold-embroidered crown of pearls to the Emperor, praising his reign as the Golden Age of Literature and Justice.

King Krishnadevaraya took the pearl crown in his hands.
He did not place it upon his own head.
The Emperor stood up from his Golden Throne, walked down the marble steps into the center of the hall, and approached Tenali Raman!

The court watched in breathless silence.
King Krishnadevaraya placed the pearl crown upon Tenali Raman’s head, and proclaimed before the entire empire:
'Scholars and kings of Bharatavarsha!
Many emperors have armies, fortresses, and treasuries of diamonds.
But the greatest treasure of Vijayanagara has been our *Vikatakavi*—Tenali Raman!

When flattery blinded my eyes, his wit gave me sight.
When anger inflamed my sword, his humor poured cooling water upon my heart.
When corruption oppressed the poor, his courage held up the mirror of justice before power.
He never flattered a monarch for gold, nor did he ever despise a humble beggar.
His laughter was the shield of the innocent, his poetry was the music of truth, and his wisdom preserved the soul of our empire!'

Tenali Raman bowed low, tears of profound emotion in his eyes.
He took off the pearl crown and placed it gently at the Emperor’s feet:
'Maharaj, a crown belongs on the head of a righteous king who loves his people.
My only crown is the joy of our citizens, the laughter in your halls, and the truth that unites our hearts.'

The entire assembly of ten thousand dignitaries, soldiers, and citizens erupted in thunderous, standing applause that echoed across the Tungabhadra River and down the corridors of history.
And so the legend of Tenali Raman lived on for centuries—remembered not merely as a jester who made a king laugh, but as the eternal poet of wisdom, courage, and righteous wit who proved that a single honest laugh can illuminate the darkest world.
moral: The true jester does not merely provoke laughter; he wields wit as the shield of justice, the sword of truth, and the soul of wisdom.

title: The Fox and the Grapes
summary: On a sweltering summer afternoon, a sly fox strolled through an orchard bathed in warm sunlight. His throat was parched, and his stomach rumbled with hunger. As he reached a high g...
full_text:
On a sweltering summer afternoon, a sly fox strolled through an orchard bathed in warm sunlight. His throat was parched, and his stomach rumbled with hunger. As he reached a high garden wall, his amber eyes caught sight of a magnificent grapevine that wound its way along a tall wooden trellis. Hanging overhead were rich, luscious clusters of dark purple grapes, glistening with delicate drops of morning dew and bursting with sweet, cool juice.

The fox licked his whiskers and grinned. "Here is a feast fit for an emperor," he muttered, stepping back a few paces to gain momentum. With a graceful leap, he sprang high into the air with jaws wide open, but his teeth snapped on empty air, missing the lowest bunch by mere inches.

Refusing to admit defeat, the fox backed up further into the dusty furrow, gathered all his strength, and sprang upward once more. Again he fell short, tumbling onto the soft earth. Three, four, five times he leaped, straining every muscle in his russet body until his breath came in ragged wheezes and his legs trembled with exhaustion.

Looking up at the purple prize that hung tantalizingly out of reach, the fox curled his snout into an arrogant sneer. He brushed the dust from his bushy tail and announced loudly to the listening birds: "Why should I waste my precious energy on such wretched fruit? I can see plainly from here that they are completely green and sour, unfit for a gentleman's palate!" And with his head held high in pretended disgust, he trotted away through the briers.
moral: It is easy to despise and pretend to scorn what you cannot possess.

title: The Tortoise and the Hare
summary: A boastful hare never tired of mocking the woodland creatures for their slow pace, reserving his sharpest jeers for the quiet tortoise. "Look at you, my plodding friend!" the hare...
full_text:
A boastful hare never tired of mocking the woodland creatures for their slow pace, reserving his sharpest jeers for the quiet tortoise. "Look at you, my plodding friend!" the hare laughed, bounding in swift circles around the turtle. "You carry your house upon your back and take an hour to cross a single cabbage patch! I am the swiftest runner in all the realm; no beast has ever outstripped my stride."

The tortoise blinked his ancient, patient eyes and replied with calm dignity, "Your legs are swift indeed, friend Hare, but boastful pride often stumbles. I challenge you to a footrace across the valley to the ancient boundary oak."

The hare laughed so heartily he fell into the clover. "A race against you? What a merry jest! Let the fox mark the course!"

The woodland animals gathered at dawn. At the fox's sharp bark, the hare shot forward like an arrow released from a bow, vanishing over the green rise in a cloud of dust. The tortoise simply tucked in his chin and placed one heavy foot after the other, moving forward with quiet, unyielding rhythm.

Halfway along the dusty course, seeing the tortoise was not even within sight, the hare felt confident and bored. "I have hours to spare," he thought, settling down beneath the cool shade of a blossoming apple tree. "A brief nap will refresh me, and I can still overtake that plodder with three bounds before the finish line." The hare closed his eyes and sank into deep slumber.

Meanwhile, the sun climbed high and began its slow descent. The tortoise neither stopped to rest nor turned aside for sweet clover. Step by steady step, his scaly claws gripped the earth. As twilight painted the hills with amber gold, the hare awoke with a start and sprinted desperately toward the boundary oak. But to his dismay, the entire forest erupted in cheers: the patient tortoise had already crossed the finish line, smiling serenely as he proved that steady determination conquers careless speed.
moral: Slow and steady perseverance wins the race over boastful arrogance.

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
summary: Throughout the long, golden days of summer, the meadow blossomed with vibrant wildflowers, sweet clover, and rich grasses. While butterflies fluttered lazily in the warm breeze, an...
full_text:
Throughout the long, golden days of summer, the meadow blossomed with vibrant wildflowers, sweet clover, and rich grasses. While butterflies fluttered lazily in the warm breeze, an industrious ant worked from dawn to twilight, hauling heavy grains of wheat, seeds, and dried corn kernels back to her underground granary. She bowed her tiny shoulders beneath burdens twice her size, sweating in the heat to store food for the cold days ahead.

Perched upon a tall thistle, a merry grasshopper sang joyful melodies on his fiddle, chirping without a care in the world. Seeing the ant struggle past with a plump barley grain, he laughed dismissively: "Why do you toil so wearily under the blazing sun, little neighbor? Put down that heavy load! Summer is made for dancing, singing, and feasting on the abundance of the earth. Winter is far away; enjoy the golden hour!"

The ant wiped her brow and replied quietly, "Summer will not last forever, friend. When the frosty winds blow and snow buries the meadow, the fields will provide nothing. I advise you to gather while the sun shines." But the grasshopper laughed, shook his green antennae, and continued fiddling his carefree tunes.

Soon autumn stripped the boughs bare, and winter arrived with howling gales and deep, freezing snow. The meadow turned into a frozen, barren desert. Shivering in the icy blast, weak with hunger and without a single crumb to eat, the grasshopper crawled to the ant's snug mound. Through the doorway, he saw the ants enjoying rich stores of grain by their warm hearth.

"Have pity on me, kind neighbor!" begged the starving grasshopper. "Grant me a few morsels of your wheat, or I shall perish in the frost!"

The ant looked at him with sorrowful sternness and asked, "What did you do all through the summer when food was plentiful and the days were long?"

"Alas," wept the grasshopper, "I made sweet music and sang for all the creatures."

"If you were foolish enough to sing away the summer," answered the ant, "then you must dance away the winter," and she closed her door, leaving the idler to face the bitter fruit of his improvidence.
moral: It is best to prepare today for the inevitable needs of tomorrow.

title: The Lion and the Mouse
summary: A mighty lion, weary from hunting across the sun-drenched savannah, lay sleeping peacefully beneath the sprawling shade of an ancient baobab tree. His massive golden mane rippled i...
full_text:
A mighty lion, weary from hunting across the sun-drenched savannah, lay sleeping peacefully beneath the sprawling shade of an ancient baobab tree. His massive golden mane rippled in the breeze, and his deep snores stirred the dust around his great paws.

A timid little field mouse, scurrying through the tall grass in search of seeds, did not notice the sleeping predator and inadvertently ran straight across the lion's broad nose.

Startled from his nap, the furious king of beasts struck out with lightning speed. His heavy paw clamped down upon the tiny creature, pinning her helpless against the hard ground. Opening his cavernous jaws, the lion prepared to crush the mouse in a single bite.

"Spare me, O King!" squeaked the terrified mouse, trembling in every whisker. "I meant no disrespect! I was running blindly from a hawk. Forgive my clumsy blunder! If you grant me my life, I promise that one day I will repay your royal mercy!"

The lion let out a roar of thunderous laughter that shook the surrounding acacia branches. "Repay me? A wretched, insignificant speck of fur repay the sovereign of the forest? What an absurd fancy!" Yet, amused by her sheer boldness, the lion lifted his paw and let the tiny creature scurry safely into the rocks.

A few days later, while patrolling his territory, the lion walked into a hunter's concealed trap. Strong hemp cords snapped tight around his limbs, hoisting him helpless into a heavy rope net. The mighty beast roared in fury and thrashing anguish, but every struggle only tightened the knots.

Hearing that familiar, desperate roar echoing through the ravines, the little mouse rushed to the scene. Without hesitation, she set her sharp, needle-like teeth against the thickest cord, gnawing with frantic determination until the fibers frayed and snapped. One by one, she severed the binding ropes until the great king stepped down, completely free.

Looking down at his tiny deliverer with humble reverence, the lion bowed his great head: "You were right, little friend. Today you have taught the King of the Forest that even the smallest heart can save the mighty."
moral: No act of kindness, however small, is ever wasted; little friends may prove great allies.

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
summary: A young shepherd boy was assigned the solitary task of tending a flock of sheep on a high pasture above a peaceful farming village. Day after day, he sat upon a rocky crag watching...
full_text:
A young shepherd boy was assigned the solitary task of tending a flock of sheep on a high pasture above a peaceful farming village. Day after day, he sat upon a rocky crag watching the sheep graze in silence. With no one to talk to and only the wind rustling through the gorse bushes, the boy grew thoroughly bored and longed for excitement.

Remembering his master's instructions to call for help if danger threatened, a mischievous plan took shape in his mind. He sprang to his feet, ran to the edge of the cliff overlooking the village, and shouted at the top of his lungs: "Wolf! Wolf! A ravenous wolf is attacking the flock! Help! Help!"

Down in the valley, the villagers dropped their scythes, hoes, and blacksmith hammers. Armed with pitchforks and heavy clubs, they sprinted breathlessly up the steep hill to drive the beast away and protect the sheep. When they arrived, sweating and panting, they found the flock grazing peacefully, while the boy rolled upon the grass in uncontrollable laughter at the prank.

"Do not cry wolf when there is no danger, lad!" warned the village elder sternly before trudging back down the mountain.

A few days later, the boy grew restless once more and shouted again: "Wolf! Wolf! Save the lambs!" Once again, the kind-hearted villagers rushed up the slope, only to be mocked and laughed at by the deceitful boy.

Then, one evening as the shadows lengthened and twilight enveloped the crags, a real, terrifying gray wolf emerged from the dark pine forest. Its eyes burned like fiery coals, and its dripping fangs bared in a menacing snarl as it sprang into the middle of the terrified flock, tearing at the helpless sheep.

Terrified out of his wits, the boy ran toward the cliff, waving his arms and screaming with genuine terror: "Wolf! Wolf! A giant wolf is slaughtering the sheep! I beg you, come quickly!"

Down in the village, the farmers heard his desperate cries and shook their heads. "There is that foolish boy again," said a weaver. "He will not trick us a third time; let him laugh alone."

No one came to his aid. The boy watched in weeping horror as the wolf decimated the flock and vanished into the shadows, leaving the deceitful shepherd to learn the bitter cost of destroying trust.
moral: A liar will not be believed, even when he speaks the absolute truth.

title: The Crow and the Pitcher
summary: A terrible drought had settled over the countryside. The streams had dried into cracked riverbeds of baked mud, the ponds had vanished, and the leaves of the olive trees drooped be...
full_text:
A terrible drought had settled over the countryside. The streams had dried into cracked riverbeds of baked mud, the ponds had vanished, and the leaves of the olive trees drooped beneath the relentless blaze of the sun. A thirsty crow, flying for leagues in search of water, felt her throat parched like hot sand and her wings growing too heavy to beat the dry air.

As she drifted down into an abandoned courtyard, she spotted an earthenware pitcher standing upon a stone bench. With a joyous caw, the crow fluttered to the rim and peered inside. To her delight, there was clear, sparkling water at the bottom!

Eagerly, she thrust her beak into the narrow neck of the pitcher, but her bill could not reach the water. She tried to insert her head, but the vessel's neck was too tight. In desperation, she attempted to push the pitcher over with her breast, hoping to spill the water onto the stone slab and drink from the puddle, but the heavy clay container was far too sturdy for her slender strength.

Weeping with frustration, the crow rested upon the bench, refusing to give up. Her keen black eyes noticed a pile of smooth river pebbles scattered near the courtyard fountain. A brilliant spark of ingenuity flashed in her mind.

Taking a smooth pebble in her beak, she flew up and dropped it into the pitcher: plunk! The water level rose an imperceptible fraction. She flew down, took a second pebble, and dropped it in: plunk! Then a third, a fourth, a fifth, and a sixth.

Dozens of times the patient bird flew back and forth in the blazing heat, never flagging in her resolve. With every stone dropped into the dark vessel, the cool water steadily mounted toward the rim. At last, the liquid reached the very top of the neck. The triumphant crow dipped her bill and drank long, refreshing draughts of cool water, saving her life through patient intellect and steady perseverance.
moral: Little by little does the trick; intelligence and patience solve problems that force cannot.

title: The Fox and the Crow
summary: A glossy black crow had swooped down onto an open farmhouse windowsill and snatched a magnificent wedge of rich, yellow Swiss cheese. Delighted with her delicious prize, she flew u...
full_text:
A glossy black crow had swooped down onto an open farmhouse windowsill and snatched a magnificent wedge of rich, yellow Swiss cheese. Delighted with her delicious prize, she flew up into the high branches of an ancient oak tree, intending to feast upon it in undisturbed peace.

A crafty fox, wandering through the woods in search of breakfast, caught the rich aroma of aged cheese drifting on the morning breeze. He followed his keen nose to the foot of the oak and looked up into the leafy canopy. Seeing the crow perched high above with the plump morsel held firmly in her beak, his mouth watered with desire.

The fox sat gracefully upon his haunches, tilted his head, and addressed the bird in a voice as smooth as melted butter: "Good morning, most radiant mistress Crow! How breathtakingly beautiful your plumage gleams in the morning sunlight! Your feathers possess a sheen finer than the finest velvet, and your graceful eyes sparkle like black diamonds. Surely, a queen of such peerless beauty must also possess a voice of celestial sweetness! If you would only sing one song for your humble admirer, I would gladly proclaim you sovereign of all winged creatures!"

The foolish crow was swept away by this lavish praise. Puffing out her chest and fluttering her wings with vanity, she resolved to prove that she was indeed the greatest singer of the forest.

She opened her beak wide and let out a harsh, rasping "Caw-w-w!"

The moment her beak parted, the heavy wedge of cheese slipped from her grasp and tumbled straight down through the branches. The nimble fox leaped forward, caught the delicious morsel in mid-air, and swallowed it in a single greedy gulp.

Licking his lips with satisfaction, the fox looked up at the mortified bird and laughed: "My dear mistress, your voice is as wretched as your feathers are dark. The song was clumsy, but the cheese was divine! In return for your meal, take this valuable advice: never trust anyone who flatters you for their own gain!"
moral: Never trust a flatterer who praises you to rob you of your prize.

title: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
summary: A humble peasant and his wife lived in a modest cottage on the outskirts of town, subsisting on the meager vegetables grown in their garden and the milk of a solitary goat. One mor...
keywords: the goose that laid the golden eggs
full_text:
A humble peasant and his wife lived in a modest cottage on the outskirts of town, subsisting on the meager vegetables grown in their garden and the milk of a solitary goat. One morning, the peasant walked into the poultry shed to gather eggs and noticed an extraordinary gleam beneath an old gray goose.

Reaching into the straw, he pulled out an egg that felt astonishingly heavy. When he wiped away the dust, the egg shone with the warm, brilliant luster of solid gold! Trembling with disbelief, he carried it to a goldsmith in the town, who weighed it and handed him a bag of silver coins, confirming it was pure, unalloyed gold.

Every morning thereafter, the miraculous goose laid another solid golden egg. The peasant and his wife quickly sold the eggs, bought fine velvet garments, built a luxurious manor house, and hired servants to attend their every whim.

Yet as their wealth expanded, an insatiable greed took root in their hearts. They grew impatient with receiving only one golden egg each morning. "Why should we wait day after day for a single egg?" whispered the greedy wife over dinner. "Inside that bird there must surely be a vast mountain of pure gold! If we cut her open, we can seize the entire treasury all at once and become richer than the king before nightfall!"

Blinded by covetousness, the peasant seized a heavy carving knife and slaughtered the miraculous goose. But when he cut the bird open, to his utter horror, her internal organs were identical in every way to those of an ordinary farmyard fowl! There was no hidden store of gold within.

The foolish couple fell to their knees in weeping despair. In their blind greed to possess everything at once, they had slain the gentle creature that provided their fortune, leaving themselves with only regret and the bitter memory of what they had squandered.
moral: Greed that seeks all at once destroys the very source of steady prosperity.

title: The Wind and the Sun
summary: A fierce argument arose between the North Wind and the Sun as to which of them possessed greater strength and power over the earth. The North Wind puffed out his icy cheeks and roa...
full_text:
A fierce argument arose between the North Wind and the Sun as to which of them possessed greater strength and power over the earth. The North Wind puffed out his icy cheeks and roared with blustering arrogance: "I am the undisputed master of might! I uproot ancient oaks with my breath, stir the oceans into mountainous waves, and strip mountains bare with icy blasts. You do nothing but shine softly like a sleepy lantern!"

The Sun smiled with serene, radiant warmth and replied gently, "True power does not lie in violent noise or harsh destruction, brother. Let us put our strength to a fair test."

Looking down through the drifting clouds, they saw a solitary traveler walking along a winding mountain highway, wrapped in a thick, woolen traveler's cloak against the autumn chill.

"Whoever can compel that traveler to remove his cloak," said the Sun, "shall be acknowledged as the mightier of the two."

"A simple task!" boomed the North Wind. "Watch and marvel!"

The North Wind unleashed his fury. He whistled down from the icy polar heights, howling with hurricane force and driving freezing gusts of sleet against the lone traveler. Leaves tore from the branches, and dust swirled in blinding storms. But the harder the fierce wind blew, the tighter the shivering traveler grasped his cloak, wrapping it doubly around his chest and pinning the collar beneath his chin. Furious, the Wind redoubled his tempest, but he only succeeded in wearying himself, leaving the man wrapped more securely than before.

At last, exhausted and defeated, the North Wind ceased his gale.

Then the Sun stepped out from behind a silver cloud. He sent forth gentle, golden rays that bathed the rugged hills in soft, soothing warmth. The chilly moisture evaporated, flowers lifted their heads, and the traveler felt the pleasant glow spreading across his tired shoulders.

As the Sun shone brighter with increasing radiance, the traveler unbuttoned his collar, wiped the beads of sweat from his forehead, and finally unclasped the heavy woolen cloak altogether, draping it over his arm and strolling merrily on his way under the pleasant sunshine. The humbled Wind was forced to concede that gentle kindness overcomes what fury fails to move.
moral: Gentle warmth and persuasion accomplish what fierce force and bluster never can.

title: The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing
summary: A cunning wolf had long hungered after the fat, tender sheep of a well-guarded pasture, but the alert shepherd and his ferocious mastiffs watched over the flock so vigilantly that...
full_text:
A cunning wolf had long hungered after the fat, tender sheep of a well-guarded pasture, but the alert shepherd and his ferocious mastiffs watched over the flock so vigilantly that the predator could never draw near without being driven off with stones and sharp spears.

Prowling around the edge of the farm one evening, the wolf discovered the complete fleece of a sheep that had been sheared and discarded by the shearers. A wicked scheme flashed in his devious mind.

"If I cannot approach as a hunter," whispered the wolf, "I shall enter as a brother."

He draped the soft, woolly skin carefully over his back, tucking his sharp snout beneath the fleece and mimicking the gentle bleat of a lamb. Disguised in snowy innocence, he strolled casually into the green pasture among the flock.

The sheep, suspecting nothing from a creature wearing wool, accepted him in their midst. Even the shepherd failed to spot the predator among his charges. When night fell, the shepherd gathered the flock into the stout wooden fold, bolted the heavy oak gate, and went to his cottage for supper, leaving the wolf locked safely inside with his intended prey.

The wolf licked his fangs, chuckling softly in the dark at how easily he had outwitted the dogs, planning to slaughter a plump lamb the moment everyone fell asleep.

Later that night, the shepherd's cook was sent out to the sheepfold with a lantern to butcher a sheep for the master's banquet the following morning. Moving through the dark pen, the cook reached blindly for the first large, heavy beast he felt in the shadows. His hand grasped the wolf in sheep's fleece. Before the predator could realize what was happening, the butcher's knife ended his life on the spot, demonstrating that those who disguise themselves in false innocence often perish by the very trap they laid.
moral: He who wears a mask of innocence to deceive others falls into the snare of his own disguise.

title: The Dog and the Bone

full_text:
A butcher had tossed a juicy, marrow-filled bone to a mastiff who lingered outside the shop. Proud of his delicious prize, the dog clamped his jaws firmly around the bone and trotted off toward his home across the river, eager to enjoy his feast in quiet solitude.

As he crossed a narrow wooden footbridge over a clear, tranquil stream, he happened to look down into the mirror-like surface of the water. There, gazing back up at him from the depths, he beheld another dog holding a bone that appeared twice as large and plump as his own!

Unaware that he was looking at his own reflection, the greedy dog was seized with an overwhelming desire to possess the second prize. "Why should I settle for one bone," he thought, "when I can easily snatch that larger one and enjoy a double banquet?"

Snarling with aggressive greed, he opened his jaws wide to snap at the rival in the stream.

The moment his teeth parted, his own precious bone slipped from his mouth, plunged into the rushing water with a splash, and sank straight to the muddy bottom, carried away by the current.

The startled dog stared down into the ripples, seeing the reflection now empty-mouthed like himself. Whimpering with regret and an empty belly, he trudged home, having learned too late that insatiable greed sacrifices present abundance for worthless illusions.
moral: He who grasps at shadows loses the real substance of what he holds.

title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse

keywords: the town mouse and the country mouse
full_text:
A humble Country Mouse who lived in an underground burrow beneath the roots of a wild hazel bush invited his aristocratic cousin, the Town Mouse, to visit him for dinner. The Country Mouse, proud of his hospitality, served the best provisions his pantry could afford: dried wheat stalks, wild berry seeds, and a hard crust of barley bread.

The Town Mouse turned up his whiskers with polite disdain, merely nibbling a seed or two. "My dear cousin," drawled the elegant visitor, "how can you endure such a dreary, monotonous existence among roots and chaff? Come with me to the grand city mansion where I reside! You shall dine upon rich cheeses, sweet pastries, and roasted meats fit for kings."

Enticed by visions of royal luxury, the Country Mouse accompanied his cousin to the city. That night, they crept into the mansion's vast dining hall, where a lavish banquet had just concluded. The Country Mouse gasped in wonder: tables groaned beneath silver platters of roast chicken, rich Brie cheese, jellies, and candied fruits.

"Eat your fill, cousin!" urged the Town Mouse grandly.

Just as the Country Mouse was sinking his teeth into a delectable cream tart, the heavy oak doors burst open with a crash. A ferocious mastiff and a sleek, sharp-clawed Persian cat bounded into the room, barking and hissing savagely!

The two mice fled in terror, scrambling frantically behind heavy draperies and squeezing through a crack in the skirting board, their tiny hearts pounding like drums. For two agonizing hours, they sat shivering in the dark, barely daring to breathe as claws scraped against the wainscot.

When quiet returned, the Country Mouse fetched his little walking stick. "Farewell, dear cousin," he whispered, heading for the garden door. "You may keep your silver platters, your rich tarts, and the terrifying terror that seasons every bite. Give me my simple barley crust and quiet safety in the meadow, where I may dine in uninterrupted peace!"
moral: A humble meal enjoyed in quiet peace is far superior to luxurious banquets seasoned with terror.

title: The Frogs Who Desired a King
summary: The frogs of a wide, fertile marsh lived in blissful freedom, leaping through the reeds, sunning themselves on water lilies, and croaking in noisy chorus whenever they pleased. But...
keywords: the frogs who desired a king
full_text:
The frogs of a wide, fertile marsh lived in blissful freedom, leaping through the reeds, sunning themselves on water lilies, and croaking in noisy chorus whenever they pleased. But over time, they grew dissatisfied with their orderly liberty. "Every kingdom on earth has a sovereign to rule over them," they argued. "Why should we be a leaderless rabble? We need a king to maintain majesty and govern our pond!"

They sent a solemn petition to the heavens, begging for a king to rule over them.

Amused by their foolishness, Jupiter tossed a colossal wooden log down into the center of the swamp. It struck the water with a tremendous splash: CRASH! The frogs, terrified by the thunderous impact, scattered beneath the mud, hiding in the dark depths for hours, convinced that their new king was a terrifying titan.

Gradually, seeing the monarch neither moved nor spoke, a bold frog poked his head above the water. Seeing only an inert piece of timber floating among the duckweed, the frogs swam closer. Within an hour, they were leaping onto the log, sunning on its bark, and mocking its total silence.

"This is no king!" they croaked in indignation. "It is a lifeless, contemptible stick! We demand a dynamic, vigorous ruler who commands respect and takes action!"

Wearied by their incessant complaining, Jupiter sent them a tall, long-legged Water Stork.

The moment the new sovereign landed in the marsh, he strode through the shallows with his sharp, spear-like beak, gobbling down the frogs one by one! The terrified survivors hid in deep crevices, weeping and praying to have their gentle log returned. But the heavens answered: "You rejected peaceful freedom and despised a gentle ruler; now you must endure the tyrant you so foolishly demanded."
moral: Be careful what you wish for; discontent with freedom often invites cruel tyranny.

title: The Fox and the Stork
summary: The fox, always fond of mischievous pranks at the expense of others, invited his neighbor the Stork to dine with him at his den. The polite bird accepted the invitation with gracio...
full_text:
The fox, always fond of mischievous pranks at the expense of others, invited his neighbor the Stork to dine with him at his den. The polite bird accepted the invitation with gracious courtesy, arriving at the appointed hour with a keen appetite.

The fox brought out dinner with a mocking grin: a thin, aromatic broth served in shallow earthenware saucers. The fox lapped up his soup in seconds with his broad tongue, but the poor Stork, with her long, slender bill, could only peck uselessly at the flat plate, wetting the very tip of her beak while the broth slipped away.

"You do not eat, neighbor Stork!" chuckled the deceitful fox. "Is the soup not spiced to your liking?"

"Do not concern yourself, friend," replied the dignified Stork politely. "I have enjoyed the visit immensely. In return, I invite you to dine with me at my nest tomorrow evening."

The following evening, the hungry fox arrived at the Stork's dwelling, eager for a free feast. The Stork welcomed him and brought out dinner: a savory stew of tender minced meat and rich gravy, served inside tall, narrow-necked glass jars with slender bases.

The Stork inserted her long bill easily into the jar, feasting delicately and savoring every mouthful. The fox, unable to squeeze his broad snout through the narrow glass neck, could only lick the rim in ravenous misery while his stomach growled in humiliation.

Seeing the fox's furious embarrassment, the Stork smiled calmly and said: "Do not grumble, friend Fox. He who plays cruel tricks upon his guests must not complain when the same hospitality is returned to him!"
moral: One bad turn deserves another; treat guests as you wish to be treated yourself.

title: The Wolf and the Lamb
summary: A sweet, innocent little lamb, having strayed from the flock, wandered down to a clear mountain brook to quench her thirst. While she was delicately lapping the fresh water, a fier...
full_text:
A sweet, innocent little lamb, having strayed from the flock, wandered down to a clear mountain brook to quench her thirst. While she was delicately lapping the fresh water, a fierce, ravenous wolf stalked out from the dark pine woods in search of prey.

Eager to devour the tender lamb, yet wishing to justify his savagery with an appearance of justice, the wolf bared his yellow fangs and snarled furiously: "How dare you muddy the water that I am trying to drink, you insolent rascal? Do you have no respect for your elders?"

The trembling lamb bleated gently in reply: "Pardon me, noble sir, but I cannot possibly be muddying your water. You are drinking high up the stream near the spring, while I am standing far below you; the current flows from you down to me!"

Frustrated by her flawless logic, the wolf scowled and barked: "Be that as it may, you are an insolent rogue! Exactly six months ago, you insulted me behind my back with slanderous words!"

"Alas, sir," cried the lamb in tears, "six months ago I was not even born! I am only three months old and still drink my mother's milk."

"If it was not you, then it was your father!" roared the savage brute. "Your entire clan hates wolves, and I shall not be cheated of my dinner!"

Without another word, the wolf sprang upon the defenseless lamb and dragged her into the dark forest, proving that when cruelty has resolved upon a deed, no plea of innocent truth can alter its wicked design.
moral: A tyrant will always invent an excuse for cruelty, and innocence cannot reason with malice.

title: The Lion's Share
summary: The Lion, the Fox, the Jackal, and the Wolf agreed to form a solemn hunting alliance, swearing upon their honor to share equally whatever game they brought down in the wilderness....
full_text:
The Lion, the Fox, the Jackal, and the Wolf agreed to form a solemn hunting alliance, swearing upon their honor to share equally whatever game they brought down in the wilderness.

After a long chase through the rocky gorges, the four companions managed to trap and bring down a magnificent, fat stag. The hunters gathered around the quarry, licking their chops in anticipation of a grand feast.

The Lion, assuming the mantle of leadership, raised his paw and commanded: "Cut the stag into four equal quarters, so that justice may be preserved among partners."

The wolf and jackal carved the carcass into four identical shares with great care. The Lion stood before the four portions, cleared his throat with a rumbling growl, and began his royal distribution:

"The first quarter belongs to me by right of my royal title, for I am sovereign of all the beasts of the forest. The second quarter falls to me on account of my superior strength and valor, since it was my claw that struck down the stag. The third quarter is mine because I contributed the greatest endurance to the hunt. And as for the fourth quarter," growled the Lion, baring his razor-sharp fangs and unsheathing his massive claws, "whoever among you dares to lay a single paw upon it must first defeat me in mortal combat!"

The Fox, the Jackal, and the Wolf exchanged silent, rueful glances, tucked their tails between their legs, and slunk away into the bushes with empty bellies, having learned the harsh lesson that an alliance with a tyrant always ends with the tyrant taking everything.
moral: Partnership with the powerful rarely brings equal rewards to the weak.

full_text:
A merchant bought several sacks of salt at the coastal saltpans, loaded them onto the back of his donkey, and set off toward the market town. The day was sweltering, and the donkey groaned beneath the heavy, abrasive burden.

While crossing a shallow river, the donkey stumbled over a slippery boulder and plunged into a deep pool. By the time the merchant helped the beast back to his feet, a large portion of the salt had dissolved into the cool water, making the sacks remarkably light! The donkey trotted on to the town with brisk joy, delighted by his good fortune.

A few days later, the merchant returned to the coast for another load of salt. Remembering the pleasant river crossing, the cunning donkey deliberately stumbled and threw himself into the water at the same ford. Once again, the salt melted away, and the donkey walked free of his heavy burden, braying in smug triumph.

The wise merchant saw through the animal's deceit and resolved to teach him a lasting lesson. On their third trip, instead of salt, the merchant packed the panniers full of dried sponges and raw wool.

Reaching the river, the foolish donkey smiled to himself and plunged intentionally into the deepest pool, waiting for the burden to melt away. But the dry sponges and dense wool soaked up gallons of water like thirsting sand! When the donkey tried to rise, the load had tripled in weight, crushing him down into the riverbed.

He had to stagger up the steep, muddy riverbank carrying a mountainous burden of waterlogged weight, learning that a trick played once too often becomes its own punishment.
moral: Tricks devised to shirk duty often turn back upon the trickster with double weight.

full_text:
An ancient miser sold his houses, his vineyards, and his orchards, converting his entire earthly estate into a single, massive lump of solid gold. Fearing that thieves might rob him or servants cheat him, he carried the golden boulder into a secluded forest clearing and buried it secretly in a deep pit beneath an old willow tree.

Every afternoon, without fail, the miser walked to the lonely spot. He would dig up the soil with trembling fingers, gaze upon the cold yellow metal with ecstatic devotion, stroke its heavy surface, and bury it once more beneath the earth.

A watchful laborer, noticing the miser's daily pilgrimages and suspicious demeanor, trailed him to the woods. The moment the old man departed, the laborer dug into the loose dirt, unearthed the colossal nugget of gold, and carried it off to enjoy its fortune.

When the miser returned the next day and found an empty hole filled with scattered pebbles, he tore his garments, beat his chest, and wept with frantic lamentations that echoed through the hills.

A wise neighbor, hearing the wailing, ran to the clearing and asked what calamity had occurred.

"My gold! My life's treasure!" shrieked the miser. "I buried a giant lump of gold in this very spot, and a vile thief has stolen it away!"

"Did you ever spend any of it?" asked the neighbor. "Did you buy food, help your family, or purchase warm clothes?"

"Never!" cried the miser in horror. "I never touched a single grain of it; I came only to look upon it every afternoon!"

The neighbor picked up a heavy, jagged river stone, threw it into the pit, and said calmly: "Cover that stone with earth and come look at it every day! It will serve you precisely as well as your gold, for when you possessed the gold, you made no more use of it than you will of that rock."
moral: Wealth unused is no better than a common stone; possession without purpose is worthless.

title: The Fox and the Cat
summary: A proud, boastful fox met a humble grey cat wandering along a woodland trail. Looking down his slender snout at the little feline, the fox puffed his chest and said arrogantly: "Go...
full_text:
A proud, boastful fox met a humble grey cat wandering along a woodland trail. Looking down his slender snout at the little feline, the fox puffed his chest and said arrogantly: "Good day, mistress cat! How can a poor, ordinary creature like you survive in these perilous woods where hounds and hunters roam?"

"I manage well enough," purred the cat modestly. "I know only one single trick, but it has never failed me."

"Only one trick?" laughed the fox with uproarious scorn. "How pitiful! I am the undisputed master of a hundred cunning strategies! I possess an entire bag full of brilliant wiles—I can double back on my trail, swim beneath water reeds, blend with autumn foliage, and baffle the keenest hounds in the kingdom!"

Just at that moment, the baying of a ferocious pack of hunting hounds shattered the forest quiet, accompanied by the blast of hunting horns and galloping hooves.

In an instant, the cat executed her one trick: she sprang gracefully up the rough bark of a tall beech tree, perching safely among the highest leafy boughs where no hound could ever reach.

"Quick, Master Fox!" called the cat from above. "Open your bag of a hundred tricks! Choose your best strategy!"

The bewildered fox darted left, sprinted right, doubled back, crawled into a briar patch, and attempted twenty clever schemes at once. But in his frantic indecision and panic, the hounds encircled him, cutting off every escape until he was caught.

Watching from her secure perch, the cat sighed: "A hundred brilliant theories are worthless when danger strikes, while one simple, practical defense preserves life and limb."
moral: One safe and reliable plan is better than a hundred brilliant schemes that fail in peril.

title: The Dog and the Wolf
summary: A gaunt, starving wolf, whose ribs showed through his matted gray fur after weeks of harsh winter blizzards, happened to meet a plump, sleek house dog strolling along the edge of a...
full_text:
A gaunt, starving wolf, whose ribs showed through his matted gray fur after weeks of harsh winter blizzards, happened to meet a plump, sleek house dog strolling along the edge of a village lane. The mastiff was glossy, round-bellied, and radiated robust health.

The wolf paused, admiring the dog's well-fed stature: "Greetings, cousin! You look magnificent! How is it that you are so delightfully fat while I, who am stronger and bolder than you, must hunt day and night only to starve in the cold?"

"It is quite simple, cousin," replied the dog cheerfully. "My master provides me with rich roasts, sweet bread, and marrow bones from his own table. All I must do in return is guard his courtyard at night, bark at passing strangers, and wag my tail when the master enters the hall. Come with me! My master will gladly give you the same easy life."

The wolf was overjoyed at the prospect of boundless meals and warm straw. "Lead on, cousin!" he exclaimed. "I am weary of sleeping in freezing bogs."

As they trotted side by side toward the manor, the wolf noticed a bare, hairless ring around the dog's thick neck, where the fur was worn down to the raw pink skin.

"What is that mark upon your neck, friend?" asked the wolf curiously.

"Oh, that is nothing," answered the dog casually. "It is merely the mark of the iron collar and chain with which they tie me up during the daytime, so that I do not wander off or bite the visitors. But at night they set me free!"

The wolf stopped dead in his tracks. His amber eyes widened. "Tie you up?" he echoed. "Do you mean you cannot roam the forests whenever you please?"

"Not by day," admitted the dog. "But what does that matter when food is abundant?"

"It matters everything," declared the wolf, backing into the shadows of the woods. "Enjoy your fat bones, cousin, and your comfortable kennel. I would rather starve as a free wanderer than grow fat as a pampered slave in chains!" And he sprinted back into the wild freedom of the wilderness.
moral: Lean freedom is far sweeter than fat luxury purchased at the price of a chain.

title: The Eagle and the Arrow
