title: Rashin-Coatie - Scotland
summary: In a kingdom of ancient Scotland lived a good king's daughter whose mother passed away, leaving her in the hands of a harsh stepmother wh...
full_text:
In a kingdom of ancient Scotland lived a good king's daughter whose mother passed away, leaving her in the hands of a harsh stepmother who made her life a misery. The stepmother dressed her in a coat woven of green wetland rushes, wherefore all the court called her 'Rashin-Coatie'.

Rashin-Coatie was forced to herd the cattle across the bogs from dawn to dusk. Her only friend was a little Red Calf, who loved her dearly.
Whenever Rashin-Coatie sat weeping on the heather, the Red Calf would say:
'Lassie, take the little bone from my foot, turn it thrice, and ask for what thy heart desires.'
The bone spread banquets of roasted meats, barley bread, and sweet milk, so that Rashin-Coatie flourished in beauty.

The jealous stepmother discovered the Red Calf and ordered it slaughtered.
The dying calf whispered: 'Bury my bones beneath the gray stone under the Rowan tree, and remember me in thy need.'

When the Yuletide feast arrived, the stepmother and her vain daughter dressed in scarlet velvets, leaving Rashin-Coatie to spin fifty skeins of coarse flax before their return.
Rashin-Coatie ran to the Rowan tree, turned the gray stone, and whispered her grief.
Flocks of songbirds flew down and spun the flax in minutes, while the stone gifted Rashin-Coatie a gown of shimmering satin woven with silver thread, and a pair of delicate green morocco leather slippers!

At the Yuletide church service, the King’s son saw her and knew his heart was won.
As Rashin-Coatie fled down the kirk steps, one green slipper slipped from her heel.
The Prince proclaimed: 'Whosoever can wear this little green slipper shall be Queen of Scots!'

The stepmother’s daughter cut off her heel to fit the shoe, but a little bird sang from the branches:
'Blood in the shoe, blood in the shoe!
Look at the lassie in the rushin-coat true!'

The Prince returned, called for Rashin-Coatie, and the green slipper slid onto her foot with flawless grace.
She drew the matching slipper from her rush coat, and the silver gown enveloped her once more.
The Prince wed Rashin-Coatie, and her reign was marked by justice for every poor hearth in the realm.
moral: Humility and gentle fortitude blossom through woven rushes into royal honor.

title: Ye Xian alternative - Vietnam / Tam and Cam
summary: In a peaceful village of Vietnam lived Tam, a sweet and dutiful maiden, and her half-sister Cam, whose mother treated Tam with unrelentin...
keywords: ye xian alternative - vietnam / tam and cam
full_text:
In a peaceful village of Vietnam lived Tam, a sweet and dutiful maiden, and her half-sister Cam, whose mother treated Tam with unrelenting cruelty.
One day, the stepmother gave each girl a basket, promising an embroidered red sash to whoever caught the most shrimp in the flooded rice paddies.
Tam worked diligently, filling her basket with plump prawns and carp. Lazy Cam played in the lotus ponds, then tricked Tam into washing her hair in deep water, stolen all Tam’s catch, and claimed the red sash.

Finding her basket empty, Tam wept beside the irrigation canal. The compassionate Bodhisattva of Mercy appeared, comforting her:
'Look into thy basket, Tam; one tiny golden goby fish remains. Take it home, release it into the well, and feed it three grains of rice each day.'

Tam tended the little fish with loving devotion. Whenever she sang at the wellhead:
'Goby, goby, rise to the light,
Eat the rice of thy mistress bright!'
the golden fish would rise to eat from her fingers.

The stepmother discovered the secret, tricked Tam into herding water buffalo in the high hills, caught the golden fish, and ate it, hiding the scales under the straw ash.
Guided by a singing rooster, Tam gathered the scales, placed them in four small clay pots, and buried them beneath the four posts of her sleeping mat.

When the King announced the Grand Autumn Festival, the stepmother mixed two bushels of rice and paddy together, commanding Tam to separate every grain before she could attend.
Swallows flew down from the banyan tree and separated the grains in an hour!
Tam then dug up the four clay pots: inside were a shimmering silk tunic, an embroidered skirt of lotus pink, a miniature white steed, and two tiny slippers embroidered with golden phoenixes!

Riding to the festival, Tam’s steed splashed across a stream, and one golden slipper fell into the water.
The royal barge found the slipper floating like a golden leaf.
The King marvelled: 'Only a maiden of peerless refinement could wear such a slipper!'
He announced that whosoever wore the slipper should be his Queen.

When Tam arrived at the royal pavilion, the shoe slipped onto her foot like a blossom upon water. She produced the matching phoenix slipper, and her lotus-pink silks shone in the sunlight.
The King took Tam to the royal citadel as his Queen.
Though the envious stepmother and Cam plotted against her, Tam’s pure spirit endured every trial, returning as a golden oriole and a fragrant persimmon fruit to restore truth, until justice prevailed, and Tam ruled Vietnam in everlasting peace and benevolence.
moral: Purity of intention and filial goodness undergo trials, but divine rebirth always vindicates the virtuous.

title: Cinderella - Native American - The Rough-Face Girl - Algonquin
summary: On the shores of Lake Ontario, in a great Algonquin village, stood a wigwam belonging to a mighty hero known as the Invisible One. None c...
keywords: cinderella - native american - the rough-face girl - algonquin
full_text:
On the shores of Lake Ontario, in a great Algonquin village, stood a wigwam belonging to a mighty hero known as the Invisible One. None could see him save his sister, a woman of deep wisdom and kindness.
It was known throughout the forest that the Invisible One would marry only the maiden who could truly see him with her own eyes.

In the village lived an impoverished father who had three daughters. The two elder daughters were proud, vain, and cruel: they forced their youngest sister to tend the wood-fire day and night, so that sparks and hot ashes burned her skin, leaving her face and arms scarred and her hair singed, wherefore they mocked her as the Rough-Face Girl.

The two elder sisters dressed themselves in fine shells and soft deerskins, painted their faces with vermilion, and walked to the Invisible One's wigwam to claim him.
The sister of the Invisible One met them at the door and asked:
'Can you see my brother?'
'Yes!' they lied eagerly.
'Of what is his bow-string made?'
'A strip of raw hide!' said the first.
'Of what is the runner of his sled made?'
'An oak branch!' said the second.
The sister shook her head: 'You have not seen him; you speak only what any fool can guess.'

The Rough-Face Girl knew in her heart that the sacred wonders of the earth were visible to those who loved with pure humility.
Having no fine furs, she took birch bark from the trees, soaked it in water, carved it into a dress, made moccasins from pine bark, and wore a necklace of broken reeds.
Her sisters and the village boys laughed and threw mud as she walked toward the sacred wigwam, but she walked with serene dignity, her eyes fixed upon the clouds and waters.

The sister of the Invisible One welcomed her with gentle eyes:
'Little sister, canst thou see my brother?'
The Rough-Face Girl looked across the lake and answered with quiet awe:
'Yes, I see him!'
'Of what is his bow made?'
'His bow is the glorious Rainbow that arches across the heavens after the summer rain!'
'And of what is his bow-string made?'
'The bow-string is the Milky Way, the luminous path of stars that spans the sky!'
'And of what is the runner of his sled made?'
'The runner of his sled is the flashing Green Fire of the Northern Lights dancing across the dark horizon!'

Tears of profound joy filled the sister’s eyes:
'Truly, thou hast seen him with the clean vision of thy soul!'

She led the Rough-Face Girl into the wigwam, bathed her scarred face in sacred water from the mountain spring, and combed her singed hair.
As the water touched her, the scars and burns dissolved: her skin became as smooth as a polished river stone, her hair grew long and lustrous like a blackbird’s wing, and her eyes shone like deep woodland pools!
She was dressed in a soft buckskin robe embroidered with porcupine quills.

The Invisible One entered the wigwam, looked upon her radiant face, and smiled with deep reverence:
'My beloved, for many seasons I have waited for the maiden whose eyes could perceive the true majesty of the Great Spirit. Thou art my bride.'

They were wed in the presence of all the forest nations, living in honor and harmony, proving that true vision belongs not to the proud, but to the humble of heart.
moral: True beauty and spiritual vision see beyond outward scars to perceive the sacred wonder of the universe.

title: The Baba Yaga and Vasilisa the Beautiful - Russia
summary: In a distant province of holy Russia lived a merchant whose wife died, leaving behind an eight-year-old daughter named Vasilisa the Beaut...
keywords: the baba yaga and vasilisa the beautiful - russia
full_text:
In a distant province of holy Russia lived a merchant whose wife died, leaving behind an eight-year-old daughter named Vasilisa the Beautiful.
On her deathbed, the mother gave Vasilisa a tiny wooden doll, saying:
'Keep this doll always in thy apron pocket, Vasilisa. Whenever trouble befalls thee, feed her a piece of bread and ask her counsel, and she will deliver thee from all harm.'

The merchant remarried a harsh widow with two envious daughters. The stepmother gave Vasilisa the hardest labor: carrying heavy logs, cleaning stoves, and scrubbing floorboards, hoping the winter winds would ruin her bloom.
Yet Vasilisa grew lovelier every day, for every night she shared her bread crusts with the little doll, who whispered:
'Sleep, Vasilisa, the morning is wiser than the evening,' and performed all the heavy tasks while Vasilisa rested.

One autumn evening, when the merchant was away on a long trading journey, the stepmother deliberately extinguished all the candles in the house.
'The hearth fire has gone out!' shrieked the elder stepsister. 'Vasilisa, go into the deep birch forest to the hut of Baba Yaga the witch, and fetch a burning skull to light our lamps!'

Vasilisa trembled, but fed her doll a crumb of rye bread.
'Fear not,' whispered the doll. 'Walk forward; no harm shall touch thee.'

Vasilisa walked through the dark, snowy woods.
A white horseman in white armor on a white horse galloped past: it was the Bright Dawn.
A red horseman on a fiery steed galloped past: it was the Red Sun.
A black horseman on a coal-black stallion rode by: it was the Dark Night.

She reached the clearing where Baba Yaga's hut stood upon giant chicken legs, surrounded by a fence of human bones topped with glowing skulls!
Baba Yaga flew down in her iron mortar, steering with the pestle and sweeping away her tracks with a silver broom:
'Foo, foo! I smell Russian blood! Who art thou?'

Vasilisa bowed with modest courtesy: 'I am Vasilisa, come for a light for my stepmother's hearth.'
'Thou shalt serve me first,' croaked Baba Yaga. 'If thou failest, I shall eat thee for supper!'

For three days Baba Yaga gave Vasilisa impossible tasks: cleaning the yard, washing three linen shirts, and sorting two bushels of poppy seeds mixed with dirt.
Each night, the little doll completed the sorting while Vasilisa slept.

Surprised by her flawless work, Baba Yaga asked:
'How dost thou accomplish my tasks so cleanly, maiden?'
'By my mother's blessing,' replied Vasilisa with serene humility.

Baba Yaga shuddered: 'Away with thee! I want no blessed souls inside my forest!'
The witch took a skull with blazing eyes from the fence, placed it upon a birch staff, and thrust it into Vasilisa's hands:
'Take thy light and go!'

Vasilisa ran home. When she entered the dark house, the blazing eyes of the skull turned upon the cruel stepmother and her daughters, scorching their envious hearts until they fled into the night, never to return.

Vasilisa buried the skull safely in the forest moss. She went to the capital city, apprenticed herself to a kind old weaver, and spun linen so translucent and fine that it could pass through the eye of a needle.
The Tsar, marvelling at the miraculous cloth, summoned the weaver and beheld Vasilisa.
Enchanted by her radiant beauty, modesty, and gentle grace, the Tsar asked for her hand.
Vasilisa became Tsaritsa of Russia, keeping the faithful little wooden doll in her pocket, ruling her people with boundless mercy and maternal love.
moral: A mother's blessing and a pure, hardworking spirit conquer the darkest terrors of the enchanted forest.

title: Cap o' Rushes - England
summary: In the rolling countryside of England lived a wealthy country squire who had three beautiful daughters. One evening, desiring to know who...
full_text:
In the rolling countryside of England lived a wealthy country squire who had three beautiful daughters. One evening, desiring to know who loved him best, he called them to his fireside:
'Tell me, daughters, how much do you love me?'
The eldest said: 'Father, I love you more than life itself, more than all the gold and rubies in the world.'
The second said: 'Father, I love you more than all the silk dresses and singing larks in England.'
The youngest, sweet and thoughtful, replied:
'Father, I love you as fresh meat loves salt.'

The squire flew into a furious rage: 'What? Thou lovest me no more than common kitchen salt? Thou hast no gratitude or filial respect! Quit my roof this night!'

Heartbroken, the youngest daughter walked into the dark marshes. She gathered green rushes, wove them into a long cloak with a hood that covered her golden hair, and made a cap of reeds, wherefore she was called Cap o' Rushes.

She walked to the mansion of a neighboring lord and found employment in the scullery, washing greasy pans, cleaning the spit, and sleeping under the kitchen stairs.

When the young lord gave three grand country dances, the kitchen staff departed to watch the festivities.
Cap o' Rushes washed the grease from her hands, cast off her rush cloak, and stood revealed in a fine silk gown she had hidden in her bundle.
She entered the ballroom, and the young lord danced with none other, captivated by her wit and beauty. Before the final dance, she slipped away and put on her cap of rushes.

On the third night, the lord placed a gold signet ring upon her finger.
When she vanished, the lord fell into a wasting love-sickness, vowing he would eat nothing unless prepared by the scullery maid.
Cap o' Rushes prepared a bowl of clear mutton broth, dropping the gold ring into the broth.
The lord found the ring, summoned Cap o' Rushes, and pulled off her reed cap, revealing her golden hair and noble countenance!
Overjoyed, the young lord asked her to be his bride.

At the wedding feast, Cap o' Rushes instructed the head cook to prepare all dishes for her estranged father without a single grain of salt.
The old squire sat at the banquet, took a mouthful of roast beef, and pushed the plate away in disgust:
'Alas! The meat has no savor, and I can eat nothing!'
He began to weep before the guests:
'I had a daughter who told me she loved me as meat loves salt, and in my blind folly I drove her into the wild. Now I understand that salt is the most precious seasoning on earth, and without it, food turns to dust!'

Cap o' Rushes stepped forward, embraced her weeping father with tears of forgiveness:
'Father, I am thy daughter who loves thee as salt loves meat!'
The father rejoiced with tears of repentance, and the wedding was celebrated with boundless joy throughout the county, proving that simple truth outshines empty praise.
moral: Flattery is empty breath, but genuine affection is essential to life as salt is to meat.

title: Catskin - England
summary: A wealthy nobleman who had long prayed for an heir was filled with disappointment when his wife bore a seventh daughter. He declared: 'I ...
full_text:
A wealthy nobleman who had long prayed for an heir was filled with disappointment when his wife bore a seventh daughter. He declared: 'I will never look upon her face, nor shall she inherit a farthing of my estate!'
The maiden grew up gentle, clever, and virtuous, hidden in a remote wing of the castle.

When an unprincipled neighboring baron demanded her hand in marriage, her father agreed to marry her off against her will.
The maiden, determined to preserve her freedom, demanded three impossible wedding gifts:
A gown made of the silver stars of heaven;
A gown made of the golden rays of the sun;
And a gown made of the shimmering feathers of every bird that flies;
Together with a warm traveling cloak made of a thousand small cat-skins.

To her dismay, the wealthy suitor provided all three gowns.
Realizing she must save herself, the maiden gathered her three wondrous dresses inside a hollow walnut shell, smeared her face with chimney soot, wrapped herself in her rough cloak of cat-skins, and fled into the forest by night.

After wandering many days, she arrived at the castle of a handsome young King and was hired as an under-scullery maid. The cooks mocked her strange fur cloak and nicknamed her Catskin, setting her to scrape iron pots and carry peat.

When the King held a grand three-night ball, Catskin begged the cook for permission to watch from the doorway.
She washed the soot from her face, cracked the walnut shell, and dressed in the Gown of Silver Stars!
She entered the ballroom like a celestial vision, dancing with the King, but vanished before midnight.
On the second night, she wore the Gown of Golden Sunbeams; on the third night, she wore the Gown of Feathered Rainbows!
As she fled on the third evening, the King slipped a jeweled diamond ring onto her finger.

When Catskin prepared the King's morning porridge, she secretly dropped the diamond ring into the bowl.
Finding the ring, the King called the scullery maid before him.
He gently pulled away her rough cat-skin cloak, and the glittering feather gown shone underneath!
The King knelt, asking her to be his Queen.
Catskin revealed her noble birth, their wedding was celebrated with nationwide rejoicings, and her estranged father, learning of her virtue and majesty, came in deep repentance to seek her pardon, which she granted with filial grace.
moral: Self-reliance, resourcefulness, and chastity navigate perils, earning honorable love through quiet dignity.

title: Nya-chan and the Golden Slipper - West Africa - Ghana
summary: Along the banks of the Volta River in Ghana lived a kind maiden named Nya-chan. Orphaned of both parents, she lived with an aunt and two ...
keywords: nya-chan and the golden slipper - west africa - ghana
full_text:
Along the banks of the Volta River in Ghana lived a kind maiden named Nya-chan. Orphaned of both parents, she lived with an aunt and two cousins who made her carry heavy calabashes of water up the steep riverbank, pound yams until her palms blistered, and wear only a tattered cloth.

Despite her toil, Nya-chan shared her meager cassava porridge with the hungry woodland animals and the little silver river crabs.
One scorching afternoon, an old, weary woman sitting by the river crossing begged for water and bread. Nya-chan immediately offered her calabash and shared her only yam cake.

The old woman was an ancient water spirit of the Volta. She smiled upon Nya-chan:
'Child of clean hands, thy kindness is recorded in the waters. Take this palm-nut shell. When the Yam Festival begins, open it beneath the great Baobab tree.'

When the Yam Harvest Festival arrived, the cousins dressed in bright kente cloths and brass bangles, leaving Nya-chan behind to weed the okra patch.
Nya-chan went to the Baobab tree and cracked the palm-nut.
Out tumbled a magnificent kente wrapper woven of gold and emerald threads, ivory bangles for her wrists, and two slippers woven of pure river gold!

Nya-chan attended the festival dance. The young Chief of the Ashanti was mesmerized by her graceful movements.
As she fled at dusk, one golden slipper slipped off her foot on the riverbank rocks.
The Chief held the golden slipper, declaring: 'The maiden whose foot fits this golden woven slipper shall sit upon the stool of honor beside me!'

Every maiden of the river towns tried the slipper, but their feet were too broad.
When the Chief’s party reached Nya-chan’s compound, her cousins locked her in the chicken coop.
A silver river crab pinched the Chief’s foot, scuttling toward the coop and rattling the wicker latch!
The Chief opened the door, brought Nya-chan forth, and placed the golden slipper upon her foot.
It embraced her toes like warm river clay! Nya-chan drew the matching slipper from her cloth, and her golden kente wrapper shone in the sunlight.

The Chief welcomed Nya-chan as Queen, where she established peaceful councils and ensured that no orphan went hungry, celebrated throughout Ghana as the Golden Maiden of the Volta.
moral: Generosity and sharing one's food with the hungry river spirits bring blessings of royal honor.

title: The Anklet (Chiriya) - India - Punjabi
summary: In the lush green fields of Punjab lived a sweet maiden named Chiriya (Little Sparrow), who lived with a harsh stepmother and two selfish...
full_text:
In the lush green fields of Punjab lived a sweet maiden named Chiriya (Little Sparrow), who lived with a harsh stepmother and two selfish stepsisters.
While her sisters lounged on velvet charpoys, Chiriya milked the water buffaloes, gathered dried cow dung for fuel, and swept the courtyard in coarse cotton homespun.

Her only refuge was an ancient Pipal tree at the edge of the mustard fields, where she sang bhajans and shared her roasted chickpeas with the green parakeets that nested in its boughs.
Moved by her gentle devotion, the spirit of the Pipal tree whispered:
'Chiriya, daughter of patience, whenever thou art in sorrow, shake my lowest branch and ask.'

When the Maharaja of the province announced a magnificent royal fair at the fort to celebrate the Baisakhi harvest, the stepmother and sisters departed in shimmering silk dupattas and gold jhumkas, leaving Chiriya to grind two sacks of wheat flour.
Chiriya went to the Pipal tree and shook its branch.
Flocks of green parakeets flew down and turned the heavy millstone, grinding the wheat into snowy flour in minutes!
The tree then showered Chiriya with an embroidered crimson lehenga woven with real silver zari, and a pair of delicate golden anklets fitted with musical silver bells!

Chiriya danced with joy at the Baisakhi fair, enchanting the young Prince with her modest beauty and rhythmic grace.
Hearing the midnight gong, she fled down the marble ghats of the river. In her haste, one musical golden anklet unclasped and fell into the swirling river water!

The Prince recovered the musical anklet, enchanted by its tiny size and sweet chime:
'I will marry only the maiden upon whose foot this golden anklet clasps with natural ease!'

The royal messengers rode through all the villages of Punjab.
At Chiriya’s house, the stepsisters rubbed their feet with mustard oil to squeeze into the anklet, but the bells remained silent and the clasp would not close.
The Prince’s minister noticed Chiriya standing quietly behind the granary door.
He asked her to step forward.
Chiriya placed her dainty foot upon the stool: the golden anklet clasped around her ankle with a clear, joyous chime! She drew the matching anklet from her dupatta, and its bells rang in perfect harmony!

The Prince welcomed Chiriya to the palace as his Princess.
True to her noble spirit, Chiriya forgave her stepmother and sisters, providing them with gifts of silk and grain, proving that a heart like a little sparrow carries the music of heaven.
moral: A pure and devoted heart cannot be dimmed by cruel malice; truth rings clear as a golden bell.

title: Cinderella - Persian Variant - Moon-Brow Girl (Mahpishani)
summary: In ancient Isfahan lived a virtuous girl named Shahrzad, whom everyone called Mahpishani (The Moon-Brow Maiden) because she had a crescen...
full_text:
In ancient Isfahan lived a virtuous girl named Shahrzad, whom everyone called Mahpishani (The Moon-Brow Maiden) because she had a crescent moon birthmark upon her forehead that glowed with gentle light when she smiled.
After her mother passed away, her father married a widow with an envious daughter.
The stepmother hated Mahpishani’s luminous forehead and forced her to wear a thick black scarf to conceal her moon-mark, sending her to spin cotton beside a swift mountain stream.

One windy afternoon, a gust of wind blew Mahpishani’s white spool of cotton into the water.
Weeping, the maiden followed the floating spool down into a subterranean cave, where she found a venerable, ancient crone stirring a cauldron of herbal water.

Instead of demanding her cotton, Mahpishani greeted the old woman with deep reverence, swept the cave floor, combed the elder’s white hair with gentle fingers, and washed her earthen dishes.
In gratitude, the wise woman returned her spool, and said:
'Go to the cave spring. Dip thy head beneath the crystal water, but touch not the black pool.'

Mahpishani stepped into the clear water. When she emerged, her hair shone like spun night-silk, her crescent moon mark glowed like the full moon, and on her chin appeared a tiny star that sparkled like a diamond!

Seeing her return in radiant splendor, the greedy stepmother sent her own lazy daughter into the cave.
The stepsister kicked the crone, demanded gold, and jumped headlong into the black pool!
She emerged with an ugly black horn on her forehead and a serpent dangling from her chin!

When the Prince of Isfahan gave a grand festival at the Pavilion of Forty Columns, Mahpishani was locked in the kitchen under a heavy wicker basket.
A friendly rooster scratched open the basket, while the cave spirit sent her a gown woven of lapis lazuli and gold, and a pair of golden slippers embroidered with turquoise!

At the pavilion, the Prince was enchanted by the maiden with the glowing moon on her brow.
Fleeing at midnight, she lost one turquoise slipper in the palace pool.
The Prince searched all of Persia for the owner of the shoe.
When the royal guards reached Mahpishani’s courtyard, the stepmother hid her in the tandoor oven.
The faithful rooster flew to the roof and crowed:
'The horned girl sits in the hall,
The Moon-Brow Queen sits in the oven wall!'

The Prince opened the oven door and beheld Mahpishani.
The turquoise slipper embraced her foot perfectly, her crescent moon shone through the soot, and she drew the matching shoe from her sleeve.
The Prince married Mahpishani with forty days of feasts, celebrated across Persia as the triumph of gentle respect and unblemished virtue.
moral: Gentle respect toward elders and genuine kindness reflect heavenly beauty, while envy brings outward ugliness.

title: Little Saddleslut - Ireland
summary: In the wild hills of Connemara lived an Irish king’s daughter whose mother passed away, leaving her in the care of an ill-tempered stepmo...
full_text:
In the wild hills of Connemara lived an Irish king’s daughter whose mother passed away, leaving her in the care of an ill-tempered stepmother.
The stepmother stripped her of her woolen kirtles, dressed her in an old leather donkey saddle tied with hemp rope, and ordered her to herd swine across the peat bogs, mocking her as 'Little Saddleslut'.

Yet the maiden’s heart was as pure as bog-cotton.
An ancient fairy trout that lived in the holy well beneath the mountain whispered to her:
'Keep heart, King’s daughter. When thou art weary, dip thy hands in the well water and make thy prayer to the stars.'

When the High King of Ireland announced three great Sunday masses at the abbey church, the stepmother and her daughter rode forth in velvet mantles, leaving the maiden in the pigsties.
The maiden ran to the holy well.
The water parted, giving her a magnificent milk-white steed, a gown of sea-green silk embroidered with golden shamrocks, and a pair of golden slippers as light as meadow mist!

At the abbey, the High King’s son could not take his eyes from her face.
As she leaped upon her horse after mass, one golden slipper slipped into the mud of the churchyard.
The Prince picked up the golden slipper and swore upon his sword:
'I will marry no woman in Ireland but she whose foot fits this golden shoe!'

The Prince rode from cabin to castle throughout the provinces.
When he arrived at the Connemara estate, the stepsister cut off her toes to force her foot into the shoe, but a robin perched on the church wall sang:
'There is blood in the shoe, Sir King,
Look for the maiden in the leather saddle ring!'

The Prince returned, searched the swine sheds, and found the maiden in her saddle cloak.
He placed the golden slipper upon her foot: it fit as though grown from her own skin!
She took off her leather saddle, revealing her sea-green gown and radiant beauty.
The Prince carried her to the royal hall of Tara, crowned her Queen of Ireland, and their days were filled with music, peace, and abundance.
moral: Faithful love and courageous endurance through cold moorlands lead to the warm hearth of true nobility.

summary: In the ancient Pueblo of Matsaki, beneath the sacred red mesas, lived a poor orphan maiden who tended the communal flock of turkeys. She ...
keywords: the turkey girl - pueblo native american - zuni
full_text:
In the ancient Pueblo of Matsaki, beneath the sacred red mesas, lived a poor orphan maiden who tended the communal flock of turkeys. She had no home, sleeping in the stone corrals, wearing ragged woven yucca skirts, and eating dry parched corn scraps.
Yet she loved her turkeys with maternal tenderness: she talked to them, carried cool water to their troughs, and shielded their fledglings from desert coyotes.

One autumn, the pueblo announced the great Sacred Dance of Matsaki, where drums beat and dancers wore turquoise beads and embroidered white mantles.
The Turkey Girl sat in the corral, listening to the drumbeats, weeping softly that she had no clothes to join the dance.

The Old Chief Turkey spread his bronze feathers, stepped forward, and spoke:
'Dear foster-mother, thou hast cared for us when all others neglected thee. We shall clothe thee for the dance.
Spread thy blanket upon the ground!'

The turkeys gathered around the blanket, shook their plumage, and miraculously produced a snowy deerskin tunic, a necklace of polished turquoise and sky-blue stones, and a pair of delicate white buckskin moccasins embroidered with red and yellow porcupine quills!
The Old Chief Turkey looked at her solemnly:
'Go and dance, little mother. But remember thy covenant: return to us before the sun sets behind the western mesa, for we need thy hands to close the pen against the coyotes. If thou forgettest us, thy blessings will vanish.'

The Turkey Girl promised with tears of gratitude.
At the pueblo plaza, she joined the dance. Her beauty was like the morning star rising over the mesa; the young cacique (chief) danced beside her, captivated by her grace.
Lost in the intoxication of music and praise, the maiden forgot her promise!
The sun dipped beneath the western cliffs, the stars appeared, and still she danced!

Suddenly remembering her turkeys, she broke away and ran frantically across the desert toward the corrals.
When she reached the stone pens, the gate was open—and the flock was gone!
Up on the mesa cliffs, she saw the turkeys flying away into the moonlight, calling mournfully:
'Thou didst forget thy duty for fleeting vanity!'

As she reached out her hands, her white buckskin tunic dissolved into ragged yucca leaves, her turquoise necklace turned to dry berries, and her moccasins became dusty dust.
The Turkey Girl sat in the empty corral and wept, learning the timeless lesson of the pueblos: that no glory or dance can replace the sacred covenant of loyalty owed to those who sustained us in our poverty.
moral: Promises made to those who help us must be honored; neglecting loyalty for selfish pleasure brings regret.

title: The Cinder Maid - Japan - Benizara and Kakezara
summary: In an ancient mountain province of Japan lived a widower who had a daughter named Benizara (Crimson Dish), whose mother had left her a sm...
keywords: the cinder maid - japan - benizara and kakezara
full_text:
In an ancient mountain province of Japan lived a widower who had a daughter named Benizara (Crimson Dish), whose mother had left her a small crimson porcelain saucer.
The father remarried a harsh woman with a daughter named Kakezara (Broken Dish).
The stepmother favored Kakezara, loading Benizara with all household drudgery: carrying water from mountain gorges, cutting bamboo, and gathering wild chestnuts in the snow.

One autumn, the stepmother gave each girl a woven bamboo basket, promising a fine silk kimono to whoever filled her basket with chestnuts first.
To Kakezara she gave a tight, strong basket; to Benizara she gave a basket with a hole in the bottom!

Benizara worked in the mountain woods, but every chestnut slipped through the hole onto the moss.
Weeping, she followed the trail of fallen nuts to a solitary mountain hut, where lived an ancient mountain woman.
Benizara bowed politely, swept the hut's hearth, prepared tea, and washed the old woman’s rice bowl.
The mountain woman smiled:
'Gentle maiden, take this woven rush basket that never empties, and take this magic box. When thou art in need, tap the lid.'

Benizara returned home with her basket overflowing with sweet chestnuts.
The envious stepmother gave Kakezara a new kimono, but left Benizara in her hemp rags.

When the young Lord of the Province traveled through their village on his ceremonial hunt, the villagers gathered to welcome him.
The stepmother locked Benizara in the rice cellar and took Kakezara to the festival.
Benizara tapped the magic box.
Instantly, her hemp rags turned into a layered silk kimono dyed the color of autumn maple leaves, with a sash of gold brocade and wooden geta clogs lacquered in vermilion!

She stood beneath a blossoming cherry tree as the Lord passed.
The Lord halted his retinue, enchanted by her graceful demeanor.
To test her mind, the Lord composed the first half of a classical waka poem:
'Upon the mountain path the autumn leaves fall deep...'
Benizara bowed modestly, completing the poem with flawless classical meter:
'Yet through the scarlet boughs the moon of virtue shines!'

The Lord was astonished by her profound learning and refined spirit.
When the stepmother pushed Kakezara forward, Kakezara spoke only crude, greedy words, humiliating her mother.
The Lord chose Benizara as his bride, escorting her to his castle with full samurai honor, celebrating her as a lady whose gentle conduct reflected the pure beauty of the mountain snow.
moral: Gentle humility, filial respect, and poetic refinement blossom into noble honor, while harshness shatters like clay.

title: Cinderella - Disney Modern Variant - 1950
summary: In a stately French chateau, a young maiden named Cinderella was reduced to servitude by her cruel stepmother, Lady Tremaine, and her two...
full_text:
In a stately French chateau, a young maiden named Cinderella was reduced to servitude by her cruel stepmother, Lady Tremaine, and her two selfish stepsisters, Anastasia and Drizella.
Banished to the chilly attic tower, Cinderella was made to cook, scrub floors, and serve her stepfamily from dawn to dusk.

Yet Cinderella’s spirit remained unvanquished. Her heart was filled with boundless kindness, befriending the birds of the eaves and the little attic mice—especially chubby Gus and quick-witted Jaq—whom she saved from mousetraps and clothed in tiny jackets of scrap cloth.
'No matter how your heart is grieving,' she would whisper to her little friends, 'if you keep on believing, the dream that you wish will come true.'

When the King proclaimed a royal ball to find a bride for the Prince, Cinderella found her mother’s old dress in an attic trunk.
The loyal mice and birds gathered ribbons, beads, and lace discarded by the stepsisters, sewing the gown into a lovely party dress!
When Cinderella appeared in her mother's dress, the jealous stepsisters tore the gown to shreds in cruel rage, departing for the palace in triumph.

Cinderella ran to the garden bench and wept in utter despair.
Suddenly, a warm glow of light gathered among the rosebushes, and her Fairy Godmother appeared:
'Dry your tears, my dear! Faith must never fade!'

With a wave of her magic wand and the words 'Bibbidi-Bobbidi-Boo!', the godmother transformed a pumpkin into a golden coach, four mice into white horses, a hound into a footman, and Cinderella’s torn rags into a dazzling gown of shimmering starlight, completed with sparkling slippers of purest glass!
'Remember, my child: at the stroke of midnight, the spell will be broken!'

At the ball, the Prince danced only with Cinderella. But at the first chime of midnight, Cinderella fled down the grand staircase, losing one glass slipper in her flight.

The Grand Duke visited every household with the glass slipper.
Lady Tremaine locked Cinderella in the attic tower, but brave little Jaq and Gus stole the heavy key from the stepmother's apron pocket, dragged it up the winding stairs, and unlocked the door!

When the stepmother deliberately tripped the footman, shattering the glass slipper upon the floor, Cinderella smiled calmly:
'Do not worry; I have the other slipper!'
She drew the matching glass slipper from her apron pocket, and it slid onto her foot with effortless perfection.

Cinderella married the Prince, forgiving her family, and welcoming her little animal friends to live in the palace gardens forever, proving that kindness and steadfast hope conquer cruelty.
moral: Kindness to the smallest creatures and unwavering hope keep dreams alive through dark hours until destiny calls.

title: Cinderella - Korea - Kongji and Patzzi
summary: In the Joseon kingdom of Korea lived a gentle maiden named Kongji (Little Bean). After her mother passed away, her father remarried a bit...
full_text:
In the Joseon kingdom of Korea lived a gentle maiden named Kongji (Little Bean). After her mother passed away, her father remarried a bitter woman who had an ugly, spiteful daughter named Patzzi (Red Bean).
The stepmother gave Kongji impossible chores, while Patzzi was spoiled with sweet rice cakes and fine silk ribbons.

One spring morning, the stepmother gave Kongji a wooden hoe and sent her to till a stony mountain field, while Patzzi received an iron hoe to weed a soft vegetable patch.
Kongji’s wooden hoe broke upon the hard rocks. Weeping, she knelt among the stones.
Suddenly, a heavenly Black Ox descended from the sky. The ox ate the stones, plowed the entire rocky field into fertile loam in minutes, and gave Kongji a basket of sweet persimmons and wild mountain herbs.

Another day, the stepmother commanded Kongji to fill an enormous earthen water jar (dok) that had a hidden hole in the bottom!
As water poured out, a giant green toad crawled out of the well and sat inside the jar, using its broad, wet back to seal the hole completely until the jar was filled to the brim!

When a grand festival was held in the provincial capital to celebrate the arrival of the new Governor, the stepmother and Patzzi dressed in silk hanboks, commanding Kongji to hull twelve bags of rice, spin ten bolts of hemp, and weave three mats before she could leave.
Flocks of sparrows flew into the courtyard, hulling the rice in an hour; a divine celestial maiden descended from the clouds, spun the hemp and wove the mats, presenting Kongji with a magnificent silk hanbok dyed the color of morning azaleas, and a pair of delicate silk shoes embroidered with golden lotus flowers!

Kongji ran toward the festival. Crossing a stepping-stone bridge over a swift stream, she heard the retinue of the handsome young Governor approaching.
Startled, she leaped across the stones, dropping one embroidered silk shoe into the clear water.

The Governor’s soldiers fished the shoe out of the river.
The Governor marveled at the miniature, artistic craftsmanship of the silk shoe, declaring:
'The maiden whose foot fits this lotus shoe must be a lady of purest virtue and refinement!'

Messengers searched every village in the province.
When they reached Kongji’s house, Patzzi jammed her clumsy heel into the shoe, tearing the silk threads, but could not fit it.
Kongji was called from the kitchen. She washed her hands, sat upon the veranda, and slipped her foot into the shoe: it fit with flawless, gentle beauty!
She drew the matching lotus shoe from her hemp sash, and the azalea silk hanbok reappeared in all its celestial glory!

The Governor recognized her extraordinary virtue and asked her to become his bride.
Kongji was escorted to the provincial palace in a palanquin of honor, where she ruled with profound compassion, opening grain warehouses for poor peasants, while Patzzi and her mother were left to reflect on how honest goodness outshines all bitter plots.
moral: Sincere devotion and filial piety receive aid from heaven and earth, whereas deceit and cruelty harvest shame.

title: The Smell of Soup and the Sound of Money
summary: One chilly winter afternoon in the bustling marketplace of Aksehir, a poor, shivering traveler walked past the steaming kitchen of a wealthy restaurant. The tavern master was boili...
keywords: the smell of soup and the sound of money
full_text:
One chilly winter afternoon in the bustling marketplace of Aksehir, a poor, shivering traveler walked past the steaming kitchen of a wealthy restaurant. The tavern master was boiling a giant cauldron of fragrant lamb broth seasoned with garlic, cinnamon, and cumin.

The penniless traveler pulled a dry crust of barley bread from his pocket and held it over the fragrant steam rising from the pot. He turned the bread around, inhaled the mouth-watering aroma deeply, and ate his softened crust with immense satisfaction.

Just as the poor man was about to walk away, the greedy restaurant owner leaped out of the shop, seized him by the collar, and roared: "Pay me five copper coins this instant!"

"For what, sir?" gasped the bewildered traveler. "I took not a single drop of your soup!"

"You nourished your bread with my rich steam!" barked the merchant. "The aroma belongs to my cauldron, and you have consumed its goodness!"

A crowd gathered, arguing loudly, when Mulla Nasruddin arrived riding his little gray donkey. Hearing the dispute, Nasruddin stroked his beard solemnly and announced: "Step aside, citizens! I shall adjudicate this case of high culinary jurisprudence!"

Nasruddin turned to the restaurant owner: "Is it true that this man ate the steam of your soup?"
"It is entirely true, Mulla!" cried the shopkeeper eagerly. "And steam costs good money to produce!"

Nasruddin reached deep into his pocket and pulled out five copper coins. He cupped the coins tightly inside his hands and shook them vigorously right next to the tavern master's ear: Jingle, jingle, clink!

"Do you hear that sound, tavern master?" asked Nasruddin with a serious frown.
"Of course I hear it, Mulla!" replied the greedy man. "What of it?"

"The judgment is settled!" proclaimed Nasruddin, pocketing the coins once more. "The sound of money pays in full for the smell of soup. Case dismissed!"

The crowd burst into uproarious laughter, while the greedy merchant slunk back into his shop, thoroughly outwitted by the Mulla's impeccable justice.
moral: A frivolous claim based on thin air deserves to be paid with nothing more than sound.

title: Who Stole the Smell?
summary: A baker who was notorious throughout the province for his extreme stinginess noticed that townsfolk often paused outside his bakery window in the early morning simply to enjoy the...
full_text:
A baker who was notorious throughout the province for his extreme stinginess noticed that townsfolk often paused outside his bakery window in the early morning simply to enjoy the delicious fragrance of fresh baking bread.

Outraged that people were enjoying his merchandise without paying, the baker posted an armed guard at his door and brought a formal lawsuit before the town magistrate, charging thirty citizens with "stealing the fragrance of fresh rye."

The magistrate, completely baffled by the absurd complaint, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to give his opinion as the resident scholar.

Nasruddin listened with grave dignity. Then he asked the baker: "How much has your bakery's fragrance diminished because these poor people inhaled it?"

"Why, it hasn't diminished at all," stammered the baker. "The street still smells just as delicious!"

"Then by the ancient law of balance," declared Nasruddin, "the defendants must pay you with an equal portion of their shadows! Tomorrow at noon, when the sun is at its zenith, all thirty citizens shall stand in front of your shop window and allow you to look at their shadows for ten minutes. If you can bake bread with their shadows, you may keep them!"

The entire town square erupted in cheers, and the baker tore down his ridiculous lawsuit in utter embarrassment.
moral: Trying to hoard what nature gives freely makes one an object of public ridicule.

title: The Donkey and the Book
summary: Timur the Lame, the fierce conqueror, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to his grand pavilion. "Mulla," boomed the tyrant, "they say you are a teacher of miraculous wisdom. Can you teach my...
full_text:
Timur the Lame, the fierce conqueror, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to his grand pavilion. "Mulla," boomed the tyrant, "they say you are a teacher of miraculous wisdom. Can you teach my favorite donkey to read the great books of philosophy? If you succeed in ten years, I will grant you a chest of rubies; if you fail, you shall lose your head!"

Nasruddin bowed to the floor: "Sire, it shall be done! I require only ten years and a monthly stipend of gold to conduct the donkey's literary education."

When Nasruddin returned home leading the donkey, his terrified wife wept: "Are you insane, husband? How can an animal learn to read? In ten years you will be executed!"

"Be calm, my dear," smiled Nasruddin with a serene wink. "Ten years is a very long time! Within ten years, either Timur will die, or I will die, or the donkey will die! And in the meantime, we shall live comfortably on the royal stipend!"

Every day, Nasruddin hid grains of barley between the parchment pages of a large book. The donkey quickly learned to flip the pages with his tongue to eat the grains. When Nasruddin brought the donkey before the court, the beast eagerly turned the pages with his muzzle, braying loudly when no more barley was found.

"Look, Your Majesty!" exclaimed Nasruddin proudly. "The donkey has already mastered reading; he has completed chapter three and is now debating the author's logic!" Timur was so amused by the spectacle that he doubled the Mulla's reward.
moral: Flattering despots with impossible promises requires a long horizon and clever strategy.

title: The Lost Key
summary: Late one moonlit evening, several neighbors walking through the town square noticed Mulla Nasruddin down on all fours in the dust beneath a bright street lamp, searching franticall...
full_text:
Late one moonlit evening, several neighbors walking through the town square noticed Mulla Nasruddin down on all fours in the dust beneath a bright street lamp, searching frantically for something.

"What have you lost, Mulla?" asked a friendly neighbor, kneeling down to help him sift through the gravel.

"I have lost the iron key to my front door," replied Nasruddin, wiping sweat from his brow.

The neighbors immediately joined the search. For nearly an hour, five men crawled upon their hands and knees, combing through every pebble beneath the lamp, but not a trace of the key could be found.

Exhausted, one of the neighbors asked: "Mulla, are you absolutely sure you dropped the key here in the square?"

"Oh, no!" answered Nasruddin casually, pointing toward the dark alleyway twenty yards away. "I dropped it inside the dark coal-cellar behind my house!"

The neighbors stared at him in utter disbelief: "Then why in heaven's name are you searching for it out here under the street lamp?"

"Can you not see?" laughed Nasruddin with wide-eyed innocence. "It is pitch black in my cellar, whereas out here under the street lamp, there is plenty of light to see!"

The neighbors groaned, but Sufi masters smiled, knowing Nasruddin had just illustrated how mortals seek truth in the superficial glitter of the world rather than searching the deep, dark caverns of their own hearts.
moral: Searching for answers where it is convenient rather than where the truth was lost is human folly.

full_text:
A group of strapping young wrestlers gathered in the village square, boasting of their mighty strength. One claimed he could lift an ox; another boasted he could uproot an olive tree.

Mulla Nasruddin, who was now well past seventy years of age with a snowy white beard and creaking joints, strode into the circle, puffing out his chest.

"You call that strength?" scoffed Nasruddin. "Why, I am just as strong today as I was when I was a fiery youth of twenty!"

The villagers were astonished. "Come now, Mulla!" said an elder. "How can an old man of seventy be as strong as a youth of twenty?"

"I have scientific proof!" declared Nasruddin proudly. "In my backyard stands an enormous stone boulder. When I was twenty years old, I tried with all my might to lift it, and I could not move it an inch. Yesterday morning, I tried with all my might to lift that very same boulder, and I still could not move it an inch! Therefore, my strength is exactly the same!"
moral: Boasting of lost youth only highlights the frailty of present vanity.

A traveling quack physician arrived in the village selling "Miraculous Elixir of Arabian Gazelle," claiming a single drop cured all ailments. He charged ten silver pieces per vial.

Nasruddin, suspecting a fraud, bought a vial, tasted a drop, and immediately spit it out: "Why, this is nothing but plain ditch water mixed with donkey vinegar!"

The quack became indignant: "How dare an ignorant villager insult imperial medicine! Bring me ten sick men, and I will prove its celestial potency!"

Nasruddin returned with his own wooden jug filled with water from his garden cistern. He had two villagers taste both the quack's potion and his own cistern water. Both villagers agreed that Nasruddin's water tasted much sweeter and fresher.

"You see?" announced Nasruddin to the crowd. "The quack sells sour donkey vinegar in gold vials, while my donkey gives pure spring water for free! Keep your silver coins in your pockets, and drink fresh water from your own wells!"
moral: Blind faith in labels often deceives people into accepting ordinary reality as magic.

title: The Coat Gets Invited
summary: A wealthy nobleman hosted a lavish banquet for the town dignitaries. Mulla Nasruddin, having worked all morning in his dusty vineyard, arrived at the palace in his worn, patched wo...
full_text:
A wealthy nobleman hosted a lavish banquet for the town dignitaries. Mulla Nasruddin, having worked all morning in his dusty vineyard, arrived at the palace in his worn, patched work clothes and mud-spattered boots.

The snobbish servants glanced at his rags and pushed him to the drafty corner near the kitchen door. The host walked past him without a word of greeting, and the waiters served him only cold broth and burnt crusts.

Nasruddin quietly slipped away, hurried home, and washed thoroughly. He put on his most magnificent holiday robe—a flowing kaftan of shimmering scarlet silk embroidered with gold thread and trimmed with luxurious fox fur—and donned a grand turban adorned with a silver brooch.

When he returned to the banquet hall, the servants bowed to the floor, opening the double doors with fanfare. The host rushed forward with open arms, embraced the Mulla, and seated him at the head of the banquet table upon velvet cushions.

Waiters immediately brought platters of roasted partridge, saffron pilaf, roasted almonds, and sweet pistachio halva.

Nasruddin smiled graciously. He picked up a spoonful of rich saffron stew and poured it directly into the sleeve of his silk robe! Then he dipped the fur hem of his kaftan into the almond sauce and rubbed sweet halva over his gold embroidery, murmuring affectionately: "Eat, my fine coat, eat! Enjoy the soup! Feast upon the pilaf!"

The host and guests were flabbergasted: "Mulla, what on earth are you doing? Why are you feeding your clothes?"

Nasruddin wiped his hands calmly and replied: "When I arrived an hour ago in my honest human body, wearing my working clothes, you turned me away into the cold corner. But when this coat arrived, you offered velvet cushions and royal delicacies! Therefore, it is obvious that this feast was prepared not for me, but for my coat! And it is only fair that the coat should enjoy what it has earned!"

The host blushed crimson with shame and apologized profusely, while the guests learned a lifelong lesson about the true worth of character over appearances.
moral: People who judge a man by his fine garments are entertaining clothes, not character.

title: How to Divide the Nuts
summary: Five boys were quarreling bitterly in the orchard over a sack of one hundred walnuts they had gathered. Unable to agree on a fair division, they saw Mulla Nasruddin approaching on...
full_text:
Five boys were quarreling bitterly in the orchard over a sack of one hundred walnuts they had gathered. Unable to agree on a fair division, they saw Mulla Nasruddin approaching on his donkey and ran to him: "O wise Mulla! Please divide these walnuts among us fairly!"

Nasruddin sat down on a boulder and smiled: "Tell me, boys: do you wish me to divide these nuts according to human division, or according to God's division?"

The boys shouted eagerly: "According to God's division, Mulla! God's division must surely be the most perfect and sublime!"

"Very well," said Nasruddin.

He opened the sack. To the first boy, he gave seventy walnuts; to the second boy, he gave fifteen; to the third boy, he gave ten; to the fourth boy, he gave four; and to the fifth boy, he gave only one single wrinkled nut!

The boys were stunned and began to protest loudly: "Mulla! This is completely unfair! One boy got almost everything, and the last boy got almost nothing!"

Nasruddin stroked his beard with a twinkle in his eye: "Did you not ask for God's division? In this world, God gives boundless wealth to one man, a modest living to another, and poverty to a third, testing the generosity of the rich and the patience of the poor! If you had wanted an equal share for everyone, you should have asked for human division!"
moral: Human justice seeks fair equality; divine providence distributes according to mysterious design.

title: The Moon is More Useful
summary: Two philosophers were debating in the tea-house whether the sun or the moon was the greater celestial blessing to humanity. The debate grew heated, with each citing ancient astrono...
full_text:
In the lively teahouse of Akşehir, where village elders, traveling merchants, and amateur philosophers gathered every afternoon to debate under the shade of a venerable plane tree, a fierce philosophical argument broke out. Two visiting scholars with elaborate turbans were disputing whether the sun or the moon was the greater celestial blessing to mankind. One argued passionately that without the sun, all crops would wither and humanity would perish in perpetual frost; the other argued with equal vehemence that the moon governed the tides, guided desert caravans by night, and inspired poets. The debate grew so loud that the tea-server spilled a pot of boiling mint tea onto the hearth.

Looking across the cushions, the two scholars spotted Mulla Nasruddin sitting peacefully in the corner, gently blowing the steam from his tea glass with an expression of serene detachment. Recognizing him as the village judge, they cried out: "Come, Mulla! You are a man whose wits cut through confusion like a sharp blade. Settle this profound question for us: which is of greater utility and service to humanity—the radiant sun or the silvery moon?"

Nasruddin placed his glass carefully upon the copper tray, stroked his gray beard with profound gravity, and paused for a long moment while the whole teahouse leaned forward in silence. "Without a shadow of a doubt," declared Nasruddin with decisive authority, "the moon is infinitely more useful and necessary to mankind than the sun!" The scholars blinked in astonishment: "How in heaven's name do you arrive at such a strange conclusion, Mulla?" "The answer is obvious to anyone who uses simple common sense!" laughed Nasruddin, spreading his arms wide. "The sun shines exclusively during the daytime, when it is already broad daylight and nobody has any need of light at all! But the glorious moon shines in the middle of the pitch-black night, precisely when the world is dark and we desperately need illumination to keep from stumbling into ditches! Therefore, the moon is far superior!" The teahouse erupted into roars of laughter, leaving the two pompous scholars shaking their heads at how easily Nasruddin turned academic pretension upside down.
moral: People often undervalue constant blessings while praising what arrives in moments of darkness.

title: Nasruddin's Donkey is Dead?
summary: Nasruddin came running into the village square, clapping his hands and shouting: "Praise be to heaven! Glory to the Almighty! What a miracle of blessings!"...
full_text:
One dusty morning in Akşehir, Mulla Nasruddin was seen sprinting into the crowded market square, his turban askew, his robes flapping in the wind, clapping his hands together and shouting at the top of his lungs: "Praise be to the Almighty! Glory to the Heavens! What a boundless miracle of divine mercy and blessings has fallen upon my humble head today!"

The merchants stopped measuring cloth, the blacksmith dropped his tongs, and Nasruddin’s neighbor ran over in great excitement, clutching the Mulla’s shoulder: "What magnificent fortune has befallen you, Mulla? Did an uncle in Samarkand pass away and leave you a chest of jewels? Did you dig up a pot of gold beneath your olive tree?" "No, no, nothing of the sort!" beamed Nasruddin, his eyes shining with radiant joy. "My faithful gray donkey broke its tether this morning, galloped wild toward the cliffs, tumbled into the rocky ravine, and broke its neck on the boulders below!"

The neighbor stared at him as if he had lost his senses: "Are you completely mad, Mulla Nasruddin? You have lost your only beast of burden, the animal that plows your patch of barley and carries your firewood to the bazaar! Why on earth are you running through the square thanking heaven that your only donkey is dead?" "O man of small understanding!" laughed Nasruddin, shaking his head with affectionate pity. "Can you not perceive the boundless miracle? I am thanking heaven with all my soul that I was not riding on its back when it tumbled into the abyss! Had I been sitting in the saddle, I would have broken my neck along with the poor beast! A lost donkey can be replaced with fifty silver coins, but where in all Anatolia could my dear wife find another Mulla Nasruddin?" The crowd chuckled at his irrepressible optimism, marveling at how a cheerful spirit finds reasons for gratitude even in the midst of loss.
moral: Finding reasons for gratitude even in misfortune preserves a cheerful spirit.

title: Whose Voice?

full_text:
A neighbor who was notoriously careless with borrowed tools knocked on Nasruddin's door: "Mulla, lend me your donkey for the afternoon; I must carry timber from the forest."

Nasruddin, who knew the neighbor never fed borrowed animals, replied from inside: "I would gladly lend it to you, my dear friend, but alas, my donkey is not here today; my son took it to the neighboring town at dawn."

Just at that moment, the donkey brayed loudly from inside the stable: "Hee-haw! Hee-haw!"

The neighbor became indignant: "Shame on you, Mulla! You tell me the donkey is in the neighboring town, when I can hear it braying with my own ears right inside your stable!"

Nasruddin stepped onto the porch, looking at the neighbor with offended dignity: "My good man! Whom do you choose to believe: an honorable scholar with a gray beard who speaks the truth, or an ignorant donkey?"
moral: Believing an animal's noise over the reasoned word of a friend exposes shallow faith.

title: The Borrowed Pot
summary: Mulla Nasruddin borrowed a large bronze cooking pot from his wealthy, greedy neighbor to prepare a family feast. A week later, he returned the pot, but inside it rested a tiny litt...
full_text:
Mulla Nasruddin borrowed a large bronze cooking pot from his wealthy, greedy neighbor to prepare a family feast. A week later, he returned the pot, but inside it rested a tiny little copper pot.

The neighbor was puzzled: "Mulla, what is this tiny pot doing inside my cauldron?"

"Rejoice, neighbor!" whispered Nasruddin solemnly. "While your pot was in my kitchen, it became pregnant and gave birth to this delightful little child! And since you own the mother, the child belongs to you by law!"

The greedy neighbor laughed to himself, thinking Nasruddin was a simpleton, and happily kept both pots.

A month later, Nasruddin came back and borrowed the big cauldron again. Weeks passed, and Nasruddin did not return it. Finally, the neighbor marched to Nasruddin's house, demanding: "Where is my cooking pot, Mulla?"

Nasruddin wiped away a tear: "Alas, my dear neighbor! I bring you tragic news! Your beloved bronze pot has passed away; it died peacefully in my kitchen yesterday, and I buried it with full honors."

"Are you out of your mind?" screamed the furious neighbor. "How can a bronze cooking pot die?"

"Come now, neighbor," smiled Nasruddin calmly. "You were perfectly willing to believe that your pot could give birth to a baby; why then can you not believe that it can die? Whatever is born must surely one day taste death!"
moral: If you accept an impossible gain based on greed, you must also accept the impossible loss.

title: The Longer Beard
summary: A visiting scholar from Baghdad boasted in the mosque: "The dignity of a scholar is proportional to the length and fullness of his beard!" His own beard reached his waist....
full_text:
One Friday afternoon, the courtyard of the grand mosque in Akşehir was filled with merchants, village elders, and eager students who had gathered to listen to a visiting scholar from the renowned academies of Baghdad. The visitor was a man of immense pomposity, adorned in shimmering silk robes trimmed with golden embroidery, and possessed an extraordinary white beard that cascaded down his chest in glorious waves, reaching all the way to his leather belt. He stroked his facial hair with supreme complacency, pausing after every sentence with a solemn air as though the heavens themselves hung upon his words.

Addressing the humble congregation with an air of condescending superiority, the scholar cleared his throat and declared: "O seekers of knowledge, let it be known that true dignity, depth of scholarship, and spiritual authority are strictly proportional to the length and fullness of a man’s beard! The longer and grander the beard, the deeper and more profound the ocean of divine wisdom that resides in the intellect beneath!" The villagers bowed their heads in bewildered awe, murmuring respectfully among themselves, too intimidated to question the distinguished guest.

From the back of the crowd, Mulla Nasruddin quietly rose to his feet, his worn felt cap slightly tilted and his fingers casually stroking his own short, modest gray beard. "Respected master," called out Nasruddin with profound gravity, bowing low with mock reverence. "Your revolutionary doctrine brings boundless illumination to our simple minds. For if wisdom, dignity, and religious authority were truly measured by the length of the hair upon one’s chin, then without a shadow of a doubt, the village billy goat tethered behind the blacksmith’s shop must be the Supreme Grand Mufti of the entire Islamic world!" The entire courtyard burst into uncontrollable laughter, while the Baghdad scholar hurriedly gathered his silk robes and vanished down the street in red-faced silence.
moral: Measuring wisdom by the length of a beard mistakes outward hair for inner intellect.

title: Half Knowledge
summary: A haughty grammarian boarded Nasruddin's ferry to cross a turbulent river. During the crossing, the scholar asked sneeringly: "Mulla, have you ever studied Arabic grammar and the r...
full_text:
Mulla Nasruddin was once earning a humble living as a ferryman, rowing passengers across a wide, turbulent river whose waters rushed swiftly from the mountain snows. One afternoon, a haughty grammarian from the imperial capital stepped into his wooden skiff. As Nasruddin pulled steadily at the heavy oars, pushing against the frothing current, the scholar adjusted his spectacles, sneered at the Mulla’s calloused hands, and asked in a condescending voice: "Tell me, ferryman, have you ever studied the intricate rules of Arabic grammar, syntax, and classical rhetoric?"

"Alas, no, respected professor," replied Nasruddin cheerfully, his muscles straining against the river's pull. "I am just a simple boatman. I know how to mend an oar, read the river eddies, and haul cargo, but I have never opened a book of grammar in my life." The scholar shook his head with theatrical sorrow and announced loudly so the other passengers could hear: "What a tragedy! You have lived like a beast in the dark! In that case, my poor man, at least half of your entire life has been completely wasted!"

Just as the scholar finished speaking, a violent mountain squall swept down the gorge. A monstrous wave slammed against the side of the skiff, snapping the steering rudder and smashing a hole through the floorboards. As icy water rushed into the boat and it began to sink rapidly beneath the white foam, the passengers screamed in terror. Nasruddin dropped his oars, stripped off his heavy coat, and turned to the trembling professor, who was clutching his parchment scrolls with white knuckles. "Professor," shouted Nasruddin above the roar of the water, "have you ever in your life studied the practical science of swimming?" "No, alas, heavens preserve me, never!" shrieked the petrified grammarian. "Then, my dear professor," shouted Nasruddin as he dove gracefully into the river, "your whole life has been completely wasted, for this boat is going straight to the bottom!"
moral: Academic arrogance is useless when the river of reality rises; practical skill saves life.

title: The Hot Soup and Cold Winter

full_text:
The village elders bet Nasruddin that he could not spend an entire freezing winter night on the snowy mountain peak without a fire, coat, or blanket. If he survived, they would buy him a grand feast.

Nasruddin accepted the wager, stood on the freezing summit all night, and survived by watching a tiny candle flame flickering in a farmhouse window a mile away.

The next morning, the greedy elders refused to pay: "You warmed yourself by the candle light a mile away! You lost the bet!"

Nasruddin said nothing. He invited them to dinner that evening. The guests arrived hungry, but after two hours, no food appeared. Looking into the kitchen, they saw Nasruddin holding a giant cauldron of soup suspended from the ceiling, with a tiny candle burning on the floor five feet below it!

"Mulla, are you crazy?" shouted the elders. "How can a candle five feet below boil a giant pot?"

"If a tiny candle a mile away could keep me warm through a winter blizzard," replied Nasruddin, "it can surely boil your soup in a few days! Sit down and wait!"

The ashamed elders apologized and paid the bet in full.
moral: Technical hair-splitting used to deny a fair reward deserves an equally absurd response.

summary: Mounting the pulpit on Friday, Nasruddin asked the congregation: "Do you know what I am going to speak about today?"...
full_text:
Mounting the pulpit on Friday, Nasruddin asked the congregation: "Do you know what I am going to speak about today?"

"No, Mulla!" replied the crowd.
"If you do not know, I have no desire to waste words on such ignorant people!" said Nasruddin, and he stepped down and went home.

The next Friday, he asked the same question. The people, determined not to be dismissed, replied: "Yes, Mulla, we know!"
"If you already know," said Nasruddin, "there is no need for me to tell you!" And he departed once more.

On the third Friday, the people agreed among themselves: half would answer "Yes" and half would answer "No."

Nasruddin asked: "Do you know what I am going to speak about?"
Half the congregation cried "Yes!" and half cried "No!"

Nasruddin beamed with delight: "Splendid! Then let those who know tell those who do not!" And he walked out into the sunshine.
moral: Teaching that relies on the community to enlighten one another achieves true harmony.

title: The Cat Ate the Meat
summary: Nasruddin bought three pounds of prime lamb at the bazaar, carried it home, and told his wife: "Prepare a rich meat stew for tonight; I have invited several honored friends."...
full_text:
Nasruddin bought three pounds of prime lamb at the bazaar, carried it home, and told his wife: "Prepare a rich meat stew for tonight; I have invited several honored friends."

While Nasruddin was at the mosque, his wife cooked the delicious stew, but could not resist tasting a piece. One piece led to another, and soon she and her gossiping neighbors had eaten every single scrap of the meat.

When Nasruddin returned with his hungry guests, his wife pretended to weep: "Alas, husband! A catastrophe! While I turned my back, your greedy black cat leaped onto the stove and ate all three pounds of lamb!"

Nasruddin did not raise his voice. He quietly picked up the black cat, carried it to the apothecary's shop next door, and placed it on the merchant's brass scale.

The weights balanced at exactly three pounds!

Nasruddin turned to his blushing wife with a serious frown: "My dear, if this three pounds of flesh on the scale is the cat—then where on earth is the meat? And if this is the meat—then where on earth is the cat?"
moral: Transparent lies crumble before the simplest test of logic.

title: Nasruddin's House is Too Small
summary: A poor peasant came to Nasruddin complaining: "Mulla, my house is a misery! I, my wife, our four children, and my mother-in-law live in a single tiny room. We are crowded, noisy, a...
full_text:
A poor peasant came to Nasruddin complaining: "Mulla, my house is a misery! I, my wife, our four children, and my mother-in-law live in a single tiny room. We are crowded, noisy, and at each other's throats. Help me!"

Nasruddin advised: "Bring your six chickens into the room to live with you."

The man was horrified, but trusted the Mulla. A week later, he returned weeping: "It is unbearable! Chickens are flapping in our faces!"

"Bring in your two goats," commanded Nasruddin. A week later: "Bring in your donkey and cow!"

The following week, the man returned in tears of madness: "I cannot live! The house is a roaring zoo of dung and noise!"

Nasruddin smiled calmly: "Now go home, take out the cow, take out the donkey, take out the goats, and take out the chickens!"

The man ran home, cleared the animals, and returned the next morning, beaming with joy: "Mulla, God bless you! Our house is so vast, quiet, and peaceful! We live in a royal palace!"
moral: True contentment is discovered by recognizing how much worse things could be.

title: The Itch
summary: Nasruddin was seen scratching his left arm furiously with both hands....
full_text:
On a sweltering summer afternoon in the bazaar of Akşehir, Mulla Nasruddin was seen sitting upon a wooden bench outside the spice shop, scratching his left arm with furious, desperate violence. Using both of his hands, he scraped his fingernails up and down his left sleeve from the elbow to the wrist, his teeth gritted in intense concentration, groaning softly with every scrape.

A passing friend, startled by the Mulla's frantic motions, stopped in his tracks and asked with concern: "Mulla! What on earth has happened to you? Did you get stung by a hornet, or brushed against a poison nettle? Why in heaven's name are you scratching your left arm with such ferocious violence?"

Nasruddin did not stop scratching for even a fraction of a second. Looking up with a sweat-streaked face, he panted: "Neither hornets nor nettles, my dear friend! title: The Empty House
summary: A traveler warned Nasruddin: "Mulla, your house has no locks, no iron bolts, and no guards! Anyone can walk in!"...
full_text:
A traveling merchant from Damascus who was passing through Akşehir stopped outside Mulla Nasruddin’s modest mud-brick cottage and was astonished by what he saw. The front door hung loosely on leather hinges without a bolt; the windows had no wooden shutters or iron grilles; and there was neither a watchdog in the yard nor a lock upon the gate.

The traveler knocked on the doorframe, where Nasruddin was sitting on a straw mat sipping warm water. "Mulla!" exclaimed the merchant with genuine alarm. "Are you mad to live in such a careless manner? Your house has no iron locks, no sturdy bolts, and no watchmen! A band of thieves could walk right in while you sleep and carry off everything you possess into the night!"

Nasruddin looked up from his cup and broke into a broad, cheerful grin. "Let them come, my dear traveler! Let them walk right in with all the crowbars and sacks they please!" chuckled the Mulla. "I have searched this house diligently with a lighted candle for twenty years, in every cupboard, corner, and floorboard, and I have never managed to find a single valuable thing myself! If a gang of hardworking burglars wants to spend all night searching through my empty jars, they will only wear themselves out; and if by some happy miracle they happen to bring a fresh loaf of bread and a wedge of cheese with them, I shall gladly get out of bed and share supper with them!" The traveler laughed heartily at the Mulla's carefree spirit, realizing that he who owns nothing possesses an invincible fortress against fear.
moral: An empty house has no fear of thieves; simplicity is an invincible fortress.

title: Nasruddin Tale 186: The Foreign Ambassador
summary: A foreign ambassador arrived who spoke only through signs. He drew a circle in the sand. Nasruddin drew a line across it. The ambassador held up three fingers; Nasruddin held up on...
full_text:
A foreign ambassador arrived who spoke only through signs. He drew a circle in the sand. Nasruddin drew a line across it. The ambassador held up three fingers; Nasruddin held up one. The ambassador held up an egg; Nasruddin held up an onion.

The ambassador bowed in deep awe: "Your scholar is a supreme genius! I showed him the earth; he showed me the equator! I showed him the three realms; he showed me divine unity! I showed him cosmic mystery; he showed me the layers of creation!"

After the envoy departed, the Sultan asked Nasruddin: "What did you say to him?"

Nasruddin laughed: "He showed me a round flatbread; I said I would cut it in half! He said he would eat three slices; I said I would eat the whole thing! Then he pulled out a boiled egg for lunch, and I showed him an onion to season it with!"
moral: Grand diplomatic gestures often conceal ordinary human appetites.

title: The Tinderbox
summary: A soldier came marching along the high road with his knapsack on his back and a sword at his side: left, right, left, right! He had been to the wars and was now returning home with...
full_text:
A soldier came marching along the high road with his knapsack on his back and a sword at his side: left, right, left, right! He had been to the wars and was now returning home with cheerful spirits, though his pockets were completely empty.

On the edge of the dark forest, he met an old witch. "Good evening, brave soldier!" croaked the witch. "How would you like to have as much gold and silver as your heart desires?"

The soldier halted and listened. The witch pointed to a giant hollow oak tree. "Climb to the top, and you will find an opening. Tie this rope around your waist, and I will lower you into the earth. At the bottom runs a great hall illuminated by three hundred burning lamps. You will pass three doors. Behind the first door sits a great chest guarded by a dog with eyes as large as teacups. Place my blue checked apron upon the floor, set the dog upon it, and take as many copper coppers as you please! Behind the second door sits a dog with eyes as large as mill-wheels; place him upon the apron, and take as much shining silver as you can carry! Behind the third door sits a monster of a dog with eyes as large as round towers; set him upon the apron, and you may fill your pockets with pure gold! In return, bring me only the old tinderbox my grandmother left behind."

The soldier boldly climbed the oak, descended into the hall, and filled his pockets, his boots, and his knapsack with gleaming gold from the third chest. Then he grabbed the old tinderbox and called out to be pulled up. When the witch refused to tell him why she desired the tinderbox above all the gold, a quarrel arose, and the soldier hurried away into the grand royal city.

Now wealthy, the soldier lived in splendor, bought fine clothes, and gave generously to the poor. But soon his gold was spent, and he moved to a dingy garret. In the darkness of the evening, remembering the tinderbox, he struck it once. Sparks flew, and instantly the dog with eyes as large as teacups appeared, barking: "What is my lord's command?"

"Bring me some money!" said the soldier. The dog darted off and returned with a heavy bag of copper. When he struck the box twice, the dog of silver appeared; when he struck it three times, the giant dog of gold arrived!

The soldier learned of the beautiful princess kept locked inside a copper castle because of a prophecy that she would marry a common soldier. Yearning to see her, he struck the box. The great dog brought the sleeping princess on its back through the midnight air. The soldier kissed her hand with tender reverence, and the dog carried her back safely.

When the queen discovered the visits by tying a bag of buckwheat with a small hole to the princess's waist, the soldier was arrested and sentenced to the gallows. But on the scaffold, the soldier asked one last wish: to smoke a final pipe of tobacco. He drew his tinderbox and struck it: once, twice, thrice!

All three enormous dogs leaped into the square, tossing the unjust judges and cruel guards into the air. The townsfolk cheered, rejoicing that an honest, generous soldier would be their king. The princess was released from her copper prison, and they were married amid seven days of joyous festivities, with the three marvelous dogs sitting at the royal banquet table, their huge eyes shining with delight.
moral: True fortune favors courage and presence of mind, but generosity toward others is what preserves genuine happiness.
