title: Paramartha Guru Tale 79
summary: While visiting the temple festival in Madurai, the five disciples stood near the tethered royal elephant, admiring its colossal limbs, br...
full_text:
While visiting the temple festival in Madurai, the five disciples stood near the tethered royal elephant, admiring its colossal limbs, broad ears, and long, flexible trunk.

Matti, who loved anatomical debate, asked: 'Brothers, is the trunk of an elephant a hand, an arm, a nose, or a fifth leg?'

Madayan expounded his Multi-Functional Organ Theory: 'According to Vedic zoology, the trunk is an elastic human arm grafted onto a pachyderm! Because it possesses finger-like lobes at the tip, it is capable of signing documents, picking flowers, and embracing friends!'

Peedan was fascinated: 'Can an elephant shake hands in friendship?'

'Of course!' declared Madayan. 'A handshake is the universal gesture of brotherhood! Matti, step forward and shake the elephant's hand!'

Matti approached the massive beast. Standing before the curling trunk, Matti smiled with courtly warmth, extended his right hand, and said: 'Greetings, noble pachyderm brother! I offer you the hand of friendship from Guru Paramartha's ashram!'

The elephant, however, had spent the morning eating ripe, sticky jaggery balls, and its trunk was coated in sweet sugar residue. Smelling salt on Matti's fingers and mistaking his hand for a sugarcane stalk, the elephant wrapped its powerful, muscular trunk around Matti's wrist, curled it tight, and lifted the terrified disciple four feet into the air!

Matti dangled above the ground, screaming in panic: 'AI-YO! HE SHAKES TOO HARD! HE HAS CAUGHT MY ARM IN AN IRON PYTHON!'

Madayan shouted instructions from a safe distance: 'Return the greeting, Matti! Squeeze back with brotherhood!'

Matti wept: 'I cannot squeeze back! He is lifting me toward his mouth!'

Peedan rushed forward and tried to tickle the elephant's knee; Asadan waved his palm leaf, and Mudan pulled Matti's legs!

Annoyed by the noisy crowd dangling from his trunk, the elephant casually swung his trunk sideways and hurled Matti across the temple yard!

Matti flew through the air and landed squarely in the middle of a vendor's cart loaded with soft, ripe, mushy jackfruits!

Yellow fruit pulp, sticky seeds, and sweet syrup exploded across Matti's face and clothes, cushioning his fall completely!

The five disciples rushed over, pulled Matti from the mush, and wiped fruit from his ears.

Madayan nodded with profound medical satisfaction: 'A magnificent diplomatic success! The elephant shook your hand, lifted you in honor, and deposited you in an abundance of sweet fruits!'

Spitting jackfruit seeds from his mouth, Matti groaned: 'Next time, Madayan, you may shake hands with the elephant's tail instead!'
moral: Mistaking a nose for a hand leads you into the giant's powerful grip.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 80
summary: The ashram was out of dried palm leaves, the customary material for inscribing sacred texts with an iron stylus.
full_text:
The ashram was out of dried palm leaves, the customary material for inscribing sacred texts with an iron stylus.

Guru Paramartha, inspired by a sudden flash of philosophical insight, summoned his scribe, Madayan: 'Madayan, an immortal thought has entered my mind regarding the transient nature of the cosmos! Fetch a stylus and record my words immediately before the inspiration evaporates!'

Madayan searched the shed, but no palm leaves remained.

The Guru became frantic: 'The thought is slipping from my memory! We must record it upon some receptive surface!'

Madayan pointed to the stone basin of clear water in the courtyard: 'Master! Water is the most receptive element in creation! It yields to the lightest touch without resistance! Inscribe your divine thought upon the water!'

The Guru agreed: 'A sublime idea! Fluid thoughts require a fluid medium!'

Madayan took a sharp iron stylus, dipped it into the water basin, and leaned over the surface.

The Guru began dictating: 'Chapter One: The Universe is an Illusion born of Maya...'

Madayan moved the iron point through the water with intense, rapid strokes: writing letters, words, and flourishes upon the surface!

The stylus churned the water, creating tiny ripples that smoothed out into flat calm the instant the point moved on.

Madayan wrote for forty-five minutes, sweating with scholarly zeal, filling 'six pages of water' with the Guru's discourse.

At last, the Guru paused: 'Now, Madayan, read back what you have inscribed, so that I may verify the syntax!'

Madayan looked down into the water basin.

The water was crystal clear, flat as glass, reflecting only Madayan's own sweating forehead. Not a single letter, mark, or scratch remained visible!

Madayan stared in dismay: 'Master! The ink has vanished! The letters have dissolved!'

Peedan examined the basin: 'Did you use indelible water-ink, Madayan?'

Madayan delivered his profound metaphysical evaluation: 'The water was so profoundly enlightened by the Master's discourse that it internalized the philosophy into its molecular essence! The words are no longer on the surface; they have achieved liberation in the depths!'

The Guru nodded in awe: 'Drink the water, disciples, and absorb the philosophy directly into your bloodstreams!'

The five disciples dipped brass cups into the basin, drank the water with reverent gulps, and sat on the veranda, feeling intensely enlightened.
moral: Inscribing records upon flowing water ensures that history vanishes with the current.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 81
summary: On a scorching summer day, when the sun reached its absolute zenith in the heavens, Guru Paramartha and his disciples were traveling acro...
full_text:
On a scorching summer day, when the sun reached its absolute zenith in the heavens, Guru Paramartha and his disciples were traveling across an open, treeless plain with their faithful gray donkey.

The heat was oppressive, and the sun beat straight down from the middle of the sky.

Matti happened to look beneath the donkey's belly. Because the sun was directly overhead, the donkey's shadow was compressed into a tiny, four-inch patch directly beneath its hooves, completely hidden by its body!

Matti shrieked in horror: 'MASTER! A DEMONIC CALAMITY! OUR NOBLE DONKEY HAS LOST HIS SHADOW!'

The Guru and disciples halted. They walked around the beast: from the left, no shadow; from the right, no shadow; from behind, no shadow!

Madayan turned pale with astrological dread: 'In occult treatises, when a living creature loses its shadow, it signifies that its soul has been stolen by the Lord of Death! Within three hours, the beast will turn into a zombie and bite our throats!'

The Guru was terrified: 'How can the shadow be restored to its rightful owner?'

Madayan expounded his Shadow Reattachment Ceremony: 'We must supply the beast with an artificial shadow until his natural shadow returns from the other world! We will drape five black woolen blankets over his back, tie them beneath his belly, and hang black umbrellas from his ears!'

The disciples draped five heavy, suffocating black horse blankets over the poor donkey, tied them with ropes, and opened two black umbrellas, tying them to the animal's halter.

The temperature beneath the five black blankets under the blazing noon sun reached boiling point!

The suffocating, sweating donkey stood for three minutes, his eyes rolling in frantic distress.

Then, with an enraged, desperate bray of rebellion, the beast kicked out with all four hooves, bucked like a mad bull, threw off the black blankets, trampled the umbrellas to splinters, and bolted across the plain toward a shady banyan tree half a mile away!

Standing beneath the spreading banyan boughs, where cool shade covered the earth, the donkey stopped, panting contentedly.

The disciples ran across the field, arriving out of breath.

Looking beneath the tree, Matti saw a massive, cool, dark shadow spreading twenty yards around the beast!

Matti cheered in ecstatic triumph: 'A MIRACLE! THE SHADOW HAS RETURNED! AND IT HAS GROWN TWENTY TIMES LARGER THAN BEFORE!'

Guru Paramartha stroked the donkey's nose with deep reverence: 'Our blankets have cured his soul; behold the magnificent expansion of his shadow!'
moral: Looking for an animal's shadow at high noon makes you believe the beast has lost its soul.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 82
summary: A clay cooking pot containing black bean soup had burnt on the kitchen hearth, and the dried bean crust was stuck like rock-hard cement t...
full_text:
A clay cooking pot containing black bean soup had burnt on the kitchen hearth, and the dried bean crust was stuck like rock-hard cement to the bottom of the pot.

Matti tried to scrape it with a wooden stick, but the wood splintered.

Guru Paramartha remembered his sole family heirloom: an antique, delicate silver spoon with a carved peacock handle, inherited from his grandfather.

The Guru handed the spoon to Matti: 'Take this solid silver instrument, Matti; its metal is noble and unyielding! Scrape the burnt crust from the clay pot!'

Matti took the delicate silver spoon, placed the tip beneath the rock-hard burnt crust, and applied his full weight to the handle to pry the crust loose!

The fragile, soft silver of the antique spoon bent like a banana!

Matti pressed harder: with a sharp SNAP!, the carved peacock handle sheared off, and the silver bowl broke in two!

Matti wailed: 'The silver spoon has broken! Our Master's heirloom is ruined!'

Madayan examined the broken silver pieces and the cheap, two-copper clay pot:

'Grieve not, Matti! The problem is purely mechanical! The silver was too soft for the task! To repair the silver spoon, we must fuse the metal together with the burnt bean crust!'

Madayan placed the broken silver pieces back into the clay pot, added water, and boiled the pot over a roaring fire for two hours, believing the silver would melt and weld itself!

Under the intense heat of the dry hearth, the cheap earthen pot cracked, broke in two, and dumped boiling water, bean sludge, and the broken silver spoon into the burning coals!

When the ashes were sifted, they retrieved two twisted, blackened, melted lumps of silver and a heap of broken clay sherds.

Guru Paramartha surveyed the wreckage with philosophical detachment: 'We have learned today that silver and clay possess incompatible karmic destinies; let us eat boiled bananas henceforth!'
moral: Using a delicate silver spoon as a pry bar breaks the silver to save the mud.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 83
summary: Winter approached, and Guru Paramartha purchased an enormous cartload of dried tamarind firewood for five silver rupees, stacking it neat...
full_text:
Winter approached, and Guru Paramartha purchased an enormous cartload of dried tamarind firewood for five silver rupees, stacking it neatly in the backyard to last through the rainy season.

Hearing that village thieves were stealing firewood by night, the Guru assigned Asadan and Mudan to guard the woodpile: 'Watch this firewood with your lives! Do not let a single stick be taken by cold thieves!'

The two disciples stood sentry beside the woodpile, armed with bamboo sticks.

By two o'clock in the morning, a freezing northern wind swept across the plain. The temperature dropped, and a heavy frost coated the grass.

Asadan's teeth chattered: 'Mudan! I am freezing to death! My fingers are numb, and my feet have turned to ice! If we freeze, who will guard the firewood?'

Mudan shivered: 'True, brother! A dead guard cannot protect property! We must warm ourselves!'

Asadan looked at the colossal stack of dry tamarind wood beside them: 'Look! Here are fifty bundles of dry firewood! Why should we freeze when warmth is at our fingertips? Let us pull out ten sticks and light a small, comforting campfire!'

They pulled ten thick logs from the pile, lit them with an ember, and warmed their frozen hands over the cheerful blaze.

After an hour, the fire burned low.

'Add five more logs!' said Mudan.

By four o'clock, the wind grew fiercer. 'Add ten more logs!' said Asadan.

To maintain their 'vigilant warmth,' the two disciples continuously fed logs from the pile into their roaring campfire. Log after log, bundle after bundle was thrown onto the blaze!

By sunrise, the two guards were sitting before a magnificent, roaring mountain of glowing embers, warm, comfortable, and sweating pleasantly!

Guru Paramartha walked into the backyard to inspect the woodpile.

He stopped in utter disbelief.

The colossal cartload of tamarind firewood was completely gone! In its place sat a mountain of white ashes, while Asadan and Mudan sat happily toasting sweet potatoes over the coals!

'WHERE IS MY FIREWOOD?' roared the Guru.

Asadan smiled with triumphant fidelity: 'Master, rejoice! Not a single stick was stolen by thieves! We burned every single log ourselves to keep warm so we could guard the pile with vigilance!'

The Guru dropped his staff, clutched his temples, and wept for his five silver rupees, while Madayan praised the guards' unshakeable devotion to duty.
moral: Burning the firewood to keep warm while guarding the wood leaves an empty stack at dawn.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 84
summary: A wandering beggar with matted hair told Matti a secret legend: 'In the royal orchard grows an ancient tree that produces the Amrita-Phal...
full_text:
A wandering beggar with matted hair told Matti a secret legend: 'In the royal orchard grows an ancient tree that produces the Amrita-Phala—The Mango of Immortality! Whoever eats of it shall never grow old, nor suffer disease, nor die!'

Matti's heart burned with devotion: 'I must secure this fruit for our beloved Guru!'

Matti crept into the royal orchard at dusk. Beneath an old, gnarled tree, he found a solitary mango lying in the mud. It was black, shriveled, covered in white mold, and smelled of fermenting vinegar—having fallen from the tree weeks earlier and rotted in the ditch.

Matti picked it up with awe: 'Notice its ancient, blackened rind! Only a fruit of extreme antiquity could possess such concentrated spiritual potency!'

Matti wrapped the rotten mango in a clean silk handkerchief and carried it to the ashram.

Presenting it to Guru Paramartha, Matti proclaimed: 'Master! I have secured the Amrita-Phala! Eat this sacred fruit, and you shall live for ten thousand years!'

The Guru unwrapped the silk. A foul, sour stench of rotting fruit filled the room. The mango was soft, black, and leaking brown liquid.

The Guru hesitated: 'Matti... it smells remarkably decayed!'

Madayan intervened with philosophical authority: 'True immortality transcends conventional olfactory aesthetics! To the mortal nose, the nectar of liberation appears rotten, because mortality cannot comprehend eternal life! Eat it with faith, Master!'

The Guru held his nose, opened his mouth, and swallowed a large bite of the rotten, fermenting fruit!

The foul, acidic slime hit his stomach like poison!

Within ten minutes, Guru Paramartha turned pale green. Violent, explosive stomach cramps seized his belly; he dropped to the floor, rolling in agony, vomiting and clutching his abdomen!

The disciples panicked: 'THE NECTAR IS EXPELING HIS MORTALITY WITH VIOLENCE!'

The village physician was summoned in haste. The physician administered castor oil, bitter ginger decoctions, and salt water, purging the Guru's stomach until midnight.

Lying pale and exhausted upon his cot, Guru Paramartha whispered in a weak, trembling voice: 'Matti...'

'Yes, Master?' wept Matti.

'If you ever bring me another fruit of immortality,' wheezed the Guru, 'I will feed it to you first, and watch you live for ten thousand years from my veranda!'
moral: Chasing a mythical fruit of immortality leads you to eat rotten fruit from the ditch.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 85
summary: Guru Paramartha woke with a stiff neck and a slight cough.
full_text:
Guru Paramartha woke with a stiff neck and a slight cough.

Madayan, eager to demonstrate his medical knowledge, declared: 'A stiff neck is caused by trapped vata wind in the cervical vertebrae! To dissolve the wind, we must apply the Fiery Mustard-Chili Thermal Poultice!'

Madayan pounded ten fiery red chilies, two ounces of black mustard seeds, four cloves of garlic, and raw ginger into a thick, crimson, burning paste.

He smeared the burning paste thickly across Guru Paramartha's neck and shoulders, wrapping it tightly with a hot wool scarf.

Within sixty seconds, the fiery capsaicin penetrated the Guru's pores!

A sensation of scorching, blistering, unbearable fire erupted across the Guru's neck!

He shrieked, tearing at the scarf: 'AI-YO! REMOVE IT! I AM BURNING! SKIN ME ALIVE!'

Madayan held his hands: 'Endure, Master! The fire of disease is fighting the fire of medicine!'

The Guru broke free, dashed into the courtyard, and threw himself into the stone water trough, splashing cold water over his burning neck!

The paste washed off, leaving his neck bright crimson, blistered, and swollen!

The Guru sat in the trough, his teeth chattering from the cold water, his neck burning like fire, glaring at his disciples.

Madayan remarked with scholarly satisfaction: 'Notice, Master: you have completely forgotten your stiff neck! You are moving your head with remarkable agility in the water! The poultice has succeeded!'

The Guru splashed a bucket of water into Madayan's face, concluding his medical treatment for the day.
moral: Applying fiery paste to sensitive skin cures nothing and sets the patient ablaze.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 86
summary: Another wandering fortune-teller arrived at the ashram, wearing rings on every finger, boasting that he could find hidden underground wat...
full_text:
Another wandering fortune-teller arrived at the ashram, wearing rings on every finger, boasting that he could find hidden underground water, buried gold, and lost cattle through divine divination.

While eating lunch on the veranda, the astrologer removed a heavy brass ring set with a red glass stone and placed it on the windowsill.

When lunch ended, the ring was gone.

The astrologer turned upon the disciples: 'One of you has stolen my magical gemstone ring! Confess, or I will curse your ashram with barrenness!'

The Guru was distressed: 'No disciple of mine is a thief! But you are a diviner of hidden treasures; use your astrological arts to locate your ring!'

The astrologer drew circles in the dirt with a stick, muttered charms, and pointed to Matti: 'The planets reveal that the ring is hidden inside this disciple's waistcloth!'

Matti was stripped and searched: no ring was found.

The astrologer pointed to Peedan: 'It is inside his sandals!'

The sandals were shaken: no ring was found.

The astrologer pointed to the ashram well: 'It has been thrown into the deep water!'

Matti was preparing to dive into the cold well with a rope, when the ashram cat jumped down from the windowsill. Beneath the cat's tail, wedged between two books on the shelf, the brass ring gleamed in the sunlight!

The cat had merely pushed it behind a manuscript while chasing a moth!

Guru Paramartha picked up the ring and handed it to the astrologer:

'Here is your ring, O seer of the cosmos! It was on the windowsill where you left it! If your stars could not distinguish between a cat's tail and my disciple's waistcloth, your divination is as hollow as an empty coconut!'

The embarrassed astrologer pocketed his ring and hurried away without his lunch.
moral: A charlatan who claims to see the stars cannot locate his own ring under his nose.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 87
summary: During the annual cattle fair in Madurai, a race was announced with a grand prize of fifty silver rupees for the fastest domestic beast.
full_text:
During the annual cattle fair in Madurai, a race was announced with a grand prize of fifty silver rupees for the fastest domestic beast.

Guru Paramartha and his disciples entered their gentle white cow, Kamadhenu.

'Our cow,' declared the Guru, 'is nourished on sacred mantras! Her spiritual energy will outstrip the swiftest steeds!'

On the day of the race, thoroughbred horses, swift bullocks, and racing camels lined up at the starting rope.

In the middle of the line stood Kamadhenu, chewing her cud peacefully, with a garland of marigolds around her horns, while Matti sat upon her back holding a bamboo switch.

The starter beat the drum: BOOM! 'GO!'

The horses galloped like the wind; the racing bullocks thundered down the track, kicking up clouds of dust!

Kamadhenu did not gallop; she did not trot.

She took three slow, dignified strides forward, stopped in the middle of the track, lowered her head, and began peacefully grazing on a patch of lush green clover growing beside the fence!

Matti shouted: 'GALLOP, KAMADHENU! FOR THE HONOR OF PHILOSOPHY, RUN!'

He tapped her with the switch.

The cow swished her tail, blinked her gentle brown eyes, and continued chewing her clover with rhythmic contentment.

The crowd in the grandstand roared with laughter!

The horses crossed the finish line half a mile away, while Kamadhenu finished her patch of clover, lay down on the track, and fell asleep in the warm sun!

Matti walked back to the Guru: 'Master, she refused to run!'

Guru Paramartha smiled with sublime philosophical detachment: 'Kamadhenu demonstrated the supreme wisdom of Non-Attachment! While worldly horses exhausted their breath for fifty perishable silver coins, our cow chose peace, clover, and meditation! She is the true spiritual victor of the race!'

The disciples bowed in awe of their cow's enlightenment.
moral: Attempting to race a placid milk cow against horses earns only laughter from the stands.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 88
summary: A bowl of fragrant, sweet ghee had been churned, and Guru Paramartha wished to protect it from stray mice.
full_text:
A bowl of fragrant, sweet ghee had been churned, and Guru Paramartha wished to protect it from stray mice.

Madayan devised an organic security system: 'Mice are terrified of stinging red ants! If we smear the outside of the bowl with honey, a protective guard of five hundred red ants will encircle the rim and bite any mouse that approaches!'

Matti smeared the outside of the bowl with honey and placed it near an anthill.

Within twenty minutes, five thousand red ants swarmed over the bowl.

They did not stay on the outside; they marched over the rim, plunged directly into the sweet, warm ghee, and formed a solid, dark, writhing layer of drowned ants upon the golden surface!

When the Guru came to eat his evening bread, the ghee was black with dead ants!

Matti reported proudly: 'Master, the defensive perimeter was established with complete success! Not a single mouse touched the bowl!'

The Guru looked at the bowl of black ants: 'Indeed, Matti; but how are we to eat the ghee?'

Madayan suggested: 'Filter the ghee through your teeth, Master! Teeth are the natural sieves of the body!'

The Guru dumped the bowl into the garden, fed the ants to the chickens, and dined on dry rice.
moral: Protecting your butter by inviting insects leaves you with butter full of ants.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 89
summary: The village temple needed to hoist a fifty-foot cedar flagpole into its stone socket. The heavy hemp ropes had rotted, and the elders deb...
full_text:
The village temple needed to hoist a fifty-foot cedar flagpole into its stone socket. The heavy hemp ropes had rotted, and the elders debated how to lift the timber.

Guru Paramartha offered the services of his disciples: 'A heavy rope is clumsy; modern engineering uses fine, multi-filament tensile cords!'

Madayan purchased fifty spools of thin cotton sewing thread from the village tailor. He twisted the threads together into a thin string: 'This composite cord possesses infinite tensile cohesion!'

They tied the thin cotton string around the fifty-foot cedar flagpole.

Matti, Peedan, Asadan, and Mudan gripped the string and heaved: 'ONE, TWO, THREE, PULL!'

The thin cotton thread snapped with a soft ping!

The four disciples tumbled backward into the temple ditch, landing in a pile of mud, while the heavy cedar flagpole rolled sideways, crushing the village council's wicker chairs!

The village headman shouted: 'Get out of here with your sewing thread, you fools!'

Guru Paramartha remarked with dignity: 'The thread was flawless, but the cedar was unspiritually heavy!'
moral: Hoisting a heavy timber with cotton thread snaps the cord and flattens the crew.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 90
summary: Following a heavy rain, the ashram courtyard was covered in deep, sticky red mud.
full_text:
Following a heavy rain, the ashram courtyard was covered in deep, sticky red mud.

Guru Paramartha wished to walk to the study hall, but refused to soil his sandals.

Madayan summoned the disciples: 'We must accelerate the evaporation of the moisture! Fetch five large palm-leaf hand fans!'

The five disciples knelt in the deep mud, fanning the wet earth with all their might: FLAP, FLAP, FLAP!

The vigorous fanning created violent gusts of air. The air did not dry the mud; instead, it picked up droplets of wet red slime and sprayed them across their faces, eyes, and white shawls!

Within ten minutes, all five disciples were coated in red mud like clay statues!

Guru Paramartha peered from the veranda: 'Is the earth dry, my children?'

Matti wiped mud from his nose: 'The earth remains moist, Master, but our faces have absorbed the mud completely!'

The Guru sighed, stepped onto wooden planks laid by the washerman, and walked across, leaving his fanners to wash in the pond.
moral: Fanning wet mud with palm leaves only spatters your own face with slime.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 91
summary: A rumor spread that a wild leopard had been seen in the forest outskirts.
full_text:
A rumor spread that a wild leopard had been seen in the forest outskirts.

Guru Paramartha instructed Peedan: 'Predators are terrified of sacred sounds! If you hear a rustle in the bushes tonight, beat the brass gong with all your might!'

At midnight, a stray goat rustled in the garden bushes.

Peedan seized the brass gong and an iron rod, beating it like thunder: CLANG! CLANG! CLANG!

The deafening noise awakened the entire village. It also awakened the local watchdogs, who began barking in chorus.

The real leopard, resting peacefully in the forest three miles away, was intrigued by the commotion. Attracted by the noise, the predator walked into the village to investigate!

Seeing the spotted beast stroll past the gate, Peedan dropped his gong, dove beneath his cot, and prayed: 'The gong was too melodious; it invited the guest instead of driving him away!'

The leopard caught a chicken from the coop and trotted back to the hills.

The Guru concluded: 'Next time, Peedan, we shall use silent meditation; it has fewer acoustic repercussions.'
moral: Ringing bells to frighten predators only summons them to the feast.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 92
summary: A wandering trickster sold Mudan a small, dried coconut for two silver coins, whispering: 'This is the Saraswati-Phala! Inscribe the alph...
full_text:
A wandering trickster sold Mudan a small, dried coconut for two silver coins, whispering: 'This is the Saraswati-Phala! Inscribe the alphabet upon the shell, grind it to powder, and drink it with milk; all the wisdom of the Vedas will instantly enter your brain!'

Mudan bought the coconut, ground the rock-hard shell into coarse, jagged brown gravel, and stirred it into a glass of hot milk.

He swallowed the mixture in three gulps!

Within an hour, the sharp, jagged coconut shell fragments began tearing through his stomach and intestines!

Mudan rolled on the floor, groaning in agony: 'MY STOMACH! THE VEDAS ARE BATTERING MY RIBS!'

The village physician administered purgatives and herbal oils, saving the fool's life.

When Mudan recovered, the Guru questioned him: 'Mudan, did the sacred knowledge manifest in your understanding?'

Mudan groaned: 'Master, I learned only one great truth: coconut shells belong on trees, not in bellies!'

The Guru nodded: 'A profound realization; knowledge has indeed commenced.'
moral: Swallowing coconut shells will not plant wisdom in an empty head.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 93
summary: Guru Paramartha had a pair of tall wooden padukas crafted, resting upon wooden pegs six inches high, designed to keep his feet above ordi...
full_text:
Guru Paramartha had a pair of tall wooden padukas crafted, resting upon wooden pegs six inches high, designed to keep his feet above ordinary puddles.

One rainy morning, he set out to inspect the vegetable garden, proudly walking upon his six-inch stilts.

He reached the garden. The soil was deep, clayey, sticky swamp mud.

The Guru took one stately step into the mud.

The thin wooden pegs sank straight down into the clay like nails driven into butter!

The Guru tried to lift his foot: the vacuum of the sticky mud held the wooden pegs fast! He pulled; his foot slipped out of the strap, and the Guru plunged knee-deep into the cold red mud!

There stood the venerable preceptor: one bare foot deep in the mire, the other perched upon a stilt, wobbling like a crane in a hurricane!

'MATTI! PEEDAN! EXTRACT ME!' roared the Guru.

Matti pulled the Guru's left arm; Peedan pulled his right. Under their combined heave, the Guru was pulled free, leaving both six-inch wooden shoes buried permanently beneath three feet of garden clay!

Carried to the veranda on his disciples' shoulders, the Guru proclaimed: 'The six-inch stilts were magnificent in theory; but the garden clay possessed an unauthorized depth!'
moral: Wearing tall wooden clogs into deep swamp mud turns the walker into a stationary statue.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 94
summary: A visiting assembly of ten visiting scholars from Kanchipuram arrived at the ashram at noon.
full_text:
A visiting assembly of ten visiting scholars from Kanchipuram arrived at the ashram at noon.

Guru Paramartha wished to display supreme Ayurvedic hospitality.

Madayan suggested: 'Bitter gourd is the king of purifying vegetables! We shall prepare a nine-course banquet consisting entirely of bitter gourd: bitter gourd soup, fried bitter gourd, boiled bitter gourd with neem, bitter gourd chutney, and bitter gourd pudding!'

The feast was served on clean banana leaves.

The ten visiting scholars took their seats, smiled, and dipped their fingers into the first course: bitter gourd soup.

The overwhelming, eye-watering, throat-searing bitterness struck their palates!

One scholar gagged; another turned pale; a third spit his mouthful into his palm!

They tried the fried gourd: more bitterness! They tried the chutney: pure gall!

The chief visiting scholar rose from his mat, his face pale: 'Guru Paramartha! Did we come to a hermitage or a poison refinery? We asked for lunch, not a therapeutic execution!'

The ten scholars marched out of the ashram, leaving their half-eaten banana leaves behind.

Guru Paramartha sat down and tasted the soup: 'PHTHOO! Madayan, this is vile!'

Madayan sighed: 'Scholars of Kanchipuram lack spiritual endurance; let us give the soup to the village goats!'

Even the goats sniffed the bitter gourd and walked away in disgust.
moral: Serving pure bitterness under the guise of medicinal hospitality clears the room of guests.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 95
summary: A rogue who had stolen a white cow from a neighboring village wished to hide her from the police. Knowing the reputation of Guru Paramart...
full_text:
A rogue who had stolen a white cow from a neighboring village wished to hide her from the police. Knowing the reputation of Guru Paramartha's ashram for gullibility, the rogue brought the cow to the gate, painted her completely green with dye, and told Matti: 'This is a rare Himalayan Emerald Cow! She yields green pistachio milk! I sell her for five rupees!'

Matti ran to the Guru, who purchased the green cow in delight.

They led the green cow to the shed.

Next morning, Matti took a brass bucket and milked the green beast.

The milk poured into the pail: white, pure, ordinary cow's milk!

Matti reported in bewilderment: 'Master! The cow is emerald green, but her milk is ordinary white!'

Madayan explained: 'The green pigment has not yet penetrated the mammary glands! We must feed her green parrot feathers and crushed grass for seven days!'

At that moment, the real owner arrived with the village police.

The police officer threw a bucket of warm water over the cow: the green dye washed off, revealing the stolen white cow!

The rogue was arrested, and the Guru lost his five rupees.

Guru Paramartha noted in his diary: 'Note: Green cows are susceptible to moisture; verify authenticity before milking.'
moral: Painting a stolen cow green does not change the flavor of her milk.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 96
summary: Visiting the seashore at Mahabalipuram, Guru Paramartha looked upon the rolling, foamy waves of the Bay of Bengal.
full_text:
Visiting the seashore at Mahabalipuram, Guru Paramartha looked upon the rolling, foamy waves of the Bay of Bengal.

The Guru mused: 'How many waves strike this shore between sunrise and sunset? If we calculate the waves, we can deduce the pulse of the cosmic ocean!'

Matti and Madayan volunteered to count the waves.

They stood at the water's edge, holding bamboo sticks, and began counting aloud as each wave broke upon the sand:

'One... two... three... forty-seven... eighty-eight...'

A large breaker surged forward, soaked their dhotis to the waist, and broke into three separate foaming surges!

Matti argued: 'Was that one large wave, or three small waves?'

Madayan declared: 'It was a composite triad wave! Count it as two and a half!'

Then an enormous roller crashed over their heads, knocking both disciples onto the sand, tumbling them into the foam, and washing away their measuring sticks!

Sputtering salt water, Matti climbed out: 'The ocean is cheating! It sent a rogue wave to wipe out our calculations!'

By sunset, they had arrived at forty thousand, two hundred, and six waves, with three lost in the foam.

The Guru accepted the report: 'A satisfactory census; the ocean may now retire for the night!'
moral: Counting the rolling waves of the ocean leaves you wet, weary, and none the wiser.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 97

full_text:
A cunning village merchant owned a small tea stall next to a magnificent, sprawling banyan tree that cast an enormous, cool shadow across the road.

The merchant told Guru Paramartha: 'Master, the land belongs to the village, but the shade of this banyan tree belongs to me! If you wish your disciples to rest in my shadow, you must pay me two silver rupees rent!'

The Guru paid the two silver rupees, and the disciples sat peacefully in the cool shade.

As the sun moved across the sky, the banyan shadow shifted toward the east, leaving the disciples sitting in the blazing, scorching sun!

Matti ran to the merchant: 'Merchant! We paid for the shade, but the shade has moved across the ditch into your tea garden!'

The merchant smiled: 'You purchased the shadow at ten o'clock, not the afternoon shadow! Pay two more rupees for the moving shade!'

The Guru was about to pay, when a passing lawyer intervened:

'If you own the shadow, merchant, then your shadow has trespassed onto the public highway and damaged the holy men's comfort! Pay them four rupees damages for trespassing shade!'

Terrified of a lawsuit, the merchant returned the Guru's two rupees and offered free tea.

The Guru praised the lawyer: 'Legal dialectic is almost as potent as Vedic philosophy!'
moral: Purchasing a moving shadow leaves you standing in the hot sun by afternoon.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 98
summary: A night burglar entered the ashram kitchen, stole two brass pots, but in his haste to squeeze through the window, his red cotton turban c...
full_text:
A night burglar entered the ashram kitchen, stole two brass pots, but in his haste to squeeze through the window, his red cotton turban caught on an iron nail and remained hanging on the sill.

Next morning, Matti found the red turban: 'Master! The thief escaped, but his headpiece was captured!'

Guru Paramartha convened a court on the veranda.

The red turban was placed upon a wooden stool.

Madayan addressed the turban: 'Accused Turban! You were caught at the scene of the burglary! Where are the two stolen brass pots?'

The turban remained motionless.

'Contempt of court!' roared the Guru. 'Sentence the accused to twenty lashes of the cane!'

The disciples beat the red turban with bamboo switches until it was frayed to threads.

Then, Guru Paramartha sentenced the turban to imprisonment: 'Lock the turban in the iron trunk for seven years!'

They locked the battered turban in the chest, proud of their swift justice, while the real thief sold the two brass pots in the next village for four rupees.
moral: Arresting a turban for a burglary lets the thief walk away with the loot.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 99
summary: Reaching a broad river during their travels, the ferryman demanded six copper coins to row the Guru and his five disciples across: one co...
full_text:
Reaching a broad river during their travels, the ferryman demanded six copper coins to row the Guru and his five disciples across: one copper per head.

The Guru opened his purse: he possessed exactly five copper coins and one silver rupee.

The Guru refused to break the silver rupee: 'The fee is six coppers! We have five! Ferryman, row five of us across, and let Matti swim!'

Matti was terrified of water: 'Master! The river has crocodiles!'

Madayan negotiated: 'Ferryman! What is the theological value of one copper coin? It is a fleeting worldly illusion! Accept five coppers and ferry all six in honor of philosophy!'

The ferryman refused: 'No six coppers, no ferry!'

The disciples spent four hours on the bank debating the ethics of transportation. They missed their banquet, their robes were soaked in the rain, and night fell.

Finally, hungry, cold, and exhausted, the Guru broke his silver rupee, paid the six coppers, and gave the ferryman a tip of two more coppers!

Madayan observed: 'We preserved our philosophical integrity for four hours at a cost of only three coppers per hour!'
moral: Spending ten rupees on philosophical arguments to save one copper coin is expensive economy.

title: Paramartha Guru Tale 100
summary: After decades of extraordinary philosophical misadventures, having crossed sleeping rivers on all fours, rescued the moon from the well, ...
full_text:
After decades of extraordinary philosophical misadventures, having crossed sleeping rivers on all fours, rescued the moon from the well, roasted in the steam blanket, and painted elephants emerald green, Guru Paramartha celebrated his seventieth birthday in the ashram.

The village elders, the headman, the blacksmith, the barber, the tailor, and hundreds of peasants from twenty neighboring villages crowded into the courtyard, laden with gifts of flowers, fruits, and sweets.

The village headman presented the Guru with a magnificent, carved sandalwood staff, speaking with heartfelt warmth:

'Venerable Guru Paramartha! Your logic has often defied mathematics, your physics has astonished the blacksmiths, and your disciples have confounded the astrologers. Yet in all these years, your ashram has never harbored malice, greed, cruelty, or deceit. You have brought laughter, innocence, and wonder to our lives, reminding us that pompous arrogance is the true folly of the world, while a gentle, humble heart is the greatest wisdom.'

Guru Paramartha stroked his silver beard, his eyes shining with tears of genuine joy.

Turning to his five faithful disciples—Matti, Madayan, Peedan, Asadan, and Mudan—who stood proudly beside him, the Guru smiled with fatherly love:

'My faithful children! We have explored the cosmos, tested the laws of nature, and survived our own experiments! Let the world laugh at our philosophy; for he who can laugh at himself walks with the gods in eternal joy!'

The disciples cheered: 'HAIL GURU PARAMARTHA! OCEAN OF WISDOM AND FATHER OF JOY!'

And the entire village joined in a magnificent feast of sweet pongal and golden laddoos, celebrating the timeless, immortal laughter of Guru Paramartha and his five beloved disciples.
moral: Laughter and innocence outlive all pretentious pomp; true affection forgives a lifetime of folly.

title: Cinderella (Aschenputtel)
summary: The wife of a rich man fell mortally ill. Calling her only daughter to her bedside, she whispered: "Dear child, remain pious and good, and heaven will always protect you; I shall l...
full_text:
The wife of a rich man fell mortally ill. Calling her only daughter to her bedside, she whispered: "Dear child, remain pious and good, and heaven will always protect you; I shall look down upon you from above." Then she closed her eyes in peace.

When winter came, snow covered the mother's grave like a white cloth. When the spring sun melted it, the man took another wife. The stepmother brought two daughters into the house, who were fair of face but vile and black of heart.

They took away the girl's fine clothes, dressed her in an old gray smock, gave her wooden clogs, and forced her into the kitchen. From dawn till dusk, she carried heavy water buckets, lit fires, cooked, and washed. In the evening, having no bed, she had to lie in the hearth ashes, so that she was always dusty and dirty; and therefore they called her Aschenputtel (Cinderella).

When the father went to the fair, he asked the two stepdaughters what gifts he should bring them. The eldest demanded pearls and diamonds; the second wanted fine silks. But Cinderella said: "Father, break off the first twig that strikes against your hat on your way home, and bring it to me."

The father brought her a hazel twig. Cinderella carried it to her mother's grave, planted it in the soil, and wept over it so bitterly that her tears watered the twig. It grew into a magnificent hazel tree. Three times a day, Cinderella went to sit beneath it, weeping and praying; and each time, a gentle white bird flew into the branches, granting whatever wish she whispered from her heart.

The king proclaimed a grand three-day festival, inviting all the maidens in the realm so the prince might choose a bride. The two stepsisters dressed in embroidered velvet, while the cruel stepmother threw a dish of lentils into the hearth ashes, saying: "If you pick these clean in two hours, you may go!"

Cinderella went to the garden door and called:
"You tame pigeons, you turtledoves, and all you birds under heaven,
The good into the pot, the bad into the crop!"

Flocks of white doves swooped down, picking out every good lentil within an hour. But the stepmother laughed mockingly: "You have no dress, you cannot dance, and you would only bring shame upon us!" And she departed with her daughters.

Cinderella ran to her mother's grave beneath the hazel tree and called:
"Shiver and shake, dear little tree,
Throw gold and silver down upon me!"

The white bird threw down a dazzling robe of pure spun gold and silver, and slippers of silk and silver! Cinderella entered the palace, and the prince took her by the hand, dancing with no other maiden all evening. At nightfall, she slipped away like a deer and returned to her ashes.

On the third evening, the bird gave her a dress radiant as the sun, with slippers of solid gold. When she fled the ballroom at midnight, the prince, having coated the palace steps with pitch, found her left golden slipper stuck fast upon the stair!

The prince rode throughout the kingdom: "She alone shall be my bride whose foot fits this golden slipper!" The elder stepsister cut off her toe to force her foot into the slipper, but two white pigeons perched on the hazel tree sang:
"Rook di goo, rook di goo!
There's blood in the shoe!
The shoe is too small,
The true bride is left at the hall!"

The second sister cut off her heel, but the doves sang again of the blood in the shoe.

Then the prince asked: "Have you no other daughter?" The father replied: "Only a stunted kitchen drudge from my first wife."

When Cinderella washed the soot from her hands and face and stepped into the room, the golden slipper slid onto her delicate foot as if molded for it! The prince looked into her eyes and recognized the beautiful maiden who had danced with his heart.

They were wed with grand rejoicings, and the faithful white doves flew down to rest upon Cinderella's shoulders, accompanying the gentle queen through a long life of wisdom and peace.
moral: True goodness and modesty shine through the darkest ashes; patience is crowned with honor.

title: Snow White (Schneewittchen)
summary: Once upon a time in midwinter, when snowflakes fell like feathers from heaven, a queen sat sewing at a window with a black ebony frame. Pricking her finger with the needle, three d...
full_text:
Once upon a time in midwinter, when snowflakes fell like feathers from heaven, a queen sat sewing at a window with a black ebony frame. Pricking her finger with the needle, three drops of blood fell into the snow. The red looked so lovely upon the white that she thought: "Oh, that I had a child as white as snow, as red as blood, and as black as the wood of this ebony frame!"

Soon after, she bore a little daughter who was as white as snow, as red as blood, and with hair as black as ebony; and she was named Snow White. But when the child was born, the good queen died.

A year later, the king married a proud, vain queen who possessed a magical mirror. Every morning she stepped before it and asked:
"Mirror, mirror, on the wall,
Who in this realm is the fairest of all?"
And the mirror answered:
"You, my queen, are the fairest of all."

When Snow White grew to be seven years old, her beauty blossomed like the dawn. The queen asked her mirror, and it replied:
"Queen, you are full fair, 'tis true,
But Snow White is a thousand times fairer than you!"

Envy turned the queen's heart green and yellow. She ordered a huntsman to take Snow White into the deep forest and slay her. But seeing the child's innocent tears, the huntsman took pity on her: "Run away, poor child!" and brought back the lungs and liver of a wild boar to deceive the queen.

Snow White ran over sharp stones and through briars until she found a charming little cottage nestled among the trees. Inside, seven little beds were neatly made, and seven little plates stood upon the table. Famished and weary, she ate a little from each plate, drank a drop from each cup, and fell asleep in the seventh bed.

The cottage belonged to seven dwarfs who mined for gold and copper in the mountains. Returning with lanterns, they found the sleeping maiden: "Heavens! What a lovely child!" When she awoke and told her tale, they said: "Keep our house, cook, knit, and spin, and you shall dwell with us in peace!"

Three times the wicked queen learned from her mirror that Snow White was alive, and three times she came disguised over the mountains to destroy her: first with a suffocating lace bodice, then with a poisoned comb, and finally with an apple—its white side sweet, but its red cheek laden with mortal poison. When the queen bit the white side to prove it safe, Snow White took a bite of the red, and fell dead upon the floor!

The weeping dwarfs could not bury her in the black earth. They crafted a transparent coffin of pure crystal glass, wrote her royal name in letters of gold, and set it upon the mountain peak, with owls, ravens, and doves keeping vigil.

Years passed, yet Snow White lay uncorrupted, fresh as if asleep. A king's son came to the mountain, fell in love with the silent maiden, and begged the dwarfs for the coffin. As the prince's servants carried it down the crags, one stumbled over a tree root. The sudden jolt dislodged the piece of poisoned apple from Snow White's throat!

She opened her eyes, lifted the glass lid, and smiled: "Where am I?"

"You are with me!" rejoiced the prince.

Their royal wedding was celebrated with great splendor. The wicked queen, summoned to the feast, choked on her own venomous rage when she beheld the living bride, and fled into the dark wilderness, never to be heard from again; while Snow White and her prince ruled their kingdom in harmony and love.
moral: Envy consumes its own host; purity of soul overcomes the snares of malice.

title: Sleeping Beauty (Dornröschen)
summary: Long ago, a king and queen longed for a child. One day while the queen was bathing, a frog hopped out of the water and prophesied: "Before a year passes, you shall bring a daughter...
full_text:
Long ago, a king and queen longed for a child. One day while the queen was bathing, a frog hopped out of the water and prophesied: "Before a year passes, you shall bring a daughter into the world!"

The prophecy came true, and the king was so overjoyed that he held a magnificent christening banquet. He invited not only his relatives, but the wise fairy women of the realm. There were thirteen in his kingdom, but having only twelve golden plates, one had to remain uninvited.

At the feast, the fairies bestowed miraculous gifts upon the infant princess: virtue, beauty, riches, and wisdom. Eleven had spoken when the uninvited thirteenth fairy burst into the hall, eyes flashing with vengeful spite. She cried in a loud voice: "In her fifteenth year, the king's daughter shall prick her finger on a spinning spindle and drop down dead!"

A shudder ran through the assembly. Then the twelfth fairy stepped forward; she could not undo the dark curse, but she could soften it: "It shall not be death, but a deep sleep of one hundred years into which the princess shall fall!"

The king, hoping to save his child, issued a royal decree banning every spinning wheel and spindle throughout the kingdom, ordering them burned to ashes.

The maiden grew into radiant youth, beloved for her gentle grace. On the day she turned fifteen, while exploring the old castle towers, she climbed a narrow winding stair to a forgotten garret. In the room sat an ancient woman spinning flax.

"What is that merry thing that rattles and hums?" asked the curious princess, reaching out her hand. The moment she touched the spindle, the ancient prophecy was fulfilled: the needle pricked her finger, and she sank down upon the bed in a profound slumber.

The deep sleep fell upon the entire palace! The king and queen fell asleep on their thrones; the courtiers fell asleep in the council chamber; the horses fell asleep in the stables, the hounds in the courtyard, the pigeons upon the roof, and the flies upon the wall! Even the hearth fire ceased its crackling, the roasting spit stopped turning, and the wind died down so that not a leaf stirred on the trees.

Around the castle grew a dense hedge of wild thorn briars. Year by year it grew taller, until it covered the battlements, towers, and flags, so that nothing of the castle could be seen. Across the land spread the legend of Dornröschen (Briar Rose), and many brave princes attempted to force their way through the hedge, but the thorns seized them like iron claws, and they perished miserably.

When the hundred years had passed, a young prince arrived in the province. An old peasant told him of the enchanted castle and the sleeping maiden. The prince boldly approached the thorn hedge; but lo! The hundred years were complete! The thorns transformed into a wall of blooming, fragrant roses that opened willingly to let him pass.

He walked through the silent halls where guards slept standing up with halberds in hand. At last he climbed the tower stairs and opened the garret door. There lay Briar Rose, looking so radiant and beautiful that he could not turn his eyes away. He bent down and kissed her lips.

At the touch of the kiss, Briar Rose opened her large, clear eyes and smiled at him.

The spell was broken! The princess arose, and with her awakened the king, the queen, the horses, the hounds, and the pigeons. The fire leaped up on the hearth, the meat began to roast again, and the royal wedding was celebrated with music and joy, living happily to the end of their days.
moral: Even when malice casts a dark shadow, destiny preserves goodness until the appointed hour of dawn.

title: Little Red Riding Hood (Rotkäppchen)
summary: Once upon a time, there was a sweet little village girl who was loved by everyone who looked at her, but most of all by her grandmother, who gave her a little cape of red velvet. I...
full_text:
Once upon a time, there was a sweet little village girl who was loved by everyone who looked at her, but most of all by her grandmother, who gave her a little cape of red velvet. It suited her so well that she would wear nothing else, and so she was called Little Red Riding Hood (Rotkäppchen).

One morning, her mother said: "Here, Little Red Riding Hood, take this cake and bottle of wine to your grandmother; she is weak and ill, and they will do her good. Walk nicely and quietly along the path, and do not stray into the forest, or you might fall and break the bottle!"

"I will take great care," promised the little girl.

The grandmother lived half an hour's walk away in the deep oak forest. When Red Riding Hood entered the woods, a wolf met her. The child did not know what a wicked beast he was, and was not afraid of him.

"Good day, Little Red Riding Hood!" said the wolf softly.
"Good day, wolf!"
"Where are you going so early?"
"To grandmother's, to take her fresh cake and wine."
"Where does grandmother live?"
"Under the three large oak trees near the hazel hedge," said the innocent child.

The wolf thought: "What a tender, juicy morsel! She will taste even sweeter than the old woman!" He pointed to the sunny glade: "Look at the lovely bluebells and yellow buttercups! Why don't you gather a fresh bouquet for your grandmother?"

Red Riding Hood thought: "A fresh bouquet will bring grandmother joy!" She left the path and wandered among the flowers, running from one bloom to the next.

Meanwhile, the wolf ran straight to the grandmother's cottage, knocked on the door, and spoke in a disguised voice: "It is Little Red Riding Hood with cake and wine!"

"Press the latch, my dear!" called the grandmother from her bed.

The wolf leaped in, swallowed the poor old grandmother whole, put on her nightgown and frilly nightcap, drew the bed-curtains, and lay down in the bed.

When Red Riding Hood had gathered as many flowers as she could carry, she ran to the cottage. Finding the door open, she felt an eerie dread. She entered the bedroom:
"Good morning, grandmother!" but received no answer. She drew the curtains.

"Oh, grandmother, what big ears you have!"
"The better to hear you with, my child!"
"Oh, grandmother, what big eyes you have!"
"The better to see you with!"
"Oh, grandmother, what big hands you have!"
"The better to hug you with!"
"Oh, but grandmother, what a terrible big mouth you have!"
"The better to eat you with!"

The wolf leaped from the bed and swallowed poor Little Red Riding Hood whole! Having satisfied his appetite, the beast lay down again and fell into a loud, snoring sleep.

A brave huntsman passed the house, thinking: "How loudly the old woman snores! I must see if she needs aid."

Peering through the window, he saw the wolf lying in the bed! "Have I found you at last, old sinner?" said the huntsman. He raised his rifle, but thought: "Perhaps the beast has swallowed the grandmother whole, and she may yet be saved!"

He took a pair of heavy shears and carefully snipped open the sleeping wolf's belly. After a few cuts, a little red cape gleamed forth! Out stepped Little Red Riding Hood, crying: "Oh, how dark and terrifying it was inside the wolf!" Then the old grandmother came out alive, though scarcely able to breathe.

Red Riding Hood gathered heavy field stones, with which they filled the wolf's belly, sewing it up neatly. When the wolf woke and tried to leap up to flee, the heavy stones dragged him down, and he collapsed dead upon the floor.

The huntsman took the wolf's pelt, the grandmother ate the cake and drank the wine, and Little Red Riding Hood thought: "Never again in my life will I stray from the path when my mother has forbidden it!"
moral: Disobeying wise counsel and straying from the honest path invites dangerous predators.

title: Hansel and Gretel (Hänsel und Gretel)
summary: Beside a great forest lived a poor woodcutter with his wife and his two children: the boy was named Hansel and the girl Gretel. They had little to bite and sup, and when a severe f...
full_text:
Beside a great forest lived a poor woodcutter with his wife and his two children: the boy was named Hansel and the girl Gretel. They had little to bite and sup, and when a severe famine struck the land, he could no longer procure daily bread.

At night, the selfish stepmother persuaded the weak father: "Tomorrow at dawn we will lead the children into the thickest part of the forest, give them a crust of bread, and leave them; we cannot feed four mouths!" The father grieved, but surrendered to her insistence.

The children, awake from hunger, heard everything. Gretel wept, but Hansel whispered: "Be quiet, Gretel, do not sorrow; I will find a way!"

Hansel crept outside in the moonlight, filled his pockets with white pebbles that shone like silver coins, and returned to bed.

At dawn, as they were led into the deep woods, Hansel lagged behind, dropping a white pebble on the path every ten paces. When evening fell and the parents abandoned them by a fire, the children waited until the full moon rose. The white pebbles glittered like silver, guiding them straight back to their father's door! The father rejoiced, for it had broken his heart to leave them.

Soon, famine struck again, and the stepmother locked the door so Hansel could not gather pebbles. This time, Hansel crumbled his single crust of bread in his pocket, dropping crumbs along the path. But when the moon rose, the bread was gone: thousands of forest birds had eaten every crumb!

Lost in the vast wilderness, the children wandered for three days until they saw a charming snow-white bird singing upon a bough. They followed it to a strange little clearing.

Lo! There stood a miraculous cottage! The roof was made of gingerbread, the walls of rich cake, and the clear windowpanes of sparkling sugar candy!

Famished, Hansel broke off a piece of the roof, and Gretel nibbled on a round windowpane. A sweet, raspy voice called from within:
"Nibble, nibble, little mouse,
Who is nibbling at my house?"

The children answered: "The wind, the wind, the heavenly child!"

The door flew open, and out hobbled an ancient woman leaning on a crutch. She smiled with sweet words, invited them inside, and fed them milk, pancakes, apples, and nuts, putting them to sleep in clean white beds.

But the old woman was a wicked cannibal witch who built gingerbread houses to lure children!

At dawn, she seized Hansel and locked him in a grated iron stall, fattening him up for her cauldron, while forcing poor Gretel to cook and scrub. Every morning the half-blind witch cried: "Hansel, stretch out your finger that I may feel if you are fat enough!" But clever Hansel held out a dry chicken bone; and the blind witch, feeling the thin bone, wondered why he remained lean.

After four weeks, impatient to feast, the witch ordered Gretel: "Crawl into the oven and see if it is hot enough to bake!" intending to shut the iron door and roast Gretel alive.

Gretel saw the trap and said innocently: "I do not know how; the opening is too small!"

"Stupid goose!" rasped the witch. "The door is big enough; look, even I could get in!" She leaned her head into the oven.

Gretel gave a mighty push! She shoved the wicked witch right inside, slammed the iron door, and bolted it fast!

Gretel unlocked Hansel's stall: "Hansel, we are saved! The old witch is gone!"

In the witch's house, they found chests filled with pearls and precious gems. Filling their pockets, they reached a great lake where a kind white duck carried them across one by one.

They ran across the fields and burst into their father's cottage, throwing their arms around his neck! The cruel stepmother had died in their absence; and Hansel and Gretel emptied their pockets of shining jewels, living with their loving father in perpetual abundance, joy, and peace.
moral: Mutual love, presence of mind, and courage overcome the darkest perils of life.

title: Rapunzel
summary: A husband and wife lived beside a witch's walled garden where lush green rampion (rapunzel) salad grew. The pregnant wife longed so desperately for the rampion that she fell ill. T...
full_text:
A husband and wife lived beside a witch's walled garden where lush green rampion (rapunzel) salad grew. The pregnant wife longed so desperately for the rampion that she fell ill. The husband climbed the wall at twilight to steal a handful, but on the second night, the powerful enchantress, Dame Gothel, caught him: "How dare you steal my rampion? You shall pay for this!"

The terrified man begged for mercy, and the witch decreed: "You may take all the rampion you desire; but when the child is born, you must surrender it to me; I will raise it like a mother."

When the child was born, Dame Gothel appeared, named the lovely girl Rapunzel, and took her away.

Rapunzel grew into the most beautiful maiden in the world. When she turned twelve, the enchantress shut her in a high stone tower in the deep forest, having neither stairs nor door, but only a tiny window at the very top.

When the enchantress wished to enter, she stood below and called:
"Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me!"

Rapunzel had magnificent, long, golden hair that shone like spun gold. She fastened her tresses around a window hook, let them tumble twenty yards to the ground, and the witch climbed up them into the tower.

Years passed. A king's son rode through the forest and heard a singing voice so exquisite that he stood spellbound. It was Rapunzel, easing her solitude with sweet melodies. The prince watched and saw how the witch gained entrance.

The next evening, the prince went to the tower and called:
"Rapunzel, Rapunzel,
Let down your hair to me!"

The golden tresses fell, the prince climbed up, and Rapunzel was startled; but the prince spoke with such tender reverence and pure love that she placed her hand in his: "I will go with you, my prince; bring a skein of silk each time you visit, and I will weave a ladder to climb down."

Their secret happiness was betrayed when Rapunzel innocently asked Dame Gothel: "Tell me, godmother, why are you so much heavier to pull up than the young prince?"

Enraged, the enchantress shrieked: "Wicked child! You have deceived me!" In fury, she seized shears and hacked off Rapunzel's golden braids, banishing the poor maiden to a desolate wilderness.

That evening, the witch fastened the severed hair to the window hook. When the prince called, she let it down. When the prince climbed into the chamber, he met not his beloved, but the venomous gaze of the sorceress: "The bird is flown, and the cat will scratch out your eyes!"

In despair, the prince leaped from the high tower. He escaped with his life, but the sharp thorn briars beneath pierced his eyes, blinding him.

Blind and heartbroken, the prince wandered through the wilderness for years, eating roots and weeping for his lost bride. At last, he reached the desolate waste where Rapunzel lived with their twin children.

He heard a voice singing that resonated in his soul! He ran toward it; Rapunzel recognized him, threw her arms around his neck, and wept.

Two of her warm tears of love fell upon his blind eyes! Instantly, the clouds cleared, and his sight was completely restored, clearer and brighter than before!

The prince led Rapunzel and their children home to his kingdom, where they were received with boundless joy and reigned in peace, righteousness, and eternal love.
moral: True devotion endures suffering and blindness, guided by love toward healing and joy.

title: Rumpelstiltskin (Rumpelstilzchen)
summary: A boastful miller told the king: "I have a daughter who can spin straw into pure gold!"...
full_text:
A boastful miller told the king: "I have a daughter who can spin straw into pure gold!"

The greedy king commanded the maiden to court, locked her in a chamber filled with straw, and ordered: "Spin this straw into gold before dawn, or you shall die!"

The poor miller's daughter wept in despair. Suddenly, a tiny little manikin stepped through the door: "What will you give me if I spin it for you?"

She gave him her necklace, and the imp sat at the wheel: whir, whir, whir! By sunrise, the room was filled with golden bobbins.

The king was thrilled, but his greed was boundless. The next night, he locked her in a larger room; she gave the little man her ring, and again the straw became gold.

On the third night, in an enormous hall of straw, the maiden had nothing left to give. The little man demanded: "Promise me your first-born child when you become queen!" Having no other choice to save her life, she promised.

The king married the miller's daughter. A year later, the young queen gave birth to a beautiful infant, having forgotten the imp.

Suddenly, the little man stepped into her bedchamber: "Now give me what you promised!"

The queen wept, offering all the treasures of the realm to keep her child. Moved by her tears, the manikin said: "I will give you three days; if you can discover my true name, you may keep your child!"

The queen sent messengers across the world to collect every name under heaven. On the first night, she guessed: "Caspar, Melchior, Balthazar!" On the second night: "Ribs-of-Beef, Sheepshanks, Spindleshanks!" But to each, the imp laughed: "That is not my name!"

On the third evening, a messenger returned from the deep forest: "High on a mountain where the fox and hare bid goodnight, I saw a fire burning; and around the fire hopped a comical little man on one leg, singing:
'Today I brew, tomorrow I bake,
Next day the queen's fair child I take;
For little does anyone know my fame,
That Rumpelstiltskin is my name!'"

When the little man arrived at dawn, demanding: "What is my name, Queen?", she asked calmly:
"Is your name Conrad?" "No!"
"Is your name Harry?" "No!"
"Can your name perhaps be... Rumpelstiltskin?"

"The devil told you that! The devil told you that!" shrieked the little man in a fury. He stamped his right foot so deep into the earth that his leg sank in up to his waist; then in his rage, he seized his left foot with both hands and tore himself in two!

The queen embraced her child in peace, freed forever from the shadow of the greedy imp.
moral: Boasting traps us in impossible debts; steadfast maternal love unmasks deceit.

title: The Frog Prince (Froschkönig)
summary: In olden times, when wishing still helped, lived a king whose daughters were all handsome, but the youngest was so beautiful that the sun itself marvelled whenever it shone upon he...
full_text:
In olden times, when wishing still helped, lived a king whose daughters were all handsome, but the youngest was so beautiful that the sun itself marvelled whenever it shone upon her.

Near the king's castle lay a dark forest, and in the forest beneath an ancient linden tree was a cool spring. On hot days, the young princess would sit by the well, tossing her favorite toy—a golden ball—high into the air and catching it.

One afternoon, the golden ball slipped through her fingers, bounced upon the ground, and plunged straight into the deep water of the well. The princess wept bitterly, for the spring was so deep that no bottom could be seen.

As she wept, an ugly frog poked its head from the water: "Why do you weep so bitterly, King's daughter?"

"My golden ball has fallen into the well!" she sobbed.

"I will fetch it for you," said the frog, "if you promise that I shall be your companion, sit beside you at your table, eat from your golden plate, drink from your cup, and sleep in your little bed."

The princess thought: "What nonsense the silly frog talks! He lives in the water with his fellows; he cannot be a companion to human beings!" So she promised everything, only wanting her ball back.

The frog dove into the depths and brought up the golden ball in its mouth, dropping it onto the grass. Overjoyed, the princess seized the ball and ran home, ignoring the frog's cries: "Wait for me! I cannot run as fast as you!"

The next day, as the royal family sat dining, a knock was heard at the door, and a voice called:
"Youngest king's daughter, open to me!
Remember the promise beneath the tree!"

The princess went to open the door, saw the slimy frog, and slammed the door shut in terror.

The wise old king saw her distress and asked what frightened her. When she confessed her promise at the well, the king spoke with firm royal majesty: "What you have promised, you must keep! Let the frog enter!"

The princess reluctantly obeyed. The frog hopped to her chair: "Lift me onto the table!" When lifted, he said: "Push your golden plate nearer, that we may eat together!" She did so with disgust, while the king watched with approval.

Finally, the frog said: "I am weary; carry me to your room that we may sleep in your silken bed."

The princess wept, horrified by the cold, clammy creature. But the king rebuked her: "You must not despise one who helped you when you were in distress!"

She carried the frog up to her chamber in two fingers, setting him in a corner. But when the frog hopped toward her bed, whispering: "Lift me up, or I will tell your father!", her patience snapped. She seized the frog and threw it against the wall with all her might: "Now you will have peace, you ugly frog!"

As he struck the wall, he tumbled down—not as a dead frog, but as a handsome young prince with noble, friendly eyes!

A wicked witch had enchanted him, and no one could release him but the king's daughter.

By her father's royal decree, they were betrothed. The next morning, a magnificent carriage drawn by eight white horses with golden plumes arrived, driven by Faithful Heinrich—the prince's devoted servant, who had bound three iron bands around his heart to keep it from breaking with grief during his master's enchantment.

As they rode to the prince's kingdom, three loud snaps were heard: the iron bands had burst from Faithful Heinrich's heart, overflowing with the joy of his master's freedom!
moral: What you have promised in your hour of need, you must faithfully fulfill in the hour of prosperity.

title: The Wolf and the Seven Young Kids
summary: An old mother goat had seven young kids whom she loved with all her heart. One day, preparing to go into the forest for food, she gathered them: "Dear children, I am going into the...
keywords: the wolf and the seven young kids
full_text:
An old mother goat had seven young kids whom she loved with all her heart. One day, preparing to go into the forest for food, she gathered them: "Dear children, I am going into the woods; beware of the wolf! If he enters, he will eat you all, skin and hair! He often disguises himself, but you will know him by his rough, gravelly voice and his pitch-black paws."

"We will take great care, mother," promised the kids.

Soon, a knock sounded at the door: "Open, dear children! Your mother is back with gifts for everyone!"

The kids heard the deep, raspy voice and called: "We will not open! You are not our mother; she has a soft, sweet voice, but your voice is rough: you are the wolf!"

The wolf went to a shopkeeper, bought a lump of chalk, and ate it to make his voice smooth and soft.

He returned and knocked: "Open, little ones, your mother has returned!"

He placed his paw on the window sill. The kids saw the black fur and cried: "We will not open! Our mother does not have black feet: you are the wolf!"

The wolf ran to a baker: "Rub some dough over my feet!" Then he ran to the miller: "Dust white flour over my paws!"

The wolf knocked a third time: "Open, children, your dear mother is here!" He showed his white paws at the window.

Deceived by the sweet voice and white feet, the kids unlatched the bolt. In sprang the wolf!

The terrified kids scrambled to hide: the first under the table, the second into the bed, the third into the stove, the fourth into the kitchen, the fifth into the cupboard, the sixth beneath the washing bowl, and the seventh into the tall clock-case!

The wolf found them and swallowed them whole, one after another—all except the youngest, who was hidden in the clock-case.

Satiated and heavy, the wolf lay down beneath a tree in the meadow and fell into a snoring sleep.

When the old mother goat returned and found her house ransacked, she wept bitter tears. The youngest kid leaped from the clock and told what had happened.

Weeping, the mother goat walked into the meadow and found the wolf snoring, with something kicking inside his bloated belly!

"Heavens!" she cried. "Can my poor children still be alive?"

She took shears and a needle. She cut open the beast's stomach, and out sprang the six little kids, alive and unhurt, for the greedy monster had swallowed them whole in his haste!

They gathered heavy field stones, filled the wolf's belly to the brim, and the mother sewed it up with deft stitches.

When the wolf woke, parched with thirst, he walked to the well to drink. The heavy stones threw him off balance; he tumbled into the deep well and drowned!

The seven kids and their mother danced around the well with joy, singing: "The wolf is dead! The wolf is dead!" and lived together in safety and peace.
moral: Heed the warnings of loving parents; smooth speech and white paws cannot conceal wolfish intentions.

title: The Bremen Town Musicians
summary: A donkey who had faithfully carried sacks to the mill for decades grew old and weak. Hearing his master plan to dispose of his hide, the donkey slipped away and set out on the road...
full_text:
A donkey who had faithfully carried sacks to the mill for decades grew old and weak. Hearing his master plan to dispose of his hide, the donkey slipped away and set out on the road to Bremen: "I can become a town musician there!"

Along the way, he met a hunting hound panting by the ditch: "I am old and can no longer hunt, so my master wanted to shoot me!"

"Come with me to Bremen," invited the donkey. "I will play the lute, and you shall beat the kettledrums!"

A little further, they met a cat with a face like three rainy days: "My teeth are blunt, and I prefer sitting by the fire to hunting mice, so my mistress wanted to drown me!"

"Join us!" said the donkey. "You understand night-music; come to Bremen!"

Then they passed a farmyard where a rooster was crowing with all his might: "The cook is putting me into the Sunday soup tomorrow, so I crow while I still have a throat!"

"Come with us, Red-Comb!" said the donkey. "Anything is better than death; your voice will make splendid harmony!"

The four companions could not reach Bremen in one day. At nightfall in the deep forest, they spotted a light shining from a cottage window. The tall donkey looked inside: "I see a table spread with roasted meat, bread, and wine, and four fierce robbers feasting!"

Hungry and cold, the animals devised a plan.

The donkey placed his forefeet upon the window sill; the hound climbed upon the donkey's back; the cat scrambled upon the hound's shoulders; and the rooster flew up to perch upon the cat's head!

At a signal, they struck up their music together: the donkey brayed, the dog barked, the cat meowed, and the rooster crowed! Then they crashed through the windowpanes with a deafening clatter of shattering glass!

Terrified by the roaring monster, the robbers fled into the woods in utter panic.

The four musicians sat down at the table, ate the feast with boundless appetite, put out the light, and went to sleep: the donkey in the yard, the dog behind the door, the cat on the warm hearth ashes, and the rooster upon the roof beam.

At midnight, seeing the house quiet, the robber captain sent a henchman to scout the cottage.

The spy crept into the pitch-black kitchen. Seeing the glowing eyes of the cat, he mistook them for live coals and held a match to them. The furious cat spat and scratched his face with sharp claws!

Terrified, the robber ran for the back door, where the dog sprang up and bit his leg! In the yard, the donkey kicked him with full force; and from the roof, the rooster crowed triumphantly: "Cock-a-doodle-doo!"

The robber fled back to his captain, trembling: "In that house sits a hideous witch who scratched my face with long nails; behind the door stands a man with a knife who stabbed my leg; in the yard lies a black monster who struck me with a wooden club; and upon the roof sits the judge, shouting: 'Bring the rascal to me!' I barely escaped with my life!"

The robbers never dared return to the forest; and the four Bremen musicians found the cottage so cozy that they never left it, living together in friendship, music, and peace.
moral: Those discarded by the world can unite their humble strengths to win freedom and a peaceful home.
