title: The Fisherman and His Wife
summary: There was once a fisherman and his wife who lived together in a filthy pigsty of a hovel close by the sea. Every day the fisherman went out with his rod and sat watching the clear...
full_text:
There was once a fisherman and his wife who lived together in a filthy pigsty of a hovel close by the sea. Every day the fisherman went out with his rod and sat watching the clear water.

One afternoon, his line was pulled deep into the depths. He hauled up an enormous flounder, who spoke in human voice: "Fisherman, spare my life! I am no common fish, but an enchanted prince! Throw me back into the water, I pray you!"

The kind fisherman threw the flounder back: "I would not kill a fish that can speak!"

When he went home and told his wife Ilsebill, she flew into a rage: "Did you ask for nothing in return? It is dreadful to live in this dirty hovel! Go back and ask the fish for a snug little cottage!"

The fisherman went to the sea; the water was green and yellow. He called:
"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
Prithee, listen unto me:
For my wife, good Ilsebill,
Wills not as I'd have her will!"

The flounder popped up: "What does she want?"
"She wants a snug cottage."
"Go home; she has it already," said the fish.

The fisherman returned and found a lovely stone cottage with a parlor, garden, and chickens. He was happy, but after a week, Ilsebill grew discontented: "This cottage is too cramped! Go back and tell the flounder I must have a great stone castle with servants and horses!"

The fisherman's heart grew heavy, but he feared his wife. The sea was now dark blue and purple. The fish granted the castle.

Next, Ilsebill demanded to be king: "I must be King of the land!" The sea turned dark gray and foamy; the flounder made her king, with crowns and golden scepters.

Then she demanded: "I must be Emperor!" The sea turned black and stormy; the fish made her Emperor.

Then: "I must be Pope!" The sea heaved with violent breakers, and sky tore with wind; the fish made her Pope, crowned with triple tiaras.

Early the next morning, as the sun began to rise, Ilsebill looked upon the golden dawn from her bed, and shook with rage: "Why can I not command the sun and moon to rise? Go back to the fish! I must become like God Almighty!"

The fisherman trembled in sheer terror. Thunder crashed, lightning cleaved the sky, and mountainous black waves roared like doom. The fisherman shouted against the hurricane:
"Flounder, flounder in the sea,
Prithee, listen unto me:
For my wife, good Ilsebill,
Wills not as I'd have her will!"

The flounder surfaced in the storm: "What does she want now?"

"Alas!" wept the fisherman. "She wants to be like God!"

"Go home," spoke the flounder solemnly. "She sits already in her dirty pigsty."

And there they sit to this very day.
moral: Unbridled ambition and insatiable greed eventually strip away everything and return one to the hovel.

title: The Golden Bird
summary: A king possessed a pleasure garden containing a tree that bore golden apples. When the apples ripened, one was found missing each morning....
full_text:
A king possessed a pleasure garden containing a tree that bore golden apples. When the apples ripened, one was found missing each morning.

The king set his three sons to keep watch. The two elder princes fell asleep, but the youngest prince kept vigil and saw a bird whose feathers were of solid gold steal an apple. He shot an arrow, knocking loose a golden feather that shone brighter than all the lamps in the palace.

The king dispatched his sons to capture the miraculous bird.

On the road, the two elder brothers met a talking fox, who warned them: "Do not choose the luxurious, noisy inn, but stay at the humble roadside tavern!" The proud brothers mocked the fox, entered the grand inn, and squandered their money in foolish pleasures.

The youngest prince met the fox, thanked him for his advice, and stayed in the humble cottage.

The grateful fox said: "Sit upon my tail, and I will carry you!"

With lightning speed, the fox carried him to a castle where the golden bird sat in a wooden cage beside a golden cage. The fox warned: "Do not put the bird into the golden cage!" But the prince yielded to vanity, touched the golden cage, alarms rang, and he was captured.

The rival king demanded the Golden Horse that ran swifter than the wind as ransom. The fox helped him again, warning: "Do not use the golden saddle; use the leather saddle!" The prince forgot the warning, touched the gold saddle, and was caught again.

To redeem himself, he was sent to bring the Princess of the Golden Palace. The fox guided him, and the prince won the princess's heart through gentle courtesy.

With the fox's clever counsel, the prince outwitted both kings, carrying off the Golden Bird, the Golden Horse, and the beautiful Princess.

On the return journey, his two jealous brothers ambushed him, threw him into a deep gorge, and brought the treasures to their father, claiming they had won them. But the horse would not eat, the bird would not sing, and the maiden wept constantly.

The faithful fox descended into the gorge, rescued the youngest prince, and brought him disguised to the palace.

The moment the true prince entered the court, the bird sang with celestial joy, the golden horse began to feast, and the princess ran to embrace him with tears of happiness!

The treacherous brothers were exiled, and the youngest prince married the princess. Finally, at the fox's request, the prince touched the animal with his sword, breaking an ancient enchantment and restoring the fox to his true form as the princess's noble brother! And they reigned in peace and prosperity.
moral: Heeding the counsel of the wise and humble guides one past temptation to true victory.

title: The Twelve Brothers
summary: A king had twelve sons, and declared that if his thirteenth child was a daughter, all twelve princes must die so that her inheritance might be boundless....
full_text:
A king had twelve sons, and declared that if his thirteenth child was a daughter, all twelve princes must die so that her inheritance might be boundless.

The good queen warned her sons. Twelve white flags were hoisted on the tower as a signal that a sister was born; and the twelve brothers fled into the deep forest, taking shelter in an enchanted cottage.

When the princess turned ten, she discovered twelve shirts in her mother's chest, learned of her brothers' exile, and vowed to find them. Guided by love, she found their forest cottage and became their devoted little housekeeper.

One morning, wanting to please them, she plucked twelve white lilies blooming in the garden. Instantly, the twelve brothers were transformed into twelve black ravens, who flew away screaming over the treetops, and the cottage vanished!

An old fairy appeared: "You have bewitched your brothers! They can be restored only if you maintain absolute silence for seven years: you must not speak, laugh, or weep. If a single word escapes you, your brothers will die!"

The maiden climbed into a tall oak tree and sat spinning flax in total silence.

A hunting king discovered the beautiful mute maiden, fell in love with her innocence, and made her his queen.

The king's jealous mother accused the silent queen of sorcery and treason, whispering lies that led to her condemnation to the stake.

Even as the flames rose around the execution scaffold, the queen remained steadfastly silent, trusting heaven.

Just as the seventh year expired to the very second, a rushing sound filled the sky! Twelve black ravens swooped down from the clouds, their wings touching the earth.

Instantly, twelve magnificent princes stood before the throne! They extinguished the flames, embraced their devoted sister, and revealed her heroic sacrifice to the king, while the wicked mother-in-law was banished forever.
moral: Pure, patient silence in the face of false accusation possesses the power to redeem.

title: The Pack of Ragamuffins
summary: Chanticleer the rooster and Partlet the hen built a miniature carriage out of walnut shells, harnessed four mice to it, and drove toward the nut-hill....
full_text:
Chanticleer the rooster and Partlet the hen built a miniature carriage out of walnut shells, harnessed four mice to it, and drove toward the nut-hill.

On the road, they picked up a duck who had lost her web-shoes, a sewing needle who thought himself a knight, and a pin who carried a sharp point.

They arrived late at an inn, demanding shelter from a grumbling landlord. They promised the landlord the duck's eggs and the rooster's feathers.

Before dawn, after eating all the bread and cheese in the kitchen, the ragamuffins prepared their escape: the needle stuck himself into the landlord's shaving towel, the pin stuck into his chair cushion, and the eggshells buried themselves in the fireplace ashes.

When the landlord awoke, he blew upon the ashes, and the eggshells exploded into his eyes; he ran to wipe his face, and the needle scratched his nose; he sat down to rest, and the pin pricked his seat!

He ran to the door shouting for guards, while the rooster crowed from the road, driving the walnut carriage merrily into freedom!
moral: Unlikely rogues who band together can turn an unfair world upside down with laughter.

title: Brother and Sister
summary: Fleeing a cruel stepmother, a little brother and sister walked into the great forest. The wicked woman had bewitched all the forest brooks....
full_text:
Fleeing a cruel stepmother, a little brother and sister walked into the great forest. The wicked woman had bewitched all the forest brooks.

At the first brook, the water murmured: "Whoever drinks of me will become a tiger!" The sister caught her brother's arm: "Do not drink, or you will tear me to pieces!"

At the second brook, it sang: "Whoever drinks will become a wolf!" The sister held him back again.

At the third brook, parched with unbearable thirst, the boy could not resist and drank. Instantly, he was transformed into a gentle white fawn!

The sister wept, took off her golden garter, fastened it around the fawn's neck, and wove a rope of rushes to lead him to a deserted woodland hut, where they lived in sweet communion.

During a royal hunt, the king chased the beautiful fawn to the cottage. Enamored by the maiden's grace, the king brought them both to his castle and married the sister, while the fawn roamed freely through the royal gardens.

When the queen bore a son, the envious stepmother slipped into the palace, smothered the queen in a heated bath, and put her own ugly one-eyed daughter in the bed.

For three nights, the ghost of the queen appeared at midnight to nurse her baby and stroke the fawn's neck, whispering:
"How fares my child? How fares my fawn?
Twice come I here, then forever gone!"

On the third night, the king stayed awake, stepped forward, and embraced her: "You are my true, living wife!"

By God's grace, she returned to life! The wicked stepmother was condemned to justice, and as she perished, the enchantment broke: the white fawn stood up as a handsome youth, restored to his human form, living in lifelong joy with his sister.
moral: Patience and gentle affection outlast cruelty; innocence is vindicated by truth.

title: The Three Little Men in the Wood
summary: A cruel stepmother dressed her gentle stepdaughter in a thin paper dress and sent her into the snowy forest in midwinter to gather a basket of fresh ripe strawberries!...
keywords: the three little men in the wood
full_text:
A cruel stepmother dressed her gentle stepdaughter in a thin paper dress and sent her into the snowy forest in midwinter to gather a basket of fresh ripe strawberries!

Shivering with cold, the maiden stumbled upon a tiny cottage where three little men (dwarfs) sat by the hearth. She greeted them with sweet courtesy, warmed herself modestly by the fire, and shared her single crust of dry bread with them.

Moved by her goodness, the three little men gave her a broom: "Sweep the snow from our back door!"

When she swept the snow, what did she find underneath? Sweet, ripe red strawberries growing in the snow!

As she departed, the three little men blessed her: the first made her grow more beautiful every day; the second decreed that a piece of gold should fall from her mouth whenever she spoke; and the third decreed that a king should marry her.

When the envious stepsister heard this, she wrapped herself in warm furs, took sweet cakes, and walked into the forest. Finding the cottage, she entered without greeting, sat on the best chair, ate her cakes without sharing, and refused to sweep the back door: "I am not your servant!"

The three dwarfs cursed her: she grew uglier each day; whenever she spoke, a toad hopped from her mouth; and she died in disgrace.

The gentle stepdaughter met a king, who marvelled at the gold coins that fell from her lips and made her his beloved queen, proving that genuine kindness receives heavenly reward.
moral: Kindness shown to strangers brings blessings upon one's lips; malice brings toads.

title: The Wishing-Table, the Gold-Ass, and the Cudgel in the Sack
summary: A tailor had three sons and a pet goat who lied to the father that the sons never fed her, driving the tailor to banish all three boys in anger....
keywords: the wishing-table, the gold-ass, and the cudgel in the sack
full_text:
A tailor had three sons and a pet goat who lied to the father that the sons never fed her, driving the tailor to banish all three boys in anger.

The eldest son became a cabinet-maker and received a magical little table: whenever he said: "Table, be covered!", it set itself with roasted meats, wine, and pastries. On his way home, a greedy innkeeper switched the table for an ordinary one while he slept.

The second son became a miller and received a miraculous donkey: whenever he said: "Bricklebrit!", gold ducats fell from its mouth. The same dishonest innkeeper switched the donkey for a common beast.

The youngest son became a wood-turner. His master gave him a stout wooden cudgel inside a burlap sack: "Whenever someone tries to harm you, say: 'Cudgel, out of the sack!' and it will dance upon their backs until you bid it stop!"

The third son arrived at the same dishonest inn, boasting of his magical sack. At midnight, the thieving innkeeper crept into his room to steal it.

The youth shouted: "Cudgel, out of the sack!"

Out leaped the wooden cudgel! It rained heavy blows upon the innkeeper's shoulders, ribs, and legs until the thief shrieked for mercy, confessing his crimes and returning the magical wishing-table and the gold-ass!

The three brothers returned to their father's house, restored family peace, provided endless feasts with the table and gold with the donkey, and lived in lasting prosperity.
moral: Honest labor earns miraculous gifts; thieves who steal from the simple receive the cudgel of justice.

title: The White Snake
summary: A wise king was served every evening with a covered dish that none of his courtiers were permitted to see. The faithful servant, consumed by curiosity, lifted the lid one night and...
full_text:
A wise king was served every evening with a covered dish that none of his courtiers were permitted to see. The faithful servant, consumed by curiosity, lifted the lid one night and found a boiled white snake. He tasted a small morsel; and instantly, he understood the language of all animals!

That day, the queen lost her diamond ring. Suspected of theft, the servant went into the courtyard and overheard a duck complaining that an iron pebble had stuck in her throat. The servant had the cook examine the duck, found the ring, and cleared his name with honors.

Setting out to see the world, the servant helped three drowning fish in the shallows; spared an ant queen whose colony had been disturbed; and fed his horse to save three starving young ravens in an oak tree.

Arriving in a great kingdom, he competed for the hand of a princess. To win her, he had to perform three impossible tasks.

First, he was ordered to retrieve a golden ring thrown into the deep sea; the three grateful fish brought it up from the ocean bed!

Second, he was ordered to gather ten sacks of millet scattered across the grass in a single night; the grateful ant queen and her millions of ants gathered every single seed before dawn!

Third, he was ordered to bring the Golden Apple from the Tree of Life; the three ravens flew across the world to the garden of heaven and dropped the golden apple into his hands!

The princess recognized his nobility of soul and married him, living together in peace and mutual love.
moral: Kindness shown to the humblest creatures of earth returns as an invincible shield in times of trial.

title: The Straw, the Coal, and the Bean
summary: An old woman dropped a straw, a glowing coal, and a broad bean while preparing her hearth fire. The three companions escaped together, setting out to seek their fortune....
keywords: the straw, the coal, and the bean
full_text:
An old woman dropped a straw, a glowing coal, and a broad bean while preparing her hearth fire. The three companions escaped together, setting out to seek their fortune.

They reached a rushing brook with no bridge. The clever straw offered: "I will lay myself across the water; you two can walk over me like a bridge!"

The glowing coal stepped boldly onto the straw. But when it reached the middle, hearing the water roar beneath, it froze in terror. The burning coal scorched through the dry straw; snap! The straw broke in two, the coal fell into the water with a hiss, and both drowned!

The bean, who had stayed safely on the bank, laughed so uproariously at their clumsy mishap that she burst her own seams!

A wandering tailor took pity on the weeping bean, drew out needle and thread, and stitched her seam closed with black cotton. And that is why, to this very day, all broad beans have a black seam down their middle!
moral: Reckless laughter at another's misfortune often ends in bursting one's own seams.

title: The Fisherman and His Wife (The Lesson of the Sea)
summary: The humble fisherman released the magical talking flounder without asking for a reward, content with his daily bread....
keywords: the fisherman and his wife variant
full_text:
Once upon a time, upon the windswept shore of a gray northern sea, there lived a humble fisherman and his wife Ilsebill in a miserable little hovel fashioned from driftwood and sea grass. Every morning at dawn, the honest fisherman walked down to the water with his hemp line, wishing for nothing more than enough fish to provide a simple supper. One calm morning, a heavy pull tugged upon his hook, and he hauled ashore an enormous golden flounder. To his astonishment, the fish spoke with a pleading human voice: 'Spare my life, kind fisherman! I am no common creature of the deep, but an enchanted prince. Cast me back into the cool brine, and may good fortune follow you!' Moved with compassion, the honest man gently released the flounder back into the sea and returned home with empty hands and a peaceful heart.

When he arrived at his hut and recounted the day's wonder to his wife, Ilsebill’s face darkened with furious indignation. 'You foolish, simple-minded man!' she scolded, shaking her wooden ladle. 'To catch a magical talking prince and ask for nothing in return? Go back to the sea at once and demand a cozy stone cottage with a blooming herb garden, a tiled chimney, and a pantry full of smoked ham!' Reluctantly, the fisherman trudged back to the beach. The water was no longer clear green, but murky yellow and purple. He called upon the flounder, and the wish was granted without delay. Yet within a fortnight, the cozy cottage was too small for Ilsebill’s surging ambition. She ordered him back again and again—first for a majestic castle of carved marble, then to be crowned queen of the land, then emperor of the realm, and finally the supreme pope! With every new demand, the sea groaned and turned from dark violet to pitch black, boiling with angry white foam and crashing against the cliffs with terrifying thunder.

At last, waking before dawn in her papal bedchamber of crimson velvet, Ilsebill looked out at the morning sky and was seized by monstrous arrogance. Shaking her terrified husband awake, she shrieked: 'I cannot bear that the sun and moon should rise without my royal command! Go to the sea this instant and tell the flounder that I must become like God!' Trembling in dread, the weeping fisherman stumbled to the shore amid a howling hurricane that uprooted ancient oaks and split the blackened heavens with lightning. He screamed his wife’s terrible demand into the roaring surf. The magical flounder surfaced through the towering waves, looked upon the weeping man with mournful pity, and whispered softly: 'Go home, fisherman. She sits once more in her muddy hovel by the shore.' And there, amid the broken driftwood and sea grass, they remain to this day, a timeless warning that boundless greed destroys the very gifts it seeks to hoard.
moral: True abundance is found in gratitude for enough; boundless greed consumes itself.

title: The Brave Little Tailor
summary: A little tailor sat on his bench sewing when seven flies landed on his jam bread. Slapping with a cloth, he killed all seven at once!...

full_text:
A little tailor sat on his bench sewing when seven flies landed on his jam bread. Slapping with a cloth, he killed all seven at once!

"What a hero I am!" he cried. He embroidered a belt with gold letters: "Seven at One Blow!" and set out to conquer the world.

Meeting an enormous giant on the mountain, the tailor challenged him. When the giant crushed a rock in his fist, the tailor squeezed a lump of soft cheese until water dripped from his hand! When the giant threw a stone high into the clouds, the tailor tossed a live bird into the air that flew away over the peaks! The giant, thinking it was a stone that never returned, was terrified.

The king promised the tailor his daughter's hand and half his kingdom if he could vanquish two wild giants, a fierce unicorn, and a rampaging wild boar.

The brave little tailor tricked the two giants into fighting each other by dropping stones on their heads while they slept; he trapped the unicorn by making it drive its horn into an oak tree; and he lured the boar into an abandoned church and locked the door!

The astonished king had to keep his royal oath, and the little tailor married the princess and became a wise, victorious king, proving that intellect and audacity conquer every giant.
moral: Audacity, quick wit, and presence of mind conquer giants where brute force fails.

title: The Little Peasant
summary: A poor peasant who owned not a single cow carved a calf out of wood and placed it in the pasture. Mocked by the wealthy village bailiff, the peasant used his sharp wits to turn eve...
full_text:
In a small village nestled between rolling hills lived a clever peasant who was so poor that he owned not a single cow or goat, having only a tiny thatch cottage and an empty barn. When the wealthy village bailiff and rich farmers drove their plump cattle to pasture, they mocked the poor peasant: 'Look at the beggar who has no livestock!' Undaunted by their cruel taunts, the little peasant carved a realistic calf out of dry pine wood, painted it with black and white spots, and carried it out to the grassy pasture, instructing the village herdsman to let it graze in peace. When the herdsman returned at evening claiming the wooden calf had run away, the peasant brought him before the magistrate and was awarded an honest cow in compensation.

Envious of his good fortune, the greedy bailiff schemed to ruin him, forcing the peasant to slaughter the cow. Not one to despair, the peasant salted the meat and took the dried hide into town to sell. On his journey through a dark forest, night overtook him, and he took shelter in the loft of a lonely wayside inn. Peering down through a knothole in the floorboards, he watched the innkeeper’s wife entertaining an illicit feast of roast fowl and wine with a corrupt local cleric. When the master of the inn knocked on the door, the wife hurriedly hid the feast in the bake-oven and pushed the cleric inside a large wooden meal chest in the parlor!

The little peasant climbed down, knocked on the door, and offered his dry cow-skin to the innkeeper, claiming it was a magical fortune-teller. Squeezing the stiff leather under his arm so it squeaked, the peasant announced: 'My hide says there is a roasted goose and jug of wine hidden inside your bake-oven!' The astonished innkeeper opened the oven, found the feast, and shared it with the peasant. Squeezing the hide again, the peasant whispered: 'My hide says the devil himself is hiding in your meal chest!' The innkeeper unlocked the chest, and the soot-blackened cleric tumbled out in terror, running into the night while leaving behind a purse of three hundred gold thalers! The little peasant returned home wealthy and respected, proving that a sharp, resourceful mind can turn every obstacle into triumphant success.
moral: The simple man who relies on wits turns the greed of dishonest oppressors against themselves.

title: The Queen Bee
summary: Two elder princes went seeking adventure and fell into reckless, idle living. Their youngest brother, whom they called Simpleton (Dummling), went to bring them home....
full_text:
Two elder princes went seeking adventure and fell into reckless, idle living. Their youngest brother, whom they called Simpleton (Dummling), went to bring them home.

Along the road, the elder brothers wanted to destroy an anthill, kill ducks on a pond, and smoke out a beehive. Dummling stood before them each time: "Leave them in peace; I will not suffer you to torment them!"

They arrived at an enchanted castle where all inhabitants were turned to stone. To break the spell, three tasks had to be solved:

First, collect a thousand pearls of the princess scattered under the moss in the forest; the grateful ants gathered every single pearl before sunset!

Second, fetch the key to the princess's bedchamber from the deep lake; the grateful ducks dove down and brought the key from the mud!

Third, identify the youngest and sweetest of the three sleeping princesses, whose lips looked identical; the grateful Queen Bee flew in and tasted the honey upon the lips of the true maiden!

The spell broke instantly: the castle awakened, and Dummling married the youngest princess, while his reformed brothers married her sisters, reigning in peace and gratitude.
moral: Kindness to the small and defenseless is rewarded with victory when the great tasks arrive.

full_text:
An old king blew three feathers into the air to determine which of his three sons should inherit the crown: the eldest followed the feather east; the second followed it west; and the third feather fell straight to the earth, where the youngest son, Simpleton, sat down in obedience.

Beside the fallen feather lay a trapdoor into the earth. Descending the stairs, the youth met an enormous fat toad surrounded by her little ones. The gentle toad rewarded his respectful courtesy with the finest carpet ever woven in the world.

His brothers brought coarse blankets, but Simpleton brought the miraculous carpet!

Next, the toad gave him a ring of dazzling gold and diamonds; and finally, the toad transformed into a breathtakingly beautiful maiden in a carriage made of a yellow carrot drawn by six white mice!

The court marveled at her grace, and the king placed the crown upon Simpleton's head, proving that humble trust in Providence outshines worldly ambition.
moral: The world mocks simplicity, but humble obedience to truth receives the kingdom.

title: The Golden Goose
summary: A young woodcutter called Dummling was despised by his family. When his elder brothers went to the forest, their mother gave them rich cakes and wine, but they refused to share wit...
full_text:
A young woodcutter called Dummling was despised by his family. When his elder brothers went to the forest, their mother gave them rich cakes and wine, but they refused to share with a little gray old man who asked for food, and were both injured by their axes.

When Dummling went to the woods with only cinder bread and sour beer, he gladly shared with the old man: "There is little, but what there is we will share together!"

The beer turned to sweet wine and the crust to rich cake. The old man said: "Because you have a good heart and share willingly, cut down that ancient oak and you will find a treasure at the roots."

At the root of the tree sat a goose whose feathers were of solid gold!

Dummling took the goose to an inn. At night, the innkeeper's eldest daughter tried to pluck a golden feather, and her hand was glued fast to the bird! The second daughter came to pull her away and was stuck to her sister! The third daughter touched her sister and was stuck fast too!

In the morning, Dummling tucked the goose under his arm and marched on, with the three sisters trailing behind! A parson shouted at them and was stuck; the sexton grabbed the parson and was stuck; two laborers tried to help and were glued fast—forming a comical procession of seven people hopping behind the golden goose!

They reached the royal capital, where the king's daughter suffered from deep melancholy and had never been known to laugh. The king had promised her hand to whoever could make her smile.

When the princess looked from her window and saw the solemn procession of seven people hopping in frantic helplessness behind Dummling and his golden goose, she burst into clear, ringing laughter!

Dummling married the princess and became a beloved king, proving that sharing with a generous heart brings joy and blessings to the whole world.
moral: A generous heart that shares simple bread unlocks laughter and brings joy to the kingdom.

title: All-Kinds-of-Fur (Allerleirauh)
summary: A king whose queen possessed golden hair was bound by a dying promise to marry only a maiden whose beauty matched hers. In his madness, he sought to marry his own gentle daughter....
full_text:
A king whose queen possessed golden hair was bound by a dying promise to marry only a maiden whose beauty matched hers. In his madness, he sought to marry his own gentle daughter.

To escape the unlawful union, the princess demanded three impossible gifts: a dress golden as the sun, a dress silver as the moon, and a dress glittering like the stars, along with a cloak made from patches of fur from every wild beast in the forest.

When the coats were delivered, the princess took three golden treasures—a ring, a tiny spinning wheel, and a reel—packed them inside a walnut shell, blackened her face with soot, wrapped herself in the fur cloak, and fled into the deep forest.

A neighboring king hunting with hounds discovered the creature in a hollow tree, named her Allerleirauh (All-Kinds-of-Fur), and put her to work in the palace kitchen sweeping ashes.

At three grand royal balls, she secretly washed the soot from her face, wore her sun, moon, and star dresses, and danced with the king, vanishing before midnight and leaving her golden treasures in the king's bread bowl.

On the third night, the king slipped a golden ring upon her finger. When she baked the bread in her fur cloak, the ring was found. The king seized her fur cloak, it slipped off, and her star-spangled dress and golden hair shone forth in royal beauty! The king embraced her, and their wedding was celebrated with great joy.
moral: True nobility cannot be obscured by rough fur; modesty and patient courage triumph over adversity.

title: Bearskin (Bärenhäuter)
summary: A discharged soldier left penniless after the wars met a mysterious stranger with a cloven foot. The stranger offered him limitless gold on one condition: for seven years, he must...
full_text:
A discharged soldier left penniless after the wars met a mysterious stranger with a cloven foot. The stranger offered him limitless gold on one condition: for seven years, he must neither wash, shave, cut his hair, comb his beard, nor say his prayers, wearing only a heavy bearskin cloak. If he died within seven years, his soul was forfeited; if he survived, he was rich and free forever.

The soldier accepted. For several years he wandered, giving boundless alms to the poor so they would pray for him. Soon his face was blackened with grime, his hair matted like a mane, and people fled screaming from "Bearskin."

He stayed at an inn where he paid off the ruinous debts of an honest father. Grateful for his salvation, the father offered Bearskin one of his three daughters in marriage.

The two elder daughters turned away in disgust, mocking his hideous appearance. But the youngest daughter said gently: "He saved our father; I will keep my word to him!"

Bearskin broke his golden ring in two, gave her half, and kept the other, promising to return in three years.

When the seven years were fulfilled, the devil arrived, cursed in defeat, washed Bearskin clean, trimmed his beard, and dressed him in magnificent royal velvet.

Bearskin returned to the inn as a handsome nobleman. The two elder sisters flirted with him, while the youngest sat quietly in her mourning dress. Bearskin dropped his half of the ring into her wine cup; she recognized her faithful groom, and they were married with joyous celebration, teaching that true love beholds the soul, not the bearskin.
moral: Inner fidelity and quiet endurance of outward contempt win the true reward of love.

full_text:
Beneath a fragrant juniper tree in the garden, a pious mother prayed for a child red as blood and white as snow. She bore a son, but died of joy, asking to be buried under the juniper tree.

The father remarried, and the second wife bore a daughter named Marlene. The stepmother loved Marlene, but despised the little boy, plotted his destruction, and killed him with a falling chest lid, cooking his flesh in a stew.

Little Marlene wept inconsolably. She gathered the little brother's bones in her silk kerchief and laid them beneath the fragrant juniper tree.

Suddenly, the tree rustled, mist rose from the branches, and out flew a magnificent golden bird singing with a voice of celestial beauty!

The bird flew through the town, singing its tragic tale to a goldsmith, a shoemaker, and twenty millers, receiving a golden chain, red shoes, and a heavy millstone in reward.

The bird flew back to the father's house, dropped the golden chain around the father's neck, dropped the red shoes for little Marlene, and dropped the heavy millstone upon the wicked stepmother, crushing her to dust!

In a flash of light, the brother stood whole and radiant once more, taking his father and sister by the hand, living in peace and eternal joy.
moral: Hidden murder cannot escape the justice of creation; truth sings through the branches.

full_text:
A king lost in a great forest married a witch's daughter to find his way out. Fearing for his six sons and one daughter, he hid them in a secret castle in the woods, finding his way by a magical ball of yarn.

The wicked queen discovered the secret, sewed six shirts of enchanted white silk, and threw them over the six princes, transforming them into six wild swans that flew away over the forest.

The little sister walked into the wilderness to find her brothers. In a hut, the six swans arrived at sunset, shedding their feathers for fifteen minutes. They told her: "We can be saved only if you sew six shirts of star-flowers, and maintain absolute silence for six years without speaking or laughing!"

The maiden lived in a tall tree, sewing silently day and night.

A king found her, loved her quiet grace, and made her his queen. But his wicked mother stole the queen's newborn children, smeared her mouth with blood, and accused her of devouring them.

Even at the stake, the queen remained steadfastly silent, finishing the sixth shirt.

As the torch touched the wood, six swans flew down! She threw the shirts over them, and six handsome princes stood before the throne! Only the youngest had a swan's wing on his left arm, because the sleeve lacked a few stitches.

The queen spoke, declaring her innocence; the stolen children were restored, and the wicked mother-in-law was brought to justice.
moral: Patient, silent sacrifice endures all false accusations to redeem those we love.

title: Little Briar Rose (The Thorn Castle)
summary: Enchanted by the uninvited thirteenth fairy to sleep for a century upon pricking her finger on a spindle, the royal maiden and the entire castle fell into motionless slumber....
full_text:
Long ago, in a magnificent kingdom bordered by whispering pine forests, a king and queen rejoiced after many years of longing at the birth of a daughter of incomparable beauty. To celebrate the royal christening, the king held a grand feast, inviting the twelve wise fairy women of the realm. Alas, he possessed only twelve golden plates, so the thirteenth fairy was left uninvited. As the feast drew to a close, eleven fairies bestowed their miraculous blessings upon the golden cradle: radiant virtue, boundless wisdom, sweet melody, and grace. Suddenly, the bronze doors burst open, and the furious thirteenth fairy entered the hall. Pointing her iron staff at the infant, she hissed: 'In her fifteenth year, the king's daughter shall prick her finger on a spinning spindle, and fall down dead!'

Before the weeping parents could despair, the twelfth fairy stepped forward, whose gift was yet unspoken. 'The curse cannot be wholly revoked,' she spoke gently, 'yet it may be softened. The maiden shall not die, but fall into a deep, peaceful slumber that shall last for a hundred years.' To shield his darling child, the king commanded every spindle and spinning wheel in the entire realm to be burned to ashes. Yet on the very day of her fifteenth birthday, while wandering through the remote towers of the castle, the princess discovered a hidden spiral staircase leading to a tiny garret room. Inside sat an ancient woman spinning flax. Fascinated by the whirling wheel, the maiden reached out her hand to touch the spindle. The sharp point pricked her finger, and that very instant, she sank onto an embroidered couch in motionless slumber.

In that same moment, a magical stillness fell upon the entire palace. The king and queen fell asleep upon their thrones, the courtiers slept in the grand hall, the horses slept in the stables, the hounds in the courtyard, the doves upon the roof, and even the flies upon the stone walls. The crackling fire on the hearth ceased its flickering and fell asleep, while the roasting meat stopped sizzling. Around the silent castle grew a dense hedge of wild briar thorns, rising year after year until not even the weather-vanes atop the towers could be seen. Many brave princes attempted to force their way through the tangled thorns, but the briars seized them like iron claws. At last, when the hundred years had fully passed, a gentle prince arrived whose heart was pure. As he approached, the briar thorns burst into millions of fragrant crimson roses, parting willingly before his footsteps. Climbing the tower, he beheld the sleeping maiden, was overwhelmed by her radiant beauty, and bent down to bestow a tender kiss. Little Briar Rose opened her shining eyes, smiled with joy, and life, music, and laughter awakened across the entire kingdom once more.
moral: The appointed hour of providence dissolves every barrier of thorn and sleep.

title: The Three Spinners
summary: A lazy maiden who hated spinning was forced by the queen to spin three rooms of flax or lose her life....
full_text:
There was once a young maiden who was so lazy that she wept bitter tears whenever she was asked to spin even a single skein of flax. Her hardworking mother scuffled with her in frustration, and the girl's loud wailing was heard by the Queen, who was riding past the village in her golden carriage. The embarrassed mother, ashamed to admit her daughter's indolence, bowed low and said: 'Gracious Majesty, my daughter loves spinning so passionately that I cannot tear her away from the wheel, and I am too poor to buy enough flax to satisfy her!' Delighted by such diligence, the Queen carried the girl to the royal palace and led her into three enormous chambers filled from floor to ceiling with the finest golden flax. 'Spin all this flax into thread,' promised the Queen, 'and you shall marry my eldest son, the Crown Prince!'

Left alone in the first chamber, the terrified maiden sat down and wept for three days, knowing she could never spin a fraction of the mountain before her. On the third evening, the chamber door creaked open, and three strange fairy women stepped inside. The first had a monstrously broad, flat right foot; the second had an enormous, drooping thumb three times the size of a mortal hand; and the third had a great hanging lower lip that reached her chin. 'Do not weep, dear child,' whispered the three visitors. 'If you will invite us to your royal wedding, seat us at the high table without being ashamed of our deformities, and introduce us as your beloved cousins, we will spin all three rooms of flax for you in the twinkling of an eye!'

The maiden agreed with heartfelt gratitude. The first woman treadled the wheel with her giant flat foot; the second twisted the thread with her monstrous thumb; and the third moistened the yarn with her hanging lip. Within three nights, all three chambers were filled with skeins of dazzling, snow-white linen! The Queen was overjoyed, and a lavish royal wedding was prepared. True to her promise, the bride welcomed the three grotesque cousins into the banquet hall and seated them in seats of honor. When the handsome Prince noticed their bizarre deformities, he asked with astonishment: 'Dear cousins, how did you come to possess such extraordinary features?' 'From treadling the wheel!' answered the first. 'From twisting the coarse yarn!' answered the second. 'From licking the dry flax!' chuckled the third. Horrified by their answers, the young Prince immediately turned to his beautiful bride, took her tender hands, and declared before the entire court: 'From this day forth, my beloved wife shall never touch a spinning wheel again as long as she lives!'
moral: Cooperation and wit save from impossible burdens without resorting to falsehood.

title: The Elves (Die Wichtelmänner)
summary: A poor, honest shoemaker had only leather left for a single pair of shoes. He cut the leather out in the evening, said his prayers, and went peacefully to sleep....
full_text:
A poor, honest shoemaker had only leather left for a single pair of shoes. He cut the leather out in the evening, said his prayers, and went peacefully to sleep.

In the morning, he found the shoes finished upon his workbench, stitched with such miraculous perfection that not a single stitch was awry! A customer bought them for double the price.

Night after night, the miracle continued: whatever leather he cut in the evening was finished by morning into magnificent footwear. The shoemaker became a prosperous man.

One night, the shoemaker and his wife hid behind a curtain to watch. At midnight, two tiny, naked little men slipped in, sat cross-legged, and stitched with lightning speed until dawn!

The grateful wife said: "These little men have made us rich; let us sew them tiny coats, shirts, breeches, and knit tiny shoes!"

On Christmas Eve, they laid the tiny clothes on the bench instead of leather. At midnight, the little elves arrived, dressed themselves in the fine coats, danced merrily upon the table, singing:
"Now we are boys so fine and neat,
Why should we longer cobble the street?"

They leaped out the window into the night. Though they never returned, good fortune and prosperity blessed the honest shoemaker to the end of his days.
moral: Unseen blessings reward honest labor; gratitude clothed in kindness blesses the helper.

The youth returned, told the cities that a toad under the fountain and a mouse at the tree root were causing the blights, and warned the ferryman to thrust his pole into the hands of the next passenger to be free.

The king rode to the river to seize the treasure, took the pole from the ferryman, and was condemned to row the ferry forever; while the lucky boy reigned in peace.

full_text:
Twelve lovely princesses slept in twelve beds in a locked royal chamber, yet every morning their slippers were found worn into holes as if they had danced all night!

The king promised his kingdom to whoever could solve the mystery in three nights; failure meant the scaffold. Many princes tried, fell into drugged slumber, and were executed.

An old wounded soldier received an invisible cloak from an old woman: "Do not drink the wine they offer you, and pretend to sleep!"

The soldier feigned sleep. At midnight, the eldest princess tapped her bed; it sank into the earth, opening a secret stair. Putting on his invisible cloak, the soldier followed them down through groves of silver trees, gold trees, and diamond trees, breaking a twig from each.

They crossed a subterranean lake in twelve boats rowed by twelve handsome princes, entering an enchanted golden castle where they danced until their satin shoes were shredded!

On the third morning, the soldier stood before the king, showed the silver, gold, and diamond twigs, and produced the golden goblet he had taken.

The princesses confessed the enchantment; the soldier chose the eldest princess as his bride and inherited the crown.
moral: Vigilance, discretion, and presence of mind solve the deepest enchantments.

title: The Old Man and His Grandson
summary: An old grandfather could scarcely walk; his knees trembled, his eyes were dim, and his hands shook so that he spilled soup on the tablecloth....
keywords: the old man and his grandson
full_text:
An old grandfather could scarcely walk; his knees trembled, his eyes were dim, and his hands shook so that he spilled soup on the tablecloth.

Disgusted, his son and daughter-in-law made him sit in the corner behind the stove, feeding him scraps from a cheap earthenware bowl. One day, the bowl broke, and they bought him a rough wooden trough.

One afternoon, the parents saw their four-year-old son fitting little wooden boards together on the floor.

"What are you making, my child?" asked the father lovingly.

The little boy replied: "I am making a little wooden trough for you and mother to eat from when I grow up and you are old!"

The husband and wife looked at each other and burst into tears of shame. They brought the old grandfather back to the master table, ate with him in honor, and never spoke another harsh word to him again.
moral: Treat your aged parents with tender reverence, as you would have your own children treat you.

title: Clever Grethel
summary: Grethel the cook roasted two fat partridges for her master's guest. Tempted by the savory aroma, she tasted a wing; then the other; then both birds were eaten completely, washed do...
full_text:
In the manor of a wealthy country gentleman lived a cook named Grethel, who loved good food and fine wine above all earthly things. Whenever she went about the kitchen in her red-buckled shoes, she would admire her reflection in the copper pans, sip from the master's best wine casks, and declare: 'A cook must know how the dishes taste, else how can she serve her master with honor?' One evening, her master announced that an honored guest was arriving for supper, commanding Grethel to roast two plump, tender partridges on the spit with butter, sage, and wild thyme.

Grethel basted the birds until their skin turned a crisp, golden brown, filling the kitchen with an aroma so heavenly that her mouth watered without ceasing. The supper hour arrived, but the guest had not yet appeared. The master decided to walk down to the village road to find him, telling Grethel to keep the spit turning. Alone beside the glowing hearth, Grethel looked at the succulent birds: 'It would be a sin to let them dry and burn!' She took a wing to taste the seasoning—it was so delicious that she promptly ate the second wing. Poured another cup of sweet wine, she reasoned: 'One bird cannot lie alone on the platter; it looks unbalanced!' Within ten minutes, the first partridge was devoured completely. Driven by the wine and the irresistible fragrance, she carved into the second bird, until only a plate of clean white bones remained on the kitchen table!

Just then, the master burst into the courtyard, calling out: 'Hurry, Grethel, the guest is coming down the lane! Bring out the carving knives!' Grethel wiped her lips and ran to the front gate just as the guest approached. Seizing his sleeve with an expression of frantic terror, she whispered: 'Flee for your life, sir! My master has invited you here only to cut off both your ears! Hear him grinding his great carving knife upon the whetstone this very moment!' Terrified by the scraping noise from the pantry, the guest gathered his cloak and sprinted down the road as fast as his legs could carry him. Grethel ran back to her master in the pantry, wailing: 'A fine guest you invited! He snatched both of your roasted partridges right off the platter and ran off down the lane!' The master ran to the doorway with his carving knife in hand, shouting: 'Just one! Leave me just one!' The fleeing guest, believing the master meant one of his ears, ran even faster into the night, while clever Grethel laughed into her apron and poured herself another cup of wine!
moral: Audacious lies to cover greed create comical panics.

full_text:
There was once a king's son who went out into the world full of thoughtful sorrow, reflecting upon the vanity of earthly pomp and the burdens of worldly crowns. Walking across lonely hills and simple meadows, he met a poor old man with silver hair sitting upon a stone, sharing a dry crust with wild birds that flocked to his weathered hand.

The prince sat beside the gentle wanderer and asked, "Father, why do you look so serene when you possess neither gold nor roof against the night?"

The old man smiled softly and answered, "My child, true wealth is not measured in jewels that rust or palaces that crumble to dust. He who walks in humility, seeks neither praise nor vanity, and opens his hand to the suffering, finds that the simplest path leads straight to heaven."

Deeply moved by the elder's peace, the prince cast aside his velvet mantle, clad himself in a plain coarse coat, and walked among the villages, nursing the sick, soothing the broken-hearted, and asking for nothing in return. When his earthly journey reached its evening, celestial light shone upon the peaceful meadow where he lay, and gentle choruses welcomed him into enduring bliss, proving that purity of spirit and quiet love outshine all the crowns of kings.
moral: A humble heart that shares even the smallest crust in love attains true peace and eternal joy.

full_text:
A young tailor, cheerful of spirit and bold of heart, journeyed deep into a vast forest where towering oaks shut out the sun. As twilight fell, he found refuge inside an underground vault, where an ancient dwarf with a snowy beard stood guarding wonders beyond mortal imagination.

Beneath crystal arches sat a magnificent glass coffin, glowing with warm radiance. Gazing through the clear crystal, the tailor beheld an extraordinarily beautiful maiden lying in enchanted slumber, adorned in silk with golden tresses flowing over her shoulders. Beside her stood miniature castles and enchanted towns sealed within glass vessels.

To release her from the wicked sorcerer's binding spell, the tailor had to overcome ferocious subterranean beasts and break the enchanted seal with fearless devotion. Undaunted by terrifying shadows, he shattered the dark runes. The glass lid swung open, and the lovely maiden awakened with a joyous breath.

She revealed herself to be a wealthy count's daughter imprisoned by an envious wizard. In gratitude for his steadfast valor, she offered him her hand, and the enchanted miniature realm expanded into a flourishing, joyful estate where they ruled in harmony and kindness for all their days.
moral: Courage and an upright spirit can break the darkest enchantments and restore beauty to the light.

full_text:
Lazy Harry was so exceedingly fond of rest that his greatest trial in life was driving his single goat out to pasture every morning. He would stretch upon the grass and sigh, "Ah, what weary work it is to watch this restless beast all day long! If only I had a wife with a goat of her own, she could pasture mine as well, and I might sleep until noon."

With this grand plan in mind, Harry courted Fat Trina, whose father owned a healthy goat. The match was struck, and the two lazy souls wed with great rejoicing. But soon Trina complained bitterly that her ankles ached from walking the pasture.

"Listen, Harry," proposed Trina. "Let us trade our two goats to neighbor Heinz for a beehive! Bees take care of themselves, fly out into the blossoms without driving, make sweet honey without our labor, and need no tending at all."

Harry marveled at her genius. They traded the goats and set the hive near the window. Yet before the first drop of honey could be enjoyed, the pair quarreled over who would stir the pot. Trina brandished her wooden hazel stick in passionate argument, accidentally striking the hive and overturning it entirely into the mud. The furious bees swarmed, stinging them both soundly, leaving the idle dreamers without honey, without goats, and nursing painful lumps as a reminder of their grand follies.
moral: Endless schemes to avoid honest toil usually collapse under the weight of their own foolishness.

There was once a king whose daughter fell gravely ill, and the physicians declared she could only be restored to health by eating apples from a miraculous tree. A poor peasant's youngest son, Hans, whom everyone mocked as simple, carried a basket of these golden apples to the palace, where they cured the princess completely.

The ungrateful king, unwilling to give his daughter to a lowly lad, set an impossible condition: "You shall not marry my daughter until you bring me a golden feather plucked from the tail of the terrifying Griffin who dwells at the edge of the world."

Hans bravely set out on the perilous journey. Along the way, he met a master of a lake who could not cross passengers without endless rowing, a king whose fountain had run dry of wine, and another whose tree of gold no longer bore fruit. Hans promised to find answers for each from the mythical Griffin.

Reaching the Griffin's mountain lair, Hans found the beast's kind-hearted wife, who hid him beneath the bed. When the Griffin returned home, hungry and grumbling, the woman gently pulled a golden feather from his tail each time he fell asleep, eliciting the secret answers to the riddles Hans had gathered.

Armed with three golden feathers and the answers, Hans returned. He revealed the toad beneath the dry fountain, the mouse gnawing the golden tree's root, and taught the boatman how to pass his oars to the next traveler. When the jealous king sought the Griffin's hoard for himself, the boatman thrust the oars into his hands, leaving the greedy monarch to row across the dark river forever, while Hans married the princess in everlasting joy.
moral: Quick wits, humble courage, and keen listening conquer monsters that brute force cannot overcome.

Returning his mother safely to his long-grieving father, Hans embarked on adventures across the realm. He joined forces with Fir-Twister and Rock-Splitter, two giants of great renown. Together they ventured into an enchanted subterranean castle to rescue a captured princess from an ancient mountain demon.

When the companions betrayed Hans and abandoned him in the abyss, Hans refused to despair. Using his wits and an enchanted ring he won from the underworld spirit, he summoned magical birds that carried him to the upper world. He confronted the false companions, rescued the grateful princess, and proved that a clean conscience and iron loyalty are mightier than any treacherous scheme.

full_text:
A poor, honest peasant arrived at the pearly gates of heaven on the very same morning as a wealthy, celebrated nobleman. When the nobleman approached, heavenly trumpets sounded, angels sang glorious hymns, and celestial gates swung wide in grand celebration.

The peasant stepped forward next, but he was admitted quietly, with gentle smiles from the gatekeeper but without brass horns or grand pageantry. The peasant stood softly in the heavenly courtyard, feeling a brief tremor of worldly doubt, wondering why rich lords were heralded with such thunder while humble plowmen entered in silence.

Saint Peter walked over to him, resting a warm, benevolent hand upon his shoulder. "My son," whispered Peter, "do not misunderstand what you have witnessed. Poor, honest peasants like yourself enter the kingdom of heaven every hour of every day; your steadfast goodness is familiar and beloved in our midst. But a wealthy lord who manages to live righteously, resist greed, and cross this threshold is so rare an arrival that all heaven rejoices when one is saved!"

Hearing this, the peasant chuckled with warm delight, understanding the divine humor and justice, and strolled happily into paradise to enjoy unending peace.
moral: True heavenly celebration welcomes every soul according to the rarity and quiet trials of its journey.

title: Lean Lisa
summary: Lean Lisa had an entirely different disposition from Lazy Harry; she was constantly restless, thrifty to a fault, and worried incessantly about how to amass a greater fortune. She...
full_text:
Lean Lisa had an entirely different disposition from Lazy Harry; she was constantly restless, thrifty to a fault, and worried incessantly about how to amass a greater fortune. She drove her poor husband Long Lenz from dawn to dusk, scolding him for every crumb he dropped and every minute he rested.

One evening, as they sat by the dim hearth, Lisa began to calculate future gains: "If we gather three silver pieces, we shall buy a young calf. The calf will grow into a cow; the cow will give rich milk and bear another calf, and soon we shall have a grand herd that fills the pasture."

"Splendid," said Lenz. "And when the herd multiplies, the boys can milk them and drink sweet cream."

"Drink cream?" shrieked Lisa, her eyes flashing fire. "Never! Do you think we raise cattle for silly children to guzzle down our profits? Every drop of cream shall be churned into butter and sold at the town market!"

"Come now, wife," Lenz reasoned, "the children must have their share."

Furious that her husband dared dispute the distribution of milk from a cow that did not yet exist, Lisa seized the heavy hearth-broom and struck him across the shoulders. Lenz caught the stick, and they scuffled across the cottage, knocking over their only water pitcher and scattering the firewood. When the dust settled, both sat bruised, cold, and exhausted, possessing neither calf nor cream, but only the bitter folly of fighting over castles in the air.
moral: Unbridled greed and arguing over imaginary possessions destroy present peace.

A poor woodcutter lived on the edge of a deep forest with his wife and three daughters. One day, the eldest daughter was sent into the woods carrying dinner to her father, but mistaking the trail of millet he had scattered, she wandered deep into the thickets until night fell.

She spotted a solitary light shining from an old thatched hut. Knocking at the door, she was greeted by an elderly grey-haired man sitting at a rustic table, while around him lay an old speckled hen, a red cock, and a spotted cow. The girl asked for food and shelter. The old man asked his animals if they agreed, and they clucked and mooed their consent. The girl ate heartily of the porridge, but offered not a crumb to the faithful creatures, nor did she bid them goodnight. When she went upstairs to sleep, the floor gave way, dropping her into a dark cellar.

The second daughter suffered the exact same fate on the following day, selfishly feeding only herself and ignoring the beasts.

On the third day, the youngest daughter ventured out. Arriving at the hut, she greeted the old man with gentle warmth, stroked the hen and the cock, and gave the spotted cow a generous handful of sweet hay. She shared her supper with all three beasts before tasting a single spoonful herself, and made sure their water trough was filled.

When she awoke next morning, the tiny hut had transformed into a dazzling royal palace of marble and gold! The old man was revealed to be an enchanted prince, transformed by a sorcerer until a maiden of pure compassion should appear who treated beasts with the same loving honor as kings. The cellar opened to release the older sisters, who were sent to learn humility, while the youngest married the prince and lived in boundless harmony.
moral: Kindness shown to the smallest and humblest creatures unlocks the door to genuine blessing.

title: Sharing Joy and Sorrow
summary: A stubborn and ill-tempered tailor married a clever, spirited woman and immediately declared: "In this household, wife, we shall share joy and sorrow equally. When I eat tasty roas...
full_text:
A stubborn and ill-tempered tailor married a clever, spirited woman and immediately declared: "In this household, wife, we shall share joy and sorrow equally. When I eat tasty roasts and drink fine wine, that is my joy, and you shall share in my pleasure by watching me eat. When you fail to obey my slightest whim, that is my sorrow, and you shall share in it by feeling my measuring yard across your shoulders!"

The clever wife said nothing, but bided her time. One morning, the tailor ordered three plump sausages fried for his supper and left for the village. The wife cooked the sausages to perfection, but realizing her husband's intolerable cruelty, she sat down and ate two of them with relish, leaving only the smallest skin behind.

When the tailor returned and saw the empty plate, he flew into a rage: "Where are my two sausages, wretched woman?"

"Husband," she replied sweetly, "I was sharing your joy! You always taught me that joy must be shared. Watching you eat gave me such radiant happiness that I thought experiencing the taste directly would double our marital joy!"

Furious, the tailor seized his measuring yard, but the wife quickly slipped behind the heavy kitchen cupboard, causing him to stumble over his own stool and overturn a kettle of cold dye upon his trousers. Shivering and soaked in indigo, he sat on the floor, while she laughed: "Now, beloved husband, we can truly share your sorrow, for your clothes are ruined, but your wit has at last been sharpened!" From that day onward, the tailor spoke far more gently to his wife.
moral: Those who demand obedience without affection find that wit can make their own harsh rules their downfall.

title: The Willow-Wren
summary: Once upon a time, the birds of the air grew tired of having no ruler and resolved to hold a contest: whichever bird could fly highest into the sky should be crowned king of all win...
full_text:
Once upon a time, the birds of the air grew tired of having no ruler and resolved to hold a contest: whichever bird could fly highest into the sky should be crowned king of all winged creatures.

On a bright summer morning, eagles, hawks, storks, and songbirds gathered in a vast meadow. At the signal, they all launched into the heavens. The smaller birds soon wearied and dropped back to earth, leaving only the mighty Eagle soaring higher and higher, brushing the very clouds. Convinced of his victory, the Eagle cried out in triumph, "I am your king!"

Suddenly, from beneath the Eagle's breast feathers, a tiny Willow-Wren popped out. He had hitched a ride unseen, and now fluttered another twenty feet into the blue, chirping proudly, "King am I! King am I!"

The birds below were outraged at this trickery. They refused to crown the little cheat unless he could prove his worth by sinking deepest into the earth. The wren hopped into a mouse-hole and refused to come out. The birds set the Owl to guard the hole, but the Owl nodded off in the morning sun, allowing the nimble wren to escape into the hazel hedges.

To this day, the Willow-Wren is called Kinglet, chirping defiantly from deep within the briars, reminding all creatures that size alone does not determine the dignity of a ruler.
moral: True sovereignty is earned not by mere size or empty flight, but through resourcefulness and integrity.

title: The Sole
summary: The fishes of the sea, having lived in wild confusion for centuries, decided they needed a king to maintain order and dispense justice in the deep waters. They agreed that whicheve...
full_text:
The fishes of the sea, having lived in wild confusion for centuries, decided they needed a king to maintain order and dispense justice in the deep waters. They agreed that whichever fish could swim fastest through the waves to the distant sandbar should be proclaimed sovereign.

The Pike, the Salmon, the Herring, and all the finned creatures lined up in the blue swell. At the signal, they darted forward with tremendous speed. The nimble Herring outpaced them all, shooting like a silver arrow through the foam and touching the sandbar first.

The Sole, a flat, boastful fish who had lagged far behind, arrived breathless and asked with arrogant disdain, "Who is it that has won the crown?"

"The Herring! The Herring!" cried the joyous assembly of fishes.

"The naked Herring?" sneered the Sole, twisting his mouth in bitter mockery and curling his lip. "That scrawny little fellow our king? What an absurd joke!"

Because of this venomous grimace of envy and disrespect, the Sole's mouth remained twisted to one side forever, his eyes shifted awkwardly to the upper surface, and he was condemned to crawl flat upon the ocean floor, bearing the permanent mark of his jealous spite.
moral: Envy and jealous mockery disfigure the soul and leave an indelible mark.

title: The Bittern and the Hoopoe
summary: In ancient times, before they took their avian forms, the Bittern and the Hoopoe were mortal herdsmen pasturing cattle in adjacent meadows....
full_text:
In ancient times, before they took their avian forms, the Bittern and the Hoopoe were mortal herdsmen pasturing cattle in adjacent meadows.

The man who became the Bittern had rich, fat cows, but he was indolent and loved his afternoon nap. While he slumbered beneath the alders, his cows strayed into treacherous bogs and sank into the mire. When he awoke and found his herd missing, he rushed wildly among the reeds, crying in desperate mournful tones, "Come back! Come back!" transformed into a marsh bird whose hollow, booming cry echoes across the fens to this day.

The man who became the Hoopoe, on the other hand, was assigned lean, unruly heifers that sprinted in all directions. He had to run up hills and down valleys, waving his staff, shouting and whistling until his breath gave out: "Up, up, up! Heifers, back!" In the end, he was changed into the crested Hoopoe, whose distinctive call "Up-up-up" still sounds from sunny glades, forever echoing the frantic cries of a herdsman trying to keep his wandering herd in line.
moral: Neglect of duty brings lamentation, while diligent care preserves honor.

title: The Owl
summary: A couple of centuries ago, an owl strayed into a town barn by mistake, seeking shelter from the blinding sunlight. When the servant went to fetch hay in the afternoon, he saw two h...
full_text:
A couple of centuries ago, an owl strayed into a town barn by mistake, seeking shelter from the blinding sunlight. When the servant went to fetch hay in the afternoon, he saw two huge fiery eyes glowing in the dark rafters and fled screaming that a terrifying demon had invaded the village.

The mayor assembled the town council, armed with pitchforks, scythes, and heavy clubs. Peeking through the door, the trembling villagers saw the bird blink its round eyes and heard it snap its beak with a quiet click. Panic gripped the crowd. "It is a monster from the abyss!" shouted the mayor. "If it escapes, it will devour our children and ruin our crops!"

Rather than confront the harmless creature, the heroic town elders decided there was only one safe course: they barricaded the barn tightly and set fire to the four corners. The flames devoured the timber, the wheat, and the hay, reducing the proudest building in the valley to smoldering ashes.

Just as the roof collapsed, the owl spread its soft wings, soared silently through the smoke into the open blue sky, and perched on a distant oak, unharmed and deeply amused, leaving the foolish villagers weeping over their self-inflicted ruin.
moral: Ignorance and irrational panic turn harmless wonders into terrifying monsters.

title: The Moon
summary: In ancient days, there was a land where the night was pitch-dark, for no moon shone in their heavens. Four wanderers journeyed to another country and saw a radiant silver sphere ha...
full_text:
In ancient days, there was a land where the night was pitch-dark, for no moon shone in their heavens. Four wanderers journeyed to another country and saw a radiant silver sphere hanging from the bough of an oak tree, shedding soft, beautiful light across the fields.

Learning that the villagers paid a small tax to keep the oil lamp burning, the four greedy travelers stole the silver moon, carried it back to their own land, and hung it in a tall tree, demanding payment from their neighbors for its light.

As the four men grew old and passed away one by one, each demanded that a quarter of the moon be cut off and buried in his coffin. When the last man died, the sky was completely dark once more, while down in the underworld, the four quarters reunited, shedding light upon the departed souls.

The spirits of the underworld awoke, mistaking the light for daylight, and began drinking, singing, and bowling in a riotous tavern brawl. Hearing the commotion shaking the earth, Saint Peter rode down on his steed to restore order. He calmed the riotous dead, took the silver moon in his hands, and carried it high into the celestial vault, hanging it forever in the open night sky where its gentle light can bless all living beings without price or ownership.
moral: Natural wonders and light belong to all humanity, not to be hoarded by selfish pride.

title: The Duration of Life
summary: When the Creator created the world and appointed the years of life to each living creature, the Donkey came first and was offered thirty years. The Donkey sighed, "Lord, thirty yea...
full_text:
When the Creator created the world and appointed the years of life to each living creature, the Donkey came first and was offered thirty years. The Donkey sighed, "Lord, thirty years of carrying heavy sacks to the mill, being beaten with sticks, and eating thistles is far too weary a burden. Spare me half of them!" And eighteen years were taken away.

Next came the Dog, who was offered thirty years. "Lord," wept the Dog, "running, barking at thieves, losing teeth, and lying stiffly in corners is too long a misery. Give me fewer!" And twelve years were removed.

Next came the Monkey, who begged for relief from thirty years of making silly faces to amuse ungrateful spectators, and ten years were lifted from him.

Finally came Man, proud and joyful, who was offered thirty years. "Thirty years?" protested Man. "Just when I build my house and plant my fields, I must depart? Give me more!"

The Creator granted him the eighteen years refused by the donkey, the twelve years refused by the dog, and the ten years refused by the monkey.

Thus it is that Man lives his first thirty years in human vigor and joy. Then follow the donkey years, bearing heavy burdens of household toil; then the dog years, sitting watchful in the corner, grumbling and guarding; and finally the monkey years, silly and weak, mocked by the young as age takes its toll.
moral: Every stage of life has its appointed character; peace comes from accepting each season with grace.

title: Death's Messengers
summary: In ancient times, a robust young giant was traveling along the highway when he encountered Death sitting exhausted by the roadside, having been beaten in a duel with a mighty champ...
full_text:
In ancient times, a robust young giant was traveling along the highway when he encountered Death sitting exhausted by the roadside, having been beaten in a duel with a mighty champion. The compassionate young man revived Death with fresh spring water and helped him to his feet.

In gratitude, Death promised: "I cannot spare you when your appointed hour strikes, for my duty is universal. But this I swear: I will never come upon you unawares. I shall send my messengers ahead to announce my coming, so you may be ready."

Years passed into decades. The young man grew into a prosperous citizen, enjoying health, wine, and laughter. But gradually, his hair turned silver, his eyesight dimmed, his joints began to ache with winter frost, and a dull ringing settled in his ears. Yet he remained carefree, thinking, "Death has not arrived; he has not sent his heralds!"

At last, a cold tap touched his shoulder, and Death stood before him. "It is time," Death declared.

"False friend!" cried the man. "Did you not swear to send messengers before taking me?"

"Foolish man," answered Death softly. "Have I not sent them every single year? Did not gray hair, failing vision, aching bones, and heavy breath knock upon your door? Every pain, every wrinkle, every weary step was my messenger whispering: prepare your house, for the evening draws near." The man bowed his head in humble understanding, and accompanied his guide into peace.
moral: The aches and changes of aging are gentle warnings to prepare the soul with wisdom and kindness.

title: Master Pfriem
summary: Master Pfriem was a cobbler so exceedingly irritable and fault-finding that nothing on earth could ever please him. If a shoe had five stitches, he complained it lacked six; if the...
full_text:
Master Pfriem was a cobbler so exceedingly irritable and fault-finding that nothing on earth could ever please him. If a shoe had five stitches, he complained it lacked six; if the leather was soft, he insisted it should be stiff; and if the apprentice was diligent, Pfriem cursed him for being slow.

When Pfriem died, he climbed up to heaven's gate and knocked loudly. Saint Peter opened the gate and warned him: "Master Pfriem, you may enter heaven, but remember this: you must keep your mouth shut. Here you must find no faults, critique no angel, and meddle in no divine affairs, or you will be cast out."

Pfriem promised to behave, but within an hour his fingers twitched with irritation. He saw two angels carrying a great beam; they held it crosswise instead of lengthwise, making it hard to pass through the golden portal. Pfriem bit his lip until blood flowed, trying to restrain himself.

Next, he saw a team of celestial horses pulling an overloaded wagon of hay, and the driver sat backward. This was too much for the compulsive fault-finder. "Hey, you clumsy blockhead!" shouted Pfriem at the top of his lungs. "Who ever saw horses harnessed that way? Turn your cart around, you foolish knave!"

At that instant, Saint Peter appeared, took Master Pfriem by the collar, and gently led him outside the gates, saying, "Go find a kingdom where perfection needs your corrections, for heaven requires only gratitude and peace."

title: The Goose-Girl (Die Gänsemagd)
summary: A beautiful royal princess was betrothed to a king's son in a distant land. When the time came for her bridal journey, her loving mother gave her a handkerchief marked with three d...
full_text:
A beautiful royal princess was betrothed to a king's son in a distant land. When the time came for her bridal journey, her loving mother gave her a handkerchief marked with three drops of maternal blood for protection, and a magnificent talking horse named Falada. She was accompanied by a treacherous maid-in-waiting.

On the long journey across parched plains, the princess asked the maid to fetch her a cup of water from the brook. The maid arrogantly refused: "I will not serve you any longer; climb down and drink yourself!" In her distress, the princess dropped her handkerchief into the stream, losing her mother's blessing.

Taking advantage of her weakness, the cruel maid forced the princess to trade dresses, switch horses, and swear a solemn oath beneath the open sky never to reveal the betrayal to any mortal living soul. At the palace, the false bride was received in grand splendor, while the real princess was sent into the meadows to herd geese alongside a boy named Conrad.

Fearing the horse would speak, the wicked maid ordered Falada beheaded. But the gentle princess begged the knacker to nail the horse's head over the dark city gateway, where she passed every morning. As she walked beneath, she sighed: "Alas, Falada, hanging there!" and the horse answered: "Alas, young queen, how sad your share! If your dear mother only knew, her loving heart would break in two."

Conrad grew furious when the princess untied her golden hair in the meadow, gleaming like the sun, and the wind blew his hat away whenever he tried to steal a strand. He complained to the old king, who observed the girl and saw her deep sorrow.

When the king questioned her, she wept that she had sworn never to tell her grief to any mortal. The wise old king said: "If you cannot speak to me, pour out your heart to the iron stove in the corner."

The princess crawled into the warm iron stove and poured forth her whole tragic story of treachery and suffering. The king, listening through the flue pipe outside, heard every word. He clothed her in royal silk, summoned a magnificent feast, and asked the false bride what punishment a traitor deserved. The wicked maid condemned herself out of her own mouth, and the true queen was restored to her rightful throne beside her joyful prince.
moral: True nobility cannot be stolen, and the quiet truth will always triumph over deceit.
