title: Birbal and the Barbers
summary: The barbers of Agra spread wild rumors that send commodity prices soaring. Birbal teaches the guild a humorous lesson in accountability.
full_text:
The barbers of Agra were the social heart of the city; while shaving beards and massaging heads, they shared news, political rumors, and market gossip. However, several unscrupulous barbers began inventing wild rumors—claiming that the salt supply was exhausted, or that the Emperor was banning grain trade—causing panicked citizens to hoard food, doubling prices in the bazaar.

Akbar asked Birbal to curb the dangerous rumor-mongering without restricting free speech.

Birbal summoned the leaders of the barbers' guild to the palace. With a very grave face, Birbal announced:

'Brothers, I have an urgent imperial assignment for your guild. His Majesty has decreed that next week, the imperial treasury will reward every barber in Agra with one gold coin for every genuine piece of news he brings to court.

'However, to ensure accuracy, if any rumor brought by a barber turns out to be false, the barber must forfeit one ear to the royal executioner!'

The barbers looked at each other in sheer terror!

'One ear?' the guildmaster stammered. 'My lord, gossip is only talk! We only repeat what we hear in the morning breeze!'

'Then let your morning breeze be silent, or verify your facts before you speak!' Birbal smiled sharply. 'If you are unwilling to risk your own ear for your words, do not risk the livelihoods of fifty thousand citizens with reckless rumors!'

The barbers bowed low, apologized, and returned to their shops. From that day, the barbers of Agra spoke only of the weather and hair oil, and market prices returned to stability. Akbar commended Birbal for solving the civic crisis with humor and firmness.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Golden Bricks
summary: A nobleman builds a house with bricks covered in gold leaf. Birbal shows him where real golden monuments are built.
full_text:
A vain and wealthy merchant of Agra named Seth Manikchand spent ten thousand gold coins building a luxurious pleasure pavilion with walls faced in bricks covered with shimmering gold leaf. He invited Emperor Akbar and the court to admire his masterpiece:

'Behold, Your Majesty! My golden mansion shall stand for centuries, proving my immense wealth to future generations!'

Akbar looked at the shining walls, but Birbal looked at the crumbling, roofless public orphanage situated right across the dusty street, where barefoot children shivered in the cold.

Birbal stepped forward and said: 'Seth Manikchand, your golden bricks are indeed bright. But tell me—what happens when the rains fall, and looters come with chisels in the night?'

'I have twenty armed guards to protect my walls!' the merchant boasted.

Birbal sighed: 'Then you are a prisoner of your own bricks! Look across the street at those fifty freezing orphan children.

'If you had used that gold to rebuild their roof, feed their hungry bellies, and teach them trades, you would have built fifty living, breathing golden monuments in the hearts of human beings! Living monuments pray for your soul, preserve your honor, and enter heaven before you. But dead bricks of gold breed only envy, theft, and vanity.'

The merchant looked at the shivering orphans, then at his cold, gilded walls. The mirror of truth shattered his vanity.

Weeping with remorse, Manikchand pledged half his fortune to rebuild the orphanage and provide food for the poor. Akbar praised Birbal for reminding everyone that the only true wealth is kindness.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Two Brothers
summary: Two farming brothers secretly carry grain sheaves to each other's barn in the night. Birbal presents them to Akbar as the true nobility of the empire.
full_text:
In a quiet village near Mathura lived two farming brothers, Dev and Ram, who farmed their late father's wheat field together. At harvest, they divided the sheaves into two equal heaps in their open threshing yard.

Dev was married with five young children, while Ram was single and lived alone.

That night, Ram lay awake thinking: 'My brother Dev has a wife and five growing children to feed and clothe. It is not fair that we divided the grain equally; he needs more than I do!'

In the dead of night, Ram crept to the threshing yard, loaded five large sheaves of wheat onto his shoulders, carried them secretly to his brother's heap, and returned to bed with a peaceful heart.

Meanwhile, Dev lay awake thinking: 'My brother Ram lives alone without a wife or sons to help him in his old age. He must save more for his future than I do!'

In the dead of night, Dev crept to the threshing yard, loaded five large sheaves of wheat onto his shoulders, carried them secretly to Ram's heap, and returned to bed with joy.

Next morning, both brothers returned to the field and were bewildered to find their grain heaps exactly equal!

This went on for three nights. On the fourth night, while carrying heavy sheaves through the moonlit field, the two brothers bumped directly into each other in the darkness!

Seeing each other laden with wheat, understanding dawned upon them. They dropped their sheaves and embraced with tears of profound love and joy.

Birbal, who had witnessed the scene while camping nearby, brought the brothers before Emperor Akbar:

'Sire, behold the true nobility of Hindustan. They do not wear silk or gold, yet their hearts are richer than the imperial treasury. Where love seeks the good of the brother above the self, heaven walks upon the earth.'

Akbar was moved to tears, and gifted the brothers a fertile tract of land and a gold medal of fraternal virtue.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Wise Minister Test
summary: Akbar asks why Birbal receives higher honors than other ministers. Birbal demonstrates the difference with a single inquiry.
full_text:
A group of senior ministers grumbled to Emperor Akbar that he favored Birbal above them all: 'Sire, we work twelve hours a day managing taxes and supplies, yet you treat Birbal like your own brother! What can he do that we cannot?'

Akbar smiled: 'Let us see.'

Just then, the sound of barking dogs and rolling cartwheels was heard outside the palace gate.

Akbar said to the first complaining minister: 'Go outside and find out what is passing by the gate.'

The minister went out, returned, and said: 'Sire, it is a bullock cart.'

Akbar asked: 'What is inside the cart?'

'I did not check,' the minister replied, and ran back out. Returning, he said: 'It is loaded with sacks of grain.'

'From where does it come?' Akbar asked.

'I will check,' the minister ran out a third time. 'It comes from Alwar, Sire.'

'And what is the price per sack?'

'I will ask,' the minister ran out a fourth time.

Akbar then called Birbal: 'Birbal, go find out what is passing the gate.'

Birbal bowed, went out, and returned five minutes later.

Birbal reported: 'Your Majesty, it is a caravan of three bullock carts carrying three hundred sacks of high-grade wheat from the district of Alwar, owned by a merchant named Seth Mohanlal.

'He is heading to the river bazaar to sell the grain at four silver rupees per sack. However, since our royal granaries are half-empty after the winter, I negotiated a bulk price of three and a half rupees per sack.

'I have already instructed the sentries to hold the carts at the second gate, and the merchant is waiting outside with samples of the wheat, should Your Majesty wish to approve the purchase.'

Akbar turned to the complaining ministers, whose mouths hung open in stunned silence:

'Now do you understand? One man runs four times to fetch four scraps of news, while Birbal anticipates every need, investigates every detail, negotiates the price, and delivers a complete solution in a single trip!'

The ministers bowed in deep shame, acknowledging Birbal's supreme competence.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The King and the Tiger
summary: A boastful general claims he fears nothing on earth and would fight a tiger bare-handed. Birbal teaches him the difference between courage and madness.
full_text:
A boastful young general named Khan Bahadur strutted through the imperial council, bragging of his fearless courage: 'Fear is for cowards! I fear nothing on earth—not cannons, not swords, and not wild beasts! If I met a royal Bengal tiger in the jungle, I would wrestle it bare-handed and tear open its jaws!'

Akbar smiled, amused by the bravado, but Birbal remarked: 'Khan Sahib, bravery without caution is madness, not virtue. Even the lion respects the thorn bush.'

The general scoffed: 'Are you calling me a coward, Birbal?'

The next week, during an imperial hunt in the dense forests of Ranthambore, word came that a ferocious man-eating tiger had been cornered in a deep rocky ravine.

Akbar and his party rode to the edge of the ravine. The tiger, colossal and striped with orange and black, paced back and forth below, its golden eyes flashing with deadly fury, unleashing a roar that rattled the leaves of the trees.

Akbar turned to the boastful general: 'Khan Bahadur! You swore you would wrestle a tiger bare-handed. Here is your chance to prove your words before the Emperor! Jump down into the ravine and wrestle the beast!'

The general's face went white as milk. His knees knocked together; his teeth chattered, and he took three steps backward, clutching his horse's saddle in sheer terror: 'Sire... I... my foot aches today... the rocks are slippery!'

Birbal stepped to the edge of the ravine with two imperial archers carrying flaming torches and heavy iron-tipped spears. With calm, measured precision, Birbal ordered the torches positioned to blind the beast, signaled the archers to cover the flanks, and guided the Emperor's hunting rifle to a clean, safe shot that dispatched the beast without endangering a single man.

Birbal turned to the trembling general:

'You see, Khan Sahib? The tongue can conquer a hundred tigers in the safety of a palace hall. But when the beast of reality roars, reckless words vanish like mist.

'True courage does not boast; it observes the danger with calm eyes, respects the enemy, and acts with prudence to protect human life.'

Akbar praised Birbal, and the general never bragged of his fearless might again.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Donkey in Lion's Skin
summary: A foolish courtier dresses in royal silk and tries to terrify the council with fierce commands. Birbal demonstrates why true majesty is quiet.
full_text:
A cowardly but wealthy courtier named Mirza Jafar purchased a magnificent cape of gold-embroidered crimson silk and a towering turban pinned with a falcon feather. Hoping to inspire awe and fear among the junior clerks and servants, Jafar paced through the palace corridors, scowling fiercely and shouting harsh commands like an imperial conqueror.

Watching this absurd spectacle, Birbal turned to Emperor Akbar and said: 'Sire, Jafar reminds me of the ancient tale of the washerman's donkey who wore a lion's skin.'

Akbar asked: 'How did that story go, Birbal?'

Birbal narrated: 'In a village near the forest, an impoverished washerman found the dried carcass of a dead lion. He skinned the beast, dried the pelt, and draped it over his skinny, hungry donkey.

'At night, the washerman drove the donkey into the villagers' lush barley fields. The farmers, seeing the yellow maned figure in the moonlight, fled in terror, crying: "A man-eating lion is in our crops!"

'Night after night, the donkey feasted upon the tender grain, growing fat and sleek under the lion's skin.

'One moonlit night, while the donkey was grazing peacefully in the barley, a female donkey in a distant pasture brayed loudly: *Hee-haw! Hee-haw!*

'Hearing the call of his own kind, the foolish donkey forgot his royal lion pelt! He lifted his snout, puffed his chest, and brayed back with all his might: *HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW!*

'The farmers, hearing the ridiculous braying emerging from the "lion," stopped running. They grabbed heavy bamboo clubs, surrounded the field, and beat the pretender until he could barely limp away!'

Akbar roared with laughter. Birbal concluded: 'Sire, a man may wrap himself in the robes of kings and adopt the snarl of a warrior. But the moment he opens his mouth to speak, the true nature of his mind is laid bare for all the world to see.'

Mirza Jafar, who had overheard the story, hung his head in mortification, took off his flamboyant cape, and learned to behave with modest dignity.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Fox and the Crow - Birbal version
summary: Birbal retells the famous fable of the crow and the cheese to warn Akbar against a flattering foreign diplomat.
keywords: the fox and the crow - birbal version
full_text:
A clever and silver-tongued ambassador from a rival principality arrived at the court of Emperor Akbar. Bowing with dramatic flourishes, the diplomat spent two hours reciting lavish praise: 'O Emperor Akbar! Your face is brighter than the full moon! Your voice is sweeter than celestial harps! Your generosity outshines the sun itself!'

Akbar, basking in the intoxicating praise, was on the verge of signing an extraordinarily one-sided trade treaty that would have surrendered the revenues of three border provinces to the foreign kingdom.

Birbal stepped forward, bowed politely to the ambassador, and turned to Akbar: 'Sire, before you seal this treaty with the royal signet, allow me to recount the Birbal version of the Fox and the Crow.'

Akbar smiled: 'Speak, Birbal.'

Birbal narrated: 'A crow was perched upon a high oak branch, holding a delicious piece of spiced mutton in its beak. A hungry fox spotted the prize and sat at the foot of the tree.

'"O magnificent bird!" the fox called out with tears of admiration. "I have heard of your royal pedigree, but I never knew your feathers were as black and lustrous as silk! And they say that when you sing, even the nightingales weep with envy! Will you not bless my humble ears with one sweet song?"

'The vain crow, intoxicated by the flattery, puffed out its chest, opened its beak wide, and croaked with all its might: *Caw! Caw!*

'The instant its beak opened, the meat fell into the grass below. The fox snapped up the savory morsel, swallowed it down, and laughed: "Thank you for the feast, foolish bird! You have a voice like a rusty gate, but a mind even weaker than your voice!"'

Akbar paused. He looked down at the treaty scroll on his desk, and then at the sweet-talking foreign ambassador who was sweating nervously.

The Emperor laughed aloud at how Birbal had shattered the diplomat's spell: 'Thank you, Birbal! You have snatched the imperial cheese before the fox could carry it away!'

Akbar tore up the unfair treaty, negotiated strict and equitable terms, and rewarded Birbal for his timely vigilance.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: Birbal's Mother-in-Law
summary: Birbal's sharp-tongued mother-in-law tests his legendary patience. Birbal handles domestic disputes with the same wit he brings to imperial governance.
full_text:
Even the wisest minister in Hindustan was not immune to domestic challenges. Birbal's elderly mother-in-law, a fiercely proud and sharp-tongued matriarch, came to visit his mansion in Agra. Accustomed to ruling her village household with an iron fist, she found fault with everything in Birbal's house—the cooking was too bland, the servants were too slow, and Birbal spent too much time at court!

One evening, while Birbal was writing an imperial dispatch, the old lady scolded him loudly: 'You may be a grand Raja in the Emperor's court, but in this house you are merely a son-in-law who cannot even ensure his wife has five new silk saris every festival! My daughter would have been happier married to a wealthy grain merchant!'

Birbal listened with a respectful smile, never losing his temper or raising his voice.

The next morning at court, Emperor Akbar noticed that Birbal looked somewhat tired and asked with a chuckle: 'Birbal, you manage thirty provinces with ease, yet today you look weary. Is there trouble in the empire?'

Birbal replied with a wry smile: 'Sire, managing thirty rebellious provinces is child's play compared to governing one household with an outspoken mother-in-law!'

Akbar laughed: 'Why do you not use your sharp wit to silence her complaints?'

Birbal shook his head with gentle wisdom:

'Sire, wit is a weapon to disarm enemies, expose frauds, and teach courtiers. But in the sacred sanctuary of family, victory does not come from winning arguments.

'My mother-in-law gave birth to my beloved wife, carried her through childhood, and protected her with her life. Her sharp tongue comes from the anxiety of old age and deep love for her daughter.

'If I humiliate an old woman with clever logic, I may win the debate, but I will break my wife's heart and destroy domestic peace. True wisdom knows when to unsheathe the sword of wit, and when to sheath it in the velvet cloak of patient love.'

Akbar was deeply moved by Birbal's emotional maturity, remarking that a man who conquers his own household with love is greater than an emperor who conquers a kingdom with iron.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Lost Book
summary: A fire destroys the imperial archive, burning a rare treatise on philosophy. Birbal comforts Akbar by demonstrating the permanence of internalized wisdom.
full_text:
A sudden fire in the library wing of the Agra palace destroyed dozens of precious illuminated manuscripts. Emperor Akbar was inconsolable over the loss of a unique, centuries-old Persian treatise on ethics and statecraft, which had been copied by master calligraphers and bound in gold leather.

Weeping with grief, Akbar said to Birbal: 'The greatest wisdom of the ancients is lost forever to the flames! Those words can never be replaced! The soul of our library has turned to ash!'

Birbal sat quietly beside the grieving monarch and said in a gentle, reassuring voice:

'Sire, fire has consumed only dried sheepskin, ink, and gold leaf. It has not burned a single grain of true wisdom.'

Akbar looked up, bewildered: 'How can you say that? The only copy in Hindustan was destroyed!'

Birbal explained:

'Your Majesty, a book is merely a wooden box that carries the fruit of knowledge. If a man reads a book and merely leaves the words on the shelf, the knowledge perishes when the paper burns.

'But if a ruler reads those words, reflects upon them in his heart, and practices justice, mercy, and compassion in his daily rule, then the book has migrated from the dead page into the living soul of the monarch!

'Can any fire burn the kindness you showed to the starving peasant yesterday? Can any ash erase the fair judgments you delivered from your throne? The words of that ancient author live on in your actions. As long as you practice righteousness, the book is alive in Hindustan!'

Akbar's heart found immediate comfort. Inspired by Birbal's words, the Emperor commissioned new scholars to compose fresh treatises based on living experience, realizing that wisdom's true temple is the human heart.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Most Valuable Thing
summary: Akbar asks his ministers to name the most valuable commodity in existence. Birbal names the one treasure that even emperors cannot purchase.
full_text:
During a discussion in the Diwan-i-Khas regarding the imperial trade monopolies, Emperor Akbar asked his ministers:

'What is the single most valuable, indispensable commodity in all the markets of the world? Is it gold, water, grain, or iron?'

The finance minister replied: 'Gold, Sire! For with gold, one can purchase armies, cities, and palaces.'

The general argued: 'Iron! For without iron swords and plows, gold is easily stolen and crops cannot be harvested.'

A physician suggested: 'Water and air! For without them, no living soul can survive for three days.'

Birbal stood up and said with profound solemnity:

'Sire, all those things are valuable, yet if you lose gold, you can earn it back. If an iron blade is broken, it can be reforged. If water dries up, the rains will fall again next season.

'The most valuable, irreplaceable thing in the universe is Time.'

Akbar leaned forward: 'Explain yourself, Birbal.'

Birbal said: 'Consider this, Your Majesty. You possess an imperial treasury overflowing with ten million gold mohurs and mountains of diamonds.

'Yet if you were lying upon your deathbed, and offered every single coin, diamond, palace, and province in your vast empire to purchase back just one single hour of yesterday—could all your wealth buy back sixty lost seconds?

'No emperor, no conqueror, no sage can ever reclaim a moment that has slipped past. The minutes we waste in idle gossip, petty quarrels, and unrighteous anger are lost forever into eternity. Therefore, Time is the supreme treasure of human life.'

Akbar fell silent in deep contemplation. He thanked Birbal for the profound reminder, and resolved to dedicate every hour of his reign to the diligent service of his people.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The True Worth
summary: A villager finds an uncut diamond and sells it for a loaf of bread. Birbal illustrates the subjective nature of human valuation.
full_text:
A poor, simple-minded woodcutter in the hills of Bundelkhand found a heavy, rough stone that sparkled faintly in the sunlight. Knowing nothing of gems, he took it to a village vegetable seller, who offered him two fresh onions for it.

The woodcutter thought: 'Two onions is not enough; let me take it to the bread seller.' The baker offered him a loaf of fresh barley bread. Being hungry, the woodcutter gladly traded the stone for the bread and ate his fill.

The baker took the stone to a brass merchant, who bought it for ten copper coins. The brass merchant showed it to a silversmith, who paid fifty silver rupees. Finally, the silversmith took it to the royal jeweler in Agra, who recognized it as a colossal, flawless blue diamond and purchased it for fifty thousand gold mohurs!

When the story reached Emperor Akbar, the Emperor was astonished: 'How tragic that the poor woodcutter gave away a fifty-thousand-gold-mohur diamond for a single loaf of bread!'

Birbal remarked with a smile: 'Sire, was the woodcutter truly foolish, or did he receive what he needed most?'

Akbar asked: 'How can a loaf of bread equal fifty thousand gold coins?'

Birbal explained:

'To the starving woodcutter on that cold morning, the stone was useless; he could not chew it, boil it, or feed his children with it. The warm bread saved his life. To him, the bread possessed supreme value.

'To the baker, it was worth ten coppers; to the silversmith, fifty rupees; and to the royal jeweler, a king's ransom.

'Value does not reside in the physical object; value is determined entirely by the knowledge, need, and capacity of the person who holds it. A fool throws away wisdom because he cannot eat it, while a sage treasures a single verse of philosophy more than a chest of gold.'

Akbar nodded in agreement, reflecting on how easily men misjudge the true worth of both goods and ideas.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: Birbal and the Cook
summary: The royal cook serves oversalted soup to the Emperor. Birbal uses an amusing salt test to help the cook correct his recipe without fear.
full_text:
The imperial head cook, Mir Baqir, had prepared meals for Emperor Akbar for fifteen years without a flaw. However, on a sweltering afternoon, overwhelmed by heat and distracted by his daughter's illness, the cook accidentally added salt twice to the Emperor's favorite saffron mutton broth.

When Akbar took his first spoonful in the private dining chamber, his face darkened with disgust: 'Ugh! This soup is like seawater! It is poisoned with salt!'

Akbar spat the broth onto the floor and shouted for the guards: 'Drag that incompetent cook here! He shall be stripped of his position and thrown into the dungeons!'

Birbal, who was dining with the Emperor, quickly tasted a drop of the broth from his own spoon. Seeing that the mistake was an honest accident, Birbal stepped in:

'Sire, allow me to question the cook. In ancient Persian culinary art, there is a rare medical reason why a master chef adds double salt.'

Curious, Akbar halted the guards. Mir Baqir was brought into the room, trembling and weeping with terror.

Birbal asked the cook solemnly: 'Mir Baqir, tell His Majesty the truth: did you oversalt this soup because you have developed a secret love affair, or because you were trying to preserve the Emperor's humors from the summer heat?'

The cook blinked in bewilderment, then fell to his knees: 'Neither, my lord! My mind was shattered because my youngest daughter is burning with a high fever at home, and in my sorrow, my hand slipped and I salted the cauldron twice! Forgive me, Sire, kill me if you must, but spare my poor child!'

Akbar's anger melted into sympathy.

Birbal smiled at the Emperor: 'Sire, salt can ruin a broth, but sorrow ruins a father's mind. The salt was an error of grief, not malice.'

Akbar ordered the imperial royal physician dispatched immediately to treat the cook's daughter with royal medicines, granted the cook three days of leave, and ordered a simple fresh broth prepared. Mir Baqir bowed with tears of gratitude, and Akbar thanked Birbal for transforming royal rage into compassionate mercy.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The King and the Elephant
summary: A rogue elephant refuses to move, blocking the palace gates. Birbal moves the giant beast without an iron hook or whip.
full_text:
A massive imperial tusker named Gajraj, known for his formidable size in battle, suddenly became stubborn and obstinate. Right in front of the main Hathipol (Elephant Gate) of the Agra Fort, the colossal elephant sat down across the stone road, folded his thick legs, and refused to budge.

Caravans, horsemen, and royal messengers were completely blocked. The mahouts beat the beast with iron ankus (hooks), yelled curses, and set off firecrackers, but Gajraj merely flapped his ears, trumpeted angrily, and planted his massive bulk even firmer into the dust.

Akbar stood on the ramparts, frustrated: 'Bring the royal cavalry! Tie twenty chains to his legs and pull him with forty horses!'

Birbal arrived and observed the scene. 'Sire, pulling a five-ton stubborn elephant with chains will only injure the beast and break our horses' backs. Force cannot conquer stubbornness; one must appeal to nature.'

Birbal walked to the palace kitchens. He returned carrying three large wicker baskets filled with fresh, juicy pineapples, sweet jaggery cakes, and tender green sugarcane stalks.

Birbal walked calmly to within twenty paces of the sitting elephant. He peeled a sweet pineapple, letting the rich, sugary aroma drift into the morning breeze.

Gajraj's trunk sniffed the air. The elephant's ears perked up.

Birbal placed a jaggery cake on the grass fifteen paces down the side road. Gajraj's trunk curled. Slowly, groaning with delight, the massive beast uncurled his legs, stood up on all fours, and ambled peacefully off the main road to eat the sweet treat!

Birbal walked ahead, dropping pieces of sugarcane every few paces, leading the docile giant gently into his stable paddock, where the gates were closed securely behind him.

The main roadway was completely clear within ten minutes, without a single blow struck!

Akbar cheered from the ramparts: 'Brilliant, Birbal! You moved with three sugar cakes what twenty iron hooks could not budge!'

Birbal smiled: 'Sire, whether dealing with stubborn beasts or rebellious citizens, sweetness and understanding lead where anger and whips only harden resistance.'
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Two Thieves
summary: Two burglars rob a merchant's vault, then try to cheat each other out of the loot. Birbal uses their mutual distrust to recover the treasure.
full_text:
Two cunning burglars, Kallu and Ballu, broke into a wealthy moneylender's mansion in Agra and escaped with a heavy iron chest containing five thousand gold mohurs. Hiding in a ruined mausoleum outside the city walls, they sat down to divide the loot.

Kallu said: 'I am hungry after our hard work. You guard the gold here, while I run to the village bazaar to buy roasted meat and sweet bread.'

As Kallu walked to the village, greed seized his heart: 'Why should I share half this fortune with Ballu? If I buy rat poison and mix it into his bread, he will die, and the entire five thousand gold coins will belong to me alone!'

Kallu bought the food, poisoned Ballu's share, and hurried back.

Meanwhile, sitting in the tomb, Ballu was thinking identical thoughts: 'Why should I share half the gold with Kallu? When he returns with the food, I will sneak behind him, strike him with this heavy stone, bury his body, and keep the entire treasure for myself!'

When Kallu returned and stepped into the dark chamber holding the bread, Ballu leaped from the shadows and crushed Kallu's skull with the heavy rock, killing him instantly!

Ballu laughed triumphantly: 'The gold is mine! All mine!'

Hungry and exhausted, Ballu sat down on the bloodstained floor and ravenously ate the sweet bread that Kallu had brought.

Within twenty minutes, the violent poison gripped his stomach. Howling in agony, Ballu collapsed across his partner's dead body and perished in the dust!

The next morning, Birbal and the city watch discovered the two corpses and the untouched iron chest.

Presenting the recovered gold to Emperor Akbar, Birbal remarked with grave irony:

'Sire, behold the fruit of unrighteous gain. The dishonest believe they can cheat the moral laws of creation. But evil carries the seeds of its own destruction; in plotting against each other, the two thieves executed justice upon themselves without needing an imperial executioner.'

Akbar ordered the gold restored to the merchant, marvelling at how divine justice operates in the shadows.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Merchant and the Donkey
summary: Birbal retells the fable of the salt merchant and the lazy donkey to illustrate the danger of habitual deceit.
full_text:
A wealthy trader was caught bribing royal customs officers at the Yamuna river bridge by declaring silk crates as common cotton. When brought before the Emperor, the merchant pleaded that he had only tried it 'once or twice as a harmless shortcut.'

Akbar turned to Birbal: 'What punishment fits a merchant who makes a habit of deceptive shortcuts?'

Birbal replied: 'Sire, let me recount the tale of the Salt Merchant and his Donkey.'

Birbal narrated: 'A merchant used to carry heavy sacks of salt on his donkey from the salt pans to the city market. To reach the road, they had to wade across a shallow stream.

'One morning, the donkey stumbled and fell into the stream. While struggling to stand, the donkey stayed in the water for several minutes. The salt in the sacks dissolved into the water!

'When the donkey stood up, the sacks were feather-light! The donkey was overjoyed.

'The next morning, the cunning donkey deliberately slipped and sat down in the middle of the stream. Again, the salt dissolved, and the burden became light. The donkey repeated this trick for four consecutive days, laughing at his master.

'The merchant soon understood the animal's lazy scheme. On the fifth morning, instead of salt, the merchant packed the sacks tightly with dry cotton wool!

'Arriving at the stream, the smug donkey threw himself into the water with a splash, waiting for his load to become light.

'However, the cotton wool soaked up gallons of heavy water like a giant sponge! When the donkey tried to stand, the sacks weighed ten times more than lead! The heavy, waterlogged cotton nearly drowned the poor beast, and he had to drag the crushing weight three miles to the bazaar under a blistering sun, groaning with every step!'

The court laughed. Birbal looked at the trembling trader:

'A deceitful trick may seem light and profitable on the first day. But repeated deceit accumulates weight like wet cotton, until it crushes the trickster beneath the burden of his own dishonesty.'

The merchant confessed his fraudulent records, paid his back taxes with a heavy fine, and vowed never to seek dishonest shortcuts again.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Rich Man and His Ring
summary: A foolish nobleman searches for a lost ring under a palace lamp instead of in his bedroom. Birbal uses the incident to satirize human escapism.
keywords: the rich man and his ring
full_text:
Late one evening, Emperor Akbar and Birbal were walking through the outer courtyard of the Agra palace when they noticed a wealthy nobleman, Mirza Asad, on his hands and knees beneath a brightly glowing oil street lamp, frantically sifting through pebbles and dust.

Akbar stopped: 'Mirza Asad, what are you doing in the dirt at this late hour?'

Asad looked up, sweating: 'Your Majesty, I have lost my priceless ruby ring, a family heirloom worth ten thousand rupees! I am searching for it!'

Akbar, feeling generous, knelt down with Birbal and helped the nobleman search. For nearly an hour, the Emperor, the minister, and the noble combed through every inch of dust beneath the lantern. The ring was nowhere to be found.

Birbal wiped his hands and asked: 'Mirza Asad, are you certain you dropped the ring right here beneath this lamp?'

Asad replied innocently: 'Oh no, Raja Birbal! I dropped it inside my dark bedroom, three corridors away inside the palace!'

Akbar jumped to his feet in disbelief: 'You dropped it in your bedroom? Then why in heaven's name are you searching for it out here in the courtyard?'

Asad blinked in surprise: 'Because it was pitch black in my bedroom, Sire, and there is such wonderful, bright light out here under this courtyard street lamp!'

Akbar stared in stunned silence, then burst into a roar of exasperated laughter.

Birbal turned to the Emperor and said with profound philosophical humor:

'Do not mock him too harshly, Your Majesty. Most of humanity behaves exactly like Mirza Asad!

'When men lose their inner peace, their health, or their moral character inside the quiet chambers of their own hearts, they never search for it within themselves where it was lost, because self-examination is dark and difficult!

'Instead, they run out into the brightly lit courtyards of the world—chasing wealth, fame, flattery, and sensual pleasures—hoping to find their lost peace where the lights are bright, even though it was never dropped there!'

Akbar was captivated by the brilliant metaphor. He ordered a lantern brought to Mirza Asad's bedroom, where the ring was promptly found under a cushion, and thanked Birbal for illuminating a profound spiritual truth.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Clever Thief
summary: A captured thief condemned to the gallows asks for one final boon: to plant a golden pomegranate seed that sprouts only for the innocent.
full_text:
A master burglar named Shafi was captured red-handed inside a royal minister's mansion. Having committed repeated burglaries across Agra, Emperor Akbar sentenced him to be hanged at the city gallows the following morning.

When the executioner asked if he had a final request, the thief replied: 'I possess an ancient family secret that must not die with me. Take me to Emperor Akbar, and I shall gift the crown a treasure of infinite wealth!'

Intrigued, Akbar summoned the thief. Shafi bowed low, held up an ordinary-looking pomegranate seed, and declared:

'Your Majesty, this is a golden seed from the gardens of Solomon. If planted in fertile soil, it will sprout into a magnificent tree within twenty-four hours, bearing fruit of pure solid gold!

'However, it possesses one mystical condition: the person who places the seed into the soil must be completely pure of heart—a man who has never in his life stolen, cheated, lied, or taken what did not belong to him! Since I am a confessed thief, if I plant it, the seed will rot. I offer it to your imperial court so that an innocent man may plant it for the prosperity of Hindustan!'

Akbar was delighted. He turned to his Prime Minister: 'Prime Minister, step forward and plant the golden seed!'

The Prime Minister coughed nervously, adjusted his sash, and stepped back: 'Sire... when I was a youth in school, I once took a gold coin from my father's desk without asking... I fear the seed would rot.'

Akbar turned to the royal treasurer: 'Treasurer, you plant it!'

The treasurer turned pale: 'Alas, Your Majesty... occasionally in my accounts, I have adjusted small expenses to my own benefit... my hands are not pure.'

Akbar looked along the line of courtiers and generals; every single nobleman looked at the floor, made excuses, and stepped backward!

Finally, Akbar thought of planting it himself, but remembered taking a neighboring kingdom's territory during his youth.

The thief looked up at the Emperor with a calm, gentle smile:

'Your Majesty, all these noble ministers, generals, and counselors live in magnificent palaces, enjoy vast estates, and eat from golden plates—yet not one of them is innocent of deceit or greed!

'I am a poor, starving wretch who stole only a handful of bread and silver to feed my dying mother, yet you are about to hang me on the gallows, while these men sit in honor!'

Akbar stood frozen. The sheer brilliance of the thief's trap struck the Emperor to the core.

Akbar smiled with deep admiration: 'Shafi, your wit and truthfulness have saved your life today!'

Akbar canceled the death sentence, granted Shafi an honest post as a night watchman in the imperial gardens, and commended Birbal for teaching the court that true justice must temper punishment with profound humility.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: Birbal and the Goldsmith
summary: A dishonest goldsmith replaces pure gold with brass while making an idol. Birbal uses acid and fire to expose the alloy.
full_text:
An elderly, devout widow named Yashoda saved all her life savings to commission a pure gold statue of a guardian angel to donate to the city temple. She handed thirty tolas of pure, 24-karat gold coins to the chief goldsmith of the bazaar, Seth Hariram, who promised to craft an exquisite idol for twenty silver rupees in labor.

Two months later, the goldsmith delivered the polished statue. It shone with a bright golden gleam.

However, an experienced jeweler who examined the statue whispered to the widow that the idol felt unusually light and had a reddish tint. Suspecting fraud, the widow confronted Hariram, who screamed with rage: 'How dare an illiterate widow insult my sacred craft! I swear on my ancestors that this statue is pure, unadulterated gold!'

The widow wept at Emperor Akbar's feet. Akbar handed the case to Birbal.

Hariram arrived in court, presenting three certificates signed by corrupt bazaar appraisers swearing the gold was pure.

Birbal examined the idol, stroked his chin, and said: 'Hariram, if this statue is indeed thirty tolas of pure gold, you have nothing to fear. We shall verify its purity using the ancient test of the royal mint.'

Birbal ordered a crucible, a charcoal furnace, and bellows brought into the Diwan-i-Khas.

Birbal turned to the widow: 'Mother, if the statue is melted to test its gold, do you consent?'

'Yes, my lord!' the widow replied. 'Better that it be melted into truth than stand in the temple as a monument of deceit!'

The statue was placed into the clay crucible and heated until it melted into glowing liquid. Birbal dropped a lump of pure nitre and borax into the crucible, blowing the flames to white heat.

Dense, foul-smelling black fumes rose from the pot, and thick green slag floated to the surface—the unmistakable sign of cheap copper and brass!

When the impurities burned away and the remaining metal cooled, Birbal weighed the pure gold button on the precision mint scale.

It weighed only twelve tolas! Eighteen tolas of pure gold had been stolen by the goldsmith and replaced with copper alloy!

Hariram fell upon his face, begging for mercy.

Birbal announced the verdict: 'Hariram shall return the thirty tolas of pure gold to the widow, pay an additional thirty tolas as a penalty for defrauding a temple offering, and spend one year in prison!'

Akbar praised Birbal for letting the incorruptible fire speak when human words lied.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Village Idiot
summary: A village boy always chooses a shiny copper coin over a dull silver coin. Akbar thinks the boy is a fool, but Birbal reveals the boy's genius.
full_text:
While traveling through a village on the road to Gwalior, Emperor Akbar was told by the local villagers about a young boy named Sukhi, whom everyone called the 'village idiot.'

The village headman laughed: 'Your Majesty, this boy has no brain at all! Every day, travelers hold out a large, shiny copper coin in one hand, and a small, dull silver coin in the other, and tell him to choose. The fool always picks the copper coin, and everyone laughs!'

Curious, Akbar called the boy over. In his right palm, Akbar placed a small, polished silver rupee. In his left palm, he placed a large, broad copper dam.

Akbar said: 'Sukhi, take whichever coin you want; it is yours.'

Sukhi looked at both coins with wide, innocent eyes, picked the large copper coin, gave a silly grin, and hopped away happily!

Akbar chuckled: 'Truly, the poor boy does not know the value of metals! A silver coin is worth thirty copper dams, yet he chooses the copper because it is bigger!'

Birbal walked over to the shade of a tamarind tree where Sukhi was sitting alone. Birbal smiled kindly and asked in a low voice: 'Sukhi, you are an observant boy. Do you truly not know that a silver coin can buy thirty times more sweets than a copper coin?'

Sukhi looked around, made sure no villagers were listening, and whispered with a mischievous grin:

'Of course I know that, wise minister! I am not a fool!'

Birbal raised his eyebrows: 'Then why do you always pick the copper coin?'

Sukhi chuckled softly:

'My lord, if I pick the silver coin just once, the travelers and villagers will realize that I know the difference, and the game will end forever!

'By picking the copper coin every day, they believe I am an idiot, so every day fifty new travelers line up to test me, and I walk home every evening with fifty copper coins in my pocket! Why should I take one silver coin today and lose fifty copper coins tomorrow?'

Birbal laughed with pure delight. He brought the boy back to Akbar and shared Sukhi's confession.

Akbar stared in astonishment, then laughed till his sides ached: 'By Allah, Birbal! The boy is smarter than half my imperial council! He lets the world call him a fool while he quietly gathers the harvest of their arrogance!'

Akbar rewarded Sukhi with a purse of silver, warning him to keep his secret safe.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The King and the Poor Brahmin
summary: Akbar forgets a casual promise of reward made to an impoverished scholar during a hunt. Birbal uses a crooked camel's neck to jog the royal memory.
keywords: the king and the poor brahmin
full_text:
While hunting in the wilderness six months earlier, Emperor Akbar's horse threw a shoe near a lonely hermitage. An elderly, impoverished Brahmin scholar named Devadatta welcomed the weary, disguised monarch, offered him sweet well water and fresh chapatis, and recited uplifting Sanskrit philosophical verses to ease his exhaustion.

Delighted by the scholar's hospitality, Akbar said before riding away: 'I am Emperor Akbar of Agra! Visit my court next month, and I shall bestow upon you a jagir of fertile land and five hundred gold coins!'

Overjoyed, the poor scholar sold his only milk cow to buy a clean white dhoti and traveled to Agra. However, arriving at the grand palace, Akbar was occupied with state treaties and military rebellions, and the guards repeatedly turned the old scholar away. Devadatta spent all his money and was reduced to begging on the city streets.

Desperate, the scholar approached Birbal and recounted the forgotten imperial promise.

Birbal felt deep sympathy: 'Do not worry, friend. The Emperor has not broken faith; he has merely forgotten in the rush of state affairs. I shall remind him today.'

That afternoon, Akbar and Birbal were strolling along the riverbank when they passed a camel caravan. One of the camels had a notoriously twisted, crooked neck that bent sharply to the left.

Akbar smiled and asked idly: 'Birbal, why is that camel's neck so crooked?'

Birbal sighed with deep solemnity:

'Sire, that camel was an emperor in its previous life! It made a sacred promise of a reward to a poor Brahmin, and then completely forgot its word! Because it broke its royal promise, heaven twisted its neck as a mark of shame for all eternity!'

Akbar stopped dead in his tracks. His face flushed bright crimson. The memory of the poor scholar at the hermitage came rushing back into his mind with the force of a thunderbolt!

'Birbal,' Akbar whispered, embarrassed, 'has that poor Brahmin scholar come to Agra?'

'He has been waiting outside your palace gates for three weeks, Sire, starving and without a single copper coin.'

Akbar immediately sent royal palanquins to bring Devadatta to court. The Emperor personally seated the scholar upon a velvet cushion, apologized for his forgetfulness, and granted him double the promised reward: two fertile villages, a thousand gold coins, and a royal pension for life.

Akbar embraced Birbal: 'Thank you for saving my neck from becoming as crooked as that camel's!'
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Talking Tree
summary: Two partners dispute a bag of gold, and one claims a sacred tree spoke from heaven to endorse his claim. Birbal lights a fire to reveal the 'tree's voice.'
full_text:
Two trading partners, Ram and Shyam, buried a bag containing two thousand gold mohurs beneath a hollow peepal tree outside Agra, agreeing that neither would touch the money without the other present.

A month later, when they went to retrieve the treasure, the hole was empty. Shyam cried: 'Ram, you dug it up in secret and stole the gold!'

Ram denied it vehemently, swearing on his children.

Shyam said: 'Let us appeal to the sacred peepal tree itself! That tree is inhabited by an ancient celestial spirit who sees all things. If the tree names you as the thief before Emperor Akbar, will you accept the judgment?'

Ram, confident in his innocence, agreed.

The next morning, Emperor Akbar, Birbal, courtiers, and village elders gathered around the colossal peepal tree.

Shyam stepped forward, bowed reverently, and cried: 'O Sacred Tree! Reveal the truth! Who stole the gold buried beneath your roots?'

To the utter astonishment and horror of Emperor Akbar and the crowd, a deep, hollow voice echoed from within the trunk of the tree:

'RAM IS THE THIEF! RAM DUG UP THE GOLD AT MIDNIGHT!'

The crowd gasped. Akbar was shaken: 'A tree that speaks! Ram, confess your crime!'

Ram fell to his knees, weeping: 'Sire, I am innocent! I do not know how a tree can speak!'

Birbal stood observing the ancient tree. He noticed a faint opening between two roots covered with freshly gathered moss, and saw that the soil near the back of the trunk was disturbed.

Birbal smiled calmly: 'Your Majesty, if this tree is indeed a sacred celestial spirit, it deserves a grand Vedic offering of incense and fragrant smoke to honor its divine wisdom.'

Birbal ordered four bundles of dry straw and pungent chili peppers placed around the hollow base of the tree, and struck a flint to ignite them!

Dense, choking clouds of smoke billowed into the hollow opening of the trunk.

Within thirty seconds, violent coughing broke out from inside the tree trunk: *Cough! Wheeze! Choke! Have mercy! I am burning!*

A scrawny man tumbled out of the hollow opening, gagging on smoke and rolling on the grass!

It was Shyam's elderly father! Shyam had hidden his father inside the hollow tree before dawn to play the part of the 'divine voice'!

The crowd erupted in outrage. Shyam and his father fell at Akbar's feet, confessing their treacherous conspiracy.

Akbar ordered the stolen gold recovered, confiscated Shyam's property, and praised Birbal's sharp eyes for smoking out the fraud.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: Birbal and the Snake Charmer
summary: A boastful snake charmer claims his cobras are entirely under his magical control. Birbal shows the court why playing with treachery always ends in ruin.
full_text:
A famous snake charmer named Ustad Madari arrived at the court of Emperor Akbar, carrying three wicker baskets containing lethal King Cobras. He played his gourd flute (pungi), and the hooded serpents swayed, hissed, and bowed their heads to the rhythm of his music.

The snake charmer boasted: 'Your Majesty, these serpents are my obedient children! Through ancient spells, I have removed all malice from their hearts! They will never bite me, for they love their master!'

Akbar was fascinated and remarked to Birbal: 'Is it not marvelous, Birbal? Even deadly cobras can be tamed by art and love!'

Birbal shook his head with grave wisdom:

'Sire, a cobra's nature is poison. It sways to the motion of the flute, not to love. A man who plays with venomous serpents is merely living on borrowed time.'

The snake charmer scoffed at Birbal's warning, boasting that he had slept with snakes for thirty years.

A month later, news reached the court that Ustad Madari had been bitten on the neck by his favorite cobra while feeding it milk, and had died within minutes.

Akbar remembered Birbal's warning with a shudder: 'Birbal, your prediction was tragically accurate.'

Birbal said with quiet sadness:

'Sire, this is a lesson not merely about serpents, but about statecraft and human companions.

'A ruler who surrounds himself with treacherous, corrupt flatterers, believing he can tame them with gifts and titles, is like that foolish snake charmer. You may feed milk to a viper and play sweet music for years, but when the moment comes, a poisonous soul will invariably strike according to its nature.

'A wise emperor eliminates venomous men from his court before their fangs find his throat.'

Akbar took the lesson deeply to heart, using it to purge corrupt ministers from the imperial administration.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Price of a Nap
summary: A miserly landlord charges a weary traveler for sleeping in the shadow of his wall. Birbal settles the account with the movement of the sun.
full_text:
On a scorching summer afternoon in Agra, when the hot Loo winds blew across the plains, an exhausted peasant named Bhola was carrying a heavy sack of grain toward the city market. Drenched in sweat and dizzy from the blistering heat, Bhola stopped beside the high stone boundary wall of a wealthy merchant named Seth Lalchand.

Finding a cool patch of dark shadow cast by the merchant's wall onto the public dusty road, Bhola rested his head on his sack and fell into a peaceful twenty-minute nap.

Presently, Seth Lalchand walked out of his iron gate. Seeing the peasant sleeping in the shadow of his wall, the miser poked Bhola with his walking stick: 'Wake up, you freeloader! Pay me five copper coins!'

Bhola rubbed his eyes: 'For what, master? I am lying on the public street!'

Lalchand shouted: 'You slept in the shadow of my wall! My wall cost two thousand rupees to build! The shadow belongs to my wall, and therefore belongs to me! If you enjoy my private shadow, you must pay for it!'

The ridiculous quarrel reached the ears of Emperor Akbar, who was sitting in the Diwan-i-Am. Akbar looked at Birbal with amusement: 'Can a man own a shadow?'

Birbal said: 'Seth Lalchand's claim must be settled with scientific justice.'

Birbal said to the merchant: 'Sethji, you are entirely right. You built the wall, so you own the shadow cast by the wall.'

Lalchand beamed: 'Thank you, wise minister!'

'However,' Birbal continued, pointing out the arched window at the afternoon sun, 'as the sun moves across the sky, your wall's shadow stretches out and covers twenty feet of the Emperor's public roadway!

'The public roadway belongs to the crown. Therefore, for every hour your private shadow encroaches upon the Emperor's road, you are trespassing and obstructing imperial traffic!

'You must pay the royal treasury a rental fee of twenty gold mohurs per hour for the land your shadow occupies! And since your shadow has fallen upon the road every afternoon for the last ten years, you owe the Emperor forty thousand gold coins!'

Lalchand turned pale as a corpse. His knees shook; he fell face-down on the floor, weeping: 'Mercy, Lord Birbal! I withdraw my claim! The shadow is free! The public may sleep in it forever!'

Akbar roared with laughter, fined the miser twenty silver coins to give to the poor peasant, and praised Birbal's brilliant legal turning of the tables.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Man Who Counted Breaths
summary: An eccentric ascetic claims he can achieve immortality by counting every breath. Birbal reveals the absurdity of mechanical existence.
full_text:
An eccentric yogi named Shvasananda arrived in Agra, boasting that he had discovered the secret of extended life. Standing before Emperor Akbar, he announced:

'Every human being is allotted exactly eight hundred million breaths by destiny! Most foolish mortals waste their breaths in laughing, shouting, running, and singing, exhausting their life in fifty years!

'I, however, count every inhale and exhale with mechanical precision, taking only four slow breaths every minute! In this manner, I shall live for three hundred years in perfect preservation!'

Akbar was intrigued: 'Is it true, Birbal? Can a man double his lifespan by counting his breaths?'

Birbal smiled: 'Let us test how much life he actually enjoys, Sire.'

Birbal invited the breath-counter to stay in the palace for three days.

During a magnificent musical performance by Mian Tansen that evening, when the entire court was swaying in ecstatic joy, Birbal watched the yogi. While everyone else smiled and wiped tears of bliss, the yogi sat rigid, eyes glazed, lips moving silently: 'One hundred... one hundred and one... one hundred and two...'

He could not listen to the music, for fear of losing his count!

At the royal banquet, when delicious saffron kebabs and sweet mangoes were served, the yogi chewed each bite with cold detachment, taking three minutes between breaths, refusing to laugh or converse.

On the third day, Birbal said to Emperor Akbar:

'Sire, observe this man. He breathes, his heart beats, and his lungs move like an iron blacksmith's bellows.

'Yet he does not enjoy music, he does not taste food, he does not love a friend, he does not smile at a child, and he does not wipe the tears of the suffering!

'He is not a living man; he is merely an animated corpse counting seconds in a tomb! What is the use of living three hundred years if those years are completely empty of joy, love, and virtue? Better to live fifty years of passionate service and deep love than three centuries of counting empty air.'

Akbar embraced Birbal's philosophy, declaring that life is measured by the depth of its moments, not by the number of its breaths.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: Birbal and the Fakir
summary: A mendicant asks Akbar for money to build a grand hermitage. Birbal shows the holy man that asking an emperor for gold is merely asking one beggar from another.
full_text:
A famous traveling fakir arrived at the imperial palace of Fatehpur Sikri, requesting an audience with Emperor Akbar. The fakir claimed to have renounced all worldly desires, yet he presented a long petition requesting twenty thousand gold mohurs from the imperial treasury to construct an opulent marble hermitage with fountains and orchards.

Akbar was performing his morning prayers in the private mosque. The fakir was ushered into the anteroom and asked to wait.

Through the arched doorway, the fakir saw Emperor Akbar kneeling upon his prayer mat, with hands raised toward heaven, praying aloud:

'O Almighty Creator! Bestow health upon my children, grant prosperity to my empire, protect my armies, and increase my treasury with wealth and blessing!'

Hearing the Emperor's prayer, the fakir quietly turned around, picked up his walking staff, and began walking toward the palace exit.

Akbar completed his prayers, stepped out into the courtyard, and saw the holy man departing. Akbar called out: 'Holy father! You came to request an imperial grant! Why are you leaving without asking for your gold?'

The fakir replied with quiet dignity:

'Your Majesty, I saw you upon your knees begging the Almighty for more wealth, health, and power.

'I thought you were a rich emperor who had treasures to give. But I see that you are merely a grand beggar, pleading before the King of Kings for your daily bread!

'If I must beg for assistance, why should I beg from a fellow beggar who is himself begging for more? It is far more honorable for me to bring my petition directly to the Almighty Creator who provides for all!'

Akbar was stunned into silence. Birbal stepped forward, bowed low to the fakir, and said to the Emperor:

'Sire, this holy man has delivered the greatest sermon ever spoken in this palace. All mortals, whether clothed in rags or crowned in diamonds, are equal paupers before the throne of the Divine. True dignity lies in relying upon providence and honest labor, not upon royal favor.'

Akbar bowed in deep reverence to the fakir, offered him food, and thanked him for the humbling reminder.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Farmer's Son
summary: Akbar challenges a poor farmer's son to solve a riddle that baffled his royal tutors. The boy's practical brilliance wins imperial honor.
full_text:
During an imperial inspection of the countryside, Emperor Akbar stopped his royal retinue near a field where a fourteen-year-old peasant boy named Suraj was guiding a pair of oxen along a furrow. Akbar decided to test the youth's intelligence with a riddle that his royal tutors had debated for hours:

'Young farmer! Can you tell me what travels around the world without ever taking a single step?'

Suraj wiped the sweat from his brow, smiled with sparkling eyes, and replied: 'Sire, the sun and the moon travel around the world every day, yet they have no legs! And beside them, the wind and human thoughts circle the earth in an instant without walking.'

Surprised, Akbar asked a second riddle: 'What grows taller the more you take away from it?'

Suraj laughed: 'A pit in the earth, Your Majesty! The more soil you dig out of it, the deeper and taller it becomes!'

Akbar was thoroughly impressed: 'And what is that which belongs to you, yet is used by everyone else far more than by yourself?'

'My name, Sire!' Suraj answered without a heartbeat's hesitation. 'It is my name, yet my neighbors and parents speak it a hundred times a day, while I rarely utter it!'

Akbar turned to Birbal with profound admiration: 'Look at this peasant youth, Birbal! He has never read Persian poetry or studied Greek logic in a palace academy, yet he answers riddles that stumped my court scholars!'

Birbal said with warm affection:

'Sire, nature and honest labor are the greatest universities. A boy who works in the soil observes the sun, the wind, the earth, and human nature every day of his life. His mind is clear, unburdened by empty pretension.

'Hindustan's true greatness resides in the sturdy huts of its farmers, where common sense and sharp wit flourish like wild wheat.'

Akbar rewarded Suraj with a scholarship to the imperial academy in Agra and granted his family tax-free farmland, proving that talent honors neither pedigree nor poverty.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Blind Judge
summary: A blind elder in an obscure village settles disputes with uncanny accuracy. Akbar investigates, and Birbal explains the secret of inner sight.
full_text:
Reports reached Emperor Akbar of an extraordinary elderly judge named Baba Rahim in a small village near Gwalior. Though completely blind from birth, Baba Rahim resolved complex theft and property disputes that had baffled imperial magistrates, delivering verdicts with infallible accuracy.

Akbar, accompanied by Birbal in disguise, traveled to the village to witness the blind judge in action.

Two women stood before Baba Rahim, fiercely arguing over a piece of woven fine silk cloth. Each woman claimed she had spun and woven the cloth herself.

Baba Rahim asked to hold the cloth. He ran his calloused fingertips gently across the weave, smelled the fabric, and listened as both women spoke.

Then, Baba Rahim asked: 'Bring me a bowl of warm water and a clean white cloth.'

He dipped a corner of the silk into the warm water, squeezed it into the bowl, and inspected the scent of the water.

Then he addressed the first woman: 'This cloth belongs to you.'

The woman wept with joy: 'Thank you, father!'

The second woman protested: 'Why do you favor her? You cannot even see!'

Baba Rahim explained: 'The first woman is a jasmine flower seller by trade; her fingertips have absorbed the subtle oil of jasmine blossoms over twenty years. When I touched the cloth, it carried the faint trace of jasmine oil woven into the threads. The second woman is a fishmonger; had she woven this cloth over weeks, it would carry the trace of fish brine. The cloth remembers the hands that made it.'

Akbar stepped forward, revealed his identity, and embraced the blind elder in awe: 'Baba Rahim, you have no eyes, yet you see the truth clearer than my royal judges!'

Birbal remarked with deep reverence:

'Sire, physical eyes are easily deceived by attractive faces, rich robes, and false tears. But this elder has no physical eyes to be distracted by outward glamour. He listens with his soul, observes with his fingertips, and weighs truth with pure reason.

'True justice is always blind to outward appearances, for it judges only by the evidence of truth.'

Akbar appointed Baba Rahim imperial judicial advisor, reminding all magistrates that discernment is an inner light.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Six Senses
summary: Akbar debates the five physical senses with Birbal. Birbal demonstrates why the sixth sense—common sense—is the supreme captain of life.
full_text:
During a philosophical symposium at Fatehpur Sikri, court scholars debated which of the five human senses—Sight, Hearing, Smell, Taste, or Touch—was the most vital for human survival and happiness.

Some argued for Sight, claiming light is the crown of experience. Others argued for Hearing, stating speech and music nourish the intellect.

Akbar turned to Birbal: 'Which of the five senses is the king, Birbal?'

Birbal replied: 'Sire, the five physical senses are merely five open windows. Without the master of the house to interpret what comes through the windows, all five senses can lead a man directly into destruction. The supreme sense is the Sixth Sense: Common Sense.'

Akbar asked: 'How does common sense rule the other five?'

Birbal explained:

'Consider a moth, Your Majesty. Its sense of sight is sharp; it sees the bright flame of the candle and is enchanted by the golden light. But because it lacks common sense, it flies directly into the fire and burns to death!

'Consider the fish. Its sense of taste and smell is acute; it smells the delicious worm on the iron hook. But because it lacks common sense, it swallows the bait and is pulled to its death!

'Consider the deer. Its hearing is so fine that it listens enraptured to the hunter's sweet flute, until an arrow pierces its chest!

'The five senses are merely scouts. It is common sense—the faculty of discernment, caution, and reason—that tells the eye: "Do not gaze upon what corrupts"; tells the ear: "Do not listen to poison flattery"; and tells the tongue: "Speak only what is true and kind."

'A man who possesses all five senses but lacks common sense is a disaster waiting to happen. But a man who possesses common sense will navigate through darkness, silence, and adversity with safety and honor.'

Akbar stood and led the court in applause, proclaiming that common sense is the true crown of human wisdom.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: Birbal and the Carpenter
summary: A hasty carpenter ruins expensive sandalwood timber for the royal throne. Birbal teaches the court a masterclass in precision and foresight.
full_text:
A master carpenter named Kalu was commissioned to build an imperial throne using rare, fragrant red sandalwood brought from the forests of Mysore at immense expense.

Eager to finish quickly and claim his gold reward, the carpenter sawed, planed, and hammered in frantic haste. When he assembled the four legs of the throne, he was horrified to discover that one leg was two inches shorter than the others, causing the throne to wobble absurdly!

Panicking, Kalu hastily sawed two inches off the second leg. Now the third leg was too long! He sawed the third leg, and then the fourth, until the majestic imperial throne was reduced to a low, comical stool!

Akbar was furious: 'You fool! You have ruined ten thousand rupees worth of rare sandalwood through your careless haste! Guards, throw him into prison!'

Birbal stepped forward: 'Sire, spare the carpenter. His folly is a living demonstration of an ancient rule of craft.'

Birbal asked the carpenter: 'Kalu, what measuring tool did you use before sawing the wood?'

Kalu wept: 'None, my lord! I merely estimated with my eye and cut in haste!'

Birbal turned to Emperor Akbar and the assembled ministers:

'Sire, Kalu's mistake is the universal error of humanity. The carpenter's proverb warns: "Measure twice, cut once." In his rush to finish, he cut without measuring, and then cut again to hide his first mistake, ruining the whole timber.

'How often do kings and ministers do the very same thing in governance? In hasty anger, a ruler passes an ill-considered decree. When the decree causes trouble, instead of pausing to measure the truth, he passes a second hasty law, and a third, until the noble throne of justice is whittled down to dust!

'Whether carving sandalwood or passing imperial laws, patience, foresight, and precise measurement before action are the only safeguards against ruin.'

Akbar took the lesson to heart. He pardoned the humbled carpenter, ordered him to rebuild the throne under Birbal's supervision, and adopted the motto: 'Deliberate with patience; act with precision.'
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The King and the Pot of Honey
summary: A single dropped spoonful of honey leads to a cascading riot in an ancient fable. Birbal reminds Akbar that small injustices must never be ignored.
keywords: the king and the pot of honey
full_text:
While eating breakfast on the palace terrace, Emperor Akbar accidentally dripped a single drop of golden honey onto the stone balustrade. An attendant rushed forward with a cloth to wipe it away, but Akbar waved his hand: 'Leave it! It is only a tiny drop of honey; it harms no one.'

Birbal, standing nearby, watched in silence.

A moment later, a fly buzzed over and alighted to drink the honey.

A hunting gecko darted out from a marble crack and snapped up the fly.

A wandering cat leaped from the garden wall, caught the gecko, and began devouring it.

The pet hound of an imperial guard spotted the cat, barked furiously, and attacked the feline, tearing at its neck.

The cat's owner, the wife of an imperial baker, rushed out and struck the dog with a heavy rolling pin, breaking its leg.

The dog's owner, the armed imperial guard, drew his sword in fury and struck down the baker!

The baker's guild brothers rushed into the street with iron ladles and knives to avenge their brother, clashing with the royal guards! Within twenty minutes, a bloody riot had erupted in the courtyard below, with swords clashing, torches burning, and dozens wounded!

Akbar watched in horror from the terrace, immediately dispatching fifty cavalrymen to quell the fighting.

Turning pale, Akbar said: 'Heavens! How did such a bloody riot break out over nothing?'

Birbal pointed to the spot on the balustrade:

'Sire, it did not break out over nothing. It began with that single, neglected drop of honey that you deemed too small to wipe away.

'In governance, no injustice is too small to ignore. A single corrupt clerk, an unaddressed peasant grievance, or an unchecked insult seems insignificant at first, like a drop of honey.

'But it attracts the fly of anger, the lizard of resentment, the dog of revenge, and the sword of rebellion, until an entire kingdom is consumed by flames!

'A wise ruler wipes away the smallest drop of discord the moment it falls, preserving the peace of his empire.'

Akbar never forgot the lesson, resolving that in his empire, no grievance, however small, would ever go unaddressed.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Man Who Sold Dreams
summary: A cunning swindler in the Agra market sells golden dreams in clay vials. Birbal uses dream coins to buy out the charlatan's shop.
full_text:
In the bustling market square outside the Delhi Gate of Agra, a silver-bearded charlatan named Hakim Khwaja set up a colorful tent surrounded by shimmering glass vials filled with colored water and scented smoke. He shouted to the passing crowds:

'Step inside, citizens! I sell the sweetest, most vivid dreams in the world! Drink one vial of this celestial nectar before bed, and you shall dream that you are an emperor seated on a golden throne, surrounded by chests of emeralds!'

Dozens of gullible citizens, poor laborers, and young apprentices spent their hard-earned copper coins buying the 'dream vials.'

A poor weaver named Shambhu spent his entire week's earnings on a vial. When he woke up the next morning, he had merely slept heavily and dreamed of nothing at all! When he went to complain, the swindler laughed: 'You did not have faith! Dreams require pure belief!'

Weeping, the weaver brought his grievance to Emperor Akbar.

Birbal stepped forward: 'Sire, selling dreams is an ancient art. Allow me to settle the account with this merchant of visions.'

Birbal summoned Hakim Khwaja to the imperial court. The swindler bowed proudly: 'Your Majesty, my dreams are authentic! Once a man drinks my potion, his mind travels to golden realms!'

Birbal smiled: 'Hakimji, our Emperor desires to purchase your entire inventory—all five hundred vials of dreams—for the royal army, so that our soldiers may dream of glorious victories before battle! The total price is five hundred gold mohurs.'

The swindler's eyes widened with greed: 'A royal bargain, my lord! I shall deliver the vials immediately!'

Birbal ordered a heavy iron chest brought into the room. He unlocked the lid and showed the swindler five hundred gleaming gold coins.

Then, Birbal closed the chest and locked it securely with a heavy brass padlock.

Birbal handed the locked chest to a palace guard and said to the swindler:

'Hakim Khwaja, tonight when you fall asleep, you shall have a magnificent, vivid dream! In your dream, you shall see yourself unlocking this heavy iron chest, taking out all five hundred gold mohurs, and filling your pockets with riches!

'Since you sell dreams for real copper, it is only fair that you be paid with dream gold for your dream vials! The exchange is complete!'

The entire court erupted in laughter. Realizing he had been trapped by his own trade, the swindler fell to the floor, confessed his fraud, returned the poor weaver's money, and was banished from Agra forever.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: Birbal and the Beggar Woman
summary: An old beggar woman refuses alms thrown into the dust with contempt by a wealthy nobleman. Birbal shows Akbar why respect is greater than charity.
full_text:
Outside the grand Jama Masjid in Agra, an elderly, blind beggar woman named Amma sat quietly, never shouting or pleading, holding out a modest clay bowl.

A wealthy and haughty nobleman, Nawab Safdar Jung, passed by on his magnificent grey stallion. Tossing a shiny silver rupee coin carelessly from his saddle, the coin missed the bowl, landed in a filthy puddle of street mud, and splashed dirty water over the old woman's face and cotton sari.

The nobleman sneered: 'Pick it up from the mud, old crone! That silver coin can buy you bread for a month!'

To the amazement of the crowd, the blind woman did not grovel in the mud. She wiped the dirty water from her face with her sleeve, left the silver coin lying untouched in the puddle, and said in a calm, clear voice:

'Keep your silver, Nawab Sahib. My hunger is only for bread, which will pass in a day. But your soul is starved of human decency, which will torment you for eternity. I am poor, but I am not a dog to eat from your insults.'

The incident caused a stir in the bazaar and was reported to Emperor Akbar.

Akbar was puzzled: 'Why did a starving beggar woman refuse a silver rupee simply because it fell in the mud? Money is money!'

Birbal replied with profound solemnity:

'Sire, charity given without respect is not a blessing; it is an assault upon the soul of the poor.

'When a man throws money into the dust with contempt, he is not helping the beggar; he is merely feeding his own disgusting vanity.

'The old woman refused the coin because her dignity was worth more to her than bread. A noble heart can beat inside rags, just as a cowardly, cruel heart can beat beneath silk.'

Akbar was deeply moved. The next morning, Akbar and Birbal walked quietly to the mosque. The Emperor knelt down in the dust, placed two gold mohurs gently into the old woman's hands, and bowed his head, saying: 'Mother, accept this humble gift from a son who honors your noble spirit.'

The old woman touched Akbar's brow, blessed him with tears of joy, and Akbar commended Birbal for teaching the court the true sanctity of human dignity.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Scholar's True Mother Tongue (TE)
summary: A brilliant visiting polyglot challenges the court of Agra to discover his native language. Birbal uses an unexpected splash of cold water to reveal the truth.
full_text:
A renowned scholar named Pandit Ramdas arrived in Agra from the southern provinces. He was an astonishing linguist who had studied in temples and universities across Asia. He spoke Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Turkish, Telugu, Tamil, Marathi, and Bengali with flawless grammar and authentic native accents.

Standing before Emperor Akbar in the Diwan-i-Khas, Ramdas delivered a greeting in five different languages, switching between them with breathtaking ease. He then issued a challenge:

'Your Majesty, I have debated scholars across Hindustan, and not a single soul has been able to identify which language is my true mother tongue! I challenge your Navratnas: determine my native language within twenty-four hours, or acknowledge that my learning surpasses all the ministers of Agra!'

Akbar summoned his linguists and courtiers. For six hours, they engaged Ramdas in discussion. He quoted Kalidasa like a scholar from Ujjain, Firdausi like an archivist from Shiraz, and Tiruvalluvar like a poet from Madurai. By sunset, the imperial scholars were completely defeated.

Akbar turned to Birbal: 'Can you uncover his mother tongue?'

'Allow me until tomorrow morning, Sire,' Birbal replied with a calm smile.

That night, Ramdas was lodged in a luxurious guest suite in the palace gardens. Around midnight, after the scholar had fallen into a deep, peaceful sleep, Birbal slipped into the bedroom carrying a brass pitcher filled with icy cold water.

Birbal crept quietly to the bedside, drew back his arm, and splashed the freezing water directly onto the sleeping scholar's face!

Shocked out of deep slumber, gasping and shivering, Ramdas leaped to his feet in the dark and screamed at the top of his lungs:

'Arey! Yevaru ra meeru? Enduku ila neellu posaaru? Pichhodlaaga unnaru!' (Hey! Who are you people? Why did you pour water on me? Have you gone mad?)

Birbal stepped back, bowed politely with a smile, and whispered: 'Good night, noble Panditji. Sleep well.'

The next morning, Ramdas stood before Akbar's throne: 'Has anyone discovered my native tongue?'

Birbal stepped forward: 'Your native mother tongue is Telugu, from the fertile delta of the Godavari!'

Ramdas gasped in astonishment. He bowed low to the marble floor: 'It is true! Telugu is the language my mother spoke to me in my cradle! But how did you discover it when I spoke only refined Persian and Sanskrit in this hall?'

Birbal explained: 'A scholar can master many languages when his intellect is alert and calculating. But when a man is startled awake in sudden shock or pain, all masks fall away, and the soul cries out in its true mother tongue!'

Akbar and the court applauded Birbal's brilliant practical psychology.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: Who Dared Pull the Emperor's Mustache? (TE)
summary: Akbar asks his ministers what punishment fits a scoundrel who dared pull his royal mustache. Courtiers demand execution, but Birbal suggests sweetmeats.
full_text:
One morning, Emperor Akbar arrived at the Diwan-i-Khas with a stern, brooding expression. The courtiers sat in nervous silence, wondering what crisis of state had troubled their sovereign.

Suddenly, Akbar slammed his fist upon the arm of the golden throne and demanded:

'My lords and counselors! Tell me at once: what punishment does a traitor deserve who had the brazen audacity to pull the royal mustache of the Emperor of Hindustan?'

The courtiers gasped in sheer horror! To touch the Emperor's body was high treason; to pull his mustache was an unforgivable sacrilege!

One bloodthirsty general jumped to his feet: 'Sire! He should be beheaded immediately, and his head mounted on a spike at the Delhi Gate!'

The chief magistrate shouted: 'He should be flayed alive and trampled under the feet of war elephants!'

The royal treasurer added: 'His entire family should be banished and his house razed to the ground!'

Every nobleman in the hall competed to propose the most gruesome, agonizing execution.

Only Birbal sat quietly in his seat, smiling with gentle amusement.

Akbar turned his piercing gaze toward Birbal: 'And you, Birbal? You sit there smiling! What punishment do you prescribe for the culprit who pulled my mustache?'

Birbal stepped forward, bowed low, and answered in a warm, melodic voice:

'Your Majesty, I propose that the culprit be rewarded with an enormous silver bowl overflowing with the sweetest, richest saffron jalebis and pistachios!'

The courtiers were stunned into dead silence. Some whispered that Birbal had finally committed treason!

Akbar smiled: 'Birbal, why do you suggest sweetmeats for such a terrible offense?'

Birbal laughed softly:

'Sire, who in all of Hindustan would have the courage or opportunity to reach up and pull the Emperor's mustache, except for your beloved little grandson, Prince Khurram, while playing upon your royal lap this morning?

'No enemy or traitor could ever get close enough to touch a single hair on your face! Only an innocent child who loves you with all his heart could pull your mustache, and for such love, sweetmeats are the only proper reward!'

Akbar threw back his head and laughed with overflowing delight, confessing that his little grandson had indeed tugged his mustache while playing that morning. Akbar embraced Birbal, praising his matchless understanding of human reality.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power
