title: The Three Daughters and the Camels (TE)
summary: A deceased merchant leaves seventeen camels to be divided among three daughters in impossible fractions. Birbal solves the mathematical paradox.
full_text:
A wealthy camel trader of Agra passed away, leaving behind seventeen fine Arabian camels and three grown daughters. His unusual will specified:

'My eldest daughter shall receive one-half (1/2) of my camels.

'My second daughter shall receive one-third (1/3) of my camels.

'My youngest daughter shall receive one-ninth (1/9) of my camels.

'However, no camel may be slaughtered, sold, or cut into pieces; the animals must be divided whole and alive!'

The three daughters and their husbands argued for weeks. Seventeen could not be divided by two (it gave 8 and a half camels)! Seventeen could not be divided by three (it gave 5 and two-thirds)! Seventeen could not be divided by nine!

The disputes grew so bitter that the case was brought before Emperor Akbar. The royal mathematicians and astronomers spent two days writing formulas in the sand, but confessed that seventeen could not be factored into whole numbers without slaughtering a camel.

Akbar turned to Birbal: 'Can this mathematical knot be untangled?'

Birbal smiled: 'With absolute ease, Your Majesty.'

Birbal ordered his own fine riding camel brought from the stables and placed among the seventeen camels of the sisters, making a total of eighteen camels!

Birbal then addressed the daughters:

'Now let us execute your father's will with mathematical precision.

'Eldest daughter, your share is one-half of the camels. One-half of eighteen is nine! Take your nine camels!' The eldest daughter happily took nine camels.

'Second daughter, your share is one-third of the camels. One-third of eighteen is six! Take your six camels!' The second daughter took six camels.

'Youngest daughter, your share is one-ninth of the camels. One-ninth of eighteen is two! Take your two camels!' The youngest daughter took two camels.

The three sisters counted their camels: nine plus six plus two equals seventeen camels!

Every sister had received more than her theoretical share, and all seventeen camels of their late father were divided whole and alive!

Birbal then stepped forward, took the reins of the one remaining eighteenth camel—his own animal—and rode back to his seat with a bow:

'And here is my camel, returned to me untouched!'

The entire court erupted in thunderous applause. Akbar was spellbound by the elegance of the solution, praising Birbal for proving that an outside perspective can effortlessly dissolve what rigid arguments declare impossible.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Stolen Mango Grove and the Dry Leaves (TE)
summary: A dishonest landlord claims he purchased an orchard twenty years ago, presenting an aged parchment. Birbal proves the ink is fresh by examining dry leaves.
full_text:
An impoverished farmer named Kanhaiya was evicted from his family's ancestral mango orchard by a wealthy landlord, Seth Ramswaroop. The landlord presented an imperial deed of sale, written on yellowed, brittle parchment, claiming he had purchased the land from Kanhaiya's father twenty years earlier.

Kanhaiya wept before Emperor Akbar: 'Sire, my father never sold our orchard! He died five years ago, blessing me to protect our trees! The deed is a forgery!'

Akbar examined the document. The parchment looked genuinely old, stained with yellow age spots and frayed at the edges.

Akbar handed the parchment to Birbal. Birbal inspected the document with a jeweler's magnifying lens, smelled the parchment, and held it up to the sunlight.

Birbal asked the landlord: 'Seth Ramswaroop, when was this deed written?'

'Exactly twenty years ago, my lord, in the presence of the village council.'

Birbal smiled calmly: 'Your Majesty, the parchment itself is indeed old—perhaps thirty years old, salvaged from an old ledger. But the black ink written upon it is less than two weeks old!'

The landlord protested: 'How can you claim that? Ink is ink!'

Birbal ordered a bowl of warm water and a fresh white blotting cloth. He gently pressed the damp cloth against one of the ink letters on the deed.

The ink immediately bled, transferring a sharp purple stain onto the white cloth!

Birbal explained:

'Ancient Indian ink prepared twenty years ago was made of soot, iron gall, and acacia gum. Once dried for over five years, it oxidizes and hardens into the fiber of the parchment, becoming completely water-resistant!

'Only fresh synthetic ink, mixed with aniline dyes introduced to the market last month, dissolves and stains a damp cloth! This deed was written two weeks ago on antique paper to forge an ancient date!'

The landlord fell to the floor in terror, confessing that he had hired a forger in the bazaar to steal the poor farmer's orchard.

Akbar ordered the landlord heavily fined, imprisoned for five years, and returned the land to the rightful farmer, praising Birbal's forensic brilliance.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Parrot with the Broken Wing (TE)
summary: Akbar rescues an injured parrot in the royal gardens and nurses it back to health. Birbal shows the court that kindness is the true measure of kingship.
full_text:
During a morning walk in the gardens of Fatehpur Sikri, Emperor Akbar heard a faint, piteous fluttering in the rose bushes. Looking down, he discovered a young green parrot with a broken wing, bleeding and unable to fly, with a hungry stray cat creeping toward it.

Without hesitation, Emperor Akbar stepped forward, chased the cat away, gently lifted the trembling bird in his silk handkerchief, and carried it to his private pavilion.

For three weeks, the Emperor of Hindustan—ruler of fifty million subjects—personally cleaned the bird's wound, applied herbal poultices, and fed it sweet mango pulp and seeds with his own hands. When the wing finally healed and the parrot fluttered to the marble railing, Akbar opened his hands and watched the bird soar joyfully into the blue sky.

A cynical courtier murmured: 'Sire, was it fitting for the Great Mughal to spend hours bandaging a worthless wild bird that cannot even speak or pay tribute?'

Birbal, who had observed the Emperor's care with deep respect, turned to the courtier:

'My lord, you measure the world by tribute and profit. But true greatness is measured by compassion toward those who can offer nothing in return.

'An emperor can command armies, execute enemies, and build golden palaces through power alone. But when an emperor bends his royal knee to cradle an injured wild bird, preserve its fragile life, and set it free to fly in the heavens, he mirrors the mercy of the Almighty Creator!

'Power makes a monarch feared, but mercy makes a monarch beloved in heaven and earth.'

Akbar smiled warmly and clasped Birbal's hand, affirming that a ruler's heart must remain tender to the humblest creature under his sky.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Brahmin Who Walked on the River (TE)
summary: An ascetic boasts that thirty years of meditation gave him the power to walk across the river Yamuna. Birbal shows him the true market value of his 'miracle.'
full_text:
A proud hermit named Sadhu Jalandhar arrived at Emperor Akbar's court, surrounded by awestruck followers. The hermit proclaimed:

'I have performed severe penance in the high Himalayas for thirty long years! I have mastered the secret art of levitation! I can walk across the deep river Yamuna upon the surface of the water without sinking, as if walking upon stone! Does Your Majesty's court possess any power that can match my divine miracle?'

Akbar was fascinated and went with Birbal and the court to the banks of the Yamuna to witness the demonstration.

Before thousands of spectators, the hermit chanted mantras, stepped onto the flowing water, and walked across the wide river to the opposite bank without sinking, stepping ashore with completely dry feet!

The crowd gasped in mystical awe. Akbar turned to Birbal: 'Birbal! He walked across the river! Thirty years of meditation to achieve such a wonder! Is it not priceless?'

Birbal walked to the river pier, approached an ordinary boatman who was rowing a wooden ferry across the river, and asked:

'Brother boatman, how much do you charge to carry a traveler across the Yamuna in your boat?'

The boatman smiled humbly: 'Two copper dams, my lord. Just two small coppers.'

Birbal returned to Emperor Akbar and the proud hermit with a radiant smile:

'Sire, I have just calculated the exact value of this holy man's thirty years of meditation!

'It is worth exactly two copper dams!

'For two copper dams, this humble boatman carries merchants, women, children, and sacks of wheat across the river safely every day, feeding his family through honest labor!

'This ascetic spent thirty years of his precious human life in cold caves, doing nothing for society, healing no sick, feeding no hungry, merely to save himself two copper dams at the river ferry!

'What a tragic waste of human life to spend thirty years acquiring a parlor trick that a boatman outperforms for two pennies!'

The entire crowd roared with laughter. The hermit blushed with profound shame, realizing that vanity had hijacked his spiritual journey, and Akbar thanked Birbal for separating genuine virtue from empty spectacles.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Merchant's Mysterious Last Will (TE)
summary: A dying merchant leaves three sealed jars of dirt, bones, and straw to his three sons. Birbal decodes the profound fatherly inheritance.
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Delhi died, leaving behind an enormous fortune and three sons. However, when his will was opened before the family elders, they found no mention of gold or property. Instead, the will instructed that three sealed ceramic jars be delivered to his sons:

To the eldest son: a jar filled with dry dirt and soil.

To the second son: a jar filled with dry animal bones.

To the youngest son: a jar filled with dry yellow straw.

The sons were insulted and bewildered. 'Our father was a millionaire, yet he has left us dirt, bones, and straw! Has our father gone mad?'

The brothers began fighting violently over their father's gold, palaces, and cattle, each claiming the entire estate. The bitter dispute was brought before Emperor Akbar.

Akbar examined the jars in confusion: 'Birbal, what father leaves dirt and bones to his children?'

Birbal smiled with deep admiration for the deceased merchant:

'Sire, this father was a man of supreme wisdom. He did not leave insults; he left a complete, fair division of his estate in symbolic code!

'To the eldest son, he gave the jar of dirt—which represents his vast real estate, farmland, orchards, and ancestral soil! Let the eldest son inherit all the lands!

'To the second son, he gave the jar of bones—which represents the cattle, horses, sheep, and livestock that possess skeletons! Let the second son inherit all the herds and animals!

'To the youngest son, he gave the jar of straw—which represents the golden harvest, the grain warehouses, the cotton stores, and the gold mohurs earned from agricultural trade! Let the youngest son inherit the treasury and warehouses!'

The three brothers stared in stunned silence. The code was so brilliant, so harmonious, and so perfectly balanced that all three brothers embraced with tears of joy, praising their late father's memory.

Akbar rewarded Birbal with a necklace of emeralds, marvelling at how wisdom can translate apparent nonsense into profound harmony.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Emperor's Cracked Mirror (TE)
summary: Akbar smashes a mirror in anger when it distorts his reflection. Birbal uses the broken shards to teach the court a lesson on emotional self-control.
full_text:
In the imperial bedchamber, Emperor Akbar was dressing for an important diplomatic summit when he looked into a large, imported Venetian looking-glass. The glass had developed an invisible hairline crack during transit, causing Akbar's reflection to appear twisted, with a distorted nose and crooked eyes!

In sudden frustration and vanity, Akbar struck the mirror with his royal staff, shattering it into a hundred shards upon the marble floor: 'Ugly, lying glass! How dare you distort my face!'

Birbal entered the chamber and observed the broken glass and the breathing Emperor.

Birbal knelt down, picked up one of the jagged shards from the floor, and looked into it.

'Birbal,' Akbar complained, 'that mirror made me look like a monster!'

Birbal held the shard before the Emperor with serene gentleness:

'Sire, look into this single broken piece now that your anger has cooled. What do you see?'

Akbar looked down. In the small shard, his reflection appeared calm, handsome, and clear.

Birbal said:

'Sire, when you struck the mirror in anger, it was not the glass that was distorted; it was your own impatient mind!

'When the mind is agitated by wrath, pride, or fear, the entire world appears hostile, twisted, and ugly. We blame our ministers, our servants, our wives, and our friends, striking out to break them like this mirror.

'Yet the moment we breathe deeply and quiet the storm within our own breast, the world reflects our own calm dignity once again.

'A ruler must never deliver judgments when his mind is cracked by anger, for he will punish his own distorted reflection instead of the truth.'

Akbar sat down in silence, deeply moved by the reminder. He apologized to his servants, ordered a new mirror placed in his chamber, and thanked Birbal for being the guardian of his emotional peace.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Sentry Who Slept at the Palace Gate (TE)
summary: A young guard falls asleep on duty after nursing his sick mother all night. Birbal saves the soldier from the executioner's sword.
full_text:
During an unannounced midnight inspection of the Agra palace ramparts, Emperor Akbar discovered a nineteen-year-old sentry named Dilip slumped against the stone parapet, sound asleep with his spear lying in the dust.

Akbar's military code was absolute and unforgiving: any sentry caught sleeping on watch was guilty of treason and sentenced to be beheaded at dawn.

The next morning, Dilip was brought before the court in chains. The young soldier wept, but did not deny his fault.

Akbar raised his hand to pronounce the death sentence: 'By the laws of our army, you must die.'

Birbal stepped forward: 'Sire, the law is just, but justice must examine the heart before it swings the sword. Dilip has served in the royal guard for three years without a single blemish. Why did he sleep last night?'

Birbal questioned the soldier's commander and neighbors.

The commander revealed: 'Sire, Dilip's widowed mother was stricken with cholera three nights ago. For seventy-two hours, the boy stayed awake by her bedside, bathing her feverish brow, carrying medicine, and weeping over her. He reported for duty last night without having slept for three days, refusing to take sick leave because he needed his daily wage to buy her milk.'

The entire court fell silent.

Birbal turned to Akbar with tears in his eyes:

'Sire, Dilip did not sleep out of treason or drunkenness. His body collapsed under the sacred weight of filial devotion and desperate poverty.

'A boy who loves his mother so deeply will fight to the death to protect the Emperor who shows his mother mercy! If we execute our most devoted sons for human exhaustion, we murder the very soul of our people!'

Akbar's stern face softened. He wiped a tear from his eye, descended from the throne, and lifted the young soldier to his feet:

'Dilip, your devotion to your mother honors this empire.'

Akbar pardoned the soldier, granted his mother a monthly medical allowance, and thanked Birbal for proving that royal mercy is the true strength of an army.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The King Who Could Not Sleep (TE)
summary: Akbar suffers from chronic insomnia despite musicians and doctors. Birbal cures the Emperor with a story that has no end.
full_text:
Emperor Akbar was plagued by severe insomnia. Night after night, musicians played soft lullabies, physicians administered herbal syrups, and storytellers recounted epic legends, but the Emperor tossed and turned until dawn, exhausted by the relentless racing of his own thoughts.

In frustration, Akbar called Birbal to his bedchamber at midnight: 'Birbal, tell me a bedtime story that will put me to sleep! But hear this: if your story ends, and I am still awake, you must start another! You must tell a story that never ends until I sleep!'

Birbal smiled, sat upon a cushion beside the imperial couch, and began in a low, soothing, rhythmic voice:

'Sire, once upon a time, a wealthy farmer built a colossal grain storehouse, towering as high as a mountain, filled to the roof with ten million bushels of golden wheat.

'However, the builder left one tiny hole near the roof, barely large enough for a single sparrow to squeeze through.

'A flock of ten thousand hungry sparrows discovered the hole.

'The first sparrow flew in through the hole... picked up a single grain of wheat in its beak... and flew away: *Chirp!*

'Then the second sparrow flew in through the hole... picked up a single grain of wheat... and flew away: *Chirp!*

'Then the third sparrow flew in... picked up a grain... and flew away: *Chirp!*'

Birbal paused. Akbar turned in his bed: 'And then what happened, Birbal?'

Birbal continued in a gentle, hypnotic monotone:

'Then the fourth sparrow flew in... picked up a grain... and flew away: *Chirp!*

'Then the fifth sparrow flew in... picked up a grain... and flew away: *Chirp!*'

'Birbal!' Akbar whispered. 'What happens after all the sparrows take their grain?'

Birbal replied softly:

'Sire, how can I tell you what happens afterward? Only five sparrows have taken five grains! There are still nine million, nine hundred and ninety-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-five bushels of wheat left in the storehouse!

'The sixth sparrow flew in... picked up a grain... and flew away: *Chirp!*

'The seventh sparrow flew in... picked up a grain... and flew away: *Chirp!*'

Akbar listened to the steady, endless, gentle rhythm of the flying sparrows. His racing thoughts surrendered their frantic grip. His eyelids grew heavy... heavier... and within ten minutes, the Emperor of Hindustan was snoring peacefully in deep, restorative slumber!

Birbal smiled, pulled the velvet blanket over the sleeping monarch, and slipped quietly out into the starlit night.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Clay Pot That Gave Birth to a Cup (TE)
summary: Birbal borrows brass pots from a greedy neighbor and returns them with 'baby' cups. When he later borrows a silver cauldron, he announces it 'died.'
full_text:
A greedy neighbor of Birbal named Seth Kundanlal was obsessed with getting something for nothing. Knowing this, Birbal decided to teach him an unforgettable lesson.

One evening, Birbal knocked on the neighbor's door: 'Sethji, I have guests arriving tonight. Could you lend me two large brass cooking pots for twenty-four hours?'

The neighbor reluctantly lent the pots.

The next evening, Birbal returned the two brass pots, along with two tiny, brand-new brass cups nested inside them!

Kundanlal looked confused: 'Birbal, what are these two small cups? They are not mine.'

Birbal smiled innocently: 'Ah, Sethji! It was a miracle! While in my kitchen last night, your two large brass pots gave birth to these two little baby cups! Since the mother pots belong to you, the baby cups belong to you as well!'

The neighbor laughed inside at Birbal's apparent stupidity, greedily pocketed the two free brass cups, and kept the pots.

A week later, Birbal visited the neighbor again: 'Sethji, I am hosting an imperial banquet for fifty nobles. Could you lend me your enormous, antique solid silver cauldron worth five thousand rupees?'

Kundanlal's eyes widened with greed: 'If his brass pots gave birth to brass cups, what will a silver cauldron give birth to? Silver bowls!'

The greedy neighbor gladly handed over his prized silver cauldron.

A week passed. Two weeks passed. Birbal did not return the cauldron.

Unable to wait any longer, Kundanlal marched to Birbal's mansion: 'Birbal! Where is my silver cauldron? And where are the silver babies it gave birth to?'

Birbal stepped out onto his veranda, his face a portrait of profound, weeping grief:

'Alas, Sethji! I bear tragic, heartbreaking news! Last night, after a sudden and violent illness, your beloved silver cauldron passed away! It died, and I had it buried with full honors in the garden!'

The neighbor turned purple with rage: 'Are you completely insane? You liar! You thief! How on earth can a metal silver cauldron die?'

Birbal looked at the shouting merchant with razor-sharp irony:

'Sethji, if a brass pot can give birth to a brass cup, then surely a silver cauldron can get sick and die!

'If you are willing to believe the impossible when it brings you dishonest profit, you must be equally willing to accept the impossible when it brings you loss!'

The dispute was dragged before Emperor Akbar, who laughed until tears filled his eyes, forcing the greedy neighbor to drop his suit and learn that greed invariably swallows its own bait.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Witness of the Ancient Banyan Tree (TE)
summary: A dishonest traveler denies borrowing money under an old banyan tree. Birbal sends the lender to summon the tree, trapping the borrower in court.
full_text:
Two travelers, Mohan and Sohan, who had known each other since childhood, journeyed together across the dry plains of Malwa. Outside a lonely village, they rested in the shade of a colossal, centuries-old banyan tree. While resting, Sohan fell ill and ran out of money. Taking pity on his friend, Mohan opened his purse and lent Sohan one hundred silver coins, saying: 'Repay me when we return to Agra.'

Sohan wept with gratitude under the tree, swearing: 'May this holy banyan tree be my witness! I shall repay every silver coin the day I return.'

A year later, both men returned to Agra. When Mohan approached Sohan's prosperous house and politely asked for his money, Sohan looked at him with icy disdain: 'What money? I never borrowed a single dam from you! Do you have a written receipt? Do you have witnesses? Get off my porch before I call the guards!'

Heartbroken by the betrayal of friendship, Mohan brought his case before Emperor Akbar's court. Akbar questioned Sohan, who swore with an innocent face: 'Sire, I swear on my sacred honor, Mohan never lent me money. He is inventing stories to extort me.'

Akbar turned to Birbal: 'There are no written documents and no human witnesses. How can this be decided?'

Birbal turned to Mohan: 'Where did you give him the money?'

'Sire, under a colossal, twisted banyan tree ten miles outside the city walls, near the old stone bridge.'

Birbal handed Mohan his royal staff: 'Take this staff, ride to that banyan tree, and say: "Raja Birbal summons you to the imperial court of Emperor Akbar to testify as a witness in this dispute!" Go at once, and we shall await the tree's reply.'

Mohan bowed and departed on a horse.

Birbal instructed Sohan to sit quietly on the floor of the court and wait. An hour passed in absolute silence. The sun climbed higher. Courtiers whispered, amused that Birbal had summoned a tree.

Suddenly, Birbal turned to Sohan and asked casually: 'Sohan, do you think Mohan has reached the banyan tree yet?'

Without thinking, Sohan replied smugly: 'Certainly not, Your Majesty! That banyan tree is more than ten miles away across rough terrain! It will take him at least two more hours to get there!'

Birbal's eyes flashed like lightning. He struck his fist upon the table:

'Caught by your own tongue, scoundrel! If Mohan never lent you money under that banyan tree, and you were never there with him, how did you know the exact distance and location of the tree so accurately?'

Sohan turned pale as death. He fell face-down upon the marble floor, trembling with terror: 'Mercy, Sire! I confessed! I remembered the tree! I will pay Mohan his hundred silver coins immediately!'

When Mohan returned hours later, exhausted, Akbar had already ordered the money recovered with a heavy penalty, praising Birbal for turning an ancient tree into an undeniable witness of truth.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Wise Washerman's Silent Donkey (TE)
summary: A quarrelsome neighbor screams insults at an old washerman. The washerman remains silent, using his donkey to illustrate the beauty of composure.
full_text:
In the riverside quarter of Agra lived a gentle, elderly washerman named Shankar, whose calm temperament was respected by all. However, his neighbor, an aggressive and foul-mouthed blacksmith named Mangal, constantly picked quarrels, shouting vile insults and cursing at the old man over everyday trifles.

Throughout every verbal attack, Shankar never raised his voice, never frowned, and never uttered a single word in reply; he merely washed his clothes and smiled.

One morning, after the blacksmith had spent twenty minutes screaming curses at Shankar's fence, Emperor Akbar and Birbal happened to pass by on their morning ride.

Akbar stopped his horse and asked: 'Shankar, why do you stand there quietly while that scoundrel heaps filthy insults upon your head? Are you a coward, or do you have no tongue to defend your honor?'

Shankar bowed with folded hands: 'Sire, allow me to ask my donkey.'

The washerman turned to his grey donkey tied to the acacia tree. The blacksmith was still screaming. The donkey chewed its hay peacefully, flicked an occasional fly with its ear, and never once looked at the screaming man.

Shankar said to the Emperor:

'Your Majesty, look at my humble donkey. Even this simple beast understands that when a wild dog barks at the fence, the donkey does not drop its hay to bark back!

'If someone offers you an ugly, filthy package wrapped in dirty rags, and you refuse to stretch out your hands to accept it—to whom does the package still belong?'

Akbar replied: 'It still belongs to the person who brought it.'

'Exactly so, Sire!' Shankar smiled. 'My neighbor brings a package of filthy anger and hatred every morning. I simply refuse to accept it.

'Since I do not receive it, his anger remains entirely his own burden, poisoning his own blood and giving him high fever, while my soul remains peaceful and clean as river water!'

Akbar was captivated by the old washerman's profound philosophy. He ordered the abusive blacksmith fined for disturbing the peace, and commended Shankar and Birbal, remarking that composure is the highest armor of the wise.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Flatterer's Grand Feast of Words (TE)
summary: A parasitic courtier promises lavish feasts to guests but never serves food. Birbal invites him to a grand royal dinner of invisible delicacies.
full_text:
A boastful courtier named Mirza Kamran was famous in Agra for inviting poor scholars and poets to his mansion, describing magnificent menus of roasted lamb, saffron pilaf, and almond halwa, yet serving only dry water and stale crusts, saying: 'Imagine the heavenly flavor, my friends!'

The hungry poets complained to Birbal about the courtier's cruel teasing.

Birbal invited Mirza Kamran to a private royal banquet in the imperial pavilion, with Emperor Akbar observing behind a carved marble screen.

Kamran arrived in his finest silk robe, starving himself all day in anticipation.

Birbal seated the courtier before an empty gold platter and said with grand gestures:

'Welcome, noble Mirza! Let us begin our feast! Do you see this magnificent, imaginary soup of mountain pheasant and wild saffron? Smell the heavenly aroma! Take your golden spoon and drink deeply!'

Kamran was bewildered, but eager to please the powerful minister, he picked up his empty spoon, dipped it into empty air, and swallowed: 'Ah... delicious, Raja Birbal!'

Birbal continued enthusiastically: 'And now, behold this giant roasted royal peacock, stuffed with pistachios and raisins! Take this carving knife, slice off a fat drumstick, and chew the tender meat!'

The hungry courtier chewed empty air, his stomach rumbling loudly: 'Mmm... succulent... exquisite!'

Birbal then 'served' twenty imaginary courses—kababs, biryanis, sherbets, and pastries—making the courtier pantomime eating for two grueling hours!

Finally, Birbal smiled: 'And now, noble Mirza, since you have enjoyed the finest feast in Hindustan, let us have the palace wrestlers wrestle you in the courtyard to test your digestive strength!'

Mirza Kamran collapsed upon the floor, clutching his starving stomach, weeping: 'Mercy, Lord Birbal! I am dying of real hunger! I have swallowed only empty air!'

Akbar stepped out from behind the screen, laughing heartily:

'Now you know how those poor poets felt when you fed them grand words instead of real bread, Kamran! Words can comfort the soul, but they can never fill a hungry belly!'

Akbar ordered real food brought for the humbled noble, who swore never to mock the hungry again.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Thief Who Robbed His Own Shadow (TE)
summary: A burglar flees in terror from his own shadow on a moonlit night. Birbal uses the incident to explain how guilt terrifies itself.
full_text:
In the middle of a clear, moonlit night, an imperial night watchman in Agra noticed a man sprinting frantically through the alleys, screaming in terror, repeatedly drawing his dagger and stabbing at the ground behind him!

The guards tackled the frantic man and brought him to the palace guardhouse.

The prisoner was an infamous burglar named Kallu, and in his pouch were three stolen diamond necklaces looted from a merchant's mansion an hour earlier.

When Emperor Akbar questioned the thief next morning: 'Why were you running and screaming like a madman if you had successfully escaped the merchant's guards?'

Kallu shivered: 'Sire, a dark, terrifying demon was chasing me through the streets! Wherever I ran, he ran behind me! When I jumped, he leaped! When I drew my dagger, he raised a blade to strike me! I was fighting for my life against a phantom of the underworld!'

Birbal smiled, walked to the open archway where the morning sun cast long shadows across the floor, and said:

'Kallu, look behind you right now! The demon is standing beside you!'

Kallu screamed and leaped away—only to see his own dark shadow moving across the marble floor!

The entire court burst into laughter.

Birbal explained to Emperor Akbar:

'Sire, the moonlight was bright last night. When Kallu committed the burglary, his guilty conscience terrified his mind.

'When he saw his own long, dark shadow stretching behind him under the street lamps, his guilt transformed his harmless shadow into an avenging officer of justice! He was running from his own reflection, fighting his own hands!

'A righteous man sleeps in peace under the stars, feared by none and fearing nothing. But the thief carries his own executioner inside his breast; even his own shadow becomes an army that drives him into chains.'

Akbar commended Birbal's psychological wisdom, sentencing the burglar while reflecting upon the inescapable terror of guilt.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Four Seasons in a Single Day (TE)
summary: Akbar asks Birbal whether a mortal can experience Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter in twelve hours. Birbal illustrates the seasons of human emotion.
full_text:
During a philosophical discussion on the terrace of Fatehpur Sikri, Emperor Akbar remarked: 'How wonderful nature is, taking twelve months to cycle through the freshness of Spring, the heat of Summer, the harvest of Autumn, and the chill of Winter! How tragic that human life cannot experience all four seasons in a single day!'

Birbal bowed: 'Sire, every human being experiences all four seasons in a single day, if he only observes the weather of his own heart.'

Akbar challenged him: 'Demonstrate this to me today, Birbal!'

Birbal took Akbar on a quiet stroll through the imperial city, observing citizens from morning till night.

At dawn, they visited the maternity pavilion of the public hospital. A young mother held her newborn son, her face glowing with tender joy, surrounded by blossoming marigolds:

'Sire,' Birbal whispered, 'this is the Spring of the human soul. Life is newborn, fragrant, innocent, and full of fresh hope.'

At noon, they observed a crowded blacksmiths' workshop where muscled men hammered glowing red iron anvils under a blistering sun, shouting and arguing over supplies:

'Here is the Summer of the soul, Sire. Passion, intense labor, heat, sweat, and burning ambitions that test human endurance.'

At sunset, they visited a bustling village threshing yard where old farmers laughed, sharing sweet jaggery cakes while stacking golden sheaves of wheat:

'Here is the Autumn of the soul. The harvest of labor, the contentment of achievement, and the quiet satisfaction of shared abundance.'

Finally, at midnight, they entered a quiet room where an elderly, white-bearded scholar sat in deep, silent meditation beneath a solitary oil lamp, completely detached from worldly desires:

'And here is the Winter of the soul, Sire. The outer world is cold and dark, but within, the mind has settled into peaceful stillness, preparing for the great dawn of eternity.'

Akbar stood in silent wonder, embracing Birbal for revealing that the great universe of nature is replicated entirely within the human soul.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Emperor's True Portrait (TE)
summary: Akbar is blind in one eye and walks with a limp. Three painters attempt his portrait. Birbal shows how true genius captures reality with grace.
full_text:
Emperor Akbar, though majestic and powerful, had two physical flaws from old battle injuries: his left eye was partially blind and clouded, and his right leg had a slight limp from a war arrow.

Akbar summoned three famous portrait artists from Delhi, Lahore, and Kashmir to paint his imperial likeness, promising ten thousand gold coins for a portrait that was both completely truthful and completely royal.

The first artist painted Akbar with both eyes wide, bright, and perfect, and both legs straight as pillars.

Akbar frowned: 'Flattery! You have painted an imaginary king, not me! You lie to please my vanity!' The first painter was dismissed without reward.

The second artist, determined to be fiercely realistic, painted Akbar with a milky, twisted, blind eye and a shriveled, deformed leg.

Akbar was offended: 'Insolence! You have focused on my infirmity, turning the Emperor of Hindustan into a wretched cripple, ignoring the majesty of the throne!' The second painter was dismissed.

The third artist, young and nervous, consulted Birbal before lifting his brush. Birbal whispered: 'Art must marry truth with dignity. Paint what the Emperor does, not merely what he suffers.'

Two weeks later, the third artist unveiled his masterpiece before the imperial durbar.

The portrait depicted Emperor Akbar mounted upon a noble Arabian stallion during a hunt.

Akbar was drawn in profile, drawing a great golden bow to shoot an arrow at a charging wild boar!

Because he was aiming his bow, his wounded left eye was naturally closed in marksman focus, while his good right eye aimed straight along the arrow!

And because he was mounted upon his horse, his legs were tucked into the stirrups under his saddle blankets, concealing the slight limp while displaying supreme equestrian grace!

The portrait was completely, undeniably true to life, yet captured the Emperor at the absolute peak of martial majesty, strength, and royal honor!

Akbar leaped from his throne with tears of admiration: 'Magnificent! You have hidden nothing, lied about nothing, and yet honored the throne with supreme dignity!'

Akbar awarded the young artist twenty thousand gold mohurs, while Birbal smiled, remarking that wisdom finds the angle where truth and beauty become one.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Golden Fishing Net of Agra (TE)
summary: A fisherman rises to become a wealthy minister and keeps a golden net in his palace. Birbal explains the profound memory behind the treasure.
full_text:
A humble, honest river fisherman named Sadhu rose through dedication, courage, and talent to become an imperial tax commissioner under Emperor Akbar. He lived in a fine mansion and received a handsome salary.

Envious courtiers noticed that in the center of his lavish reception hall, Sadhu had mounted an old, frayed, mud-stained hemp fishing net inside a glass cabinet lined with velvet and gold leaf.

The courtiers mocked him: 'Look at that peasant! He has become a high minister, yet he displays a filthy fishnet in his palace to insult the nobility!'

Akbar was curious and asked Sadhu in court: 'Commissioner, why do you keep a dirty old fishing net in a golden cabinet?'

Before Sadhu could speak, Birbal stepped forward with deep respect:

'Sire, allow me to honor Commissioner Sadhu's golden net.

'Many men who rise from humble poverty into royal wealth immediately become arrogant, look down upon the poor, and pretend they were born of kings.

'Sadhu keeps his old fishing net where he must gaze upon it every single morning before putting on his silk robes and signing tax decrees.

'The net reminds him: "Remember that you were once a hungry, barefoot fisherman on the muddy banks of the Yamuna, and that your power is a trust from the Emperor to serve the poor, not to oppress them!"

'That frayed net is the anchor of his humility, preserving his soul from the intoxicating poison of pride.'

Akbar was so moved by the explanation that he walked across the hall and embraced Commissioner Sadhu:

'Blessed is the empire whose ministers remember their humble origins! Would to God that all my courtiers kept their old plows and fishnets in their palaces!'

Akbar rewarded Sadhu with a jade seal, praising Birbal for defending the beauty of humility.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Silver Coin in the Palace Courtyard (TE)
summary: Akbar drops a silver coin on the floor to see which of his noble courtiers will stoop to pick it up. Birbal's reaction provides a lesson in self-respect.
full_text:
One afternoon in the Diwan-i-Khas, while testing the character of his courtiers, Emperor Akbar casually reached into his sash, pulled out a single silver rupee coin, and let it drop onto the polished marble floor.

*Clink!*

The coin rolled across the floor, coming to rest near a group of senior courtiers and ministers.

Instantly, three wealthy nawabs and two imperial scribes dove forward onto their hands and knees, scrambling across the floor, shoving each other aside, and pawing through the dust to grab the single silver coin!

A general snatched it triumphantly, dust coating his silk sleeves.

Meanwhile, Birbal stood quietly beside the Emperor, his hands folded, watching the undignified scramble with a calm, amused gaze.

Akbar smiled with disdain at the scrambling courtiers, then turned to Birbal: 'Birbal, you did not jump to pick up the silver coin. Do you despise money?'

Birbal replied with quiet grace:

'Sire, I respect honest wealth earned through labor and service. But a man who wears the robes of an imperial counselor should possess dignity worth more than thirty copper dams!

'When noblemen who govern provinces dive into the dirt to scramble over a single coin dropped from a monarch's hand, they show that they possess the minds of hungry street dogs, not the souls of statesmen!

'He who scrambles for petty crumbs will eventually sell his honor, his judgment, and his empire for a handful of silver. A true minister bows only to justice, never to dust.'

The scrambling courtiers stood up, red-faced with burning shame, brushing the dust from their knees.

Akbar commended Birbal, stating that character is measured not by how high a man climbs, but by how low he refuses to stoop.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Magic Lamp of Fatehpur Sikri (TE)
summary: A merchant sells an 'Aladdin's lamp' to a gullible prince. Birbal demonstrates that real genies are summoned through human sweat.
full_text:
A foreign trickster arrived at the court of Prince Salim (the future Emperor Jahangir), carrying an antique, tarnished brass oil lamp covered in mysterious Arabic inscriptions. The trickster whispered secretly to the young prince:

'Your Highness! This is an authentic magic lamp from the cavern of Baghdad! If you rub the brass with saffron oil at midnight, a giant celestial genie will emerge to build golden palaces and defeat your enemies in battle! I offer it to you for merely ten thousand gold mohurs!'

Salim was fascinated and paid the ten thousand gold coins from his royal allowance.

For seven nights, the young prince rubbed the lamp with scented oil, chanted spells, and waited in the dark, but nothing emerged except greasy brass soot!

Realizing he had been swindled, Salim was furious and complained to his father, Emperor Akbar.

Akbar summoned Birbal to track down the swindler.

Birbal caught the trickster at the city gates, retrieved the prince's gold, and brought the lamp into the council chamber.

Young Prince Salim asked: 'Raja Birbal, is there truly no magic lamp in the world that commands a genie?'

Birbal picked up the brass lamp, handed Salim an iron spade and a book of mathematics, and said with affectionate warmth:

'My Prince, there is indeed a magic lamp that commands the greatest genie in creation, but it is not made of brass.

'The magic lamp is the Human Intellect!

'The oil that fuels it is Diligent Study and Truth!

'The flame that burns upon it is Moral Virtue!

'And the mighty genie that emerges from it to build golden cities, drain swamps, heal diseases, and conquer empires is the genie of Honest Human Labor and Science!

'He who rubs the lamp of his own mind with hard work and study can command the universe. But he who sits in the dark rubbing a metal pot, waiting for magic to do his work, is a fool who loses his gold to swindlers!'

Prince Salim bowed in deep respect, took the lesson to heart, and dedicated himself to his studies, while Akbar praised Birbal's inspiring pedagogy.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Grateful River Fisherman (TE)
summary: A fisherman finds a lost royal emerald in the stomach of a fish and returns it to Akbar. Birbal ensures the honest man's reward blesses his village.
full_text:
While boating upon the river Yamuna during a festival, Emperor Akbar slipped his favorite emerald signet ring from his finger, and it splashed into the deep, swirling waters, sinking forever out of sight. Divers searched for two days, but found nothing.

A week later, an impoverished river fisherman named Mangal caught a colossal carp three leagues downriver. While cleaning the fish for his family's dinner, his knife struck something hard inside the fish's belly. Wiping away the scales, he uncovered the gleaming imperial signet ring, engraved with Akbar's royal seal!

The fisherman's wife gasped: 'Husband! This emerald can buy us five houses and make us rich for life! Let us sell it to a jeweler in Delhi!'

Mangal shook his head firmly: 'No, wife. This ring bears the imperial seal of our Emperor. What is found must be returned to its owner. Dishonest bread brings a curse upon the children.'

The next morning, Mangal walked to the Agra palace in his patched rags, knelt before the throne, and presented the emerald ring to Akbar.

Akbar was overjoyed: 'Fisherman, you have restored my father's heirloom! Ask for whatever reward you desire!'

Mangal bowed humbly: 'Sire, I am an uneducated fisherman. If you give me gold coins, I may lose them to thieves.

'I ask only this: build a small stone school and a clean drinking water well in our riverside village, so that our children may learn to read and write and our wives need not walk miles for water.'

The entire court was hushed by the peasant's selfless request.

Birbal stepped forward, his eyes shining with admiration:

'Sire, look at the nobility of this honest fisherman. A greedy nobleman would have asked for titles, land, and gold for himself.

'This poor man asks only for knowledge and clean water for his neighbors! True virtue thinks not of its own pocket, but of the community's future.'

Akbar ordered the school and well built immediately, appointed Mangal the royal superintendent of the river fisheries with a handsome salary, and rewarded Birbal for celebrating the pure hearts of the people.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Riddle of the Seven Sealed Pots (TE)
summary: A foreign merchant presents seven identical sealed clay pots containing gold, mud, honey, vinegar, salt, jewels, and ashes. Birbal identifies the contents without opening them.
full_text:
A clever merchant from Samarkand arrived at Emperor Akbar's court, wheeling a cart bearing seven identical, unglazed earthenware pots, each sealed tightly with wax and stamped with the merchant's seal.

The merchant challenged the court: 'Your Majesty, these seven identical jars contain seven different substances: pure Gold, river Mud, sweet Honey, sour Vinegar, white Salt, precious Jewels, and dry Ashes.

'I challenge your wise minister Raja Birbal: tell the court the exact contents of each jar without breaking the wax, without opening the lids, and without shaking the jars!'

The courtiers shook their heads in dismay: 'How can anyone see through opaque clay without opening it?'

Birbal smiled, walked calmly around the table, and made a few simple arrangements.

First, Birbal placed all seven jars in the warm morning sun near the open garden archway.

Within twenty minutes, two honeybees flew in from the garden and landed persistently upon the lid of the third jar, sipping the faint microscopic vapors that seeped through the porous clay: 'The third jar contains sweet Honey!' Birbal announced.

Next, tiny black ants marched across the floor and climbed up the outside of the third jar, confirming the sweetness.

Birbal picked up a sharp metal needle, warmed it in a candle flame, and tapped the jars gently with a small bronze mallet.

The fourth jar, when tapped, emitted a faint pungent sour vapor through the clay pore: 'This is sour Vinegar!'

The first jar, when lifted, was immensely heavy—far heavier than all the others: 'This contains pure Gold!'

The sixth jar, when tapped with the needle, rattled with a hard, ringing crystalline chime: 'These are precious uncut Jewels!'

The fifth jar felt cold and damp to the touch, absorbing moisture from the air: 'This is white Salt!'

The second jar smelled of river silt: 'This is Mud!'

And the seventh jar was feather-light, completely dry and soundless: 'These are dry Ashes!'

The merchant broke the wax seals before the court. Every single jar matched Birbal's identification with absolute, flawless precision!

The court erupted in cheers, and the merchant bowed low: 'Your wisdom uses nature's senses to see through clay!' Akbar rewarded Birbal with a royal robe.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The False Witness and the Clay Dog (TE)
summary: A false witness testifies that he saw a theft committed in pitch-black darkness. Birbal uses a clay dog to shatter the perjurer's testimony.
full_text:
A greedy landlord named Seth Hiralal accused a poor tenant farmer of sneaking into his stables on a stormy, moonless night and stealing an ox.

To prove his case, Hiralal brought a hired witness—a shady gambler named Jaggu—who swore on the holy river: 'Your Majesty, I saw the theft with my own eyes! At two o'clock in the morning, during the pitch-black new moon, while torrential rain fell, I was standing fifty paces away and I clearly saw this tenant untie the ox and lead it into the woods!'

The poor tenant cried out his innocence, swearing he was asleep in his hut with his children.

Akbar was inclined to believe the eyewitness testimony. Birbal stepped in:

'Your Majesty, allow me to question this remarkable witness.'

Birbal asked Jaggu: 'You say you saw the theft at two in the morning, during a moonless, stormy night, from fifty paces away?'

'Yes, my lord! My vision is sharp as a hawk!'

Birbal pointed to a small wooden table in the corner of the council hall, thirty paces away, where a small clay statue rested.

Birbal asked: 'Jaggu, in this brightly lit hall, tell the court: what animal is depicted by that clay statue on the corner table?'

Jaggu squinted and replied: 'It is a clay dog, my lord!'

Birbal walked to the table, picked up the statue, and showed it to Emperor Akbar and the court:

It was an intricately carved clay lion, with a thick mane, fangs, and a curved tail!

Birbal smiled with razor-sharp irony:

'Behold, Your Majesty! In this brightly lit palace hall, in broad daylight, from only thirty paces away, this man cannot tell a lion from a dog!

'Yet he expects this court to believe that in the pitch-black darkness of a midnight storm, without a single lamp, from fifty paces away, he recognized the exact face of the tenant farmer in the rain!

'A hired liar always overreaches his script, forgetting that nature makes sight impossible in the dark!'

Jaggu broke down in terror, confessed that the landlord had paid him twenty silver coins to bear false witness, and begged for mercy.

Akbar ordered the landlord heavily fined, the false witness imprisoned, and the innocent farmer acquitted, praising Birbal's brilliant cross-examination.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Man Who Carried His Bullock on His Head (TE)
summary: Birbal meets a traveler carrying his luggage and riding an oxcart, claiming he is sparing the animals. Birbal exposes the comedy of misplaced self-sacrifice.
full_text:
While traveling along the dusty highway between Agra and Mathura, Emperor Akbar and Birbal rode past a bullock cart loaded with sacks of grain. Inside the cart sat a well-dressed passenger who was holding a heavy, wooden iron-banded trunk firmly balanced upon his own head!

The two bullocks were straining to pull the heavy cart through the deep dust.

Akbar reined in his horse in complete disbelief: 'Look at that man, Birbal! He is sitting inside the cart, yet he is carrying his heavy iron trunk upon his own head! Is he mad?'

Akbar rode alongside the cart and called out: 'Friend! Why on earth are you carrying that heavy iron trunk on your head instead of placing it on the floor of the cart?'

The passenger wiped sweat from his eyes and replied with sincere piety:

'Noble rider! My heart is full of tender compassion! These two poor bullocks are already pulling this heavy cart and thirty sacks of grain!

'If I placed this heavy iron trunk on the floor of the cart as well, it would increase the weight and break the poor animals' backs!

'So I carry the trunk upon my own head, so that I bear its weight myself and spare the poor beasts!'

Akbar stared in astonishment, then burst into a roar of laughter.

Birbal smiled and explained to the passenger:

'Brother, think for one second! Whether you place the trunk on the wooden floor of the cart, or hold it upon your own head—are you not sitting inside the cart?

'Your body is supported by the cart, and the cart is pulled entirely by the bullocks! Every ounce of weight on your head presses down through your body onto the cart, and onto the bullocks' shoulders!

'You are not sparing the bullocks a single grain of weight; you are merely giving yourself a terrible headache and looking like a premier fool!'

The passenger looked down at the cart floor, then up at his trunk, and sheepishly placed the trunk down with a sigh of relief.

Akbar laughed all the way back to Agra, remarking that many men endure useless misery in life because they do not understand the simple laws of reality.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Barber Who Wanted to Be Prime Minister (TE)
summary: Akbar's royal barber demands to be made Prime Minister for a day. Birbal gives him a complex diplomatic dispute to resolve, curing his delusions.
full_text:
The royal barber, Karim, had shaved Emperor Akbar's head and trimmed his beard for twenty years. Because Akbar often conversed pleasantly during his morning grooming, the barber grew absurdly conceited, imagining that statecraft was no more difficult than trimming a mustache.

One morning, Karim complained: 'Your Majesty, ministers like Birbal do nothing but make witty jokes and write poems, yet they receive palaces and gold! If you made me Prime Minister for just one day, I would govern Hindustan with unmatched precision!'

Amused, Akbar mentioned it to Birbal. Birbal smiled: 'Sire, let his wish be granted tomorrow morning.'

The next day, Karim was dressed in grand brocade robes, a towering ministerial turban, and seated upon the chief minister's velvet cushion in the Diwan-i-Am. He puffed out his chest, looking immensely proud.

Soon, two foreign ambassadors from Central Asia entered the hall. They bowed and presented a complex border dispute regarding pasture water rights along the Indus river, speaking rapidly in high, ornate Persian:

'Noble Prime Minister! The treaty of 1572 cedes the seasonal snowmelt of the upper tributaries to the Khans of Balkh, but the spring herds of the Mughal frontier claim riparian rights under the imperial firman! Does the crown mandate riparian division by head of cattle, or by seasonal runoff?'

The barber's eyes widened in sheer terror. He did not understand a single word of the Persian legal terms! He sweated profusely beneath his heavy turban.

The ambassadors waited. The ministers stared. The court was dead silent.

Karim stammered: 'Uh... well... you see... we must cut... trim... shave the water equally...'

The ambassadors looked insulted: 'Shave the water? Is the Prime Minister mocking our sovereign?'

The ambassadors drew their daggers in outrage!

Karim panicked, dropped his ministerial staff, tore off his heavy turban, and dove under the council table, screaming: 'Help! Mercy! I am not a minister! I am only a barber! Forgive me, Sire!'

Birbal stepped forward, greeted the ambassadors in fluent Persian, resolved the treaty terms within five minutes, and smoothed over the diplomatic crisis with impeccable grace.

Birbal pulled the trembling barber out from under the table and handed him his wooden razor case:

'Here are your tools, Karim. A razor can trim hair, but it cannot navigate the treaties of nations. Honor your own trade, and leave statecraft to those who have dedicated their lives to wisdom.'

Karim bowed in deep shame, cured forever of his foolish political ambitions.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Peacock's Dance on the Terrace (TE)
summary: A vain prince boasts of his flawless elegance. Birbal uses the peacock's dance to remind him that even the most beautiful creatures have humble feet.
full_text:
A visiting young prince from Rajputana was celebrated for his dazzling physical beauty, tall stature, and fashionable silk attire. However, he was insufferably conceited, spending hours admiring himself in mirrors and openly mocking the plain features of older scholars in Akbar's court.

During an afternoon reception on the palace terrace overlooking the gardens, a wild peacock flew onto the marble balustrade. The bird spread its magnificent tail into a giant fan of shimmering emerald, sapphire, and bronze feathers, dancing gracefully in the breeze.

The young prince exclaimed: 'Look at that peacock! It possesses supreme beauty, like myself! It has no flaw in all creation!'

Birbal smiled gently: 'Prince, observe the peacock closely as it dances.'

As the magnificent bird completed its graceful turn, its eyes glanced down at its own legs. Its feet were coarse, wrinkled, grey, and scaly, covered in dirt and sharp claws.

The instant the peacock looked down at its ugly feet, it ceased its proud dance, dropped its tail, and let out a harsh, mournful shriek: *Kaa-ooo! Kaa-ooo!*

Birbal said to the young prince:

'You see, noble Prince? The peacock has the most magnificent feathers in the world, yet the moment it glances down at its coarse, wrinkled feet, its vanity is shattered, and it weeps with shame!

'Nature has given every human being some gift of beauty, intelligence, or strength, but nature has also given every mortal coarse "feet of clay"—flaws, vulnerabilities, and mortality—to remind us to remain humble!

'He who gazes only upon his glittering feathers becomes an arrogant fool. But he who remembers his humble feet walks through life with grace, kindness, and modesty.'

The young prince stood silent. The lesson touched his conscience deeply. He bowed to Birbal, apologized to the elders, and resolved to cultivate inner virtue above outward vanity.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Merchant Who Lost His Memory (TE)
summary: A dishonest merchant claims he forgot borrowing five hundred gold coins due to a medical condition. Birbal restores his 'memory' with an unexpected debt.
full_text:
A wealthy trader named Seth Goverdhan borrowed five hundred gold mohurs from an elderly scholar named Shastriji to finance a spice caravan to Surat. The transaction was made verbally on mutual trust.

A year later, the spice caravan returned with vast profits. When the poor scholar visited Goverdhan's shop to ask for his five hundred coins, the merchant stared blankly and sighed:

'Alas, Shastriji! Six months ago, I was thrown from a horse and suffered a severe blow to the head! Since that tragic day, I have completely lost my memory! I do not remember borrowing a single coin from you! The physician says my memory can never return! Please leave, for you pain my infirmity!'

Weeping, Shastriji brought his grievance to Emperor Akbar.

Akbar summoned Goverdhan, who put on a convincing display of amnesia, staring with glassy eyes and repeating: 'I remember nothing! I know neither numbers nor loans!'

Akbar turned to Birbal: 'Can medical amnesia be cured by justice?'

Birbal smiled: 'Certainly, Your Majesty. I have an infallible psychological remedy for lost memories.'

Birbal addressed the court: 'Goverdhan's amnesia is indeed tragic. However, we have an urgent state matter.

'Three weeks ago, an imperial auditor inspecting the provincial customs registers discovered that Goverdhan's firm owes the imperial crown a back tax penalty of two thousand gold mohurs!

'Because Goverdhan has lost his memory and can no longer manage finances, the imperial treasury shall seize his warehouses, mansion, and spice stores today to satisfy the two-thousand-gold debt!'

Goverdhan's glassy eyes instantly widened with sheer terror! He leaped to his feet, waving his arms:

'Wait! Halt! It is coming back to me! My memory has returned! A miracle from heaven!'

Birbal asked calmly: 'What has returned to you, Goverdhan?'

Goverdhan cried frantically: 'I remember everything! I remember that my firm paid all imperial taxes three years ago! And I suddenly remember that I borrowed exactly five hundred gold mohurs from Shastriji for my Surat caravan!'

The entire court erupted in roaring laughter.

Birbal smiled with razor sharpness: 'Behold, Your Majesty! The mention of a two-thousand-gold penalty has instantly cured a medical condition that baffled all the physicians of Agra!'

Akbar ordered the five hundred gold coins paid to Shastriji immediately, along with an additional two hundred coins penalty for feigning illness, praising Birbal's swift cure for convenient memories.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Secret of the River Yamuna (TE)
summary: Akbar stands on the riverbank and grieves over the passing of his youth. Birbal uses the flowing current to explain the eternal renewal of existence.
full_text:
On an autumn twilight, Emperor Akbar stood upon the river terrace of the Agra Fort, gazing down at the dark, swirling waters of the Yamuna river. The monarch looked weary and somber, noticing a few silver hairs in his beard and the deepening lines upon his brow.

Akbar sighed deeply: 'Birbal, looking at this river fills my heart with sorrow. Time flows like this river, washing away our youth, our strength, and our companions. In fifty years, I shall be dust in a tomb, and this water will still be flowing past these walls, indifferent to emperors and empires. What is the meaning of all our conquests and glory if time washes everything away?'

Birbal stepped to the stone parapet, dipped a brass bowl into the flowing current, and poured the water slowly back into the river.

Birbal spoke in a gentle, melodious voice:

'Sire, you see the river as a thief of time, but consider the river as the great giver of life!

'The water that flows past your terrace today was snow on the highest peaks of the Himalayas yesterday. Tomorrow, it will irrigate the wheat fields of peasant farmers; next week, it will nourish thirsty cattle; next month, it will join the great ocean, rise as clouds into the heavens, and fall as sweet rain upon your rose gardens once again!

'Nothing in this universe is truly destroyed; life merely changes its form in eternal renewal!

'An emperor does not live forever in his physical flesh, but he lives forever in the justice he established, the schools he built, the peace he protected, and the tears he wiped from the eyes of the poor!

'Do not mourn that the river flows; rejoice that you have been chosen by heaven to build bridges of justice and mercy across its waters while your day lasts.'

Akbar felt a profound peace wash over his spirit. The melancholy lifted from his heart like morning mist before the sun. He embraced Birbal, thanking him for transforming sorrow into sublime purpose.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The King's Bad Omen at Sunrise (TE)
summary: Akbar encounters an ugly sweeper at sunrise and fears an evil omen. Birbal shows the Emperor that the sweeper is the true benefactor of the city.
full_text:
Early one morning, Emperor Akbar stepped out onto the east-facing terrace to perform his morning devotions at sunrise. Just as the golden rim of the sun crested the horizon, Akbar looked down into the courtyard and his eyes fell upon a municipal sweeper named Kalu—an impoverished, one-eyed man in ragged clothes carrying a broom of twigs and a basket of horse dung.

Akbar turned back in dismay: 'What an ill-omened sight! To see an ugly sweeper with a basket of dung at the very moment of sunrise! This day will bring misfortune to the empire!'

Later that morning, during the council assembly, Akbar was irritable and nervous, jumping at every noise.

Birbal noticed the Emperor's distress and inquired: 'Sire, why are you troubled today?'

Akbar explained: 'At sunrise, the first creature I saw was an ugly sweeper carrying a basket of dung! My day is cursed!'

Birbal smiled gently, stepped out, and brought the sweeper Kalu into the Diwan-i-Am. The poor man was trembling with fear, clutching his broom.

Birbal said to the Emperor:

'Your Majesty, you consider Kalu an evil omen because he carries a basket of waste.

'Yet consider what would happen to your magnificent capital if Kalu and his fellow sweepers stayed home for just one single week!

'The streets of Agra would be choked with filth, disease and pestilence would sweep through every household, and the imperial palace itself would become unlivable!

'This humble man cleans away the filth of our lives so that we may breathe clean air and walk on clean stones! His labor is an act of pure public service.

'A corrupt minister who smiles with a handsome face while stealing public gold is the true evil omen! A humble sweeper who works honestly at sunrise to keep your city pure is a blessing from heaven!'

Akbar looked at the trembling sweeper, felt deep shame for his superstition, and stepped down from the dais.

Akbar placed a purse of fifty gold mohurs into the sweeper's calloused hands, granted him a warm woolen coat, and vowed never to judge human beings by superstition again.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Salt Seller and the Cotton Trader (TE)
summary: Two merchants cross a flooded river with salt and cotton. Birbal illustrates the poetic justice of natural elements.
full_text:
In the marketplace of Mathura, two rival merchants—Seth Hariram the salt dealer and Seth Mohanlal the cotton dealer—set out together with their pack bullocks to cross a swollen river during the monsoon.

Hariram, an arrogant and malicious man, secretly laughed at the cotton dealer: 'Look at your fluffy sacks of cotton! If a single splash of water touches them, they will absorb water, double in weight, and break your bullocks' backs!'

As they waded into the deep, turbulent current, both bullocks stumbled and fell into the swirling river water, submerging their loads for several minutes.

When they dragged the animals out onto the opposite bank:

Hariram's sacks of salt had completely dissolved into the river! His heavy sacks were empty; his entire fortune had washed away into the current!

Meanwhile, Mohanlal's cotton sacks had indeed become soaked and heavy. But when spread out beneath the hot sun on the riverbank, the cotton dried completely within three hours, undamaged and ready for sale!

Hariram wept bitterly, shaking his fist at the river.

Birbal, who was traveling past on an imperial inspection tour, observed the two merchants.

Birbal said to the weeping salt merchant:

'Hariram, you rejoiced at the thought of your neighbor's cotton becoming waterlogged and ruined.

'Yet nature has balanced the scales with poetic justice. Salt is rigid and dissolves when it meets the water it mocks; cotton is humble and flexible, yielding to moisture but drying under the sun.

'He who schemes for his brother's downfall invariably falls into the pit he wished upon another. Rejoice that your life was spared, and learn to trade with goodwill toward your fellows.'

Humbled by the lesson, the salt merchant apologized to his neighbor and resolved to abandon spite.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Emperor's Whispering Rose Garden (TE)
summary: Akbar asks why the royal rose garden feels so peaceful compared to the noisy council chamber. Birbal reveals the secret of silent cooperation.
full_text:
After a grueling, chaotic six-hour durbar filled with shouting ministers, territorial disputes, and angry petitions, Emperor Akbar walked into the private palace rose gardens with Birbal. The garden was a paradise of serenity: crimson, yellow, and white roses bloomed in neat beds, honeybees hummed softly among the petals, and crystal fountains murmured gently over marble basins.

Akbar breathed in the fragrant, cool air and sighed in relief: 'Birbal, what a miracle! In the council hall, fifty learned men argue, yell, and make my head throb with noise. Yet here in this garden, ten thousand roses bloom together in absolute, divine peace! Why can human beings not live like flowers?'

Birbal smiled, walked to a rosebush, and pointed to the blooming flowers:

'Sire, consider the wisdom of the garden.

'The crimson rose does not scream at the white rose, claiming that crimson is the only true color!

'The tall yellow rose does not boast over the humble jasmine creeping on the ground!

'The sweet petals do not curse the sharp thorns that protect them from grazing goats!

'The roots drink water in the dark soil without demanding praise; the leaves absorb sunlight without boasting; and the blossoms exhale their sweet fragrance freely to king, beggar, child, and saint alike, asking nothing in return!

'A garden flourishes because every flower, leaf, and root performs its own duty in quiet harmony with the Creator, without vanity, without envy, and without the poison of selfish competition.

'When human beings learn to perform their honest duty and bless the world with kindness instead of fighting for dominance, human society will become as sweet and peaceful as this rose garden.'

Akbar sat on the marble bench, his soul rejuvenated by the allegory, promising to cultivate the harmony of the garden within his imperial court.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Royal Test of Four Noble Virtues (TE)
summary: Akbar tests four young noble candidates for governorship. Birbal arranges four secret trials to reveal their true character.
full_text:
Four young noble princes competed for the prestigious appointment of Governor of the wealthy province of Gujarat. Each candidate was polished, eloquent, and presented glowing letters of recommendation from high ministers.

Emperor Akbar was unsure whom to choose: 'Birbal, all four speak like angels! How can I know which one will govern with genuine justice?'

Birbal smiled: 'Sire, let us test them not with examinations of words, but with secret trials of action.'

Birbal arranged four secret scenarios along the road as the four candidates traveled to the palace for their final interview.

Candidate One passed an old woman whose cart was stuck in a ditch. He ignored her, saying: 'I cannot soil my silk coat; I must meet the Emperor!'

Candidate Two found a leather purse containing fifty gold coins dropped on the trail. He pocketed the gold in secret, whispering: 'A lucky windfall!'

Candidate Three encountered a wounded stray dog whining in pain. He kicked the animal aside to clear his path.

Candidate Four, named Prince Vijay, saw the stuck cart, dismounted his horse, rolled up his sleeves, and helped the old woman push her cart free. When he found an iron ring dropped in the mud, he handed it to the village watchman. And when he saw the wounded dog, he bound its paw with his own silk handkerchief and left water for the beast.

When the four candidates assembled before the throne, Akbar was about to begin the interview when Birbal stepped forward, accompanied by the old woman, the watchman, and the bandaged dog!

Birbal revealed the secret trials:

'Sire, governance is tested in the shadows, not on the stage!

'A man who will not help a stuck cart will never help a starving peasant. A man who steals a purse in the dark will embezzle your provincial revenues. And a man who kicks a wounded animal will be a cruel tyrant to his subjects!

'Only Prince Vijay passed every test of compassion, honesty, and mercy. He alone possesses the noble character to govern Gujarat!'

Akbar appointed Prince Vijay Governor on the spot, praising Birbal for proving that secret deeds reveal the true soul of a ruler.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Scholar Who Forgot How to Swim (TE)
summary: An arrogant scholar mocks a simple boatman for not studying grammar and astronomy. When the boat leaks, the boatman asks a vital question.
full_text:
A proud scholar named Pandit Vidyadhar, who had spent forty years memorizing ancient texts of grammar, logic, and astronomy, hired a humble wooden ferry to cross the wide, turbulent river Yamuna during the monsoon.

As the boatman rowed with steady strokes, the scholar puffed his chest and asked: 'Boatman! Have you ever studied the sacred rules of Sanskrit grammar?'

The boatman replied humbly: 'No, master, I cannot read.'

The scholar scoffed: 'Alas! One-fourth of your entire life is completely wasted!'

A few minutes later, the scholar pointed to the sky: 'Boatman! Do you understand the planetary motions of Mars and Saturn and the science of astronomy?'

'No, master, I know only the river currents.'

The scholar shook his head: 'Tragic! Half of your entire life has been wasted in ignorance!'

Presently, the scholar asked: 'Do you know the twelve schools of Greek and Persian philosophy?'

'No, master, I know only how to row.'

'Hopeless!' the scholar declared. 'Three-fourths of your life is completely wasted!'

Just then, a sudden violent gale blew down the river. The small wooden ferry struck a submerged rock; water gushed into the hold, and the boat began to sink rapidly in the swirling, deep waves!

The boatman quickly took off his cotton tunic, turned to the trembling scholar, and asked:

'Master! Have you ever studied the art of swimming?'

The scholar screamed in terror, clutching the sinking gunwale: 'No! No! I never learned to swim! I studied only books!'

The boatman leaped into the water, shouting back:

'Alas, master! Then I fear your ENTIRE life is about to be wasted in the next two minutes!'

The boatman swam back, pulled the drowning scholar by the collar, and dragged him ashore, coughing water and shivering with cold.

Birbal, who had observed the rescue from the bank, helped the wet scholar up and said with a gentle smile:

'You see, Panditji? Book learning is splendid, but if you lack practical wisdom and humble skill, all the philosophy in the world cannot keep your head above water when the storms of life strike!'

The humbled scholar bowed to the boatman, cured forever of his intellectual arrogance.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Horse That Grazed on the Palace Roof (TE)
summary: Akbar jokingly commands Birbal to show him a horse grazing on a rooftop. Birbal arranges a spectacle that fulfills the royal whim.
full_text:
During an idle afternoon in the imperial palace, Emperor Akbar decided to tease Birbal with a nonsensical riddle:

'Birbal, travelers tell me that in certain mystical kingdoms of the north, horses graze upon the rooftops of houses! I command you: show me a horse grazing upon a roof in Agra by tomorrow noon, or admit that your wit has failed!'

The courtiers smiled, expecting Birbal to confess defeat.

The next day at noon, Akbar walked out onto the royal balcony of the Agra Fort, overlooking the sprawling city.

In a courtyard just below the palace wall stood a small, flat-roofed mud outhouse used for storing garden tools.

Upon the flat roof, Birbal had arranged several bundles of fresh, juicy green clover and sugarcane.

Standing upon a wooden ramp beside the outhouse was an ordinary donkey! But Birbal had tied a pair of tall wooden horse-ears to the donkey's bridle, draped a magnificent horse blanket over its back, and pinned a bushy horse tail to its rear!

The donkey was munched happily on the clover upon the roof!

Birbal stood on the ground below, bowed low to Akbar on the balcony, and announced:

'Behold, Your Majesty! There is the horse grazing upon the roof, exactly as you commanded!'

Akbar stared in disbelief, then laughed: 'Birbal, that is not a horse! That is merely an ordinary donkey dressed up in horse clothes!'

Birbal looked up with innocent surprise:

'Sire! If an Emperor can issue a decree demanding that a horse graze on a rooftop like a bird, then surely an ordinary donkey has every right to believe it is an imperial warhorse!'

The entire court erupted in laughter. Akbar shook his head in fond amusement: 'You turn every absurd challenge back upon me, Birbal!' Akbar rewarded him with a purse of gold for his playful genius.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Broken Earthen Water Pot (TE)
summary: A servant weeps uncontrollably after breaking an antique water pot. Birbal uses the broken pieces to teach the court the wisdom of moving forward.
full_text:
A young palace servant named Mohan was carrying an antique earthenware water pot, painted with intricate Persian motifs, through the council hallway when his foot caught on a carpet. The pot crashed to the marble floor, shattering into dozens of fragments, spilling water across the stones.

Terrified of punishment, the young servant collapsed beside the shards, weeping hysterically, tearing his hair, and crying: 'Oh, my life is ruined! If only I had looked at the carpet! If only I had walked slower! If only I had taken the other corridor!'

For an hour, the servant remained paralyzed on the floor in useless sorrow.

Birbal walked down the hallway, knelt beside the weeping youth, picked up a handful of broken clay shards, and asked:

'Mohan, look at these shards in my hand. Can all your bitter tears reassemble this pot?'

The boy sniffled: 'No, my lord.'

'Can all your weeping dry the spilled water back into the pitcher?'

'No, my lord.'

'Can beating your chest undo the step you took an hour ago?'

'No, wise minister.'

Birbal helped the youth to his feet, handed him a broom and a mop, and said with gentle firmness:

'Then stand up, my boy, wipe your tears, and pick up the broom!

'What is broken is broken. What has passed has passed into eternity. Crying over spilled water does not clean the floor; it merely wastes the hours of today on the regrets of yesterday!

'Sweep away the shards, dry the stones, and walk forward with greater care. The wise man does not mourn what is shattered; he applies his energy to building what lies ahead.'

The young servant smiled through his tears, cleaned the floor diligently, and returned to his duties with a peaceful heart. Akbar, who had observed the scene, remarked that Birbal's practical wisdom was the greatest medicine for human regret.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power

title: The Emperor's Riddle on True Mortality (TE)
summary: Akbar asks what separates an emperor from a beggar after death. Birbal takes the Emperor to an ancient graveyard to find the answer.
full_text:
During a quiet evening walk outside the city walls, Emperor Akbar and Birbal passed an ancient, crumbling graveyard where kings, warriors, merchants, and beggars had been buried over five centuries.

Akbar paused, looking at the overgrown mounds of dust, and asked in a somber tone: 'Birbal, look at these graves. In life, emperors sleep on golden thrones and beggars sleep in the mud. What is the difference between a king and a beggar after death?'

Birbal walked among the broken tombstones, picked up two ancient, weathered human skulls from an eroded grave pit, and brought them to the Emperor.

Birbal held one skull in his right hand, and the other in his left hand.

Both skulls were grey, hollow, and weathered by centuries of rain and wind.

Birbal said: 'Your Majesty, examine these two skulls carefully.

'One belonged to an ancient, mighty emperor who commanded armies of a hundred thousand soldiers and ruled three kingdoms!

'The other belonged to a penniless beggar who walked barefoot and begged for crusts of barley bread!

'Tell me, Sire: which of these skulls is the emperor, and which is the beggar?'

Akbar looked at both skulls. They were completely identical. There were no crowns, no rags, no gold, and no poverty written upon the hollow bone.

Akbar whispered in deep humility: 'It is impossible to tell, Birbal. They are completely equal in the dust.'

Birbal nodded with profound solemnity:

'Yes, Your Majesty. Death is the great leveler of humanity. The grave asks not how many diamonds you wore, nor how many palaces you built.

'The only thing that survives the dust is the righteousness of your deeds, the justice you delivered, and the kindness you sowed in the hearts of your people. An emperor's crown rots in the soil, but his virtue shines in the presence of the Divine forever.'

Akbar bowed his head in reverence, and returned to the palace with a renewed commitment to justice and humility.
moral: నీతి: Wit beats power
